\title{Cumulative-Score Routes Toward Polylogarithmic Loss\\
for Optimal Data-Dependent Euclidean ANN}
\author{Anonymous Authors}
\date{Draft, June 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
   For fixed $c>1$, the optimal balanced exponent for data-dependent approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space is
   \[
      \rho_c=\frac{1}{2c^2-1}.
   \]
   Known worst-case constructions achieve $n^{\rho_c+o(1)}$ query time and $n^{1+\rho_c+o(1)}$ space. The goal here is to remove the subpolynomial loss, not merely optimize it. This draft isolates which parts of that program are now self-contained and which part remains a genuine mixed score/geometric stopping problem.

   The unconditional milestone is a restartable slice construction with
   \[
      Q(n,d)=
      d\,n^{\rho_c}
      \exp\!\left(
         O_c\!\left((\log n)^{2/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3}\right)
      \right),
   \]
   and
   \[
      \qquad
      S(n,d)=
      dn+n^{1+\rho_c}
      \exp\!\left(
         O_c\!\left((\log n)^{2/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3}\right)
      \right).
   \]
   The key self-contained ingredient is a spherical continuation-mass decoder with polylogarithmic loss; it lets the restart architecture improve from the older $7/9$ optimization to the $2/3$ exponent above. For terminal spherical search we also give a constant-depth smooth product filter with constant single-table recall and the same optimal exponent.

   We then record the remaining clean-endpoint routes.  The low-rate
   score-band separator is no longer left as an abstract LP/SA certificate:
   leave-one-out overlap on a distance-three panel collapses to the true
   codeword hull, and greedy packing gives such panels with only polylogarithmic
   ambient slack.  For the geometric one-tree route, the work side can be paid
   unconditionally by a canonical budget-thinning supermartingale.  The
   remaining conditional target is now the near-side aggregate value delivery:
   the saturated route value, equivalently every route-cut activation mass, must
   stay inverse-polylogarithmic.  A structured posterior route gives another
   implementation target: if pure posterior children can be decoded
   output-sensitively across dyadic mass scales, the continuous likelihood-ball
   geometry plus negative-moment arithmetic already gives the same
   polylogarithmic bound.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

The $(c,r)$-approximate nearest neighbor problem asks us to preprocess a set $P\subseteq\R^d$ of $n$ points so that, given a query $q\in\R^d$ satisfying
\[
   \min_{p\in P}\|p-q\|_2\le r,
\]
the data structure returns some $p'\in P$ with
\[
   \|p'-q\|_2\le cr.
\]
Throughout the paper, $c>1$ is fixed. The data structure is randomized and data-dependent, and succeeds with a fixed constant probability. Candidate points are verified using their true Euclidean distances, so the structure never reports an incorrect answer.

For Euclidean space, the optimal balanced data-dependent exponent is
\[
   \rho_c=\frac{1}{2c^2-1}.
\]
The landmark construction of Andoni and Razenshteyn obtains query time $d\,n^{\rho_c+o(1)}$ and space $dn+n^{1+\rho_c+o(1)}$ for worst-case data sets~\cite{AR15}. Its geometric component removes dense spherical caps, recenters them as smaller certified balls, and applies a spherical filtering primitive to the residual data. The $o(1)$ term absorbs several losses: shell discretization, geometric slack, spherical list decoding, and the repeated restarting of the filtering process after recentering.

The purpose of the one-tree program is to stop optimizing that restart loss and instead remove it. The central design choice is to keep one cumulative score process across geometric recentering. Recentered children are not fresh spherical instances; they are edges inside the same score tree. This forces two changes:
\begin{itemize}
   \item the spherical decoder must survive with only polylogarithmic loss under continuation-mass pruning;
   \item geometric recursion must be paid by a potential identity rather than by restarting a full score tree in every child.
\end{itemize}
The first point is a one-sided branching-random-walk problem. We prove it first for the spherical block and then for predictable adaptive score schedules. The second point is handled by randomized cap thinning: always search the residual child, search the cap child with probability $z^s\Psi(R_C)/\Psi(R)$, and use the padded radius potential $\Psi(R)=1+(R/r)^4$. This makes the recursive query potential contract directly.

\subsection{Main result}

All logarithms are natural.

\begin{theorem}[Main self-contained theorem]\label{thm:main}
   Fix $c>1$. There is a randomized data-dependent data structure for worst-case $(c,r)$-approximate nearest neighbor search in $\R^d$ with constant success probability, query time
   \[
      Q(n,d)
      =
      d\,n^{\rho_c}
      \exp\!\left(
         O_c\!\left((\log n)^{2/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3}\right)
      \right),
   \]
   and space
   \[
      S(n,d)
      =
      dn+n^{1+\rho_c}
      \exp\!\left(
         O_c\!\left((\log n)^{2/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3}\right)
      \right),
   \]
   where $\rho_c=1/(2c^2-1)$. The bounds hold in expectation over preprocessing; standard truncation and rebuilding convert them to capped bounds with only constant-factor changes in success probability and asymptotic cost.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{What changes}

The algorithm in this draft differs from a restart construction in the following ways:
\begin{itemize}
   \item score prefixes are kept or discarded by continuation mass, not by a fresh hard threshold at every level;
   \item recentering changes the geometric coordinates but preserves the cumulative score state through an explicit offset;
   \item almost-total cap children are followed by randomized thinning probabilities chosen to contract the radius potential;
   \item cap-free terminal score leaves are scanned and charged to their low-correlation mass;
   \item every geometric child is certified by its actual maximum radius.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Where the proof stands}

The expected-work calculation for continuation-mass pruning is exact, and the restartable slice construction built from it proves \cref{thm:main}. The smooth product terminal filter gives constant one-table recall once localization has reduced the instance to a spherical gap. The randomized cap split has an exact one-step potential contraction, and the cap-thinning probabilities telescope along a true near-neighbor lineage.

The older mixed-frontier work condition is no longer the preferred
polylogarithmic target.  The budget-thinned one-tree variant proves the
activated geometric work bound by optional stopping for the canonical mixed
budget, so the remaining one-tree obstruction is near-side value delivery:
after budget-stable edges and cap-free scans are removed, the saturated value
of the remaining tame-route trie should be inverse-polylogarithmic.  Equivalently,
every route cut should have inverse-polylogarithmic activation mass, or a
route law should have only polylogarithmic cut energy against the activation
prefix weights.

We also record a fractional certified-cover formulation because it is the cleanest way to reason about dense overlap.  Dense balls, score caps, facility buckets, additive-quantization buckets, and ordinary spherical filters are all columns in one near-pair LP.  A failed cover gives demand prices, query-load prices, and a storage price; the remaining theorem is a weighted dense/spherical separator saying that every such dual obstruction either exposes a cheaper radius-contracting child or is pseudo-random enough for a large-range spherical filter.  This makes dense merging a reduced-gain separation problem rather than a hard recursive decomposition.

For the LP/SA structured-panel route we freeze the target at the finite
score-band condition \((LNN2)\), with the chart-incidence tail
\((LNP5)\)--\((LNZ4)\) as its diagonal random-code diagnostic.  The uniform
full-price version is not a theorem to chase: the singleton chart obstruction
forces the cost to scale with \(\max_j e^{\lambda(M-W(c_j))}\).  The viable
local theorem is instead the leave-one-out overlap lift.  If the local panel
has minimum Hamming distance at least \(3\), the projected overlap polytope is
exactly the true codeword hull; greedy packing supplies such panels with only
polylogarithmic slack.  Thus projected local pseudowords are no longer the
source of subpolynomial loss in this route.

Finally, we record posterior formulations because they are useful routes to more general certified child hierarchies. The finite-channel version is a coarse explicit-enumeration special case; the structured version is the sharper target suggested by the negative-moment accounting. The older cohort route still has a route-level cohort-or-leaf coupling condition, while the almost-total cap-thinning route isolates a narrower mixed-operator condition.

\section{Preliminaries}

\subsection{Correlation parameters}

For unit vectors $x,q\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$,
\[
   \|x-q\|_2^2=2-2\ip{x}{q}.
\]
A spherical filtering instance is specified by two correlations
\[
   -1<b<a<1.
\]
A near pair satisfies $\ip{x}{q}\ge a$, while an ordinary far pair satisfies $\ip{x}{q}\le b$. The balanced Gaussian filtering exponent is
\[
   \rho(a,b)
   =
   \frac{(1-a)(1+b)}{(1+a)(1-b)}.
\]
At the critical Euclidean normalization,
\[
   a_0=1-\frac{1}{c^2},
   \qquad
   b_0=0,
\]
and therefore
\[
   \rho(a_0,b_0)=\frac{1}{2c^2-1}=\rho_c.
\]

We repeatedly use the smoothness of $\rho$ near $(a_0,b_0)$.

\begin{lemma}[Stability of the balanced exponent]\label{lem:rho-stability}
   For every fixed $c>1$, there are constants $C_c>0$ and $\eta_c>0$ such that, whenever $0<\eta\le\eta_c$ and
   \[
      a\ge a_0-C_c\eta,
      \qquad
      b\le C_c\eta,
   \]
   we have
   \[
      \rho(a,b)\le \rho_c+C_c\eta.
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The denominator $(1+a)(1-b)$ is bounded away from zero in a fixed neighborhood of $(a_0,0)$. The rational function $\rho(a,b)$ is continuously differentiable there. The claim follows from the mean-value theorem, after enlarging $C_c$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Polylogarithmic slack}

All geometric discretization parameters are chosen as inverse powers of $\log n$ with constants depending only on $c$. We write $\log^{O_c(1)}n$ for any resulting polynomial in these logarithmic factors. The restartable theorem still has the displayed $\exp(O((\log n)^{2/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3}))$ loss; the cumulative one-tree target is to absorb every additional nonconstant loss into $\log^{O_c(1)}n$.

\subsection{Expected cost and truncation}

The filtering constructions naturally give expected numbers of explored nodes and candidate occurrences. We use the following standard conversion. If one copy succeeds with probability at least $p_0>0$ and has expected query work at most $T$, stop it after $K T$ work for a sufficiently large constant $K=K(p_0)$. Markov's inequality shows that the truncation probability is at most $1/K$, so the truncated copy still succeeds with constant probability. A constant number of independent copies then restores any desired fixed success probability below one. The same idea applies to space: rebuild whenever the realized space exceeds a fixed multiple of its expectation. We therefore state expected bounds in intermediate lemmas and capped bounds in the final theorem.

\subsection{Preprocessing convention}

The main scarce resources in this draft are query work and retained index
space.  Preprocessing may be polynomial, quasipolynomial, or superpolynomial in
the local node size when a statement explicitly invokes an offline certified
cover compiler.  Such preprocessing may enumerate huge proposal pools, solve
exact integer programs, run repeated randomized or learned proposal generators,
and discard every failed attempt.  The stated query and space bounds count only
the certified children, residual blocks, decoder data, and point copies present
in the final index.  In particular, huge temporary LPs, pattern enumerations,
and saturated candidate universes are free only if they are discarded after
certification; any pattern table, cohort, routing metadata, or learned decoder
used by the query is retained index space and must be charged explicitly.

\subsection{Dimension and diameter localization}

The score-and-ball proof below works inside projected cells whose diameter is only polylogarithmically larger than $r$. We record the reduction explicitly.

\begin{lemma}[Projected bounded-diameter localization]\label{lem:localization}
   Fix $c>1$. It is enough to solve $(c',r')$-ANN instances in dimension
   \[
      D=\log^{O_c(1)}n
   \]
   whose point sets lie in balls of radius
   \[
      R_0\le r'\log^{O_c(1)}n,
   \]
   with exponent $\rho_{c'}\le\rho_c+O_c(1/\log n)$. The reduction uses only $\log^{O_c(1)}n$ instances and changes query time and space by polylogarithmic factors, plus the unavoidable $dn$ storage and $d\log^{O_c(1)}n$ projection work.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Choose a large constant $C_0=C_0(c)$ and set
   \[
      \varepsilon=\frac{1}{C_c\log n},
      \qquad
      D=C_0\varepsilon^{-2}\log n,
   \]
   and draw $T=C_c\log n$ independent Gaussian maps
   \[
      \Pi_t:\R^d\to\R^D,
      \qquad
      \Pi_t x=\frac1{\sqrt D}(g_1\cdot x,\ldots,g_D\cdot x),
   \]
   where the $g_i$ are standard Gaussian vectors. For a fixed query $q$, a standard chi-square tail gives
   \[
      \Prb\!\left[
         \left|\|\Pi_t(p-q)\|_2^2-\|p-q\|_2^2\right|
         >\varepsilon\|p-q\|_2^2
      \right]
      \le
      2\exp(-\Omega(\varepsilon^2D))
      \le
      n^{-C_0/10}
   \]
   for every fixed data point $p$, after increasing the absolute constant in $D$. A union bound over $P$ shows that one projection is \emph{good for $q$}, meaning all $n$ squared distances from $q$ are preserved within a factor $1\pm\varepsilon$, with probability at least $1-n^{-C_0/20}$. This statement is only over the data-structure randomness for the fixed query; no uniform guarantee over all possible queries is needed.

   In each projected copy, put a randomly shifted axis-aligned grid of side length
   \[
      h=20\sqrt D\,r',
      \qquad
      r'=(1+\varepsilon)r.
   \]
   If $\|p-q\|_2\le r$ and the projection is good, then
   \[
      \|\Pi_t p-\Pi_t q\|_2\le r'.
   \]
   For a random grid shift, the probability that two projected points at distance at most $r'$ are separated by some grid hyperplane is at most
   \[
      \frac{\|\Pi_t p-\Pi_t q\|_1}{h}
      \le
      \frac{\sqrt D\,r'}{20\sqrt D\,r'}
      \le
      \frac1{20}.
   \]
   Hence, in a good projection, a near neighbor shares the query cell with probability at least $19/20$ over the grid shift. With $T=C_c\log n$ independent projected grids, at least one copy is good and keeps the near pair together with constant probability; increasing $C_c$ gives any fixed success probability below one.

   Each grid cell has projected diameter at most $h\sqrt D=20Dr'$, so it is contained in a ball of radius $R_0=10Dr'=r\log^{O_c(1)}n$. We build one score-and-ball instance for every nonempty projected cell. The total number of stored projected point occurrences over one grid is $n$, and over all grids is $n\log^{O_c(1)}n$.

   A point with original distance greater than $cr$ from $q$ has projected distance greater than $(1-\varepsilon)cr$ in a good projection. Therefore a projected $(c',r')$-ANN answer with
   \[
      c'=\frac{(1-\varepsilon)c}{1+\varepsilon}
   \]
   is guaranteed, after verification in the original metric, to contain a valid $c$-approximate neighbor whenever one exists. Since $c\mapsto 1/(2c^2-1)$ is smooth in a fixed neighborhood of the chosen $c>1$, $\rho_{c'}\le\rho_c+O_c(\varepsilon)$, so $n^{\rho_{c'}}\le e^{O_c(1)}n^{\rho_c}$.

   At query time we project $q$ into all $T$ copies, query the cell containing $\Pi_tq$ in each copy, and verify returned candidates in the original metric. The projection work is $dD T=d\log^{O_c(1)}n$, and the number of localized instances queried is polylogarithmic.

   Bad projected copies do not spoil the expected work. The query implementation caps each localized copy by falling back to a brute-force scan of its projected cell, so a bad copy costs at most $n$ distance checks. Its expected contribution is at most
   \[
      T\cdot n\cdot n^{-C_0/20}=o(1)
   \]
   after increasing $C_0$. Good copies satisfy the promised projected near/far gap and bounded diameter, so the localized bounds apply. This preserves the claimed asymptotic query and space bounds.
\end{proof}

\section{The cumulative-score spherical primitive}

The spherical stage uses one cumulative Gaussian score tree and prunes by continuation mass. This avoids the two-sided tube that causes the $\exp(O(k^{1/3}))$ loss in the earlier analysis.

Choose a constant branching factor $B\ge2$, write $\ell_B=\log B$, and let
\[
   t^2=(1+a)\ell_B.
\]
A path of depth $k$ carries independent Gaussian edge vectors $g_e\sim N(0,I_d)$ and cumulative score
\[
   S_v(x)=\sum_{e\preceq v}\ip{g_e}{x}.
\]
The depth is
\[
   k
   =
   \left\lceil
      \frac{2(1+b)\log m}
      {(1+a)(1-b)\ell_B}
   \right\rceil
   =
   \Theta_{a,b}(\log m),
\]
and a leaf accepts $x$ when $S_v(x)\ge kt$.

For a node $v$ at level $\ell$ with score $s$, put $r=k-\ell$ and define the continuation mass
\[
   H_\ell(s)
   =
   B^r
   \overline\Phi\!\left(\frac{kt-s}{\sqrt r}\right).
\]
This is exactly the expected number of accepting descendant leaves of $v$, conditional on the current score $s$. The decoder retains a prefix only while
\[
   H_\ell(S_v(x))\ge k^{-A}
\]
for a sufficiently large constant $A=A_{a,b}$. Equivalently, up to lower-order tail terms, a retained prefix satisfies
\[
   S_v(x)\ge
   kt-\sqrt{2r(r\log B+A\log k)}.
\]
Early scores may lie well below the final linear trajectory; the barrier tightens only near the leaf. See \cref{fig:barrier}.

\begin{figure}[t]\centering

\draw[->] (0,0) -- (8.4,0) node[right]{level $\ell$};
\draw[->] (0,0) -- (0,4.6) node[above]{score $S$};
\node[below] at (8,0) {$k$};
\draw[dashed] (8,0) -- (8,4);
\node[left] at (0,4) {$kt$};
\draw[dashed] (0,4) -- (8,4);
\draw[gray,thick] (0,0) -- (8,4) node[pos=0.5,above,sloped,font=\scriptsize,black]{linear target $\tfrac{\ell}{k}\,kt$};
\draw[blue,very thick,domain=0:8,samples=80,smooth] plot (\x,{4*(\x/8) - 1.7*sqrt((8-\x)/8)});
\node[blue,font=\scriptsize,right] at (2.0,0.5) {continuation barrier $S\ge kt-\sqrt{2r(r\ell_B+A\log k)}$};
\draw[red,thick]
   (0,0) -- (1,0.15) -- (2,0.05) -- (3,0.9) -- (4,1.3) -- (5,1.7) -- (6,2.6) -- (7,3.2) -- (8,4.05);

\caption{Continuation-mass pruning keeps a score prefix as long as it stays above the soft barrier $S_v\ge kt-\sqrt{2r(r\ell_B+A\log k)}$ (blue), where $r=k-\ell$. The barrier is far below the linear trajectory to the accepting threshold $kt$ early on, and tightens to it only near the leaf, so the decoder tolerates prefixes whose scores start low. \begin{lemma}[Exact expected work]\label{lem:continuation-work}
   For fixed $-1<b<a<1$, continuation-mass pruning gives expected query path work
   \[
      m^{\rho(a,b)}\log^{O_{a,b}(1)}m,
   \]
   expected ordinary-far candidate occurrences
   \[
      m^{\rho(a,b)}\log^{O_{a,b}(1)}m,
   \]
   and stored point-path occurrences
   \[
      m^{1+\rho(a,b)}\log^{O_{a,b}(1)}m.
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   At any fixed level, summing $H_\ell(S_v(x))$ over all prefixes $v$ counts the expected number of accepting descendant leaves for $x$. Since every retained prefix has continuation mass at least $k^{-A}$, the expected number of retained prefixes at that level is at most $k^A$ times the expected number of accepting leaves. Summing over $k$ levels gives only a polynomial factor in $k$.

   The expected number of accepting leaves for one point is
   \[
      B^k\overline\Phi(t\sqrt{k})
      =
      m^{\rho(a,b)}k^{O(1)}.
   \]
   For a pair of correlation at most $b$, the Gaussian joint-tail estimate
   \[
      \Prb[X\ge u,\,Y\ge u]
      \le
      \exp\!\left(-\frac{u^2}{1+b}\right)
   \]
   gives expected common accepting leaves at most
   \[
      m^{-(1-\rho(a,b))}k^{O(1)}.
   \]
   Summing over $m$ ordinary far points proves the far-candidate bound. Summing the one-point bound over stored data points proves the storage bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Tame good near leaf]\label{def:good-near-leaf}
   Fix a near pair $(p,q)$ with $\ip{p}{q}=a$. For a prefix $u$ at level $\ell$, write
   \[
      Y_u(x)=S_u(x)-\ell t
   \]
   and define the centered common coordinate
   \[
      M_u=\frac{Y_u(p)+Y_u(q)}{\sqrt{2(1+a)}}.
   \]
   A leaf $v$ is tame good for $(p,q)$ if
   \[
      S_v(p),S_v(q)\in[kt,kt+1]
   \]
   every prefix $u\preceq v$ satisfies the continuation-mass pruning rule for both $p$ and $q$, and every prefix satisfies the analytical upper barrier
   \[
      M_u\le H_{a,b}
   \]
   for a sufficiently large fixed constant $H_{a,b}$. This upper barrier is used only in the proof; the algorithm does not enforce it.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Tame-good first moment]\label{lem:good-first-moment}
   For every fixed $-1<b<a<1$ and sufficiently large pruning constant $A$, if $Z$ is the number of tame good near leaves for a pair of correlation exactly $a$, then
   \[
      \E Z\ge k^{-O_{a,b}(1)}.
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Work at the critical correlation $a$, which is the least favorable near case. Exponentially tilt the two-dimensional Gaussian increment $(X,Y)$ so that both coordinates have mean $t$. Since
   \[
      \Sigma=
      \begin{pmatrix}
         1&a\\
         a&1
      \end{pmatrix},
      \qquad
      \theta=\frac{t}{1+a}(1,1),
   \]
   the tilted law has mean $\Sigma\theta=(t,t)$ and
   \[
      \frac12\theta^\top\Sigma\theta=\frac{t^2}{1+a}=\ell_B.
   \]
   Let $Q$ denote the tilted measure. On the endpoint event
   \[
      S_v(p),S_v(q)\in[kt,kt+1],
   \]
   the likelihood ratio satisfies
   \[
      B^k\frac{dP}{dQ}=\exp(O_{a,b}(1)).
   \]
   Therefore the expected number of tame good leaves under the original measure is, up to constant factors, the $Q$-probability that one tilted two-dimensional walk has endpoint in the unit square, stays above the two continuation barriers, and stays below the common-coordinate upper barrier.

   Under $Q$, after subtracting the linear drift $\ell t$, each coordinate is a centered Gaussian walk. The endpoint has covariance $k\Sigma$, so the probability that both centered endpoints lie in $[0,1]$ is $\Theta_{a,b}(1/k)$.

   It remains to check that the path barriers do not cost more than a polynomial factor. Write $r=k-\ell$ and let
   \[
      d_r=\sqrt{2r(r\ell_B+A\log k)}-rt.
   \]
   A prefix at level $\ell$ is retained whenever the centered coordinate is at least $-d_r$, up to harmless constant tail corrections. Since $t^2=(1+a)\ell_B<2\ell_B$, there is a constant $c_{a,b}>0$ such that
   \[
      d_r\ge c_{a,b}r
      \qquad\text{for } r\ge C_{a,b}\log k,
   \]
   and, for $1\le r\le C_{a,b}\log k$,
   \[
      d_r\ge c_{a,b}\sqrt{A r\log k}
   \]
   after increasing $A$. Conditioned on endpoints in $[0,1]^2$, each coordinate is a Gaussian bridge whose variance at distance $r$ from the endpoint is $O(r)$. A union bound over $r$ therefore gives failure probability
   \[
      \sum_{r\ge C\log k}\exp(-\Omega_{a,b}(r))
      +
      \sum_{1\le r\le C\log k} k^{-\Omega_{a,b}(A)}
      =
      o(1)
   \]
   for $A$ large enough.

   The common coordinate $M_u$ is a standard one-dimensional centered Gaussian bridge, independent of the difference coordinate. By the reflection principle for a Gaussian bridge, conditioned on its endpoint lying in a fixed bounded interval below $H_{a,b}$,
   \[
      \Prb_Q\!\left[\max_{u\preceq v}M_u\le H_{a,b}\right]
      \ge k^{-O_{a,b}(1)}.
   \]
   On this upper-barrier event, violation of either continuation lower barrier would force the difference-coordinate bridge to make an excursion of size at least $d_r-O_{a,b}(1)$ at distance $r$ from the endpoint. The same union bound as above shows that this has probability $o(1)$ after increasing $A$. Thus, conditional on the endpoint event, all barriers in the definition of tame good hold with probability at least $k^{-O_{a,b}(1)}$. Hence $\E Z\ge k^{-O_{a,b}(1)}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Tame-good second moment]\label{lem:tame-second-moment}
   For every fixed $-1<b<a<1$, the tame-good leaf count $Z$ from \cref{lem:good-first-moment} satisfies
   \[
      \E Z^2\le k^{O_{a,b}(1)}.
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\small,>=stealth]
\draw[very thick] (0,0) -- (3,0) node[midway,above=2pt,font=\scriptsize]{shared prefix (length $j$)};
\node[circle,fill,inner sep=1.3pt,label=left:{root}] at (0,0){};
\node[circle,fill,inner sep=1.3pt] (split) at (3,0){};
\node[below=2pt,font=\scriptsize] at (split) {LCA, depth $j$};
\draw[thick] (split) -- (6,0.9) node[right]{$v$};
\draw[thick] (split) -- (6,-0.9) node[right]{$w$};
\node[font=\scriptsize] at (4.6,0.92) {$r=k-j$};
\node[font=\scriptsize] at (4.6,-0.92) {$r=k-j$};
\node[draw,rounded corners,fill=gray!10,font=\scriptsize] at (7.3,0.9) {$S_v(p),S_v(q)\in[kt,kt+1]$};
\node[draw,rounded corners,fill=gray!10,font=\scriptsize] at (7.3,-0.9) {$S_w(p),S_w(q)\in[kt,kt+1]$};
\node[align=left,font=\scriptsize,anchor=west] at (0,-2.0)
  {common coord.\ $C_\ell=\dfrac{S_\ell(p)+S_\ell(q)}{\sqrt{2(1+a)}}$ \quad(drift $\mu=\sqrt{2\ell_B}$, capped $\le H_{a,b}$ at the split)};
\node[align=left,font=\scriptsize,anchor=west] at (0,-2.9)
  {difference coord.\ $D_\ell=\dfrac{S_\ell(p)-S_\ell(q)}{\sqrt{2(1-a)}}$ \quad(centered; variance $k$, covariance $j$)};
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Second-moment decomposition by the lowest common ancestor. Two tame-good leaves $v,w$ share a prefix of length $j$ and then run independently for $r=k-j$ steps. After multiplying the conditional endpoint probability by the $B^{2k-j}$ ordered pairs at split depth $j$, the common-coordinate drift $\mu^2=2\ell_B$ cancels the exponential growth; the upper cap $M_u\le H_{a,b}$ at the split kills prolific high shared prefixes, leaving a summable $\sum_j (j{+}1)^{-1/2}(k{-}j)^{-3/2}k^{-1/2}=O(1)$.}
\label{fig:lca}
\end{figure}

\begin{proof}
   We decompose pairs of leaves by the depth $j$ of their lowest common ancestor. Write $r=k-j$, and first consider $0\le j<k$. There are at most $B^{2k-j}$ ordered pairs with split depth $j$.

   Use the independent common and difference coordinates
   \[
      C_\ell=\frac{S_\ell(p)+S_\ell(q)}{\sqrt{2(1+a)}},
      \qquad
      D_\ell=\frac{S_\ell(p)-S_\ell(q)}{\sqrt{2(1-a)}}.
   \]
   The common coordinate has unit Gaussian increments and endpoint threshold
   \[
      \mu k,
      \qquad
      \mu=\sqrt{\frac{2}{1+a}}\,t=\sqrt{2\ell_B}.
   \]
   If both leaves are tame good, then at the split prefix the centered common value $y=C_j-\mu j$ satisfies $y\le H_{a,b}$, and both common-coordinate suffixes end in a fixed unit interval around $\mu k$. Ignoring all other constraints, the common-coordinate probability is at most
   \[
      \int_{-\infty}^{H_{a,b}}
      \frac{1}{\sqrt{j+1}}
      \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\mu j+y)^2}{2j}\right)
      \left[
         \frac{C}{\sqrt r}
         \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\mu r-y)^2}{2r}\right)
      \right]^2dy,
   \]
   with the evident interpretation when $j=0$. Multiplying by the pair count $B^{2k-j}$ and using $\mu^2=2\ell_B$ cancels the exponential main term and leaves
   \[
      C_{a,b}\frac{1}{\sqrt{j+1}\,r}
      \int_{-\infty}^{H_{a,b}}\exp(\mu y)\,dy
      \le
      \frac{C_{a,b}}{\sqrt{j+1}\,r}.
   \]

   The difference coordinates for the two leaves are centered jointly Gaussian with variances $k$ and covariance $j$. The event that both endpoint differences lie in the fixed interval forced by
   \[
      S_v(p),S_v(q),S_w(p),S_w(q)\in[kt,kt+1]
   \]
   has probability at most the maximum bivariate Gaussian density times a constant area:
   \[
      O_{a,b}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{k^2-j^2}}\right)
      =
      O_{a,b}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{kr}}\right).
   \]
   Since the common and difference coordinates are independent, the total contribution of split depth $j<k$ to $\E Z^2$ is at most
   \[
      \frac{C_{a,b}}{\sqrt{j+1}\,r^{3/2}\sqrt k}.
   \]
   Summing over $j<k$ gives a bounded quantity:
   \[
      \sum_{j=0}^{k-1}
      \frac{1}{\sqrt{j+1}\,(k-j)^{3/2}\sqrt k}
      =
      O(1).
   \]

   The diagonal contribution $v=w$ is at most the first moment of accepting near leaves, hence at most $k^{O_{a,b}(1)}$ by the same endpoint calculation used in \cref{lem:good-first-moment}. Therefore $\E Z^2\le k^{O_{a,b}(1)}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[One-sided spherical survival]\label{cor:spherical-survival}
   If a query $q$ has a data point $p$ with $\ip{p}{q}\ge a$, then the continuation-mass decoder produces a common accepting leaf for $(p,q)$ with probability at least $\log^{-O_{a,b}(1)}m$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   By \cref{lem:good-first-moment} and \cref{lem:tame-second-moment}, Paley--Zygmund gives
   \[
      \Prb[Z>0]\ge \frac{(\E Z)^2}{\E Z^2}
      \ge k^{-O_{a,b}(1)}.
   \]
   Since $k=\Theta_{a,b}(\log m)$, this is the desired inverse-polylogarithmic survival probability. Correlation larger than $a$ can only improve the tilted endpoint exponent; the same constants cover a fixed compact neighborhood of the critical parameters after the usual slack adjustment.
\end{proof}

The spherical primitive therefore has polylogarithmic loss: expected work follows from continuation mass, and near-pair survival follows from the tame-good first and second moments. No algorithmic two-sided tube is imposed.

\subsection{Budgeted score blocks}

The spherical block can be run with a budget parameter larger than the number of resident points. This is useful in the Euclidean recursion because the natural query potential is
\[
   F(m,R)=m^\rho\left(\frac Rr\right)^{2(1-\rho)},
\]
not just $m^\rho$.

\begin{corollary}[Budgeted continuation block]\label{cor:budgeted-block}
   Fix $-1<b<a<1$ and write $\rho=\rho(a,b)$. Let a spherical node contain $m$ points, and let $N\ge m$. Run the continuation-mass decoder exactly as above, except choose the depth
   \[
      k
      =
      \left\lceil
         \frac{2(1+b)\log N}
         {(1+a)(1-b)\ell_B}
      \right\rceil .
   \]
   Then the expected query path work is
   \[
      N^\rho\log^{O_{a,b}(1)}N,
   \]
   the expected ordinary-far candidate occurrences are at most
   \[
      mN^{-(1-\rho)}\log^{O_{a,b}(1)}N
      \le
      N^\rho\log^{O_{a,b}(1)}N,
   \]
   and the stored point-path occurrences are at most
   \[
      mN^\rho\log^{O_{a,b}(1)}N.
   \]
   If a query has a near point with correlation at least $a$, the success probability is at least $\log^{-O_{a,b}(1)}N$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   The proof of \cref{lem:continuation-work} depends on the depth only through the expected one-point accepting-leaf count and the far joint-tail count. With the displayed depth these become $N^\rho\log^{O(1)}N$ and $N^{-(1-\rho)}\log^{O(1)}N$, respectively. Summing the latter over the $m$ resident points gives the stated far-candidate bound, and $m\le N$ gives the displayed simplification. The storage bound is the one-point accepting count summed over $m$ data points.

   The first- and second-moment near-pair arguments in \cref{lem:good-first-moment}, \cref{lem:tame-second-moment}, and \cref{cor:spherical-survival} use only the score depth $k=\Theta_{a,b}(\log N)$ and the fixed correlations. Replacing $m$ by $N$ in that depth therefore gives success probability $\log^{-O_{a,b}(1)}N$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Radius-budgeted score block]\label{cor:radius-budgeted-block}
   Fix $\rho=\rho_c$ and $s=1-\rho$. At a Euclidean node with $m$ points in radius $R\ge r$, set
   \[
      N=m\left(\frac Rr\right)^{2s/\rho}.
   \]
   Then one continuation-mass score block has expected query path work and ordinary-far candidate occurrences
   \[
      F(m,R)\log^{O_c(1)}N,
      \qquad
      F(m,R)=m^\rho\left(\frac Rr\right)^{2s},
   \]
   stored point-path occurrences
   \[
      mF(m,R)\log^{O_c(1)}N,
   \]
   and inverse-polylogarithmic near-pair survival.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Since $R\ge r$, the chosen $N$ is at least $m$. Also
   \[
      N^\rho=m^\rho\left(\frac Rr\right)^{2s}=F(m,R).
   \]
   Apply \cref{cor:budgeted-block}. In the bounded-diameter instances used below, $\log N=\log^{O_c(1)}n$, so the logarithmic factors are absorbed into $\log^{O_c(1)}n$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A constant-recall smooth terminal filter}

The continuation-mass decoder above is designed to survive adaptive score schedules and recentering. For a terminal spherical search, where no further geometric edge has to be coupled to a score prefix, there is a simpler constant-depth smooth product filter with constant one-table recall. This gives a non-channel terminal layer for any localization scheme that can reduce the remaining instance to a spherical near/far gap.

Let
\[
   \phi(\gamma)=\frac{1-\gamma}{1+\gamma},
   \qquad
   \rho(a,b)=\frac{\phi(a)}{\phi(b)}.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Smooth product terminal filter]\label{thm:smooth-product-terminal}
   Fix $-1<b<a<1$ and a fixed integer $k\ge 2/(1-a)$. Let $m$ be the spherical instance size. Put
   \[
      t^2=\frac{2\log m}{\phi(b)}+O_{a,b}(\log\log m),
      \qquad
      u=\frac{t}{\sqrt k}.
   \]
   For each block $i\in[k]$, sample
   \[
      g_{i,1},\ldots,g_{i,B}\sim N(0,I_d),
      \qquad
      B=\Theta_{a,b}\!\left(J_a(u)^{-1}\right),
   \]
   where $J_\gamma(u)=\Pr[X\ge u,Y\ge u]$ for correlated standard Gaussians with correlation $\gamma$. A leaf is a tuple $j=(j_1,\ldots,j_k)\in[B]^k$ with aggregate normal
   \[
      G_j=\frac1{\sqrt k}\sum_{i=1}^k g_{i,j_i},
   \]
   and accepts a point $x$ if $\ip{G_j}{x}\ge t$.

   Then one table has constant success probability for every near pair of correlation at least $a$. Its expected query leaves, update leaves per point, and ordinary far candidates are
   \[
      m^{\rho(a,b)}\log^{O_{a,b}(1)}m,
   \]
   and its expected storage is
   \[
      m^{1+\rho(a,b)}\log^{O_{a,b}(1)}m.
   \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
   For a near pair $(p,q)$ of correlation at least $a$, one block contains a column satisfying
   \[
      \ip{g_{i,j},p}\ge u,
      \qquad
      \ip{g_{i,j},q}\ge u
   \]
   with probability bounded below by a positive constant, by the choice $B=\Theta(J_a(u)^{-1})$. The blocks are independent and $k$ is fixed, so with constant probability every block contains such a common column. Choosing one such column per block gives a tuple accepted by both $p$ and $q$, since
   \[
      \ip{G_j,p},\ip{G_j,q}\ge\frac{k u}{\sqrt k}=t.
   \]

   The number of implicit leaves is
   \[
      M=B^k
      =
      \exp\!\left(\frac{t^2}{1+a}\right)\log^{O_{a,b}(1)}m,
   \]
   using the standard bivariate Gaussian tail
   \[
      J_a(u)=u^{-O_{a,b}(1)}
      \exp\!\left(-\frac{u^2}{1+a}\right).
   \]
   For each fixed tuple, $G_j\sim N(0,I_d)$. Hence the expected number of leaves entered by one query, and also by one stored point, is
   \[
      M\overline\Phi(t)
      =
      \exp\!\left(\frac{t^2}{1+a}-\frac{t^2}{2}\right)
      \log^{O_{a,b}(1)}m
      =
      m^{\rho(a,b)}\log^{O_{a,b}(1)}m,
   \]
   because $t^2=2\log m/\phi(b)+O(\log\log m)$ and $\rho(a,b)=\phi(a)/\phi(b)$. This proves the query-leaf and storage bounds.

   For a far data point $x$ with $\ip{x}{q}\le b$, the pair $(\ip{G_j,x},\ip{G_j,q})$ is bivariate Gaussian with correlation at most $b$. Therefore
   \[
      M J_b(t)
      \le
      \exp\!\left(\frac{t^2}{1+a}-\frac{t^2}{1+b}\right)
      \log^{O_{a,b}(1)}m
      =
      m^{-(1-\rho(a,b))}\log^{O_{a,b}(1)}m.
   \]
   Summing over the $m$ resident far points gives the far-candidate bound.
\end{proof}

The leaf set $[B]^k$ is implicit. For a query or data point, sort the $B$ scores in each block and enumerate tuples whose block-score sum is at least $t\sqrt k$ by a best-first heap over the $k$ sorted lists. If $L$ tuples are output, this costs $O_k(B\log B+L\log L)$. The condition $k\ge2/(1-a)$ gives $B\le m^{\rho(a,b)}\log^{O_{a,b}(1)}m$, so the enumeration overhead is absorbed into the stated polynomial logarithmic factors.

The smooth product filter is not a replacement for \cref{lem:adaptive-continuation}: it has no long prefix process on which to hang many recentering decisions. Its role is terminal. Once a localization method produces a bounded spherical subproblem with the critical near/far angular gap, \cref{thm:smooth-product-terminal} gives constant one-table recall and removes the last inverse-polylogarithmic amplification loss.

\begin{corollary}[Random-position tensoring baseline]\label{cor:random-position-tensoring}
   Fix \(c>1\), and put
   \[
      a_0=1-\frac1{c^2},
      \qquad
      \rho_c=\frac1{2c^2-1}.
   \]
   Let \(q\in\mathbb S^{D-1}\) be a terminal spherical query with a near point
   \(p\) satisfying \(\ip{p}{q}\ge a_0\).  Suppose every invalid resident point
   \(x\) satisfies
   \[
      \ip{x}{q}\le b_m,
      \qquad
      0\le b_m\le\frac{C_c}{\log m}.
   \]
   Then the constant-depth product construction, with
   \(k=\lceil 2/(1-a_0)\rceil=O(c^2)\) tensor blocks, gives one-table constant
   recall and expected query work, update work per point, and invalid
   candidate work
   \[
      m^{\rho_c}\log^{O(c^2)}m .
   \]
   Its expected storage is
   \[
      m^{1+\rho_c}\log^{O(c^2)}m .
   \]

   In particular, the same conclusion holds with high probability in the
   random-position model in which the invalid points are independent uniform
   directions and \(D\ge C'_c\log^3 m\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Apply \cref{thm:smooth-product-terminal} with \(a=a_0\) and \(b=b_m\).
   The Gaussian tail estimates in its proof are uniform for
   \(0\le b_m\le C_c/\log m\).  Since
   \[
      \rho(a_0,b_m)=\rho_c+O_c(b_m)
      =
      \rho_c+O_c\!\left(\frac1{\log m}\right),
   \]
   the factor \(m^{\rho(a_0,b_m)}\) is \(O_c(m^{\rho_c})\).  The polynomial
   tail factors in the \(k\) tensor blocks contribute
   \(\log^{O(k)}m=\log^{O(c^2)}m\).

   For the final statement, a standard spherical cap bound gives
   \[
      \Prb[\ip{X}{q}>\varepsilon]\le \exp(-D\varepsilon^2/3)
   \]
   for a uniform direction \(X\), after adjusting the absolute constant.  With
   \(\varepsilon=C_c/\log m\) and \(D\ge C'_c\log^3 m\), a union bound over the
   \(m\) invalid points gives the displayed deterministic correlation
   condition with probability at least \(1-m^{-2}\), after increasing \(C'_c\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What tensoring leaves open]\label{rem:tensoring-random-open}
   \Cref{cor:random-position-tensoring} is the clean random-position baseline:
   the tensor product itself supplies the storage, far-load, and near-hit
   spectrum, so no posterior channel or finite-envelope construction is
   needed.  The worst-case obstruction is different.  If a queried filter
   bucket is large, the relevant quantity is not its raw size but its
   recursive cost divided by the conditional probability that the same bucket
   still contains the near point.

   A possible worst-case extension is therefore a success-normalized
   bucket-compression recursion.  For a split parameter \(1<\alpha<c\), replace
   a filter bucket by an \((\alpha-1)r\)-net \(N_F\) and recurse on
   approximation \(c/\alpha\).  Writing \(\rho'=\rho_{c/\alpha}\), the query
   recurrence does not need a new Renyi list-decoding theorem: since
   \(N_F\subseteq B_F\) and \(\rho'\le1\), the usual success-normalized
   expected candidate-load estimate already implies
   \[
      \E\!\left[
         |N_F|^{\rho'}\mid q\in Q_F
      \right]
      \le
      \E\!\left[
         |B_F|\mid q\in Q_F
      \right] .
   \]
   The genuinely new storage condition is the shared-DAG version for
   canonicalized bucket nets,
   \[
      \sum_A |A|^{1+\rho'}
      \le
      m^{1+\rho_c}\polylog m .
   \]
   The occurrence multiplicities are still charged as filter metadata and
   through the query sampling law, but the recursive child index is stored once
   per distinct canonical net.
   The query inequality is only a success-normalized first-moment statement:
   since \(N_F\subseteq B_F\) and \(\rho'\le1\), ordinary candidate-load control
   implies the recursive query moment.  The genuinely Renyi list-decoding part
   is the shared storage inequality for distinct canonical bucket nets, after
   the dense part has been quotiented out.  In worst-case tangent-cap
   configurations the correct proof target is split: low-correlation tuple
   profiles should be paid by Gaussian cap-intersection energy, while
   high-correlation tuple mass should be reported as smaller-radius star
   containers and charged through the dense-cover LP.  These storage
   certificates hold in the random-position tensor calculation above, but the
   corresponding low-correlation/dense-star dichotomy is not yet proved for
   arbitrary dense tangent-cap configurations.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Bucket-net recursion geometry]
   \label{lem:bucket-net-recursion-geometry}
   Let \(P\) be a metric subproblem, let \(B\subseteq P\), and let
   \(N\subseteq B\) be a \(\Delta\)-cover of \(B\): every point of \(B\) is
   within distance \(\Delta\) of some point of \(N\).  Fix \(1<\alpha<c\) and
   put \(\Delta=(\alpha-1)r\).  If a query \(q\) has a near witness
   \(p\in B\) with \(\|p-q\|\le r\), then \(N\) contains a point \(t\) with
   \[
      \|t-q\|\le\alpha r .
      \tag{BNG1}
   \]
   Consequently, a \((c/\alpha,\alpha r)\)-ANN child built on \(N\), followed
   by verification in the parent metric, is a valid recursive replacement for
   scanning \(B\): any successful child answer is within \(cr\) of \(q\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Since \(p\in B\) and \(N\) \(\Delta\)-covers \(B\), choose \(t\in N\) with
   \(\|t-p\|\le\Delta=(\alpha-1)r\).  The triangle inequality gives
   \[
      \|t-q\|\le\|t-p\|+\|p-q\|\le\alpha r.
   \]
   If the child returns a point \(x\in N\) within
   \((c/\alpha)(\alpha r)=cr\) of \(q\), the parent verifier accepts it.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Success-normalized compressed-bucket compiler]
   \label{prop:success-normalized-bucket-dag}
   Fix a finite approximation ladder
   \[
      c=c_0>c_1>\cdots>c_h=1,
      \qquad
      \alpha_j=\frac{c_j}{c_{j+1}}>1,
   \]
   and put
   \[
      \rho_j=\frac1{2c_j^2-1}\quad(j<h),
      \qquad
      \rho_h=1 .
   \]
   Let \(L(m)=\log^{A_c}(m+2)\).  Suppose that, for every rung \(j<h\), every
   local \((c_j,r_j)\)-ANN subproblem \(P\) of size \(m\) has a randomized
   compressed-filter step with the following properties.

   First, each sampled filter \(F\) has an update bucket \(B_F\subseteq P\) and
   stores a maximal \((\alpha_j-1)r_j\)-separated net
   \(N_F\subseteq B_F\).  Nets are canonicalized into classes \(A\), so all
   filter occurrences with the same retained net point to the same recursive
   child.  The retained filter metadata and occurrence pointers have space at
   most \(m^{1+\rho_j}L(m)\).

   Second, for every promised query \(q\) and near witness \(p\in P\) with
   \(\|p-q\|\le r_j\), one probe samples a filter occurrence from a law
   \(\mu_q\) in \(dL(m)\) expected nonrecursive work.  If
   \[
      a_j(q,p)=\Pr_{F\sim\mu_q}[p\in B_F],
   \]
   then
   \[
      a_j(q,p)^{-1}\le m^{\rho_j}L(m),
      \tag{CB0}
   \]
   and the success-normalized query moment satisfies
   \[
      \E_{F\sim\mu_q}|N_F|^{\rho_{j+1}}
      \le
      a_j(q,p)\,m^{\rho_j}L(m).
      \tag{CB1}
   \]

   Third, the coordinates of the original resident points are stored once
   globally; recursive children store only point identifiers, filter metadata,
   and their own incidence structures.  The distinct canonical child nets obey
   \[
      \sum_A |A|^{1+\rho_{j+1}}
      \le
      m^{1+\rho_j}L(m).
      \tag{CB2}
   \]

   Then the recursive compressed-filter DAG gives, at rung \(j\), constant
   success probability with expected query work
   \[
      d\,m^{\rho_j}\log^{O_c(1)}(m+2)
   \]
   and expected space
   \[
      dm+m^{1+\rho_j}\log^{O_c(1)}(m+2).
   \]
   In particular, at the original rung \(j=0\) this is the desired
   \(m^{\rho_c}\polylog m\) query and \(m^{1+\rho_c}\polylog m\) space bound.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
   We prove the claim by backward induction on \(j\).  At \(j=h\) the
   approximation factor is \(1\), and a brute-force scan of the resident set
   costs \(dm\), succeeds deterministically whenever a point within \(r_h\)
   exists, and uses no index space beyond the coordinates.  This is exactly the
   displayed bound because \(\rho_h=1\).

   Assume the claim is known at rung \(j+1\).  Build the retained filter
   metadata for \(P\), using references to the one global coordinate array.
   For every canonical net \(A\), build one recursive child for the
   \((c_{j+1},r_{j+1})\)-ANN problem on \(A\), where
   \(r_{j+1}=\alpha_jr_j\).  We apply the induction hypothesis to the
   non-coordinate part of the child indices; the coordinate term is not
   duplicated because every child point is an original resident point addressed
   by identifier.  By \((CB2)\), the total recursive non-coordinate space is at
   most
   \[
      \log^{O_c(1)}(m+2)
      \sum_A |A|^{1+\rho_{j+1}}
      \le
      m^{1+\rho_j}\log^{O_c(1)}(m+2),
   \]
   after absorbing the retained metadata.  Adding the single global coordinate
   array gives \(dm+m^{1+\rho_j}\log^{O_c(1)}(m+2)\).  Thus the space bound
   holds.

   On query \(q\), repeat independent probes until a verified \(c_jr_j\)-near
   neighbor is found, and cap the resulting expected algorithm as in the
   preliminaries.  Consider a true near witness \(p\).  If a sampled filter
   \(F\) contains \(p\), then maximality of \(N_F\) gives a net point
   \(t\in N_F\) satisfying \(\|t-q\|\le\alpha_jr_j=r_{j+1}\), by
   \cref{lem:bucket-net-recursion-geometry}.
   Therefore the child on \(N_F\) is a valid \((c_{j+1},r_{j+1})\)-ANN
   instance, and a successful child answer is within
   \[
      c_{j+1}r_{j+1}=c_jr_j
   \]
   of \(q\), so verification accepts it.

   One probe succeeds with probability at least a fixed constant times
   \(a_j(q,p)\), by the induction hypothesis for the child.  Its expected child
   work is, again by induction,
   \[
      d\,\E_{F\sim\mu_q}|N_F|^{\rho_{j+1}}\log^{O_c(1)}(m+2),
   \]
   where \(m\) bounds all child sizes.  Adding the probe-generation work and
   dividing by the success probability gives expected query work
   \[
      \frac{dL(m)}{a_j(q,p)}
      +
      d\,\frac{
         \E_{F\sim\mu_q}|N_F|^{\rho_{j+1}}
      }{a_j(q,p)}
      \log^{O_c(1)}(m+2).
   \]
   The first term is at most
   \(d\,m^{\rho_j}\log^{O_c(1)}(m+2)\) by \((CB0)\), and the ratio in the
   second term is at most \(m^{\rho_j}L(m)\) by \((CB1)\).  This proves the
   desired expected query bound.  The standard truncation paragraph converts
   the expected geometric repetition into a capped constant-success query
   procedure.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Fractional probing form of compressed buckets]
   \label{cor:fractional-probe-compressed-bucket}
   In \cref{prop:success-normalized-bucket-dag}, the two query hypotheses
   \((CB0)\)--\((CB1)\) may be replaced by the following single
   cost-normalized fractional probing condition.  For each promised query \(q\),
   let \(\lambda_{q,F}\ge0\) be a finite intensity measure on the retained
   filter occurrences visible to \(q\), sampleable after normalization in
   \(dL(m)\) expected nonrecursive work.  For every near witness \(p\) with
   \(\|p-q\|\le r_j\), assume
   \[
      H_q(p):=\sum_{F:p\in B_F}\lambda_{q,F}>0
      \tag{FPB0}
   \]
   and
   \[
      \sum_F\lambda_{q,F}
      \left(L(m)+|N_F|^{\rho_{j+1}}\right)
      \le
      H_q(p)\,m^{\rho_j}L(m).
      \tag{FPB1}
   \]
   Then the same recursive query bound as in
   \cref{prop:success-normalized-bucket-dag} holds, with the same storage
   hypothesis \((CB2)\).

   Equivalently, after rescaling \(\lambda_q\) separately for each witness, the
   condition says that the visible compressed buckets form a fractional cover of
   \(p\) whose total one-probe price
   \(L(m)+|N_F|^{\rho_{j+1}}\) is at most \(m^{\rho_j}L(m)\).  Thus the query
   invariant is exactly recursive cost divided by near-witness coverage
   probability, not raw bucket size and not a fixed hit probability.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Put \(\Lambda_q=\sum_F\lambda_{q,F}\).  If \(\Lambda_q=0\), then
   \((FPB0)\) is impossible for a promised near witness, so assume
   \(\Lambda_q>0\) and sample
   \[
      \mu_q(F)=\lambda_{q,F}/\Lambda_q .
   \]
   For a fixed near witness \(p\), the one-probe hit probability is
   \[
      a_j(q,p)=\Pr_{F\sim\mu_q}[p\in B_F]
      =
      \frac{H_q(p)}{\Lambda_q}.
      \tag{FPB2}
   \]
   The expected normalized child work is
   \[
      \E_{F\sim\mu_q}|N_F|^{\rho_{j+1}}
      =
      \frac1{\Lambda_q}\sum_F\lambda_{q,F}|N_F|^{\rho_{j+1}} .
      \tag{FPB3}
   \]
   Therefore the whole one-probe cost divided by hit probability is
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      \frac{L(m)+\E_{F\sim\mu_q}|N_F|^{\rho_{j+1}}}{a_j(q,p)}
      &=
      \frac{
         \sum_F\lambda_{q,F}
         \left(L(m)+|N_F|^{\rho_{j+1}}\right)
      }{H_q(p)}  \\
      &\le m^{\rho_j}L(m)
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{FPB4}
   \]
   by \((FPB1)\).  The query analysis in
   \cref{prop:success-normalized-bucket-dag} used \((CB0)\)--\((CB1)\) only
   through this ratio bound: the \(dL(m)\) probe-generation cost contributes the
   \(L(m)\) term in the numerator, and the child recursion contributes
   \(|N_F|^{\rho_{j+1}}\) up to the common polylogarithmic induction factor.
   Substituting \((FPB4)\) in that display gives the same
   \(d\,m^{\rho_j}\log^{O_c(1)}(m+2)\) expected query time.  The space argument is
   unchanged because it depends only on the retained metadata and \((CB2)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[First-moment query compression]\label{lem:first-moment-query-compression}
   In the query part of \cref{prop:success-normalized-bucket-dag}, suppose
   that the sampled filter law satisfies the stronger but simpler
   success-normalized expected-load bound
   \[
      \E_{F\sim\mu_q}|N_F|
      \le
      a_j(q,p)\,m^{\rho_j}L(m).
      \tag{FMQ1}
   \]
   Then the Renyi query moment \((CB1)\) follows.

   In particular, it is enough to prove \((FMQ1)\) with \(|B_F|\) in place of
   \(|N_F|\).  Thus the query side of the compressed-bucket recursion is just
   the usual LSH/LSF success-normalized candidate-load estimate: recursive
   compression and spherical list-size effects are needed for storage, not for
   this query moment.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The net size is an integer and \(0\le\rho_{j+1}\le1\).  Hence
   \[
      |N_F|^{\rho_{j+1}}\le |N_F|
   \]
   pointwise, with the convention \(0^{\rho_{j+1}}=0\).  Averaging and applying
   \((FMQ1)\) gives \((CB1)\).  Since \(N_F\subseteq B_F\), the same conclusion
   follows from the corresponding expected-load bound for \(|B_F|\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Occurrence moments dominate shared-DAG storage]
   \label{lem:occurrence-moments-dominate-dag}
   Let \(\mathcal F\) be a finite set of retained filter occurrences, each with
   a canonical net \(N_F\), and let \(\mathcal A\) be the set of distinct
   canonical nets.  For \(0\le r\le1\),
   \[
      \sum_{A\in\mathcal A}|A|^{1+r}
      \le
      \sum_{F\in\mathcal F}|N_F|^{1+r}.
      \tag{OMD1}
   \]
   Moreover, with
   \[
      S_1=\sum_{F\in\mathcal F}|N_F|,
      \qquad
      S_2=\sum_{F\in\mathcal F}|N_F|^2,
   \]
   the occurrence moment satisfies
   \[
      \sum_{F\in\mathcal F}|N_F|^{1+r}
      \le
      S_1^{1-r}S_2^r .
      \tag{OMD2}
   \]
   Consequently, the shared-DAG storage hypothesis \((CB2)\) follows if the
   retained occurrences have
   \[
      S_1\le m^{1+\rho_j}L(m),
      \qquad
      S_2\le m^{1+\rho_j}L(m),
   \]
   and it also follows from any sharper direct bound on the distinct-net sum in
   \((OMD1)\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Choose one occurrence \(F(A)\) for each distinct canonical net \(A\).  Since
   \(N_{F(A)}=A\),
   \[
      \sum_{A\in\mathcal A}|A|^{1+r}
      =
      \sum_{A\in\mathcal A}|N_{F(A)}|^{1+r}
      \le
      \sum_{F\in\mathcal F}|N_F|^{1+r},
   \]
   proving \((OMD1)\).

   The interpolation inequality is Holder's inequality applied to
   \[
      |N_F|^{1+r}=|N_F|^{1-r}\bigl(|N_F|^2\bigr)^r:
   \]
   \[
      \sum_F |N_F|^{1-r}\bigl(|N_F|^2\bigr)^r
      \le
      \left(\sum_F |N_F|\right)^{1-r}
      \left(\sum_F |N_F|^2\right)^r .
   \]
   Substituting the two displayed bounds on \(S_1,S_2\) gives \((CB2)\), after
   absorbing \(L(m)\) into the polylogarithmic factor.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Compressed-bucket rung checklist]
   \label{cor:compressed-bucket-rung-checklist}
   In one rung \(j\) of
   \cref{prop:success-normalized-bucket-dag}, it is enough to verify the
   following three certificates.

   First, the retained filter metadata and occurrence pointers use at most
   \(m^{1+\rho_j}L(m)\) space, and each bucket net \(N_F\subseteq B_F\) is a
   maximal \((\alpha_j-1)r_j\)-separated net of \(B_F\).

   Second, for every promised query \(q\) and near witness \(p\), the sampling
   law \(\mu_q\) has hit probability
   \[
      a_j(q,p)=\Pr_{F\sim\mu_q}[p\in B_F],
      \qquad
      a_j(q,p)^{-1}\le m^{\rho_j}L(m),
      \tag{CBK1}
   \]
   and satisfies the ordinary success-normalized candidate-load bound
   \[
      \E_{F\sim\mu_q}|B_F|
      \le
      a_j(q,p)\,m^{\rho_j}L(m).
      \tag{CBK2}
   \]

   Third, the distinct canonical child nets obey the shared storage bound
   \[
      \sum_A |A|^{1+\rho_{j+1}}
      \le
      m^{1+\rho_j}L(m).
      \tag{CBK3}
   \]
   Then all hypotheses of
   \cref{prop:success-normalized-bucket-dag} hold at rung \(j\).

   If \((CBK3)\) is not proved directly, it is enough to prove the occurrence
   moment bounds
   \[
      \sum_F|N_F|\le m^{1+\rho_j}L(m),
      \qquad
      \sum_F|N_F|^2\le m^{1+\rho_j}L(m),
      \tag{CBK4}
   \]
   or any sharper tuple-profile certificate implying them.

   Thus the compressed-bucket route has only one genuinely nonstandard
   query/storage obstruction: shared canonical-net storage.  The query side
   uses the usual LSF first moment; no separate query-side Renyi list-decoding
   theorem is needed.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   A maximal separated net is a cover of its bucket, so recursive correctness is
   exactly \cref{lem:bucket-net-recursion-geometry}.  The lower bound on
   \(a_j(q,p)\) is \((CB0)\).  Since \(N_F\subseteq B_F\) and
   \(0\le\rho_{j+1}\le1\),
   \[
      |N_F|^{\rho_{j+1}}\le |N_F|\le |B_F|.
   \]
   Averaging and using \((CBK2)\) gives \((CB1)\).  The distinct-net storage
   condition \((CBK3)\) is \((CB2)\), so
   \cref{prop:success-normalized-bucket-dag} applies.  Finally, \((CBK4)\)
   implies \((CBK3)\) by
   \cref{lem:occurrence-moments-dominate-dag}, with
   \(r=\rho_{j+1}\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Positive-correlation occurrence-moment obstruction]
   \label{lem:positive-correlation-occurrence-obstruction}
   Fix \(0<\varepsilon<\min\{\beta,1-\beta\}\), \(0<r\le1\), and
   \(\rho\ge0\).  For arbitrarily large \(m\), in dimension
   \(D=O_{\beta,\varepsilon}(\log m)\) there is a set
   \(P=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\subset\mathbb S^{D-1}\) such that
   \[
      \beta-\varepsilon
      \le \ip{x_i}{x_j}\le
      \beta+\varepsilon
      \qquad(i\ne j).
      \tag{PC0}
   \]
   Put
   \[
      \delta=\sqrt{2(1-\beta-\varepsilon)},
      \qquad
      T=\sqrt{2\log m},
   \]
   and let \(\mathcal F\) consist of
   \(M=\lfloor m^{1+\rho}\rfloor\) independent Gaussian cap occurrences
   \[
      U_G=\{x:\ip{G}{x}\ge T\},
      \qquad G\sim N(0,I_D).
   \]
   Since \(P\) is already \(\delta\)-separated, the canonical net in each
   occurrence is \(N_G=P\cap U_G\).  Then
   \[
      \E\sum_{F\in\mathcal F}|N_F|^2
      \ge
      m^{1+\rho+2-\frac{2}{1+\beta-\varepsilon}}
      \log^{-O_{\beta,\varepsilon}(1)}m.
      \tag{PC1}
   \]
   Thus the first/second occurrence co-load certificate in
   \cref{lem:occurrence-moments-dominate-dag} is polynomially too strong as
   soon as \(\beta>\varepsilon\).

   Moreover, if
   \[
      \beta-\varepsilon>\frac{1-r}{1+r},
      \tag{PC2}
   \]
   then the occurrence-weighted \((1+r)\)-moment itself satisfies
   \[
      \E\sum_{F\in\mathcal F}|N_F|^{1+r}
      \ge
      m^{1+\rho+\Omega_{\beta,\varepsilon,r}(1)} .
      \tag{PC3}
   \]
   Hence an occurrence-weighted list-size theorem cannot be the final
   worst-case storage proof in positive-correlation tangent caps; the
   distinct-net quotient in \((CB2)\), or an equivalent dense-cap sharing
   mechanism, is essential.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   We first construct \(P\).  Let \(e_0\) be a fixed unit vector and choose
   \(y_1,\ldots,y_m\) independently on the unit sphere in \(e_0^\perp\).  For
   \(D\ge C_{\beta,\varepsilon}\log m\), the standard spherical cap bound and
   a union bound give, with positive probability,
   \[
      |\ip{y_i}{y_j}|\le \frac{\varepsilon}{1-\beta}
      \qquad(i\ne j).
   \]
   Set
   \[
      x_i=\sqrt{\beta}\,e_0+\sqrt{1-\beta}\,y_i .
   \]
   Then
   \[
      \ip{x_i}{x_j}
      =
      \beta+(1-\beta)\ip{y_i}{y_j},
   \]
   and \((PC0)\) follows.  The upper bound in \((PC0)\) gives
   \(\|x_i-x_j\|\ge\delta\), so the whole set \(P\cap U_G\) is a valid
   \(\delta\)-separated net in its bucket.

   It remains to lower-bound the co-load of one correlated pair.  Let
   \((X,Y)\) be a centered bivariate normal pair with correlation
   \(\theta\in[\beta-\varepsilon,\beta+\varepsilon]\).  On the rectangle
   \([T,T+1/T]^2\), its density is at least
   \[
      C_{\beta,\varepsilon}
      \exp\!\left(-\frac{(T+1/T)^2}{1+\theta}\right).
   \]
   Therefore
   \[
      \Pr[X\ge T,\ Y\ge T]
      \ge
      T^{-2}C_{\beta,\varepsilon}
      \exp\!\left(-\frac{(T+1/T)^2}{1+\theta}\right)
      \ge
      m^{-\frac{2}{1+\beta-\varepsilon}}
      \log^{-O_{\beta,\varepsilon}(1)}m .
      \tag{PC4}
   \]
   For one occurrence,
   \[
      \E |N_G|^2
      \ge
      \sum_{i\ne j}\Pr[x_i,x_j\in U_G]
      \ge
      m^{2-\frac{2}{1+\beta-\varepsilon}}
      \log^{-O_{\beta,\varepsilon}(1)}m .
   \]
   Multiplying by \(M\) proves \((PC1)\).

   Since \(|N_G|\le m\),
   \[
      |N_G|^{1+r}\ge m^{-(1-r)}|N_G|^2 .
   \]
   Combining this with the previous lower bound gives
   \[
      \E\sum_{F\in\mathcal F}|N_F|^{1+r}
      \ge
      m^{1+\rho+1+r-\frac{2}{1+\beta-\varepsilon}}
      \log^{-O_{\beta,\varepsilon}(1)}m .
   \]
   The exponent exceeds \(1+\rho\) exactly under \((PC2)\), proving
   \((PC3)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Packing-list moments by separated tuples]
   \label{lem:packing-list-tuple-moment}
   Let \(P\subset\mathbb S^{D-1}\), let \(\delta>0\), and let
   \(\{U_z:z\in\mathcal Z\}\) be any family of update regions.  For a label
   \(z\), define the bucket packing number
   \[
      L_\delta(z)=
      \max\{|Y|:\ Y\subseteq P\cap U_z,\ \|x-y\|\ge\delta
      \text{ for all distinct }x,y\in Y\}.
   \]
   For an integer \(k\ge1\), let \(\mathcal T_k(P,\delta)\) be the set of
   ordered \(k\)-tuples \((x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in P^k\) whose distinct entries are
   pairwise \(\delta\)-separated.  Then every probability law \(\nu\) on
   labels satisfies
   \[
      \E_{Z\sim\nu} L_\delta(Z)^k
      \le
      \sum_{(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in\mathcal T_k(P,\delta)}
      \Pr_{Z\sim\nu}[x_i\in U_Z\text{ for every }i].
      \tag{TM1}
   \]
   Consequently, for \(0\le r\le1\),
   \[
      \E L_\delta(Z)^r
      \le
      \left(
      \sum_{x\in P}\Pr[x\in U_Z]
      \right)^r,
      \tag{TM2}
   \]
   while for \(1\le r\le2\),
   \[
      \E L_\delta(Z)^r
      \le
      A_1^{\,2-r}A_2^{\,r-1},
      \tag{TM3}
   \]
   where
   \[
      A_1=\sum_{x\in P}\Pr[x\in U_Z],
      \qquad
      A_2=
      \sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal T_2(P,\delta)}
      \Pr[x,y\in U_Z].
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   For each label \(z\), choose one maximum \(\delta\)-separated subset
   \(Y_z\subseteq P\cap U_z\).  Every ordered \(k\)-tuple from \(Y_z\), with
   repetitions allowed, belongs to \(\mathcal T_k(P,\delta)\) and all its
   entries lie in \(U_z\).  Hence
   pointwise
   \[
      L_\delta(z)^k
      \le
      \sum_{(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in\mathcal T_k(P,\delta)}
      \mathbf 1\{x_i\in U_z\text{ for every }i\}.
   \]
   Integrating over \(z\) gives \((TM1)\).

   The case \(0\le r\le1\) follows from Jensen's inequality applied to the
   concave function \(u^r\), together with \((TM1)\) for \(k=1\).  For
   \(1\le r\le2\), log-convexity of \(L_p\)-moments gives
   \[
      \E L_\delta^r
      \le
      (\E L_\delta)^{2-r}(\E L_\delta^2)^{r-1}.
   \]
   Applying \((TM1)\) with \(k=1\) and \(k=2\) gives \((TM3)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Gaussian cap-intersection energy]
   \label{lem:gaussian-cap-intersection-energy}
   Let \(G\sim N(\mu,I_D)\), let \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\mathbb S^{D-1}\), and
   write \(K=(\ip{x_i}{x_j})_{i,j\le k}\).  For the Gaussian cap
   \(U_G=\{x:\ip{G}{x}\ge T\}\), put
   \[
      b_i=T-\ip{\mu}{x_i},
      \qquad
      \mathcal I(K,b)=
      \sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^k}
      \left\{
         \sum_i\lambda_i b_i
         -
         \frac12\lambda^\top K\lambda
      \right\}.
      \tag{GE1}
   \]
   Then
   \[
      \Pr[x_i\in U_G\text{ for every }i]
      \le
      e^{-\mathcal I(K,b)}.
      \tag{GE2}
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   For every \(\lambda\ge0\),
   \[
      \Pr[\ip{G}{x_i}\ge T\ \forall i]
      \le
      \exp\!\left(
         -\sum_i\lambda_i b_i
      \right)
      \E\exp\!\left(\sum_i\lambda_i\ip{G-\mu}{x_i}\right).
   \]
   The centered Gaussian moment-generating function is
   \[
      \E\exp\!\left(\sum_i\lambda_i\ip{G-\mu}{x_i}\right)
      =
      \exp\!\left(\frac12\lambda^\top K\lambda\right).
   \]
   Taking the infimum over \(\lambda\ge0\), equivalently the exponential of
   minus the supremum in \((GE1)\), proves \((GE2)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Two-point Gaussian cap energy]
   \label{lem:two-point-gaussian-cap-energy}
   In the setting of \cref{lem:gaussian-cap-intersection-energy}, take
   \(k=2\), write \(x=x_1\), \(y=x_2\), and
   \[
      \theta=\ip{x}{y}>-1,
      \qquad
      b_x=T-\ip{\mu}{x},
      \qquad
      b_y=T-\ip{\mu}{y}.
   \]
   Then
   \[
      \mathcal I(K,b)
      \ge
      \frac{(b_x+b_y)_+^2}{4(1+\theta)}.
      \tag{TGE1}
   \]
   In particular, if \(b_x,b_y\ge\beta\ge0\) and
   \(\theta\le\theta_0\) for some \(-1<\theta_0<1\), then
   \[
      \Pr[x,y\in U_G]
      \le
      \exp\left(-\frac{\beta^2}{1+\theta_0}\right).
      \tag{TGE2}
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   In the variational formula \((GE1)\), restrict to
   \(\lambda_1=\lambda_2=\lambda\ge0\).  Since
   \[
      (1,1)K(1,1)^\top=2(1+\theta),
   \]
   the objective is bounded below by
   \[
      \lambda(b_x+b_y)-\lambda^2(1+\theta).
   \]
   Maximizing this one-dimensional concave quadratic over \(\lambda\ge0\) gives
   \((TGE1)\).  If \(b_x,b_y\ge\beta\), then
   \((b_x+b_y)_+^2\ge4\beta^2\); if also \(\theta\le\theta_0\), then
   \(1+\theta\le1+\theta_0\).  Combining this with
   \cref{lem:gaussian-cap-intersection-energy} gives \((TGE2)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Gaussian tail ratio]
   \label{lem:gaussian-tail-ratio}
   Let
   \[
      \overline\Phi(t)=\Pr[Z\ge t],
      \qquad Z\sim N(0,1).
   \]
   There is a universal constant \(C\) such that, for all
   \(0\le u\le v\),
   \[
      \frac{\overline\Phi(u)}{\overline\Phi(v)}
      \le
      C(1+v)\exp\!\left(\frac{v^2-u^2}{2}\right).
      \tag{GTR1}
   \]
   Consequently, for \(0<\theta\le1\) and \(M\ge0\),
   \[
      \frac{\overline\Phi(M)}{\overline\Phi(M/\sqrt\theta)}
      \le
      C_\theta(1+M)
      \exp\!\left(\frac{(1/\theta-1)M^2}{2}\right).
      \tag{GTR2}
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The Chernoff bound gives
   \(\overline\Phi(u)\le\exp(-u^2/2)\) for \(u\ge0\).  For the lower bound,
   integrate the Gaussian density on the interval
   \([v,v+(1+v)^{-1}]\):
   \[
      \overline\Phi(v)
      \ge
      \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}(1+v)}
      \exp\!\left(-\frac12\left(v+\frac1{1+v}\right)^2\right)
      \ge
      \frac{c}{1+v}e^{-v^2/2}
   \]
   with a universal constant \(c>0\).  Dividing the two estimates proves
   \((GTR1)\).  Taking \(u=M\) and \(v=M/\sqrt\theta\) proves \((GTR2)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Positive-correlation Gaussian cap lower bound]
   \label{lem:positive-correlation-gaussian-cap-lower}
   Let \(G\sim N(\mu,I_D)\), let \(x,y\in\mathbb S^{D-1}\), and put
   \[
      U_G=\{u:\ip{G}{u}\ge T\},
      \qquad
      m_x=T-\ip{\mu}{x},
      \qquad
      m_y=T-\ip{\mu}{y}.
   \]
   Let
   \[
      \overline\Phi(t)=\Pr[Z\ge t],
      \qquad Z\sim N(0,1).
   \]
   If \(0<\theta_-\le\ip{x}{y}\le1\) and \(m_x,m_y\le M\) for some
   \(M\ge0\), then
   \[
      \Pr[x,y\in U_G]
      \ge
      \frac14\,
      \overline\Phi\!\left(\frac{M}{\sqrt{\theta_-}}\right).
      \tag{PGL1}
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Write \(\theta=\ip{x}{y}\).  If \(\theta<1\), the centered pair
   \[
      X=\ip{G-\mu}{x},
      \qquad
      Y=\ip{G-\mu}{y}
   \]
   has the representation
   \[
      X=\sqrt\theta Z_0+\sqrt{1-\theta}Z_1,
      \qquad
      Y=\sqrt\theta Z_0+\sqrt{1-\theta}Z_2,
   \]
   with \(Z_0,Z_1,Z_2\) independent standard Gaussians.  On the event
   \[
      Z_0\ge\frac{M}{\sqrt\theta},
      \qquad
      Z_1\ge0,
      \qquad
      Z_2\ge0,
   \]
   both \(X\) and \(Y\) are at least \(M\), hence at least \(m_x\) and \(m_y\).
   This event has probability
   \[
      \frac14\,\overline\Phi\!\left(\frac{M}{\sqrt\theta}\right)
      \ge
      \frac14\,\overline\Phi\!\left(\frac{M}{\sqrt{\theta_-}}\right).
   \]
   If \(\theta=1\), then \(X=Y\), so
   \[
      \Pr[X\ge m_x,\ Y\ge m_y]\ge\overline\Phi(M),
   \]
   which is even larger than the right-hand side of \((PGL1)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Finite tuple-profile Renyi certificate]
   \label{cor:tuple-profile-renyi-certificate}
   In the setting of \cref{lem:packing-list-tuple-moment}, suppose the labels
   are Gaussian caps \(U_G=\{x:\ip{G}{x}\ge T\}\) with
   \(G\sim N(\mu,I_D)\).  For \(k=1,2\), partition
   \(\mathcal T_k(P,\delta)\) into finitely many profile classes \(\Pi_k\).
   If each profile \(\pi\in\Pi_k\) has size \(M_\pi\), and every tuple in that
   profile has Gaussian energy at least \(I_\pi\) in the sense of
   \cref{lem:gaussian-cap-intersection-energy}, then
   \[
      \E L_\delta(G)^k
      \le
      \sum_{\pi\in\Pi_k}M_\pi e^{-I_\pi}.
      \tag{TP1}
   \]
   Hence, for \(1\le r\le2\),
   \[
      \E L_\delta(G)^r
      \le
      \left(\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_1}M_\pi e^{-I_\pi}\right)^{2-r}
      \left(\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_2}M_\pi e^{-I_\pi}\right)^{r-1}.
      \tag{TP2}
   \]
   For \(0\le r\le1\), the first parenthesis alone gives
   \[
      \E L_\delta(G)^r
      \le
      \left(\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_1}M_\pi e^{-I_\pi}\right)^r.
      \tag{TP3}
   \]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Apply \cref{lem:gaussian-cap-intersection-energy} to every tuple in
   \((TM1)\), then sum by profile class.  This gives \((TP1)\).  The
   fractional bounds are exactly \((TM2)\) and \((TM3)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Two-point tuple-profile Gaussian certificate]
   \label{cor:two-point-tuple-profile-gaussian}
   In the pair case \(k=2\) of
   \cref{cor:tuple-profile-renyi-certificate}, suppose each pair profile
   \(\pi\in\Pi_2\) has size \(M_\pi\), and there are parameters
   \(-1<\theta_\pi<1\), \(\beta_\pi\ge0\) such that every
   \((x,y)\in\pi\) satisfies
   \[
      \ip{x}{y}\le\theta_\pi,
      \qquad
      T-\ip{\mu}{x}\ge\beta_\pi,
      \qquad
      T-\ip{\mu}{y}\ge\beta_\pi .
      \tag{TPG1}
   \]
   Then
   \[
      \E L_\delta(G)^2
      \le
      \sum_{\pi\in\Pi_2}
      M_\pi
      \exp\left(-\frac{\beta_\pi^2}{1+\theta_\pi}\right).
      \tag{TPG2}
   \]
   More generally, it is enough to replace the two lower bounds in \((TPG1)\)
   by
   \[
      T-\ip{\mu}{x}+T-\ip{\mu}{y}\ge s_\pi\ge0,
      \tag{TPG3}
   \]
   in which case the exponential factor in \((TPG2)\) becomes
   \[
      \exp\left(-\frac{s_\pi^2}{4(1+\theta_\pi)}\right).
      \tag{TPG4}
   \]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   By \cref{lem:two-point-gaussian-cap-energy}, every pair in profile \(\pi\)
   has Gaussian cap-intersection energy at least
   \(\beta_\pi^2/(1+\theta_\pi)\), or \(s_\pi^2/(4(1+\theta_\pi))\) under
   \((TPG3)\).  Substitute these profile energies into \((TP1)\) for \(k=2\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Tuple-profile storage certificate for compressed buckets]
   \label{cor:tuple-profile-compressed-bucket-storage}
   Let \(P\subset\mathbb S^{D-1}\), let \(\delta>0\), and let
   \(0\le s\le1\).  Let \(G_1,\ldots,G_M\), \(M\ge1\), be independent copies of
   a Gaussian cap label \(G\sim N(\mu,I_D)\), with
   \[
      U_G=\{x:\ip{G}{x}\ge T\}.
   \]
   For each occurrence choose any \(\delta\)-separated net
   \(N_i\subseteq P\cap U_{G_i}\), and let \(\mathcal A\) be the set of distinct
   canonical nets represented among the \(N_i\)'s.  Suppose that, for a target
   storage budget \(B>0\),
   \[
      M\sum_{x\in P}\Pr[x\in U_G]\le B,
      \tag{TPS1}
   \]
   Let
   \[
      \mathcal T_2^\ne(P,\delta)
      =
      \{(x,y)\in P^2:x\ne y,\ \|x-y\|\ge\delta\}.
   \]
   Suppose the distinct separated pair tuples are partitioned into finitely many
   profiles \(\Pi_2^\ne\) with \(M_\pi=|\pi|\) and certified cap-intersection
   energies \(I_\pi\) satisfying
   \[
      M\left(
         \sum_{x\in P}\Pr[x\in U_G]
         +
         \sum_{\pi\in\Pi_2^\ne}M_\pi e^{-I_\pi}
      \right)\le B .
      \tag{TPS2}
   \]
   Then
   \[
      \E\sum_{i=1}^M |N_i|^{1+s}\le B,
      \qquad
      \E\sum_{A\in\mathcal A}|A|^{1+s}\le B .
      \tag{TPS3}
   \]

   In particular, for one rung of the compressed-bucket recursion, \((TPS1)\)
   and \((TPS2)\) with \(s=\rho_{j+1}\) certify the occurrence-weighted storage
   moment and therefore the shared-DAG storage hypothesis \((CB2)\) in
   expectation.  The pair energies \(I_\pi\) may be supplied by the explicit
   correlation-margin bound of
   \cref{cor:two-point-tuple-profile-gaussian}; the diagonal part of the second
   moment is exactly the first moment already present in \((TPS1)\)--\((TPS2)\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Let \(L_\delta(G)\) be the maximum \(\delta\)-separated list size from
   \cref{lem:packing-list-tuple-moment}.  Since each \(N_i\) is
   \(\delta\)-separated inside \(P\cap U_{G_i}\),
   \[
      |N_i|\le L_\delta(G_i).
   \]
   Put
   \[
      A_1=\sum_{x\in P}\Pr[x\in U_G],
      \qquad
      A_2=\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal T_2(P,\delta)}
      \Pr[x,y\in U_G].
   \]
   Split \(A_2\) into the diagonal contribution \(A_1\) and the distinct-pair
   contribution.  By \cref{cor:tuple-profile-renyi-certificate}, or directly by
   \cref{lem:gaussian-cap-intersection-energy} summed over the distinct-pair
   profiles,
   \[
      A_2
      \le
      A_1+\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_2^\ne}M_\pi e^{-I_\pi}.
   \]
   Thus \((TPS1)\)--\((TPS2)\) give \(A_1\le B/M\) and \(A_2\le B/M\).
   Applying \((TM3)\) with exponent \(1+s\) gives
   \[
      \E L_\delta(G)^{1+s}\le A_1^{1-s}A_2^s\le B/M .
   \]
   Summing over the \(M\) independent occurrences proves the first inequality in
   \((TPS3)\).

   The second inequality is pointwise weaker than the first by
   \cref{lem:occurrence-moments-dominate-dag}: selecting one representative
   occurrence for each distinct canonical net gives
   \[
      \sum_{A\in\mathcal A}|A|^{1+s}
      \le
      \sum_{i=1}^M |N_i|^{1+s}.
   \]
   Taking expectations completes the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Polylogarithmic low-correlation co-load cutoff]
   \label{cor:polylog-low-correlation-coload}
   Let \(m\ge3\), \(P\subset\mathbb S^{D-1}\) with \(|P|\le m\), and let
   \(G_1,\ldots,G_M\) be independent centered Gaussian cap labels
   \(G_i\sim N(0,I_D)\) with
   \[
      U_G=\{x:\ip{G}{x}\ge T\}.
   \]
   Fix constants \(A,K\ge0\), \(0\le\rho\le1\), and assume
   \[
      M\le m^{1+\rho}\log^A m,
      \qquad
      T^2\ge 2\log m-A\log\log m.
      \tag{PLC1}
   \]
   Put
   \[
      \theta_m=K\,\frac{\log\log m}{\log m},
      \tag{PLC2}
   \]
   and assume \(\theta_m<1\).  Let
   \(E_{\rm lo}\subseteq P\times P\) be any set of ordered pairs with
   \(|E_{\rm lo}|\le m^2\) and \(\ip{x}{y}\le\theta_m\) for every
   \((x,y)\in E_{\rm lo}\).  Then
   \[
      M\sum_{x\in P}\Pr[x\in U_G]
      \le
      m^{1+\rho}\log^{3A/2}m
      \tag{PLC3}
   \]
   and
   \[
      M\sum_{(x,y)\in E_{\rm lo}}
      \Pr[x,y\in U_G]
      \le
      m^{1+\rho}\log^{2A+2K+1}m .
      \tag{PLC4}
   \]
   Consequently, if all distinct separated pair profiles charged to the
   Gaussian storage term are contained in \(E_{\rm lo}\), then the hypotheses
   \((TPS1)\)--\((TPS2)\) of
   \cref{cor:tuple-profile-compressed-bucket-storage} with
   \(B=m^{1+\rho}\log^{O_{A,K}(1)}m\) hold.  Thus centered spherical cap
   buckets have only polylogarithmic shared-storage co-load from all pairs of
   correlation at most \(O(\log\log m/\log m)\); any polynomial storage
   obstruction must lie in the complementary tiny positive-correlation branch
   and be routed to the dense/star or quotient separator.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   The one-point Chernoff bound gives
   \[
      \Pr[x\in U_G]\le e^{-T^2/2}
      \le m^{-1}\log^{A/2}m .
   \]
   Since \(|P|\le m\) and \(M\le m^{1+\rho}\log^A m\), this proves
   \((PLC3)\).

   For \((x,y)\in E_{\rm lo}\), \cref{lem:two-point-gaussian-cap-energy} with
   \(\mu=0\), \(\beta=T\), and \(\theta_0=\theta_m\) gives
   \[
      \Pr[x,y\in U_G]
      \le
      \exp\!\left(-\frac{T^2}{1+\theta_m}\right).
   \]
   Writing \(L=\log m\) and \(\ell=\log\log m\), and using
   \(\theta_m=K\ell/L\), we have
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      2L-\frac{T^2}{1+\theta_m}
      &\le
      2L-\frac{2L-A\ell}{1+\theta_m}  \\
      &=
      \frac{2L\theta_m+A\ell}{1+\theta_m}
      \le (2K+A)\ell ,
   \end{aligned}
   \]
   where the last inequality uses \(1+\theta_m\ge1\).  Hence
   \[
      |E_{\rm lo}|
      \exp\!\left(-\frac{T^2}{1+\theta_m}\right)
      \le
      \log^{A+2K}m .
   \]
   Multiplying by \(M\le m^{1+\rho}\log^A m\) proves \((PLC4)\), with the
   harmless extra logarithmic power absorbing small values of \(m\) and the
   integer rounding of constants.

   Taking one pair profile equal to \(E_{\rm lo}\), with energy
   \(T^2/(1+\theta_m)\), and refining it arbitrarily into subprofiles only
   decreases the displayed upper bound after summation.  Thus, whenever the
   Gaussian-charged profiles are all contained in \(E_{\rm lo}\),
   \((PLC3)\)--\((PLC4)\) supply \((TPS1)\)--\((TPS2)\) with
   \(B=m^{1+\rho}\log^{O_{A,K}(1)}m\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Low/high storage screen for compressed cap buckets]
   \label{cor:low-high-compressed-cap-storage}
   Work in the setting of
   \cref{cor:polylog-low-correlation-coload}.  Let
   \(0\le s\le1\), and for every retained cap occurrence \(i\le M\), let
   \(N_i\subseteq P\cap U_{G_i}\) be any \(\delta\)-separated bucket net.  Let
   \(\mathcal A\) be the set of distinct canonical nets represented among the
   \(N_i\)'s.  Define the realized high-correlation ordered pair tail
   \[
      H_{\rm hi}
      =
      \sum_{i=1}^M
      \left|
      \{(x,y)\in N_i^2:\ x\ne y,\ \ip{x}{y}>\theta_m\}
      \right|.
      \tag{LHS1}
   \]
   Then
   \[
      \E\sum_{A\in\mathcal A}|A|^{1+s}
      \le
      m^{1+\rho}\log^{O_{A,K}(1)}m
      +
      \E H_{\rm hi}.
      \tag{LHS2}
   \]
   In particular, if the high-correlation tail is itself paid by dense/star,
   sponsor, or shared-prefix certificates so that
   \[
      \E H_{\rm hi}\le m^{1+\rho}\log^{O_{A,K}(1)}m,
      \tag{LHS3}
   \]
   then the expected form of the shared-DAG storage hypothesis \((CBK3)\) of
   \cref{cor:compressed-bucket-rung-checklist} holds, with the cap-panel
   exponent \(\rho=\rho_j\) and \(s=\rho_{j+1}\).  If preprocessing verifies
   the realized value of the left side of \((CBK3)\), Markov's inequality gives
   a Las Vegas build-time realization satisfying the deterministic bound after
   only constant expected resampling, with the usual constant-factor slack.

   Thus centered cap buckets at the large-range threshold have an exact
   storage split: the diagonal and all pairs of correlation
   \(O(\log\log m/\log m)\) are already polylogarithmic, and any polynomial
   storage survivor must be visible as the high-correlation pair tail
   \(H_{\rm hi}\).  The dense separator only has to repair or sponsor this
   tail; it does not have to reprove the diffuse cap co-load estimate.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   For an integer \(K\ge0\) and \(0\le s\le1\),
   \(K^{1+s}\le K^2\).  Hence, for each occurrence,
   \[
      |N_i|^{1+s}
      \le
      |N_i|^2
      =
      |N_i|
      +
      \left|\{(x,y)\in N_i^2:\ x\ne y\}\right|.
      \tag{LHS4}
   \]
   Split the ordered distinct pairs in \((LHS4)\) into
   \(\ip{x}{y}\le\theta_m\) and \(\ip{x}{y}>\theta_m\).  Since
   \(N_i\subseteq P\cap U_{G_i}\), the first moment and the low-correlation
   pair count are bounded pointwise by the corresponding cap-incidence sums.
   Taking expectations and applying \((PLC3)\)--\((PLC4)\) gives
   \[
      \E\sum_i |N_i|^{1+s}
      \le
      m^{1+\rho}\log^{O_{A,K}(1)}m+\E H_{\rm hi}.
      \tag{LHS5}
   \]
   Finally, selecting one occurrence representative for each distinct canonical
   net gives
   \[
      \sum_{A\in\mathcal A}|A|^{1+s}
      \le
      \sum_i|N_i|^{1+s}
   \]
   pointwise, as in
   \cref{lem:occurrence-moments-dominate-dag}.  Combining this with
   \((LHS5)\) proves \((LHS2)\), and \((LHS3)\) gives the expected storage
   bound.  If the realized storage exceeds a fixed constant times this
   expectation, preprocessing discards the sampled panel and resamples; Markov's
   inequality gives constant acceptance probability, and accepted panels satisfy
   the deterministic \((CBK3)\) bound after absorbing that constant.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Diffuse compressed-cap rung certificate]
   \label{cor:diffuse-compressed-cap-rung}
   Work in one rung \(j\) of
   \cref{cor:compressed-bucket-rung-checklist}, and let \(m=|P|\).  Suppose
   the retained bucket occurrences are centered Gaussian caps satisfying
   \((PLC1)\) in \cref{cor:polylog-low-correlation-coload} with
   \(\rho=\rho_j\), and let \(N_i\subseteq P\cap U_{G_i}\) be the maximal
   \((\alpha_j-1)r_j\)-separated bucket nets.  Put \(s=\rho_{j+1}\).

   Assume the filter metadata and occurrence pointers have size
   \(m^{1+\rho_j}\log^{O_c(1)}m\), and assume the query sampling law satisfies
   the success-normalized hit and active-load conditions \((CBK1)\)--\((CBK2)\)
   with \(L(m)=\log^{O_c(1)}m\).  If the cap-panel law is diffuse at the
   low-correlation cutoff, in the sense that every retained realization obeys
   \[
      \ip{x}{y}\le\theta_m
      \qquad
      (i\le M,\ x,y\in N_i,\ x\ne y),
      \tag{DCR1}
   \]
   then, after the usual verified Las Vegas resampling of the cap panel, all
   hypotheses of \cref{prop:success-normalized-bucket-dag} hold at this rung
   with polylogarithmic loss.

   More generally, \((DCR1)\) may be replaced on an accepted realization by the
   certified high-tail bound
   \[
      H_{\rm hi}
      \le
      m^{1+\rho_j}\log^{O_c(1)}m
      \tag{DCR2}
   \]
   or by the corresponding expectation followed by verified resampling of both
   the high tail and the left side of \((CBK3)\).

   In particular, the diffuse case is already a complete polylogarithmic
   compressed-bucket rung.  If the resident data themselves satisfy
   \[
      \max_{x\ne y\in P}\ip{x}{y}
      \le K\frac{\log\log m}{\log m},
      \tag{DCR3}
   \]
