   \(\theta\) uniformly from \([0,1]\).  If \(c_i=a_i\), the coordinate
   contributes one erasure exactly when \(\theta>\gamma_i\), so its expected
   contribution to \(2e+s\) is \(1-\gamma_i\).  If \(c_i\ne a_i\), the
   coordinate contributes two when kept and one when erased, so its expected
   contribution is \(1+\gamma_i\).  Therefore
   \[
      \E_\theta[2e(c,y^\theta)+s(y^\theta)]
      =
      h
      -
      \sum_{i:c_i=a_i}\gamma_i
      +
      \sum_{i:c_i\ne a_i}\gamma_i
      <\Delta .
   \]
   Some threshold \(\theta\in[0,1]\) has
   \(2e(c,y^\theta)+s(y^\theta)<\Delta\).  The erasure pattern changes only
   when \(\theta\) crosses one of the values \(\gamma_i\), so the finite sweep
   contains a threshold with the same pattern.  The decoder returns \(c\) on
   that pattern.  There are at most \(h+2\) thresholds and hence at most that
   many decoder calls and distinct decoded words.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Soft-score margin compiler for GMD]
   \label{lem:soft-score-gmd-margin}
   Let \(\mathcal C\subseteq\Sigma^h\) have Hamming distance \(\Delta\), and
   let a query assign coordinate scores \(\omega_i(a)\).  Choose a hard symbol
   \(a_i\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in\Sigma}\omega_i(a)\), numbers
   \(\gamma_i\in[0,1]\), and a scale \(\kappa>0\) such that
   \[
      \omega_i(a_i)-\omega_i(a)\ge\kappa\gamma_i
      \qquad(a\ne a_i).
      \tag{GMS1}
   \]
   Put
   \[
      M(q)=\sum_{i=1}^h\omega_i(a_i),
      \qquad
      \Gamma(q)=\sum_{i=1}^h\gamma_i,
   \]
   and \(S_q(c)=\sum_i\omega_i(c_i)\).  Then the
   reliability-erasure sweep of
   \cref{lem:reliability-erasure-sweep} includes every codeword satisfying
   \[
      S_q(c)>
      M(q)-\frac{\kappa}{2}\bigl(\Gamma(q)-h+\Delta\bigr).
      \tag{GMS2}
   \]
   Consequently, for any soft threshold \(\Theta\) with
   \[
      \Theta\ge
      M(q)-\frac{\kappa}{2}\bigl(\Gamma(q)-h+\Delta\bigr),
      \tag{GMS3}
   \]
   the GMD sweep followed by exact filtering \(S_q(c)\ge\Theta\) is a
   certified threshold reporter for all codewords of score at least
   \(\Theta\), using at most \(h+2\) errors-and-erasures decoder calls.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   For a codeword \(c\), let \(I(c)=\{i:c_i\ne a_i\}\).  By \((GMS1)\),
   \[
      M(q)-S_q(c)
      =
      \sum_{i\in I(c)}
      \bigl(\omega_i(a_i)-\omega_i(c_i)\bigr)
      \ge
      \kappa\sum_{i\in I(c)}\gamma_i .
   \]
   If \((GMS2)\) holds, then
   \[
      \sum_{i\in I(c)}\gamma_i
      <
      \frac{\Gamma(q)-h+\Delta}{2}.
   \]
   Since
   \[
      \sum_{i:c_i=a_i}\gamma_i-\sum_{i:c_i\ne a_i}\gamma_i
      =
      \Gamma(q)-2\sum_{i\in I(c)}\gamma_i,
   \]
   condition \((GMD)\) follows.  The inclusion is therefore
   \cref{lem:reliability-erasure-sweep}.  If \((GMS3)\) holds, every codeword
   with \(S_q(c)\ge\Theta\) satisfies \((GMS2)\), and the final exact filter
   removes any lower-score decoder outputs.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[GMD block certificate]
   \label{cor:gmd-block-certificate}
   Let \(\mathcal C\subseteq\Sigma^h\) have Hamming distance \(\Delta\) and a
   certified errors-and-erasures decoder.  For a query \(q\), let
   \(S_q(c)=\sum_i\omega_i(q,c_i)\), choose hard symbols \(a_i(q)\),
   confidences \(\gamma_i(q)\in[0,1]\), and a scale \(\kappa(q)>0\) satisfying
   \((GMS1)\), and define \(M(q)\) and \(\Gamma(q)\) as in
   \cref{lem:soft-score-gmd-margin}.  If a requested threshold \(\Theta(q)\)
   satisfies
   \[
      \Theta(q)\ge
      M(q)-\frac{\kappa(q)}2\bigl(\Gamma(q)-h+\Delta\bigr),
   \]
   then the GMD erasure sweep followed by exact filtering \(S_q(c)\ge\Theta(q)\)
   returns exactly
   \[
      \{c\in\mathcal C:S_q(c)\ge\Theta(q)\}
   \]
   using at most \(h+2\) errors-and-erasures decoder calls and at most \(h+2\)
   reported codewords.  Equivalently, the query-side sweep has only \(O(h)\)
   erasure-threshold transcripts before the compact outer decoder output; in
   the output-sensitive decoder-DAG certificate, scan work is charged only to
   the distinct decoded codewords actually reported.

   Therefore, in the finite-signature or decoder-DAG rate-coverage
   certificates, a retained block only has to certify the top-gap inequality
   above on each query signature; no repeated-coordinate list-recovery oracle
   is needed in such high-margin signatures.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   The inclusion of every codeword with \(S_q(c)\ge\Theta(q)\) is exactly
   \cref{lem:soft-score-gmd-margin}.  The final exact filter guarantees that
   no lower-score codeword is output.  The decoder-call and output bounds are
   those of \cref{lem:reliability-erasure-sweep}.  The transcript statement is
   the same sweep viewed as a compact decoder: one branch for each distinct
   erasure threshold, followed by the certified errors-and-erasures decoder
   call and duplicate removal.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Chase--GMD reporter]
   \label{lem:chase-gmd-reporter}
   Let \(\mathcal C\subseteq\Sigma^h\) have Hamming distance \(\Delta\) and a
   certified errors-and-erasures decoder as in
   \cref{lem:reliability-erasure-sweep}.  Fix hard symbols \(a_i\in\Sigma\)
   and confidences \(\gamma_i\in[0,1]\).  Let \(T\subseteq[h]\) be a branch
   set, and for each \(i\in T\) let \(L_i\subseteq\Sigma\) be a candidate
   symbol list.  For every branch
   \(b=(b_i)_{i\in T}\in\prod_{i\in T}L_i\), set
   \[
      a^b_i=
      \begin{cases}
         b_i, & i\in T,\\
         a_i, & i\notin T,
      \end{cases}
      \qquad
      \gamma^b_i=
      \begin{cases}
         1, & i\in T,\\
         \gamma_i, & i\notin T.
      \end{cases}
   \]
   Run the reliability-erasure sweep of
   \cref{lem:reliability-erasure-sweep} for every pair
   \((a^b,\gamma^b)\), and output the distinct decoded codewords.

   This reporter makes at most
   \[
      (h+2)\prod_{i\in T}|L_i|
   \]
   errors-and-erasures decoder calls and outputs at most that many distinct
   codewords.  It includes every \(c\in\mathcal C\) such that
   \(c_i\in L_i\) for all \(i\in T\) and
   \[
      |T|
      +
      \sum_{\substack{i\notin T\\ c_i=a_i}}\gamma_i
      -
      \sum_{\substack{i\notin T\\ c_i\ne a_i}}\gamma_i
      >
      h-\Delta .
      \tag{CH1}
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   For a codeword \(c\) satisfying the displayed hypotheses, choose the branch
   \(b_i=c_i\) on \(T\).  With respect to \((a^b,\gamma^b)\), every coordinate
   in \(T\) is a correct hard decision with confidence \(1\).  Thus the GMD
   weighted agreement margin for this branch is exactly the left-hand side of
   \((CH1)\), so \cref{lem:reliability-erasure-sweep} outputs \(c\).  The
   number of calls is the number of branches times the \(h+2\) erasure
   thresholds per branch, and each call returns at most one codeword.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Chase--GMD soft-score block certificate]
   \label{cor:chase-gmd-block-certificate}
   Work in the setting of \cref{lem:chase-gmd-reporter}, and let a query assign
   coordinate scores \(\omega_i(a)\).  For \(i\notin T\), choose
   \(a_i\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in\Sigma}\omega_i(a)\),
   \(\gamma_i\in[0,1]\), and a scale \(\kappa>0\) such that
   \[
      \omega_i(a_i)-\omega_i(a)\ge\kappa\gamma_i
      \qquad(i\notin T,\ a\ne a_i).
      \tag{CH2}
   \]
   For a branch \(b\in\prod_{i\in T}L_i\), put
   \[
      M_b(q)=
      \sum_{i\in T}\omega_i(b_i)
      +
      \sum_{i\notin T}\omega_i(a_i),
      \qquad
      \Gamma_T(q)=\sum_{i\notin T}\gamma_i,
   \]
   and \(S_q(c)=\sum_i\omega_i(c_i)\).  Then the Chase--GMD reporter includes
   every codeword \(c\) with \(c_i\in L_i\) for \(i\in T\) and
   \[
      S_q(c)>
      M_{c_T}(q)
      -
      \frac{\kappa}{2}\bigl(\Gamma_T(q)+|T|-h+\Delta\bigr).
      \tag{CH3}
   \]
   Consequently, if a requested threshold \(\Theta(q)\) satisfies
   \[
      \Theta(q)\ge
      \max_{b\in\prod_{i\in T}L_i}M_b(q)
      -
      \frac{\kappa}{2}\bigl(\Gamma_T(q)+|T|-h+\Delta\bigr),
      \tag{CH4}
   \]
   then the Chase--GMD reporter followed by exact filtering
   \(S_q(c)\ge\Theta(q)\) returns every codeword of score at least
   \(\Theta(q)\) whose symbols on \(T\) lie in the candidate lists.  If
   \(L_i=\Sigma\) for all \(i\in T\), it is a certified threshold reporter for
   the whole code.  Its query-side transcript count is
   \[
      O\!\left(h\prod_{i\in T}|L_i|\right).
   \]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Fix \(c\) with \(c_i\in L_i\) on \(T\), and let
   \(I(c)=\{i\notin T:c_i\ne a_i\}\).  By \((CH2)\),
   \[
      M_{c_T}(q)-S_q(c)
      =
      \sum_{i\in I(c)}
      \bigl(\omega_i(a_i)-\omega_i(c_i)\bigr)
      \ge
      \kappa\sum_{i\in I(c)}\gamma_i .
   \]
   If \((CH3)\) holds, then
   \[
      \sum_{i\in I(c)}\gamma_i
      <
      \frac{\Gamma_T(q)+|T|-h+\Delta}{2}.
   \]
   Hence
   \[
      |T|
      +
      \sum_{\substack{i\notin T\\ c_i=a_i}}\gamma_i
      -
      \sum_{\substack{i\notin T\\ c_i\ne a_i}}\gamma_i
      =
      |T|+\Gamma_T(q)-2\sum_{i\in I(c)}\gamma_i
      >
      h-\Delta .
   \]
   \Cref{lem:chase-gmd-reporter} therefore includes \(c\).  If \((CH4)\)
   holds, then every codeword with \(S_q(c)\ge\Theta(q)\) and \(c_T\in\prod_iL_i\)
   satisfies \((CH3)\), and exact filtering removes lower-score outputs.  The
   transcript count is the call bound in \cref{lem:chase-gmd-reporter}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Top-list Chase completeness]
   \label{cor:top-list-chase-completeness}
   Work in the setting of
   \cref{cor:chase-gmd-block-certificate}.  Assume that every list
   \(L_i\), \(i\in T\), contains a maximizer of \(\omega_i\), and define
   \[
      M_*(q)=
      \sum_{i\in T}\max_{a\in\Sigma}\omega_i(a)
      +
      \sum_{i\notin T}\omega_i(a_i).
   \]
   Let
   \[
      \delta_{\rm list}(q)
      =
      \min_{i\in T}
      \left(
         \max_{a\in\Sigma}\omega_i(a)
         -
         \max_{a\notin L_i}\omega_i(a)
      \right),
   \]
   with the convention that the inner maximum is \(-\infty\) when
   \(L_i=\Sigma\), and that \(\delta_{\rm list}(q)=+\infty\) when
   \(T=\emptyset\).  If
   \[
      \Theta(q)>M_*(q)-\delta_{\rm list}(q)
      \tag{TL1}
   \]
   and
   \[
      \Theta(q)\ge
      M_*(q)
      -
      \frac{\kappa}{2}\bigl(\Gamma_T(q)+|T|-h+\Delta\bigr),
      \tag{TL2}
   \]
   then the Chase--GMD reporter followed by exact filtering
   \(S_q(c)\ge\Theta(q)\) is a certified threshold reporter for the entire
   code:
   \[
      \{c\in\mathcal C:S_q(c)\ge\Theta(q)\}.
   \]
   Its transcript count is \(O(h\prod_{i\in T}|L_i|)\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Because each \(L_i\) contains a maximizer of \(\omega_i\), the quantity
   \(\max_{b\in\prod_{i\in T}L_i}M_b(q)\) in \((CH4)\) is exactly \(M_*(q)\).
   Thus \((TL2)\) is the Chase margin condition \((CH4)\).

   It remains only to show that every codeword with score at least
   \(\Theta(q)\) has its \(T\)-coordinates in the lists.  If \(c_j\notin L_j\)
   for some \(j\in T\), then
   \[
      S_q(c)
      \le
      M_*(q)
      -
      \left(
         \max_{a\in\Sigma}\omega_j(a)
         -
         \max_{a\notin L_j}\omega_j(a)
      \right)
      \le M_*(q)-\delta_{\rm list}(q)
      <\Theta(q).
   \]
   Hence every codeword with \(S_q(c)\ge\Theta(q)\) satisfies
   \(c_i\in L_i\) for all \(i\in T\).  Applying
   \cref{cor:chase-gmd-block-certificate} and then exact filtering proves the
   claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Information-set threshold reporter]
   \label{lem:information-set-threshold-reporter}
   Let \(\mathcal C\subseteq\Sigma^h\) be a code and let
   \(I\subseteq[h]\).  Write
   \(D_I=\{c_I:c\in\mathcal C\}\), and assume that the projection
   \(c\mapsto c_I\) is injective on \(\mathcal C\).  Let
   \(E_I:D_I\to\mathcal C\) be its certified inverse.  For query scores
   \(\omega_i(q,a)\), define
   \[
      S_q(c)=\sum_{i=1}^h\omega_i(q,c_i),
      \qquad
      m_i(q)=\max_{a\in\Sigma}\omega_i(q,a),
   \]
   and for \(b\in D_I\)
   \[
      U_I(q,b)
      =
      \sum_{i\in I}\omega_i(q,b_i)
      +
      \sum_{i\notin I}m_i(q).
   \]
   Suppose a query routine returns a set \(\mathsf B_I(q,\Theta)\subseteq D_I\)
   containing every \(b\in D_I\) with \(U_I(q,b)\ge\Theta\).  Then extending
   all \(b\in\mathsf B_I(q,\Theta)\) by \(E_I\) and filtering by
   \(S_q(c)\ge\Theta\) returns exactly
   \[
      \{c\in\mathcal C:S_q(c)\ge\Theta\}.
   \]

   In particular, when \(D_I=\Sigma^I\), the standard best-first product
   enumerator over the sorted coordinate symbol lists supplies such a routine.
   If
   \[
      N_I(q,\Theta)=
      \left|
      \left\{
      b\in\Sigma^I:
      \sum_{i\in I}\omega_i(q,b_i)
      \ge
      \Theta-\sum_{i\notin I}m_i(q)
      \right\}
      \right|,
   \]
   then its work is
   \[
      O\!\left(
      |I||\Sigma|\log|\Sigma|
      +
      N_I(q,\Theta)\log(2+N_I(q,\Theta))
      \right)
   \]
   plus the cost of extending and scoring the listed words.  For every
   \(\beta>0\),
   \[
      N_I(q,\Theta)
      \le
      \exp\!\left(
         -\beta\Theta
         +
         \beta\sum_{i\notin I}m_i(q)
      \right)
      \prod_{i\in I}
      \sum_{a\in\Sigma}\exp(\beta\omega_i(q,a)).
      \tag{IS1}
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Let \(c\in\mathcal C\) satisfy \(S_q(c)\ge\Theta\), and put
   \(b=c_I\).  Since each coordinate outside \(I\) is bounded above by
   \(m_i(q)\),
   \[
      U_I(q,b)
      \ge
      \sum_{i\in I}\omega_i(q,c_i)
      +
      \sum_{i\notin I}\omega_i(q,c_i)
      =
      S_q(c)
      \ge\Theta .
   \]
   Hence \(b\) is listed and \(E_I(b)=c\) is tested.  The exact score filter
   removes every extended word below threshold, proving exactness.

   For the product case, sort the symbols in each coordinate by decreasing
   score and use a heap on rank vectors, starting from the all-top vector and
   inserting each unvisited neighbor obtained by increasing one rank.  The heap
   always pops the largest remaining information-set score, so stopping below
   the displayed threshold lists exactly the \(N_I(q,\Theta)\) tuples.  The
   stated work is the sorting and heap cost.  Finally,
   \[
      \mathbf 1\left\{
      \sum_{i\in I}\omega_i(q,b_i)
      \ge
      \Theta-\sum_{i\notin I}m_i(q)
      \right\}
      \le
      \exp\!\left(
         \beta\sum_{i\in I}\omega_i(q,b_i)
         -
         \beta\Theta
         +
         \beta\sum_{i\notin I}m_i(q)
      \right),
   \]
   and summing over \(b\in\Sigma^I\) gives \((IS1)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Ordered-statistics information-set certificate]
   \label{cor:ordered-statistics-information-set}
   Work in the product information-set case of
   \cref{lem:information-set-threshold-reporter}.  For \(i\in I\), choose
   \(a_i(q)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in\Sigma}\omega_i(q,a)\), and put
   \[
      D_I(q,b)=
      \sum_{i\in I}
      \bigl(m_i(q)-\omega_i(q,b_i)\bigr),
      \qquad
      \Delta_I(q,\Theta)=
      \sum_{i=1}^h m_i(q)-\Theta .
   \]
   Enumerating all \(b\in\Sigma^I\) with
   \(D_I(q,b)\le\Delta_I(q,\Theta)\), extending by \(E_I\), and exact filtering
   is a certified threshold reporter for \(\mathcal C\).

   Moreover, let
   \[
      \delta_i(q)=
      \min_{a\ne a_i(q)}
      \bigl(m_i(q)-\omega_i(q,a)\bigr),
      \qquad i\in I,
   \]
   with \(\delta_i(q)=+\infty\) if \(|\Sigma|=1\), and let
   \(\delta_{(1)}(q)\le\cdots\le\delta_{(|I|)}(q)\) be these gaps in
   nondecreasing order.  The order-\(s\) ordered-statistics enumeration of all
   information words differing from \(a_I(q)\) in at most \(s\) positions is
   complete whenever
   \[
      \Delta_I(q,\Theta)
      <
      \sum_{\ell=1}^{s+1}\delta_{(\ell)}(q),
      \tag{IS2}
   \]
   with the right-hand side interpreted as \(+\infty\) when \(s=|I|\).  Its
   number of candidate information words is at most
   \[
      \sum_{\ell=0}^s \binom{|I|}{\ell}(|\Sigma|-1)^\ell .
   \]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Since
   \[
      U_I(q,b)
      =
      \sum_{i=1}^h m_i(q)-D_I(q,b),
   \]
   the condition \(D_I(q,b)\le\Delta_I(q,\Theta)\) is exactly
   \(U_I(q,b)\ge\Theta\).  The first claim is therefore
   \cref{lem:information-set-threshold-reporter}.

   If \(b\) differs from \(a_I(q)\) in at least \(s+1\) positions, then
   \(D_I(q,b)\) is at least the sum of the \(s+1\) smallest coordinate gaps.
   Under \((IS2)\), no such \(b\) can satisfy the required discrepancy bound.
   Hence order-\(s\) enumeration contains every threshold-relevant information
   word, and the displayed count is the number of possible support sets and
   non-top symbols on those sets.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Minimum-entropy information-set reporter]
   \label{lem:min-entropy-information-set}
   Let \(\mathcal C\le\mathbb F^h\) be a \(k\)-dimensional linear code with
   generator matrix \(G\in\mathbb F^{k\times h}\).  For an information set
   \(I\subseteq[h]\), \(|I|=k\), write \(G_I\) for the \(k\times k\) submatrix
   of columns in \(I\), and assume \(G_I\) is nonsingular.  Then
   \(D_I=\mathbb F^I\), and the certified extension map is
   \[
      E_I(b)=bG_I^{-1}G .
   \]

   Fix \(\beta>0\), query scores \(\omega_i(q,a)\), and threshold \(\Theta\).
   Put
   \[
      m_i(q)=\max_{a\in\mathbb F}\omega_i(q,a),
      \qquad
      \lambda_i(q)=
      \log\sum_{a\in\mathbb F}
      \exp\bigl(\beta(\omega_i(q,a)-m_i(q))\bigr),
   \]
   and
   \[
      \Delta(q,\Theta)=\sum_{i=1}^hm_i(q)-\Theta .
   \]
   Let
   \[
      \Lambda_*(q)=
      \min_{\substack{I\subseteq[h]\\ |I|=k,\ \operatorname{rank}G_I=k}}
      \sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i(q).
   \]
   Choose an information set \(I_*(q)\) attaining this minimum and run the
   information-set reporter of
   \cref{lem:information-set-threshold-reporter} with \(I=I_*(q)\).  It is a
   certified threshold reporter for
   \[
      \{c\in\mathcal C:S_q(c)\ge\Theta\},
   \]
   and its information-word list size satisfies
   \[
      N_{I_*}(q,\Theta)
      \le
      \exp\bigl(\beta\Delta(q,\Theta)+\Lambda_*(q)\bigr).
      \tag{ME1}
   \]

   The minimizing information set is found by the usual greedy basis rule:
   sort the coordinates by nondecreasing \(\lambda_i(q)\), scan them in that
   order, and keep a coordinate exactly when its column of \(G\) increases the
   rank of the kept columns.  If \(h\), \(|\mathbb F|\), and the linear-algebra
   work are polylogarithmic in the local subproblem size \(m\), then the
   reporter has polylogarithmic query overhead whenever
   \[
      \beta\Delta(q,\Theta)+\Lambda_*(q)=O(\log\log m).
      \tag{ME2}
   \]

   Two useful upper bounds on \(\Lambda_*(q)\) are immediate.  If
   \(\mathcal C\) is MDS, then \(\Lambda_*(q)\) is the sum of the \(k\)
   smallest values among \(\lambda_1(q),\ldots,\lambda_h(q)\).  More generally,
   for any distribution \(\nu\) on information sets,
   \[
      \Lambda_*(q)
      \le
      \sum_{i=1}^h \pi_i\lambda_i(q),
      \qquad
      \pi_i=\Pr_{I\sim\nu}[i\in I].
      \tag{ME3}
   \]
   In particular, a coordinate-transitive family with a uniform information-set
   distribution satisfies
   \[
      \Lambda_*(q)\le\frac{k}{h}\sum_{i=1}^h\lambda_i(q).
      \tag{ME4}
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Since \(G_I\) is nonsingular, every information word \(b\in\mathbb F^I\)
   determines the unique message \(u=bG_I^{-1}\), hence the unique codeword
   \(uG=E_I(b)\).  Thus the information-set reporter applies.

   For any information set \(I\), the exponential bound \((IS1)\) becomes
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      N_I(q,\Theta)
      &\le
      \exp\!\left(
         -\beta\Theta+\beta\sum_{i\notin I}m_i(q)
      \right)
      \prod_{i\in I}
      \sum_{a\in\mathbb F}\exp(\beta\omega_i(q,a))\\
      &=
      \exp\!\left(
         \beta\sum_{i=1}^hm_i(q)-\beta\Theta
         +
         \sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i(q)
      \right).
   \end{aligned}
   \]
   Minimizing over information sets gives \((ME1)\).  The polylogarithmic
   claim follows by substituting \((ME2)\) into this bound and adding the
   stated coordinate sorting, symbol sorting, rank-test, extension, and exact
   scoring costs.

   It remains to justify the greedy minimization.  The columns of \(G\) form a
   rank-\(k\) linear matroid, whose bases are exactly the information sets.
   Let \(B\) be the greedy basis and \(O\) any minimum-weight basis.  Order the
   elements of \(B\) as they are chosen, \(b_1,\ldots,b_k\).  By induction,
   after the first \(r-1\) greedy choices there exists a minimum-weight basis
   \(O_{r-1}\) containing \(b_1,\ldots,b_{r-1}\).  At step \(r\), if
   \(b_r\in O_{r-1}\), take \(O_r=O_{r-1}\).  Otherwise, because
   \(O_{r-1}\) is a basis, \(b_r\) has a linear representation in the columns
   of \(O_{r-1}\).  Since \(b_r\) is independent of
   \(\{b_1,\ldots,b_{r-1}\}\), there is a column
   \(o\in O_{r-1}\setminus\{b_1,\ldots,b_{r-1}\}\) that appears with nonzero
   coefficient in this representation.  Replacing that column by \(b_r\)
   preserves the span, so
   \[
      O_r=O_{r-1}-\{o\}+\{b_r\}
   \]
   is still a basis.  Also \(o\) is not in the span of
   \(\{b_1,\ldots,b_{r-1}\}\), otherwise \(O_{r-1}\) would be dependent.  Thus
   \(o\) was feasible for the greedy scan at step \(r\), so the sorted greedy
   rule gives
   \(\lambda_{b_r}(q)\le\lambda_o(q)\).  Hence \(O_r\) is no heavier than
   \(O_{r-1}\), and it is also minimum-weight.  After \(k\) steps the greedy
   basis itself is minimum-weight.

   If \(\mathcal C\) is MDS, every \(k\)-subset is an information set, so the
   minimum is the sum of the \(k\) smallest weights.  For a distribution
   \(\nu\) on information sets,
   \[
      \Lambda_*(q)
      \le
      \E_{I\sim\nu}\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i(q)
      =
      \sum_i\Pr[i\in I]\lambda_i(q),
   \]
   proving \((ME3)\).  The transitive specialization has
   \(\pi_i=k/h\) for every coordinate, giving \((ME4)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[OSD blocks are superset reporters]
   \label{cor:osd-superset-block-reporter}
   Let a block code \(\mathcal C\le\mathbb F^h\) and coordinate scores
   \(\omega_i(q,a)\) be as in \cref{lem:min-entropy-information-set}, and
   write
   \[
      S_q(c)=\sum_{i=1}^h\omega_i(q,c_i),
      \qquad
      M(q)=\sum_{i=1}^h\max_{a\in\mathbb F}\omega_i(q,a).
   \]
   For a fixed \(\beta>0\), choose the minimum-entropy information set
   \(I_*(q)\) and let \(\Lambda_*(q)\) be as in
   \cref{lem:min-entropy-information-set}.  For every threshold \(\theta\),
   enumerate all information words \(b\in\mathbb F^{I_*(q)}\) satisfying
   \[
      U_{I_*}(q,b)\ge\theta,
   \]
   extend them to codewords, and exact-filter by \(S_q(c)\ge\theta\).
   This is a certified threshold reporter for
   \(\{c\in\mathcal C:S_q(c)\ge\theta\}\).  Before exact filtering, the number
   of candidate extensions is at most
   \[
      \exp\bigl(\beta(M(q)-\theta)+\Lambda_*(q)\bigr).
      \tag{OSD1}
   \]
   Hence the block supplies the superset reporter required by
   \cref{lem:superset-product-panel-decoder} with
   \[
      B(q)=\exp\bigl(\beta M(q)+\Lambda_*(q)\bigr),
      \tag{OSD2}
   \]
   and \(A(q)\) equal to the polylogarithmic chart-construction, sorting, and
   heap-initialization cost.

   In a product panel whose block upper bounds split as
   \(R_{\ell+1}(q)=\sum_{j>\ell}M_j(q)\), the OSD candidate term for block
   \(j=\ell+1\) in \(\widehat P_\beta(q)\) is exactly
   \[
      \exp(\Lambda_j(q))\,e^{\beta R_{\ell+1}(q)}Z_{\le\ell}(q).
      \tag{OSD3}
   \]
   Therefore the query-list certificate for an OSD product panel is the usual
   product-panel prefix moment, with the extra multiplier
   \(\exp(\Lambda_j(q))\) only at the block being decoded.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   The first claim is \cref{lem:min-entropy-information-set} applied with
   \(\Theta=\theta\).  The candidate count bound \((OSD1)\) is \((ME1)\) with
   \(\Delta(q,\theta)=M(q)-\theta\).  Thus the threshold-dependent part of the
   reporter work is bounded by \(B(q)e^{-\beta\theta}\), proving \((OSD2)\).
   The remaining operations do not depend on \(\theta\) except through the heap
   enumeration already charged by the candidate count, so they are absorbed
   into \(A(q)\).

   For the product-panel identity, substitute
   \(B_j(q)=\exp(\beta M_j(q)+\Lambda_j(q))\) into the third sum of
   \cref{lem:superset-product-panel-decoder}:
   \[
      B_{\ell+1}(q)e^{\beta R_{\ell+2}(q)}Z_{\le\ell}(q)
      =
      e^{\Lambda_{\ell+1}(q)}
      e^{\beta(M_{\ell+1}(q)+R_{\ell+2}(q))}
      Z_{\le\ell}(q).
   \]
   Since \(M_{\ell+1}(q)+R_{\ell+2}(q)=R_{\ell+1}(q)\), this is \((OSD3)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[GMD and Chase as compressed list decoders]
   \label{rem:gmd-chase-compressed-decoder}
   \Cref{lem:reliability-erasure-sweep} is the self-contained form of the
   generalized minimum-distance idea of Forney and of its Euclidean-code and
   lattice extensions by Forney--Vardy~\cite{For66,FV96}.  It is weaker than a
   full soft list-recovery oracle, because each coordinate contributes one hard
   symbol and one confidence, but it has a much smaller transcript space than
   the repeated-coordinate lift of \cref{lem:hard-list-recovery-lift}: the
   query tries only \(O(h)\) erasure patterns.  This is exactly the kind of
   decoder DAG charged by
   \cref{cor:output-sensitive-decoder-dag-rate-coverage}.

   Chase decoding enlarges the same template by branching over a few
   low-confidence coordinates or low-confidence symbols before running the
   outer decoder~\cite{Cha72}.  In the present language, those trials are just
   additional branches of a compact decoder DAG, as formalized in
   \cref{lem:chase-gmd-reporter} and
   \cref{cor:chase-gmd-block-certificate}.  The useful theoretical target is
   therefore not Lloyd-style cell convergence, but a reliability map for which
   the true near route satisfies the soft top-gap inequality \((GMS2)\), or the
   Chase margin \((CH4)\) after branching over a polylogarithmic ambiguity set,
   while the retained outputs pass the same rate-coverage scan and storage
   certificates as the other panels.  \Cref{cor:top-list-chase-completeness}
   makes the usual practical restriction to top lists self-contained: symbols
   outside the lists are harmless whenever their score deficit already puts the
   codeword below the reporting threshold.

   \Cref{lem:information-set-threshold-reporter} gives the ordered-statistics
   alternative inspired by Prange information sets and the Fossorier--Lin OSD
   decoder~\cite{Pra62,FL95}.  Instead of asking an outer decoder to correct
   low-confidence coordinates, one chooses a reliable information set, lists
   only high-score information words, extends them through the systematic chart,
   and filters by the exact Euclidean score.  This is often a better match for
   expensive preprocessing: the build stage may search for good systematic
   charts, rotations, or quotient bases, while the retained query algorithm pays
   only for the short discrepancy list certified by
   \cref{cor:ordered-statistics-information-set}.
   \Cref{lem:min-entropy-information-set} makes this search objective exact:
   for a linear block, the right chart is the minimum-weight information set
   with coordinate weights equal to the local soft entropy
   \(\lambda_i(q)\).  For MDS or Reed--Solomon style blocks this is just the
   \(k\) most reliable coordinates, while for a general retained linear block
   it is a greedy minimum-basis computation.  The remaining geometric spectrum
   theorem can therefore ask for the scalar entropy margin \((ME2)\), instead
   of a full soft list-recovery oracle.
   The nearest-neighbor-accelerated information-set-decoding line of
   May--Ozerov~\cite{MO15} is the dual use case: high-dimensional nearest
   neighbor search is used to speed up code decoding.  Here the reduction runs
   in the opposite direction.  A retained code or lattice decoder supplies an
   implicit nearest-neighbor panel, so the charged object must be the compact
   discrepancy or closest-pair transcript, not the raw universe of possible
   codewords.
   \Cref{lem:superset-product-panel-decoder} and
   \cref{cor:osd-superset-block-reporter} then connect this scalar margin back
   to the product-panel accounting: false OSD candidates are not hidden in the
   output-sensitive scan term, but are charged by an explicit
   \(e^{\Lambda_j(q)}\) multiplier in the prefix moment.
   \Cref{cor:superset-product-panel-rate-bookkeeping} is the rate form of the
   same statement: the query exponent only has to absorb
   \((1+A_j(q)+e^{\Lambda_j(q)})
   e^{\beta(M_j(q)-\theta_{Q,j})}\) block-by-block.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Outer list recovery as the clean codebook target]
   \label{rem:outer-list-recovery-codebook}
   \Cref{cor:euclidean-list-decoder-reporter},
   \cref{lem:hard-list-recovery-lift}, and
   \cref{lem:reliability-erasure-sweep} are the most useful transfers from
   Reed--Solomon, expander-code, polar-code, and Euclidean-code list decoding
   to the present data-structure problem.  The codebook need not be the full
   Cartesian product
   \(\prod_j\mathcal C_j\).  It may be a sparse outer code
   \(\mathcal C\subseteq\prod_j\Sigma_j\), a Construction-A or Construction-D
   lattice coset, or a Barnes--Wall style recursive lattice family.  The query
   supplies soft Euclidean reliabilities for the symbols.  If those
   reliabilities are actual embedded Euclidean scores, then
   \cref{cor:euclidean-list-decoder-reporter} turns any Euclidean-metric list
   decoder into the threshold reporter directly.  For more general bounded
   scores, the lift converts reliabilities into ordinary list-recovery
   constraints at \(h\lceil M/\Delta\rceil\) repeated positions, and the
   decoder returns a short certified list of high-score global codewords before
   metric verification.  When one symbol per coordinate is dominant, the
   reliability-erasure sweep gives the cheaper \(O(h)\)-transcript GMD
   surrogate instead.  Signed scores are handled by adding a query-dependent
   constant to all symbols in a coordinate and shifting the final threshold.

   This is a sharper alternative to \(k\)-means or Lloyd cells.  \(k\)-means++
   or other expensive build-time procedures can still be used to propose
   rotations, cosets, scalings, or inner score panels, but the retained index is
   certified by a code/list-recovery theorem and by the spectrum inequalities
   \((PP1)\)--\((PP4)\), not by convergence of the clustering heuristic.  When
   \(M/\Delta=\log^{O_c(1)}m\), the repeated-coordinate lift costs only a
   polylogarithmic factor; direct Euclidean decoding removes even this
   discretization overhead when it applies.  Thus folded Reed--Solomon/list-recovery
   constructions~\cite{GR08}, Koetter--Vardy soft decoding~\cite{KV03},
   Barnes--Sloane lattice decoding via soft Reed--Solomon scores~\cite{MP20},
   expander-code list recovery~\cite{ST25}, and polar-code multiprobing
   \cite{TV12,TH23} all point to the same theorem object: a compact panel whose
   soft-score threshold reporter is output-sensitive and whose retained buckets
   have the random-like ANN spectrum.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[List decoding as learned routing without Lloyd analysis]
   \label{rem:list-decoding-routing}
   The useful transfer from list decoding is not a black-box decoding radius.
   It is the interface in \cref{lem:soft-list-recovery-reporter} and
   \cref{cor:euclidean-list-decoder-reporter}: a structured code or lattice gives an
   implicit family of candidate centers together with a certified
   output-sensitive enumerator for the centers relevant to a query.
   \Cref{lem:hard-list-recovery-lift} is the fallback that reduces arbitrary
   bounded soft scores to ordinary list recovery with only polylogarithmic mesh
   loss.
   This is a cleaner theorem object than Lloyd or \(k\)-means routing.  Lloyd
   may find excellent empirical centers, but its iterations do not by
   themselves provide a worst-case list-size majorant for every query.  A
   code/lattice panel instead stores a compact seed, coset, syndrome, or
   frozen-set description, and the query runs a list decoder whose stack size is
   charged by the partition certificates \(P_\beta\) and \(T_\beta\).

   Since preprocessing time is not charged in the model, the build routine may
   search aggressively over random rotations, cosets, Construction-A moduli,
   block scalings, frozen sets, evaluation points, and pruning profiles.  Only
   the retained panel descriptions, bucket incidences, and query decoder are
   charged.  The proof obligation remains exactly the rate bookkeeping above:
   random-like point load, random-like far co-load, output-sensitive decoding,
   and inverse-polylogarithmic near-pair hit probability.  Recent Euclidean
   list-decoding work gives relevant building blocks and benchmarks for this
   target: random spherical and Construction-A Euclidean codes give the list
   size baseline~\cite{ZV21}, Reed--Solomon and related soft decoders give
   coordinatewise Euclidean list-recovery mechanisms~\cite{KV03,MP20,PH26},
   and polar-code nearest-neighbor search shows the practical value of using a
   high-dimensional latent code plus list decoding for multiprobe
   search~\cite{TV12,TH23}.  Recent expander-code list-decoding and
   list-recovery results also make it plausible to use an explicit outer code
   to combine many small soft blocks without paying a linear scan over all
   products~\cite{ST25}.  Folded Reed--Solomon and multiplicity-code
   algorithms give another candidate outer layer after the soft scores have
   been discretized by the dyadic lift: recent near-linear list-decoding and
   list-recovery routines make the decoder side close to output-sensitive for
   the relevant capacity regime~\cite{AHS26,GHKS25}.  What is still missing
   here is the simultaneous ANN spectrum theorem at the critical exponent, not
   the decoder interface.

   This is the main distinction to keep from the coding and lattice
   literature.  Barnes--Wall and Barnes--Sloane decoding, Euclidean
   Reed--Solomon decoding, Construction-A quotient decoding, ordered-statistics
   decoding, and expander or folded-Reed--Solomon list recovery are primarily
   \emph{decoder-side} results: they say that a structured implicit family can
   be threshold-enumerated, sampled, or reduced to ordinary list recovery with a
   controlled transcript.  The ANN theorem also needs a \emph{spectrum-side}
   result: after the rotations, cosets, pruning profile, and bucket weights are
   fixed, the retained family must have the critical storage moment, far
   co-load moment, and tilted near-pair mass.  The finite verifier and
   reduced-cost separator are designed exactly to keep these two claims
   separate.  Existing decoders may expose candidate labels or certify that no
   positive dual obstruction remains in their implicit universe; the paper's
   rate-coverage inequalities decide whether the resulting panel is a valid ANN
   index.

   The sharpest formulation of that missing object is the smooth decodable
   subcode problem isolated by Becker--Ducas--Gama--Laarhoven.  Their random
   product-code construction gives the right spherical filtering intuition and
   a lattice-enumeration decoder, but the random-behavior guarantee carries a
   \(2^{\widetilde O(\sqrt d)}\) slack.  In logarithmic dimension this is
   \(m^{o(1)}\), which is enough for the traditional \(o(1)\)-exponent
   accounting but not for the polylogarithmic overhead target pursued here.
   Thus the self-contained replacement for \(k\)-means is not a black-box
   lattice decoder.  It is a block code or lattice subcode of the prescribed
   size whose wedge/cap loads satisfy the one-block rate inequalities of
   \cref{cor:product-panel-rate-bookkeeping} with only polylogarithmic slack,
   and whose threshold reporter is output-sensitive.  Expensive preprocessing
   may search over random rotations, Construction-A or Construction-D
   parameters, Barnes--Wall or Reed--Solomon derived blocks, or repulsive
   spherical codebooks; after certification, the retained object is just a
   compact decodable panel.  In this sense the cumulative score tree is an
   online randomized lattice decoder, and the product-panel program asks for a
   fixed implicit lattice whose decoder has the same moment certificates.

   The route-lattice viewpoint also clarifies how such a panel can simplify the
   near-value side of the proof.  A black-box approximate closest-vector answer
   is too weak, because it gives neither pointwise domination nor a cut-mass
   certificate.  A threshold list decoder with admissible prefix upper scores
   is strong enough: every decoded continuation is a unit-success edge in the
   route trie.  After the contraction in
   \cref{lem:port-skeleton-saturated-comparison}, the decoded block contributes
   only its Fano/list-decoder prefix moment and its polylogarithmic depth, not a
   separate detector-vote or cohort-materialization loss.  Thus the lowest
   overhead code/lattice replacement is one that turns nonunit probabilistic
   ports into certified deterministic threshold enumeration, or else into a
   sampler with an explicit state-DAG envelope and the same cut certificate.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Sharp LP bounds give output-sensitive soft decoding]
   \label{cor:sharp-lp-soft-decoder}
   Let \(C\subseteq[q]^b\) be a finite code, and let
   \[
      W(c)=\sum_{i=1}^b w_{i,c_i}
   \]
   be a query-dependent soft score.  Fix a threshold \(T\).  Suppose a
   branch-and-bound decoder uses a rooted partition tree of depth \(H\) whose
   nodes \(u\) carry disjoint subcodes \(C_u\subseteq C\), with leaves singleton
   codewords.  At node \(u\), the decoder computes a certified upper bound
   \(U(u)\ge\max_{c\in C_u}W(c)\), prunes when \(U(u)<T\), branches otherwise,
   and verifies every singleton leaf it reaches.

   Assume the relaxation upper bound is \(\Gamma\)-sharp on this tree:
   \[
      U(u)
      \le
      \max_{c\in C_u}W(c)+\Gamma
      \qquad(u\text{ in the partition tree}).
      \tag{LPS1}
   \]
   Put
   \[
      N_{\ge s}=\bigl|\{c\in C:W(c)\ge s\}\bigr|.
      \tag{LPS2}
   \]
   Then the number of visited nodes is at most
   \[
      (H+1)N_{\ge T-\Gamma}.
      \tag{LPS3}
   \]
   In particular, if each LP, Sherali--Adams, dynamic-programming, or other
   certified relaxation solve costs \(B_{\rm lp}\), then the query work is
   \[
      O\!\left(B_{\rm lp}(H+1)N_{\ge T-\Gamma}\right)
      \tag{LPS4}
   \]
   plus the final metric-verification cost for the reported codewords.

   Now assume additionally that, for every fixed codeword \(c\), the random
   panel construction makes \(W(c)\sim N(0,b)\).  Write
   \(T=\tau\sqrt b\) and \(\Gamma=\delta\sqrt b\), with
   \(\tau\ge1\) and \(0\le\delta\le\tau/2\).  Then
   \[
      \E N_{\ge T-\Gamma}
      \le
      \exp\!\bigl(O(1+\tau\delta)\bigr)\,\E N_{\ge T}.
      \tag{LPS5}
   \]
   Consequently, in the logarithmic terminal regime
   \[
      b=\Theta\!\left(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\right),
      \qquad
      \tau=\Theta(\sqrt{\log n}),
      \qquad
      \Gamma=O(\sqrt{\log\log n}),
      \tag{LPS6}
   \]
   the expected lowered-threshold list is only a \(\log^{O(1)}n\) factor larger
   than the true threshold list.  A relaxation satisfying \((LPS1)\) with
   \(\Gamma=O(\sqrt{\log\log n})\), together with
   \(H,B_{\rm lp}=\log^{O(1)}n\), is therefore an output-sensitive Gaussian soft
   decoder with only polylogarithmic overhead.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   If a node \(u\) is visited, then \(U(u)\ge T\).  By \((LPS1)\), there is a
   codeword \(c\in C_u\) with \(W(c)\ge T-\Gamma\).  Hence every visited node
   contains at least one codeword counted by \(N_{\ge T-\Gamma}\).  Since the
   node sets form a partition tree, any fixed codeword belongs to at most one
   node at each depth and therefore to at most \(H+1\) nodes total.  Counting
   pairs \((u,c)\) with \(u\) visited, \(c\in C_u\), and
   \(W(c)\ge T-\Gamma\) gives \((LPS3)\).  Multiplying by the per-node certified
   solve cost gives \((LPS4)\).

   For the Gaussian comparison let \(Z\sim N(0,1)\).  By linearity of
   expectation,
   \[
      \frac{\E N_{\ge T-\Gamma}}{\E N_{\ge T}}
      =
      \frac{\Pr[Z\ge\tau-\delta]}{\Pr[Z\ge\tau]} .
   \]
   Since \(\delta\le\tau/2\),
   \[
      \Pr[Z\ge\tau-\delta]
      \le
      \Pr[Z\ge\tau]+\delta\sup_{x\in[\tau-\delta,\tau]}\phi(x)
      \le
      \Pr[Z\ge\tau]+\delta\,\phi(\tau-\delta),
   \]
   where \(\phi\) is the standard Gaussian density.  The elementary lower
   bound
   \(\Pr[Z\ge\tau]\ge c(1+\tau)^{-1}\phi(\tau)\) for \(\tau\ge1\) gives
   \[
      \frac{\Pr[Z\ge\tau-\delta]}{\Pr[Z\ge\tau]}
      \le
      1+C(1+\tau)\delta
      \exp\!\left(\tau\delta-\frac{\delta^2}{2}\right)
      \le
      \exp\!\bigl(O(1+\tau\delta)\bigr).
   \]
   This is \((LPS5)\).  In \((LPS6)\),
   \(\delta=\Gamma/\sqrt b=O(\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})\), so
   \(\tau\delta=O(\log\log n)\), and \((LPS5)\) is polylogarithmic.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The LP gap scale is sharp]
   \label{cor:lp-gap-scale-sharp}
   In the Gaussian comparison of
   \cref{cor:sharp-lp-soft-decoder}, let \(T=\tau\sqrt b\),
   \(\Gamma=\delta\sqrt b\), and \(0\le\delta\le\tau/2\).  There are absolute
   constants \(c,C>0\) such that, for \(\tau\ge1\),
   \[
      c\exp\!\left(\tau\delta-\frac{\delta^2}{2}\right)
      \le
      \frac{\E N_{\ge T-\Gamma}}{\E N_{\ge T}}
      \le
      C(1+\tau\delta)
      \exp\!\left(\tau\delta-\frac{\delta^2}{2}\right).
      \tag{LPS7}
   \]
   In particular, in the terminal logarithmic regime
   \[
      b=\Theta\!\left(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\right),
      \qquad
      \tau=\Theta(\sqrt{\log n}),
      \tag{LPS8}
   \]
   the lowered-threshold list is inflated by
   \[
      \exp\!\bigl(\Theta(\Gamma\sqrt{\log\log n})\bigr)
      \tag{LPS9}
   \]
   whenever \(\Gamma=o(\sqrt b)\).  Thus an
   \(O(\sqrt{\log\log n})\) additive LP gap is not merely sufficient for
   polylogarithmic overhead; in the random Gaussian tail model it is the
   largest scale one can tolerate up to constants.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   As in \cref{cor:sharp-lp-soft-decoder}, the expectation ratio is the
   Gaussian tail ratio
   \[
      \frac{\Pr[Z\ge\tau-\delta]}{\Pr[Z\ge\tau]} .
   \]
   The upper bound in \((LPS7)\) is the estimate proved in \((LPS5)\), with
   the harmless polynomial prefactor kept explicit.  For the lower bound, the
   elementary Mills estimates
   \[
      \Pr[Z\ge x]\ge c_0(1+x)^{-1}\phi(x),
      \qquad(x\ge0),
   \]
   and
   \[
      \Pr[Z\ge x]\le C_0x^{-1}\phi(x)
      \qquad(x\ge1)
   \]
   give, using \(\delta\le\tau/2\),
   \[
      \frac{\Pr[Z\ge\tau-\delta]}{\Pr[Z\ge\tau]}
      \ge
      c_1
      \frac{\tau}{1+\tau-\delta}
      \frac{\phi(\tau-\delta)}{\phi(\tau)}
      \ge
      c\exp\!\left(\tau\delta-\frac{\delta^2}{2}\right).
   \]
   Finally, under \((LPS8)\),
   \[
      \tau\delta=\tau\Gamma/\sqrt b
      =
      \Theta(\Gamma\sqrt{\log\log n}),
   \]
   and \(\delta=o(1)\) when \(\Gamma=o(\sqrt b)\), proving \((LPS9)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[No-good cuts are an implementation detail]
   \label{rem:no-good-lp-cuts}
   The one-hot LP formulation also supports the usual repeated-enumeration
   implementation.  After an integral word \(c\) is output, the linear cut
   \[
      \sum_{i=1}^b z_{i,c_i}\le b-1
      \tag{LPS10}
   \]
   removes exactly that word, and the LP may be re-solved to expose the next
   candidate.  This is a convenient way to implement a threshold reporter, but
   it does not change the proof obligation.  For accounting, the run should be
   unfolded into the same kind of certified decision tree used in
   \cref{cor:sharp-lp-soft-decoder}: a no-good residual is simply the child
   subproblem \(C_u\setminus\{c\}\), and fractional optima are ordinary branch
   nodes.  Every surviving residual node still needs the same sharp upper
   certificate, or the sharper false-survivor certificate of
   \cref{cor:false-survivor-lp-accounting}.

   Thus no-good cuts give duplicate-free enumeration, not a replacement for
   the Gaussian pseudocodeword-spectrum theorem.  \Cref{cor:lp-gap-scale-sharp}
   explains why this distinction matters: a relaxation whose fractional
   optima exceed the true subproblem optimum by
   \(\omega(\sqrt{\log\log n})\) creates a superpolylogarithmic lowered-tail
   inflation even before any implementation overhead is counted.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Anchored Gaussian-width certificate for LP sharpness]
   \label{cor:anchored-lp-width-certificate}
   Let \(C\subseteq[q]^b\), and write
   \(\iota(c)\in\{0,1\}^{bq}\) for the one-hot encoding of \(c\).  Let
   \(\mathcal U\) be a finite family of possible branch-and-bound nodes.  Each
   \(u\in\mathcal U\) has a subcode \(C_u\subseteq C\) and a certified
   relaxation \(P_u\subseteq\R^{bq}\) with
   \(\iota(C_u)\subseteq P_u\).  The LP upper bound at \(u\) is
   \[
      U(u)=\sup_{z\in P_u}\ip{w}{z},
      \qquad
      W(c)=\ip{w}{\iota(c)} .
      \tag{LPC1}
   \]
   Suppose that, for every \(u\), there is an anchor map
   \(a_u:P_u\to C_u\).  Define the anchored excess set
   \[
      E_u=\{z-\iota(a_u(z)):z\in P_u\},
      \qquad
      r_u=\sup_{h\in E_u}\|h\|_2,
      \tag{LPC2}
   \]
   and its Gaussian width
   \[
      \omega_u
      =
      \E_g\sup_{h\in E_u}\ip{g}{h},
      \qquad
      g\sim N(0,I_{bq}).
      \tag{LPC3}
   \]
   Let \((\eta_u)_{u\in\mathcal U}\) be positive numbers with
   \(\sum_u\eta_u\le\eta\).  If
   \[
      \omega_u+r_u\sqrt{2\log(1/\eta_u)}
      \le \Gamma
      \qquad(u\in\mathcal U),
      \tag{LPC4}
   \]
   then, with probability at least \(1-\eta\) over the Gaussian score table
   \(w\), every \(u\in\mathcal U\) satisfies
   \[
      U(u)\le \max_{c\in C_u}W(c)+\Gamma .
      \tag{LPC5}
   \]
   Consequently, on this event, any branch-and-bound decoder whose node tree is
   contained in \(\mathcal U\) satisfies the sharpness hypothesis \((LPS1)\) of
   \cref{cor:sharp-lp-soft-decoder}.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Fix a node \(u\), and put
   \(X_u(g)=\sup_{h\in E_u}\ip{g}{h}\).  The map \(g\mapsto X_u(g)\) is
   \(r_u\)-Lipschitz, so the standard Gaussian concentration inequality for
   Lipschitz suprema gives
   \[
      \Prb[X_u(g)>\omega_u+t]\le \exp(-t^2/(2r_u^2))
      \tag{LPC6}
   \]
   with the evident deterministic interpretation when \(r_u=0\).  Taking
   \(t=r_u\sqrt{2\log(1/\eta_u)}\) and applying a union bound over
   \(\mathcal U\) shows that, with probability at least \(1-\eta\),
   \(X_u(w)\le\Gamma\) for every \(u\).

   On this event, for any \(z\in P_u\),
   \[
      \ip{w}{z}
      =
      W(a_u(z))+\ip{w}{z-\iota(a_u(z))}
      \le
      \max_{c\in C_u}W(c)+X_u(w)
      \le
      \max_{c\in C_u}W(c)+\Gamma .
   \]
   Taking the supremum over \(z\in P_u\) proves \((LPC5)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[False-survivor accounting for LP branch-and-bound]
   \label{cor:false-survivor-lp-accounting}
   Work in the branch-and-bound setting of
   \cref{cor:sharp-lp-soft-decoder}, and write
   \[
      M(u)=\max_{c\in C_u}W(c),
      \qquad
      \Delta(u)=U(u)-M(u)\ge0 .
      \tag{LPF1}
   \]
   Let
   \(0<\gamma_0<\gamma_1<\cdots<\gamma_J\).  Define the false-survivor count
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      F(\gamma_0,\ldots,\gamma_J)
      &=
      \sum_{j=0}^{J-1}
      \bigl|\{u:
         T-\gamma_{j+1}\le M(u)<T-\gamma_j,\,
         \Delta(u)\ge\gamma_j
      \}\bigr| \\
      &\quad+
      \bigl|\{u:
         M(u)<T-\gamma_J,\,
         \Delta(u)\ge\gamma_J
      \}\bigr| .
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{LPF2}
   \]
   Then the number of visited nodes is at most
   \[
      (H+1)N_{\ge T-\gamma_0}
      +
      F(\gamma_0,\ldots,\gamma_J).
      \tag{LPF3}
   \]
   Hence, for random score tables,
   \[
      \E[\#\text{ visited nodes}]
      \le
      (H+1)\E N_{\ge T-\gamma_0}
      +
      \E F(\gamma_0,\ldots,\gamma_J).
      \tag{LPF4}
   \]
   In particular, if the terminal Gaussian regime has
   \(\gamma_0=O(\sqrt{\log\log n})\),
   \(H,B_{\rm lp}=\log^{O(1)}n\), and
   \[
      \E F(\gamma_0,\ldots,\gamma_J)
      \le
      \log^{O(1)}n\cdot \E N_{\ge T},
      \tag{LPF5}
   \]
   then the decoder is output-sensitive with only polylogarithmic overhead.

   If, in addition, the LP upper bound is represented by anchored excess sets
   as in \cref{cor:anchored-lp-width-certificate}, then
   \[
      \Delta(u)
      \le
      X_u(w):=\sup_{h\in E_u}\ip{w}{h},
      \tag{LPF6}
   \]
   and it is enough to prove the joint false-survivor tail bound
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      &\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}\sum_u
      \Prb\!\left[
         T-\gamma_{j+1}\le M(u)<T-\gamma_j,\,
         X_u(w)\ge\gamma_j
      \right] \\
      &\qquad+
      \sum_u
      \Prb\!\left[
         M(u)<T-\gamma_J,\,
         X_u(w)\ge\gamma_J
      \right]
      \le
      \log^{O(1)}n\cdot \E N_{\ge T}.
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{LPF7}
   \]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Consider a visited node \(u\).  If \(M(u)\ge T-\gamma_0\), then \(u\)
   contains a codeword counted by \(N_{\ge T-\gamma_0}\).  As in the proof of
   \cref{cor:sharp-lp-soft-decoder}, any fixed codeword belongs to at most
   \(H+1\) nodes, so all such visited nodes contribute at most the first term
   in \((LPF3)\).

   It remains to consider a visited node with \(M(u)<T-\gamma_0\).  Since it is
   visited, \(U(u)\ge T\), hence
   \(\Delta(u)=U(u)-M(u)\ge T-M(u)\).  If
   \(T-\gamma_{j+1}\le M(u)<T-\gamma_j\), then
   \(T-M(u)>\gamma_j\), so \(u\) is counted in the \(j\)-th summand of
   \((LPF2)\).  If \(M(u)<T-\gamma_J\), it is counted in the last summand.
   This proves \((LPF3)\), and expectation gives \((LPF4)\).  The Gaussian
   tail comparison \((LPS5)\) turns
   \(\E N_{\ge T-\gamma_0}\) into a polylogarithmic multiple of
   \(\E N_{\ge T}\) when
   \(\gamma_0=O(\sqrt{\log\log n})\), proving the stated output-sensitive
   consequence under \((LPF5)\).

   Finally, \((LPF6)\) follows from the last display in the proof of
   \cref{cor:anchored-lp-width-certificate}, without taking a high-probability
   union bound.  Replacing \(\Delta(u)\) by the larger \(X_u(w)\) in
   \((LPF2)\) and taking expectations gives \((LPF7)\) as a sufficient
   condition for \((LPF5)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exponential false-survivor certificate]
   \label{cor:exponential-false-survivor-certificate}
   Work in the setting of \cref{cor:false-survivor-lp-accounting}, and assume
   the anchored excess domination \((LPF6)\).  For any \(\gamma>0\), put
   \[
      S_\gamma
      =
      \bigl|\{u:M(u)<T-\gamma,\ M(u)+X_u(w)\ge T\}\bigr|.
      \tag{LPE1}
   \]
   Then the number of visited nodes is at most
   \[
      (H+1)N_{\ge T-\gamma}+S_\gamma .
      \tag{LPE2}
   \]
   Consequently, if \(W(c)\sim N(0,b)\) for every fixed codeword, if
   \(T=\tau\sqrt b\), and if
   \(\gamma=O(\sqrt{\log\log n})\) in the logarithmic terminal regime, then the
   decoder has polylogarithmic expected overhead whenever
   \(H,B_{\rm lp}=\log^{O(1)}n\) and, for some \(\lambda>0\),
   \[
      \sum_u
      \E\!\left[
         \exp\!\bigl(\lambda(M(u)+X_u(w)-T)\bigr)
         \mathbf 1_{\{M(u)<T-\gamma\}}
      \right]
      \le
      \log^{O(1)}n\cdot \E N_{\ge T}.
      \tag{LPE3}
   \]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   If a visited node \(u\) has \(M(u)\ge T-\gamma\), then it is charged to a
   codeword in \(N_{\ge T-\gamma}\), with multiplicity at most \(H+1\) as
   before.  If \(M(u)<T-\gamma\), then \(U(u)\ge T\), so
   \[
      T\le U(u)=M(u)+\Delta(u)\le M(u)+X_u(w).
   \]
   Hence \(u\) is counted by \(S_\gamma\).  This proves \((LPE2)\).

   By Markov's inequality applied termwise,
   \[
      \E S_\gamma
      \le
      \sum_u
      \E\!\left[
         \exp\!\bigl(\lambda(M(u)+X_u(w)-T)\bigr)
         \mathbf 1_{\{M(u)<T-\gamma\}}
      \right].
   \]
   The first term in \((LPE2)\) is a polylogarithmic multiple of
   \(\E N_{\ge T}\) by the Gaussian tail comparison \((LPS5)\), and the second
   term is controlled by \((LPE3)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Conditional tilted-excess certificate]
   \label{cor:conditional-tilted-excess-certificate}
   Work in the setting of
   \cref{cor:exponential-false-survivor-certificate}.  Let \(\mathcal T\) be
   the full branch-and-bound node tree, and let
   \[
      \mathcal G_u=\sigma(W(c):c\in C_u)
      \tag{LPT1}
   \]
   be the score information carried by the true codewords in node \(u\).  If
   for some \(\lambda>0\) and \(A_\lambda\ge1\),
   \[
      \E\!\left[\exp(\lambda X_u(w))\mid\mathcal G_u\right]
      \le A_\lambda
      \qquad(u\in\mathcal T)
      \tag{LPT2}
   \]
   almost surely, then
   \[
      \sum_u
      \E\!\left[
         \exp\!\bigl(\lambda(M(u)+X_u(w)-T)\bigr)
         \mathbf 1_{\{M(u)<T-\gamma\}}
      \right]
      \le
      A_\lambda(H+1)|C|\exp(-\lambda T+\lambda^2b/2).
      \tag{LPT3}
   \]
   In particular, taking the Gaussian tilt \(\lambda=T/b\) gives
   \[
      \sum_u
      \E\!\left[
         \exp\!\bigl(\lambda(M(u)+X_u(w)-T)\bigr)
         \mathbf 1_{\{M(u)<T-\gamma\}}
      \right]
      \le
      O(1+\tau)\,A_\lambda(H+1)\,\E N_{\ge T},
      \tag{LPT4}
   \]
   where \(T=\tau\sqrt b\).  Thus a polylogarithmic bound on
   \(A_{T/b}\), together with \(H,B_{\rm lp}=\log^{O(1)}n\), implies the
   polylogarithmic expected-overhead conclusion of
   \cref{cor:exponential-false-survivor-certificate}.  This reduction uses only
   the one-codeword marginal law \(W(c)\sim N(0,b)\), not independence among the
   codeword scores.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Since \(M(u)\) and \(\mathbf 1_{\{M(u)<T-\gamma\}}\) are
   \(\mathcal G_u\)-measurable, \((LPT2)\) gives
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      &\E\!\left[
         \exp\!\bigl(\lambda(M(u)+X_u(w)-T)\bigr)
         \mathbf 1_{\{M(u)<T-\gamma\}}
      \right]\\
      &\qquad\le
      A_\lambda
      \E\!\left[
         \exp(\lambda(M(u)-T))
         \mathbf 1_{\{M(u)<T-\gamma\}}
      \right]\\
      &\qquad\le
      A_\lambda e^{-\lambda T}\E e^{\lambda M(u)} .
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{LPT5}
   \]
   Pointwise,
   \[
      e^{\lambda M(u)}
      \le
      \sum_{c\in C_u}e^{\lambda W(c)}.
      \tag{LPT6}
   \]
   Summing over all nodes, each codeword appears in at most one node at each
   depth and hence in at most \(H+1\) nodes.  Therefore
   \[
      \sum_u\E e^{\lambda M(u)}
      \le
      (H+1)\sum_{c\in C}\E e^{\lambda W(c)}
      =
      (H+1)|C|e^{\lambda^2b/2},
      \tag{LPT7}
   \]
   proving \((LPT3)\).

   For \(\lambda=T/b\), the right hand side of \((LPT3)\) becomes
   \(A_\lambda(H+1)|C|e^{-T^2/(2b)}\).  With \(T=\tau\sqrt b\) and
   \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), the elementary Gaussian lower tail used in
   \cref{cor:sharp-lp-soft-decoder} gives
   \[
      |C|e^{-\tau^2/2}
      \le
      O(1+\tau)\,|C|\Pr[Z\ge\tau]
      =
      O(1+\tau)\,\E N_{\ge T},
   \]
   which is \((LPT4)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Conditional Gaussian projection certificate]
   \label{cor:conditional-gaussian-projection-certificate}
   Work in the setting of
   \cref{cor:conditional-tilted-excess-certificate}.  For a node \(u\), let
   \[
      L_u=\operatorname{span}\{\iota(c):c\in C_u\}\subseteq\R^{bq},
      \tag{LPG1}
   \]
   and let \(\Pi_u\) and \(\Pi_u^\perp\) be the orthogonal projections onto
   \(L_u\) and \(L_u^\perp\).  For the anchored excess set \(E_u\), define the
   conditional projection bias
   \[
      B_u(w)=\sup_{h\in E_u}\ip{\Pi_u w}{\Pi_u h},
      \tag{LPG2}
   \]
   and the orthogonal width/radius
   \[
      \omega_u^\perp
      =
      \E_g\sup_{h\in E_u}\ip{g}{\Pi_u^\perp h},
      \qquad
      r_u^\perp=\sup_{h\in E_u}\|\Pi_u^\perp h\|_2,
      \tag{LPG3}
   \]
   where \(g\sim N(0,I_{bq})\).  If, almost surely for every \(u\in\mathcal T\),
   \[
      \exp\!\left(
         \lambda B_u(w)
         +\lambda\omega_u^\perp
         +\frac{\lambda^2(r_u^\perp)^2}{2}
      \right)
      \le A_\lambda,
      \tag{LPG4}
   \]
   then the conditional tilted-excess bound \((LPT2)\) holds with the same
   \(A_\lambda\).  Hence, at the Gaussian tilt \(\lambda=T/b\), a
   polylogarithmic bound in \((LPG4)\) is sufficient for the LP/SA decoder to
   have polylogarithmic expected overhead.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Conditioning on \(\mathcal G_u\) is equivalent to conditioning on
   \(\Pi_u w\): the linear functionals
   \(\ip{w}{\iota(c)}\), \(c\in C_u\), determine the projection of \(w\) onto
   their span \(L_u\).  The residual \(\Pi_u^\perp w\) remains an independent
   standard Gaussian vector on \(L_u^\perp\).  Therefore, conditionally on
   \(\mathcal G_u\),
   \[
      X_u(w)
      =
      \sup_{h\in E_u}
      \left(
         \ip{\Pi_u w}{\Pi_u h}
         +
         \ip{\Pi_u^\perp w}{\Pi_u^\perp h}
      \right)
      \le
      B_u(w)+Y_u,
      \tag{LPG5}
   \]
   where
   \[
      Y_u=\sup_{h\in E_u}\ip{g}{\Pi_u^\perp h},
      \qquad
      g\sim N(0,I_{bq})
      \tag{LPG6}
   \]
   is independent of \(\mathcal G_u\), has expectation \(\omega_u^\perp\), and
   is \(r_u^\perp\)-Lipschitz as a function of \(g\).  The Gaussian
   concentration moment bound for Lipschitz functions gives
   \[
      \E\exp(\lambda Y_u)
      \le
      \exp\!\left(
         \lambda\omega_u^\perp
         +\frac{\lambda^2(r_u^\perp)^2}{2}
      \right).
      \tag{LPG7}
   \]
   Combining \((LPG5)\)--\((LPG7)\) yields
   \[
      \E[\exp(\lambda X_u(w))\mid\mathcal G_u]
      \le
      \exp\!\left(
         \lambda B_u(w)
         +\lambda\omega_u^\perp
         +\frac{\lambda^2(r_u^\perp)^2}{2}
      \right),
   \]
   so \((LPG4)\) implies \((LPT2)\).  The final sentence follows from
   \cref{cor:conditional-tilted-excess-certificate}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[False-survivor projected-bias certificate]
   \label{cor:false-survivor-projection-certificate}
   Work in the setting of
   \cref{cor:exponential-false-survivor-certificate}, and use the projection
   notation of \cref{cor:conditional-gaussian-projection-certificate}.  It is
   enough to control the projected bias on the false-survivor frontier.  More
   precisely, if for some \(\lambda>0\) and \(\gamma>0\),
   \[
      \sum_u
      \E\!\left[
         \exp(\lambda(M(u)-T))
         \mathbf 1_{\{M(u)<T-\gamma\}}
         \exp\!\left(
            \lambda B_u(w)
            +\lambda\omega_u^\perp
            +\frac{\lambda^2(r_u^\perp)^2}{2}
         \right)
      \right]
      \le
      \log^{O(1)}n\cdot \E N_{\ge T},
      \tag{LPA1}
   \]
   then the tilted crossing bound \((LPE3)\) holds.  Consequently, under the
   Gaussian terminal assumptions of
   \cref{cor:exponential-false-survivor-certificate}, \((LPA1)\) implies the
   same polylogarithmic expected-overhead conclusion.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   For a fixed node \(u\), \(M(u)\) and
   \(\mathbf 1_{\{M(u)<T-\gamma\}}\) are \(\mathcal G_u\)-measurable.  The
   proof of \cref{cor:conditional-gaussian-projection-certificate} gives the
   conditional estimate
   \[
      \E[\exp(\lambda X_u(w))\mid\mathcal G_u]
      \le
      \exp\!\left(
         \lambda B_u(w)
         +\lambda\omega_u^\perp
         +\frac{\lambda^2(r_u^\perp)^2}{2}
      \right).
      \tag{LPA2}
   \]
   Multiplying \((LPA2)\) by
   \(\exp(\lambda(M(u)-T))\mathbf 1_{\{M(u)<T-\gamma\}}\), taking expectation,
   and summing over \(u\) shows that \((LPA1)\) implies \((LPE3)\).  The final
   claim is then exactly
   \cref{cor:exponential-false-survivor-certificate}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Gram form of the projection certificate]
   \label{cor:gram-projection-certificate}
   Fix a node \(u\), and enumerate
   \(C_u=\{c_1,\ldots,c_N\}\).  Let \(A_u\) be the \(bq\times N\) matrix with
   columns \(\iota(c_j)\), let
   \[
      G_u=A_u^\top A_u,
      \qquad
      W_u=A_u^\top w=(W(c_1),\ldots,W(c_N)),
      \tag{LPB1}
   \]
   and for \(h\in E_u\) write
   \[
      v_u(h)=A_u^\top h .
      \tag{LPB2}
   \]
   Thus \(G_u(j,k)\) is the number of coordinates on which \(c_j\) and \(c_k\)
   agree.  With \(G_u^+\) denoting the Moore--Penrose inverse,
   \[
      B_u(w)
      =
      \sup_{h\in E_u} W_u^\top G_u^+v_u(h),
      \tag{LPB3}
   \]
   and
   \[
      (r_u^\perp)^2
      =
      \sup_{h\in E_u}
      \left(
         \|h\|_2^2-v_u(h)^\top G_u^+v_u(h)
      \right),
      \tag{LPB4}
   \]
   while
   \[
      \omega_u^\perp
      =
      \E_g
      \sup_{h\in E_u}
      \ip{g}{h-A_uG_u^+v_u(h)}.
      \tag{LPB5}
   \]
   Therefore the projected-bias certificate is an exact statement about the
   codeword overlap Gram matrix \(G_u\) and the overlap vectors \(v_u(h)\) of
   the anchored pseudocodeword excesses.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   The column span of \(A_u\) is \(L_u\), and
   \(A_uG_u^+A_u^\top\) is the orthogonal projection onto that span.  Hence
   \[
      \Pi_u h=A_uG_u^+A_u^\top h=A_uG_u^+v_u(h).
      \tag{LPB6}
   \]
   Since \(v_u(h)\in\operatorname{range}(G_u)\),
   \[
      \|\Pi_u h\|_2^2
      =
      v_u(h)^\top G_u^+v_u(h),
   \]
   which gives \((LPB4)\), and \((LPB5)\) is the definition of orthogonal
   width applied to \(h-\Pi_u h\).  Finally,
   \[
      \ip{\Pi_u w}{\Pi_u h}
      =
      \ip{w}{\Pi_u h}
      =
      W_u^\top G_u^+v_u(h),
   \]
   and taking the supremum over \(h\in E_u\) proves \((LPB3)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Shifted overlap-coefficient certificate]
   \label{cor:shifted-overlap-coefficient-certificate}
   Work in the setting of \cref{cor:gram-projection-certificate}.  For
   \(h\in E_u\), define the coefficient vector
   \[
      a_u(h)=G_u^+v_u(h),
      \qquad
      \kappa_u(h)=\sum_{j=1}^N a_u(h)_j,
      \qquad
      a_u(h)_j^-=\max\{-a_u(h)_j,0\}.
      \tag{LPD1}
   \]
   Let \(\Theta_u\) be any \(\mathcal G_u\)-measurable upper score satisfying
   \[
      \Theta_u\ge M(u)=\max_{c\in C_u}W(c).
      \tag{LPD2}
   \]
   Then
   \[
      B_u(w)
      \le
      D_u(\Theta_u,w),
      \tag{LPD3}
   \]
   where
   \[
      D_u(\Theta_u,w)
      =
      \sup_{h\in E_u}
      \left[
         \Theta_u\kappa_u(h)
         +
         \sum_{j=1}^N a_u(h)_j^-\bigl(\Theta_u-W(c_j)\bigr)
      \right].
      \tag{LPD4}
   \]
   Consequently, the false-survivor projected-bias condition \((LPA1)\) may be
   replaced by the same condition with \(B_u(w)\) replaced by
   \(D_u(\Theta_u,w)\).

   In particular, on the false-survivor event \(M(u)<T-\gamma\), one may take
   the deterministic frontier \(\Theta_u=T-\gamma\).  Thus the projected-bias
   task reduces to controlling
   \[
      D_{u,\gamma}(w)
      =
      \sup_{h\in E_u}
      \left[
         (T-\gamma)\kappa_u(h)
         +
         \sum_{j=1}^N a_u(h)_j^-\bigl(T-\gamma-W(c_j)\bigr)
      \right]
      \tag{LPD5}
   \]
   under the tilted false-survivor weighting.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   By \((LPB3)\), it suffices to upper-bound
   \(a_u(h)^\top W_u\) for a fixed \(h\in E_u\).  Since
   \(W(c_j)\le\Theta_u\) for every \(j\),
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      a_u(h)^\top W_u
      &=
      \Theta_u\kappa_u(h)
      +
      \sum_{j=1}^N a_u(h)_j\bigl(W(c_j)-\Theta_u\bigr)\\
      &\le
      \Theta_u\kappa_u(h)
      +
      \sum_{j=1}^N a_u(h)_j^-\bigl(\Theta_u-W(c_j)\bigr).
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{LPD6}
   \]
   Taking the supremum over \(h\in E_u\) proves \((LPD3)\).  Replacing \(B_u\)
   by the larger \(D_u\) in \((LPA1)\) preserves the sufficient condition, and
   the deterministic-frontier statement follows from
   \(M(u)<T-\gamma\Rightarrow T-\gamma\ge M(u)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Balance witness for scalar leakage]
   \label{cor:balance-witness-scalar-leakage}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:shifted-overlap-coefficient-certificate}.  Suppose there is a
   vector \(\ell_u\in\R^{bq}\) such that
   \[
      A_u^\top\ell_u=\mathbf 1_N,
      \qquad
      \ip{\ell_u}{h}=0\quad(h\in E_u),
      \tag{LPL1}
   \]
   where \(\mathbf 1_N\) is the all-ones vector in \(\R^N\).  Then
   \[
      \kappa_u(h)
      =
      -\ip{\Pi_u^\perp\ell_u}{\Pi_u^\perp h}
      \qquad(h\in E_u),
      \tag{LPL2}
   \]
   and hence, with
   \[
      \epsilon_u(\ell_u)=\|\Pi_u^\perp\ell_u\|_2,
      \tag{LPL3}
   \]
   one has
   \[
      |\kappa_u(h)|
      \le
      \epsilon_u(\ell_u)\|\Pi_u^\perp h\|_2
      \le
      \epsilon_u(\ell_u)r_u^\perp .
      \tag{LPL4}
   \]
   In particular, if \(\ell_u\in L_u\), then
   \[
      \kappa_u(h)=0
      \qquad(h\in E_u).
      \tag{LPL5}
   \]

   If \(P_u\) is contained in the coordinate simplex constraints
   \[
      \sum_{a\in[q]}z_{i,a}=1
      \qquad(i=1,\ldots,b),
      \tag{LPL6}
   \]
   then every coordinate-block indicator
   \[
      e_i=\mathbf 1_{\{(i,a):a\in[q]\}}
      \tag{LPL7}
   \]
   is a valid balance witness.  Thus the scalar leakage in \((LPD5)\) is
   bounded above by
   \[
      (T-\gamma)\,
      \Bigl(\min_{1\le i\le b}\|\Pi_u^\perp e_i\|_2\Bigr) r_u^\perp
      \tag{LPL8}
   \]
   whenever \(T\ge\gamma\).  Equivalently one may use the averaged witness
   \(b^{-1}\mathbf 1_{bq}\), giving the bound
   \[
      (T-\gamma)\frac{\|\Pi_u^\perp\mathbf 1_{bq}\|_2}{b}\,r_u^\perp .
      \tag{LPL9}
   \]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Let \(a=a_u(h)=G_u^+v_u(h)\).  Since \(A_u^\top\ell_u=\mathbf 1_N\),
   \[
      \kappa_u(h)=\mathbf 1_N^\top a
      =
      \ip{\ell_u}{A_ua}
      =
      \ip{\ell_u}{\Pi_u h}.
      \tag{LPL10}
   \]
   By the balance assumption \(\ip{\ell_u}{h}=0\), and
   \(h=\Pi_u h+\Pi_u^\perp h\), this equals
   \[
      \kappa_u(h)
      =
      -\ip{\ell_u}{\Pi_u^\perp h}
      =
      -\ip{\Pi_u^\perp\ell_u}{\Pi_u^\perp h},
   \]
   proving \((LPL2)\).  Cauchy's inequality gives \((LPL4)\), and
   \((LPL5)\) follows when \(\Pi_u^\perp\ell_u=0\).

   If \(P_u\) satisfies \((LPL6)\), then for any
   \(h=z-\iota(a_u(z))\in E_u\),
   \[
      \ip{e_i}{h}
      =
      \sum_a z_{i,a}-1
      =
      0.
   \]
   Also every codeword has exactly one symbol in coordinate \(i\), so
   \(A_u^\top e_i=\mathbf 1_N\).  Hence each \(e_i\) satisfies \((LPL1)\), and
   \((LPL8)\) follows from \((LPL4)\).  The averaged witness
   \(b^{-1}\mathbf 1_{bq}=b^{-1}\sum_i e_i\) also satisfies \((LPL1)\), giving
   \((LPL9)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Frontier-gap cancellation for negative coefficients]
   \label{cor:frontier-gap-negative-coefficients}
   Work in the setting of
   \cref{cor:shifted-overlap-coefficient-certificate}, and put
   \[
      \beta_u(h)=\sum_{j=1}^Na_u(h)_j^- .
      \tag{LPN1}
   \]
   Assume that
   \[
      \beta_u(h)\le1
      \qquad(h\in E_u)
      \tag{LPN2}
   \]
   for every branch-and-bound node \(u\).  Define the internal-gap functional
   \[
      J_{u,\gamma}(w)
      =
      \sup_{h\in E_u}
      \left[
         (T-\gamma)\kappa_u(h)
         +
         \sum_{j=1}^N a_u(h)_j^-\bigl(M(u)-W(c_j)\bigr)
      \right].
      \tag{LPN3}
   \]
   Then, on the false-survivor event \(M(u)<T-\gamma\),
   \[
      \exp(\lambda(M(u)-T))
      \exp\!\left(\lambda D_{u,\gamma}(w)\right)
      \le
      e^{-\lambda\gamma}\exp\!\left(\lambda J_{u,\gamma}(w)\right).
      \tag{LPN4}
   \]
   Consequently, the projected-bias condition \((LPA1)\) follows from
   \[
      e^{-\lambda\gamma}
      \sum_u
      \E\!\left[
         \mathbf 1_{\{M(u)<T-\gamma\}}
         \exp\!\left(
            \lambda J_{u,\gamma}(w)
            +\lambda\omega_u^\perp
            +\frac{\lambda^2(r_u^\perp)^2}{2}
         \right)
      \right]
      \le
      \log^{O(1)}n\cdot \E N_{\ge T}.
      \tag{LPN5}
   \]
   If scalar leakage is killed or absorbed using
   \cref{cor:balance-witness-scalar-leakage}, the only projected-bias term
   left in \(J_{u,\gamma}\) is the negative coefficient mass against the
   \emph{internal} gaps \(M(u)-W(c_j)\) within the same branch subcode.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   On the event \(M(u)<T-\gamma\), write
   \[
      \theta_u=T-\gamma-M(u)>0.
      \tag{LPN6}
   \]
   For every \(h\in E_u\),
   \[
      T-\gamma-W(c_j)=\theta_u+M(u)-W(c_j),
      \tag{LPN7}
   \]
   so
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      &M(u)-T+
      \left[
         (T-\gamma)\kappa_u(h)
         +\beta_u(h)\theta_u
         +\sum_{j=1}^Na_u(h)_j^-\bigl(M(u)-W(c_j)\bigr)
      \right]\\
      &\qquad=
      -\gamma
      +(\beta_u(h)-1)\theta_u
      +(T-\gamma)\kappa_u(h)
      +\sum_{j=1}^Na_u(h)_j^-\bigl(M(u)-W(c_j)\bigr)\\
      &\qquad\le
      -\gamma+J_{u,\gamma}(w),
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{LPN8}
   \]
   where the last line uses \((LPN2)\).  Taking the supremum over
   \(h\in E_u\) and exponentiating gives \((LPN4)\).
   Finally, \cref{cor:shifted-overlap-coefficient-certificate} lets us replace
   \(B_u\) by \(D_{u,\gamma}\) in \((LPA1)\), and then \((LPN4)\) gives the
   sufficient condition \((LPN5)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Leader-shift near-leader certificate]
   \label{cor:leader-shift-near-leader-certificate}
   Work in the setting of
   \cref{cor:shifted-overlap-coefficient-certificate}.  For a nonempty branch
   subcode \(C_u=\{c_1,\ldots,c_N\}\), put
   \[
      \widehat J_u(w)
      =
      \sup_{h\in E_u}
      \left[
         M(u)\kappa_u(h)
         +
         \sum_{j=1}^N a_u(h)_j^-\bigl(M(u)-W(c_j)\bigr)
      \right].
      \tag{LPM1}
   \]
   If, for some \(\lambda>0\) and \(A_\lambda\ge1\), almost surely for every
   branch-and-bound node \(u\),
   \[
      \exp\!\left(
         \lambda\widehat J_u(w)
         +\lambda\omega_u^\perp
         +\frac{\lambda^2(r_u^\perp)^2}{2}
      \right)
      \le A_\lambda,
      \tag{LPM2}
   \]
   then the conditional tilted-excess bound \((LPT2)\) holds with this
   \(A_\lambda\).  Consequently, at the Gaussian tilt \(\lambda=T/b\), a
   polylogarithmic bound in \((LPM2)\) gives the LP/SA decoder
   polylogarithmic expected overhead.

   A concrete sufficient condition is the following.  Suppose that for each
   node \(u\) there are bounds \(R_u,\Delta_u\ge0\) such that, for every
   \(h\in E_u\),
   \[
      M(u)\kappa_u(h)\le R_u,
      \qquad
      \sum_j a_u(h)_j^-\le1,
      \tag{LPM3}
   \]
   and all negative coefficient mass is supported on the \(\Delta_u\)-near
   leaders,
   \[
      a_u(h)_j^->0
      \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
      W(c_j)\ge M(u)-\Delta_u .
      \tag{LPM4}
   \]
   Then \(\widehat J_u(w)\le R_u+\Delta_u\).  Hence \((LPM2)\) follows from
   \[
      \exp\!\left(
         \lambda(R_u+\Delta_u)
         +\lambda\omega_u^\perp
         +\frac{\lambda^2(r_u^\perp)^2}{2}
      \right)
      \le A_\lambda
      \qquad(u\in\mathcal T).
      \tag{LPM5}
   \]
   In the exact-balance case \(\kappa_u(h)=0\), this reduces the projected
   part of the terminal LP/SA theorem to proving that negative Gram
   coefficients of anchored pseudocodeword excesses are carried only by true
   codewords whose scores are within \(\Delta_u\) of the local maximum.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   In \cref{cor:shifted-overlap-coefficient-certificate}, take
   \(\Theta_u=M(u)\).  Since \(M(u)\ge W(c_j)\) for every \(c_j\in C_u\), the
   shifted bound gives
   \[
      B_u(w)
      \le
      \widehat J_u(w).
      \tag{LPM6}
   \]
   Therefore \((LPM2)\) implies the projection certificate \((LPG4)\), and
   \cref{cor:conditional-gaussian-projection-certificate} gives the
   conditional tilted-excess bound.  The overhead conclusion follows from
   \cref{cor:conditional-tilted-excess-certificate}.

   Under \((LPM3)\)--\((LPM4)\), every nonzero term in the negative part
   satisfies \(0\le M(u)-W(c_j)\le\Delta_u\), so
   \[
      \sum_j a_u(h)_j^-\bigl(M(u)-W(c_j)\bigr)
      \le
      \Delta_u\sum_j a_u(h)_j^-
      \le
      \Delta_u .
      \tag{LPM7}
   \]
   Together with \(M(u)\kappa_u(h)\le R_u\), this proves
   \(\widehat J_u(w)\le R_u+\Delta_u\), and \((LPM5)\) implies \((LPM2)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Boltzmann negative-tail certificate]
   \label{cor:boltzmann-negative-tail-certificate}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:leader-shift-near-leader-certificate}, and assume
   \[
      \sum_j a_u(h)_j^-\le1
      \qquad(h\in E_u)
      \tag{LMQ1}
   \]
   for every branch-and-bound node \(u\).  For \(\lambda>0\), define the
   internal negative-tail partition function
   \[
      \mathcal Z_{u,\lambda}(w)
      =
      \sup_{h\in E_u}
      \exp\!\bigl(\lambda M(u)\kappa_u(h)\bigr)
      \left(
         1+
         \sum_{j=1}^N
         a_u(h)_j^-
         \exp\!\bigl(\lambda(M(u)-W(c_j))\bigr)
      \right).
      \tag{LMQ2}
   \]
   If, almost surely for every node \(u\),
   \[
      \mathcal Z_{u,\lambda}(w)
      \exp\!\left(
         \lambda\omega_u^\perp
         +\frac{\lambda^2(r_u^\perp)^2}{2}
      \right)
      \le A_\lambda ,
      \tag{LMQ3}
   \]
   then the conditional tilted-excess bound \((LPT2)\) holds with
   \(A_\lambda\).  Hence, at \(\lambda=T/b\), a polylogarithmic bound in
   \((LMQ3)\) gives polylogarithmic expected overhead for the LP/SA decoder.

   In particular, if for some \(R_u,\Xi_u\ge0\),
   \[
      M(u)\kappa_u(h)\le R_u,
      \qquad
      \sum_j
      a_u(h)_j^-\exp\!\bigl(\lambda(M(u)-W(c_j))\bigr)
      \le \Xi_u
      \tag{LMQ4}
   \]
   for every \(h\in E_u\), then
   \[
      \mathcal Z_{u,\lambda}(w)\le e^{\lambda R_u}(1+\Xi_u).
      \tag{LMQ5}
   \]
   The hard near-leader condition \((LPM4)\) is the special case
   \(\Xi_u\le e^{\lambda\Delta_u}\).  Thus one does not need literal support
   on near leaders; it is enough that the negative coefficient mass has small
   Boltzmann tail under the internal gaps \(M(u)-W(c_j)\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Fix \(h\in E_u\), and write
   \[
      b_j=a_u(h)_j^-,
      \qquad
      g_j=M(u)-W(c_j)\ge0,
      \qquad
      \beta=\sum_j b_j\le1 .
      \tag{LMQ6}
   \]
   By convexity of the exponential, adding mass \(1-\beta\) at the zero gap
   gives
   \[
      \exp\!\left(\lambda\sum_j b_jg_j\right)
      \le
      (1-\beta)+\sum_j b_j e^{\lambda g_j}
      \le
      1+\sum_j b_j e^{\lambda g_j}.
      \tag{LMQ7}
   \]
   Therefore
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      \exp\!\left(
         \lambda M(u)\kappa_u(h)
         +\lambda\sum_j a_u(h)_j^-\bigl(M(u)-W(c_j)\bigr)
      \right)
      &\le
      \exp\!\bigl(\lambda M(u)\kappa_u(h)\bigr)\\
      &\quad\cdot
      \left(
         1+\sum_j
         a_u(h)_j^-
         e^{\lambda(M(u)-W(c_j))}
      \right).
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{LMQ8}
   \]
   Taking the supremum over \(h\in E_u\) gives
   \[
      e^{\lambda\widehat J_u(w)}
      \le
      \mathcal Z_{u,\lambda}(w).
      \tag{LMQ9}
   \]
   Thus \((LMQ3)\) implies \((LPM2)\), and the first claim follows from
   \cref{cor:leader-shift-near-leader-certificate}.

   The bound \((LMQ5)\) follows immediately from \((LMQ4)\).  If
   \((LPM4)\) holds and \(\sum_j a_u(h)_j^-\le1\), then every term with
   nonzero negative coefficient has \(g_j\le\Delta_u\), so the second
   inequality in \((LMQ4)\) holds with \(\Xi_u=e^{\lambda\Delta_u}\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Cumulative internal-tail certificate]
   \label{cor:cumulative-internal-tail-certificate}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:boltzmann-negative-tail-certificate}.  For \(h\in E_u\), define
   the cumulative negative mass below the local leader by
   \[
      A_{u,h}(s)
      =
      \sum_{\substack{j:\\ M(u)-W(c_j)\ge s}} a_u(h)_j^-,
      \qquad s\ge0 .
      \tag{LMR1}
   \]
   Assume \(\sum_j a_u(h)_j^-\le1\).  Then
   \[
      \sum_j
      a_u(h)_j^-\exp\!\bigl(\lambda(M(u)-W(c_j))\bigr)
      \le
      1+\lambda\int_0^\infty e^{\lambda s}A_{u,h}(s)\,ds .
      \tag{LMR2}
   \]
   Consequently, if for every \(h\in E_u\),
   \[
      M(u)\kappa_u(h)\le R_u,
      \qquad
      \lambda\int_0^\infty e^{\lambda s}A_{u,h}(s)\,ds\le I_u ,
      \tag{LMR3}
   \]
   then
   \[
      \mathcal Z_{u,\lambda}(w)
      \le
      e^{\lambda R_u}(2+I_u).
      \tag{LMR4}
   \]
   In particular, the exponential tail condition
   \[
      A_{u,h}(s)\le C_u e^{-(\lambda+\eta_u)s}
      \qquad(s\ge0,\ h\in E_u)
      \tag{LMR5}
   \]
   gives
   \[
      \mathcal Z_{u,\lambda}(w)
      \le
      e^{\lambda R_u}\left(2+\frac{\lambda C_u}{\eta_u}\right).
      \tag{LMR6}
   \]

   There is also a finite dyadic form.  For a mesh \(\delta>0\), set
   \[
      B_{u,h,k}
      =
      \sum_{\substack{j:\\ k\delta\le M(u)-W(c_j)<(k+1)\delta}}
      a_u(h)_j^- .
      \tag{LMR7}
   \]
   If
   \[
      M(u)\kappa_u(h)\le R_u,
      \qquad
      \sum_{k\ge0} e^{\lambda(k+1)\delta}B_{u,h,k}\le I_u
      \tag{LMR8}
   \]
   for every \(h\in E_u\), then
   \[
      \mathcal Z_{u,\lambda}(w)\le e^{\lambda R_u}(1+I_u).
      \tag{LMR9}
   \]
   Hence it is enough to prove the cumulative dyadic decay
   \[
      A_{u,h}(k\delta)\le C_u e^{-(\lambda+\eta_u)k\delta}
      \qquad(k=0,1,\ldots)
      \tag{LMR10}
   \]
   because then \((LMR8)\) holds with
   \[
      I_u=
      \frac{e^{\lambda\delta}C_u}{1-e^{-\eta_u\delta}} .
      \tag{LMR11}
   \]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Put \(g_j=M(u)-W(c_j)\ge0\) and \(b_j=a_u(h)_j^-\).  The layer-cake identity
   for the finite nonnegative family \(\{g_j\}\) gives
   \[
      e^{\lambda g_j}
      =
      1+\lambda\int_0^{g_j}e^{\lambda s}\,ds .
      \tag{LMR12}
   \]
   Summing with weights \(b_j\) yields
   \[
      \sum_j b_j e^{\lambda g_j}
      =
      \sum_j b_j
      +
      \lambda\int_0^\infty
      e^{\lambda s}
      \sum_{j:g_j\ge s}b_j\,ds .
      \tag{LMR13}
   \]
   Since \(\sum_j b_j\le1\), this is \((LMR2)\).  Combining \((LMR2)\) with
   \((LMQ2)\) proves \((LMR4)\), and \((LMR6)\) follows by integrating
   \(e^{-\eta_us}\).

   For the dyadic statement,
   \[
      \sum_j b_je^{\lambda g_j}
      \le
      \sum_{k\ge0}e^{\lambda(k+1)\delta}B_{u,h,k}.
      \tag{LMR14}
   \]
   Thus \((LMR8)\) implies \((LMR9)\).  Finally \(B_{u,h,k}\le A_{u,h}(k\delta)\),
   so \((LMR10)\) gives
   \[
      \sum_{k\ge0}e^{\lambda(k+1)\delta}B_{u,h,k}
      \le
      e^{\lambda\delta}C_u\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\eta_uk\delta}
      =
      \frac{e^{\lambda\delta}C_u}{1-e^{-\eta_u\delta}},
   \]
   proving \((LMR11)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Support-function form of internal tails]
   \label{cor:support-function-internal-tail-certificate}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:gram-projection-certificate} and
   \cref{cor:cumulative-internal-tail-certificate}.
   For \(s\ge0\), let
   \[
      S_u(s)=\{j:\ M(u)-W(c_j)\ge s\},
      \qquad
      \mathcal R_u(s)=\{r\in[0,1]^N:\ r_j=0\text{ for }j\notin S_u(s)\}.
      \tag{LMS1}
   \]
   Define the anchored-excess support function
   \[
      \Phi_u(y)=\sup_{h\in E_u}\ip{y}{h}.
      \tag{LMS2}
   \]
   Then, for every \(s\ge0\),
   \[
      \sup_{h\in E_u}A_{u,h}(s)
      =
      \sup_{r\in\mathcal R_u(s)}
      \Phi_u\!\left(-A_uG_u^+r\right).
      \tag{LMS3}
   \]
   Consequently, the cumulative exponential tail condition \((LMR5)\) follows
   from the finite support-function bounds
   \[
      \sup_{r\in\mathcal R_u(s)}
      \Phi_u\!\left(-A_uG_u^+r\right)
      \le
      C_u e^{-(\lambda+\eta_u)s}
      \qquad(s\ge0).
      \tag{LMS4}
   \]
   Likewise, the dyadic condition \((LMR10)\) follows from the finite family of
   bounds
   \[
      \sup_{r\in\mathcal R_u(k\delta)}
      \Phi_u\!\left(-A_uG_u^+r\right)
      \le
      C_u e^{-(\lambda+\eta_u)k\delta}
      \qquad(k=0,1,\ldots).
      \tag{LMS5}
   \]

   Thus the remaining negative-tail theorem can be phrased without explicit
   negative parts of \(G_u^+v_u(h)\): every low-score down-set \(S_u(s)\) and
   every fractional selector \(r\) on it must have small support over the
   anchored excess set in the direction \(-A_uG_u^+r\).  If such a bound
   fails, the maximizing \(r\) is an explicit separating objective for the
   local LP/SA relaxation.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   For fixed \(h\in E_u\), write \(a=a_u(h)=G_u^+A_u^\top h\).  Since
   \(a_j^-=\max\{-a_j,0\}\),
   \[
      A_{u,h}(s)
      =
      \sum_{j\in S_u(s)}a_j^-
      =
      \sup_{r\in\mathcal R_u(s)}\left(-\sum_j r_ja_j\right).
      \tag{LMS6}
   \]
   Using the symmetry of \(G_u^+\),
   \[
      \sum_j r_ja_j
      =
      r^\top G_u^+A_u^\top h
      =
