   Applying \(A_u^\top\) to \((LNQ4)\) gives
   \[
      A_u^\top d_\tau(\mu)+A_u^\top K_\tau(\alpha)+G_u\theta=0.
      \tag{LNQ12}
   \]
   By the definitions of \(d_\tau\), \(K_\tau\), and \(h_\tau\),
   \(A_u^\top d_\tau(\mu)=h_\tau(\mu)\) and
   \(A_u^\top K_\tau(\alpha)=h_\tau(\alpha)\), proving \((LNQ6)\).  Conversely,
   if \((LNQ6)\) holds, then
   \(A_u^\top(d_\tau(\mu)+K_\tau(\alpha)+A_u\theta)=0\), which is equivalent to
   membership in \(L_u^\perp\).  Thus the Gram-system form is equivalent to
   \((LNQ3)\).

   Finally, applying \((LNQ3)\) with
   \(\omega=\Omega_u\) in every chart and using
   \cref{cor:min-chart-band-residual-verifier} proves the last assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Off-chart majorant form of the min-chart certificate]
   \label{cor:off-chart-majorant-min-chart}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:min-chart-deficit-transport-dual}.  For a chart \(\tau\), write
   \(\zeta\ge_\tau\mu\) for \(\zeta\in\R_+^{bq}\) when
   \[
      \zeta_{i,a}\ge\mu_{i,a}
      \qquad(i\in[b],\ a\ne\tau_i),
      \tag{LNR1}
   \]
   with no constraint on the unused chart-minimum coordinates
   \(\zeta_{i,\tau_i}\).  Then
   \(\mathsf B_{u,\tau}(\mu,\omega)\) is equal to
   \[
      \inf
      \left\{
         \sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\theta_j^+:
         \begin{array}{l}
            \zeta\ge_\tau\mu,\quad \sum_j\theta_j=0,\\
            h_\tau(\zeta)+G_u\theta=0
         \end{array}
      \right\}.
      \tag{LNR2}
   \]
   Consequently \((LNO2)\) holds with \(\Omega_u,\Xi_u\) if and only if, for
   every chart \(\tau\), there is an off-chart majorant \(\zeta^\tau\ge_\tau
   \mu_u\) and a zero-total coefficient vector \(\theta^\tau\) such that
   \[
      h_\tau(\zeta^\tau)+G_u\theta^\tau=0,
      \qquad
      \sum_j\Omega_{u,j}(\theta^\tau_j)^+\le\Xi_u .
      \tag{LNR3}
   \]
   Thus the residual-localization target can be stated without the auxiliary
   upward-move variables: each chart asks for a nonnegative enlargement of the
   residual off the minimum symbols whose chart-incidence score vector has a
   cheap zero-total Gram decomposition.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   For any \(\eta\ge0\),
   \[
      d_\tau(\eta)=K_\tau(\eta)
      \tag{LNR4}
   \]
   because both vectors have coordinate \(a\ne\tau_i\) equal to \(\eta_{i,a}\)
   and coordinate \(\tau_i\) equal to \(-\sum_{a\ne\tau_i}\eta_{i,a}\).  Hence
   \[
      d_\tau(\mu)+K_\tau(\alpha)=K_\tau(\mu+\alpha),
      \tag{LNR5}
   \]
   and
   \[
      h_\tau(\mu)+h_\tau(\alpha)=h_\tau(\mu+\alpha).
      \tag{LNR6}
   \]
   Since \(K_\tau\) and \(h_\tau\) ignore the chart-minimum coordinates, the
   possible vectors \(\mu+\alpha\) with \(\alpha\ge0\) are exactly the
   off-chart majorants \(\zeta\ge_\tau\mu\), up to arbitrary values on
   \(a=\tau_i\).  Substituting this into \((LNQ6)\) and the objective in
   \((LNQ3)\) proves \((LNR2)\).  Applying this equivalence with
   \(\omega=\Omega_u\) for all charts and using
   \cref{cor:min-chart-deficit-transport-dual} proves \((LNR3)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Canonical zero-sum inverse certificate]
   \label{cor:canonical-zero-sum-min-chart}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:off-chart-majorant-min-chart}.  Let
   \[
      Z_N=\{\theta\in\R^N:\mathbf 1_N^\top\theta=0\},
      \qquad
      \mathcal L_{u,0}=G_u Z_N,
      \tag{LNS1}
   \]
   and let \(G_{u,0}^\dagger:\mathcal L_{u,0}\to Z_N\) denote the
   Moore--Penrose inverse of the linear map \(G_u:Z_N\to\mathcal L_{u,0}\).
   Thus \(G_{u,0}^\dagger v\) is the minimum-norm zero-sum solution of
   \(G_u\theta=v\).  If, for every chart \(\tau\), there is a nonnegative
   off-chart majorant \(\zeta^\tau\ge_\tau\mu_u\) such that
   \[
      h_\tau(\zeta^\tau)\in\mathcal L_{u,0}
      \tag{LNS2}
   \]
   and
   \[
      \sum_j\Omega_{u,j}
      \left(-G_{u,0}^\dagger h_\tau(\zeta^\tau)\right)_j^+
      \le \Xi_u,
      \tag{LNS3}
   \]
   then the band-limited residual condition \((LNO2)\) holds.

   In particular, suppose the chart score vectors are balanced,
   \[
      h_\tau(\eta)\in Z_N
      \qquad(\eta\in\R_+^{bq},\ \tau\in[q]^b),
      \tag{LNS4}
   \]
   and the codeword Gram matrix is scalar on the zero-sum subspace,
   \[
      G_u\theta=\chi_u\theta
      \qquad(\theta\in Z_N)
      \tag{LNS5}
   \]
   for some \(\chi_u>0\).  Then \((LNO2)\) follows from the scalar lower-tail
   checks
   \[
      \frac1{\chi_u}
      \sum_j\Omega_{u,j}\bigl(h_\tau(\zeta^\tau)_j\bigr)^-
      \le \Xi_u
      \qquad(\tau\in[q]^b)
      \tag{LNS6}
   \]
   for some nonnegative off-chart majorants \(\zeta^\tau\ge_\tau\mu_u\).
   The balance condition \((LNS4)\) is implied by coordinate-symbol balance of
   the subcode:
   \[
      |\{j:c_j(i)=a\}|=|\{j:c_j(i)=a'\}|
      \qquad(i\in[b],\ a,a'\in[q]).
      \tag{LNS7}
   \]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   If \((LNS2)\) holds, set
   \[
      \theta^\tau=-G_{u,0}^\dagger h_\tau(\zeta^\tau).
      \tag{LNS8}
   \]
   Then \(\theta^\tau\in Z_N\) and
   \(G_u\theta^\tau=-h_\tau(\zeta^\tau)\), so the Gram equation in
   \((LNR3)\) holds.  The positive-mass bound is exactly \((LNS3)\).  Hence
   \cref{cor:off-chart-majorant-min-chart} gives \((LNO2)\).

   Under \((LNS4)\)--\((LNS5)\), every \(h_\tau(\zeta^\tau)\) lies in
   \(\mathcal L_{u,0}=Z_N\), and
   \[
      -G_{u,0}^\dagger h_\tau(\zeta^\tau)
      =
      -\chi_u^{-1}h_\tau(\zeta^\tau).
      \tag{LNS9}
   \]
   Thus \((LNS3)\) becomes \((LNS6)\).  Finally, \((LNS7)\) implies
   \((LNS4)\) by summing the definition of \(h_\tau(\eta)_j\) over \(j\):
   for each coordinate \(i\), the number of codewords with symbol \(a\) equals
   the number with symbol \(\tau_i\), so each summand has zero total.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Perturbed scalar zero-sum certificate]
   \label{cor:perturbed-scalar-zero-sum-min-chart}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:canonical-zero-sum-min-chart}.  Suppose the chart score vectors
   are balanced as in \((LNS4)\), and suppose \(G_u\) preserves \(Z_N\) and is
   spectrally close to a scalar there:
   \[
      G_u Z_N\subseteq Z_N,
      \qquad
      \left\|\chi_u^{-1}G_u-I_{Z_N}\right\|_{Z_N\to Z_N}
      \le \delta_u<1
      \tag{LNT1}
   \]
   for some \(\chi_u>0\).  Then \((LNO2)\) follows if, for every chart
   \(\tau\), there is a nonnegative off-chart majorant
   \(\zeta^\tau\ge_\tau\mu_u\) such that, writing
   \(v^\tau=h_\tau(\zeta^\tau)\),
   \[
      \frac1{\chi_u}\sum_j\Omega_{u,j}(v^\tau_j)^-
      +
      \frac{\delta_u}{\chi_u(1-\delta_u)}
      \|\Omega_u\|_2\,\|v^\tau\|_2
      \le \Xi_u .
      \tag{LNT2}
   \]

   Thus the exact diagonal model in \((LNS5)\) is stable: a spectral Gram
   error \(\delta_u\) only adds the weighted perturbation term in \((LNT2)\).
   Coordinate-symbol balance implies \((LNS4)\), and together with constant
   row sums of \(G_u\) it gives the invariant subspace
   \(G_uZ_N\subseteq Z_N\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   By balance, \(v^\tau\in Z_N\).  The spectral assumption implies that
   \(G_u:Z_N\to Z_N\) is invertible and
   \[
      \left\|G_{u,0}^{-1}-\chi_u^{-1}I_{Z_N}\right\|_{Z_N\to Z_N}
      \le
      \frac{\delta_u}{\chi_u(1-\delta_u)} .
      \tag{LNT3}
   \]
   Indeed, write \(G_u=\chi_u(I+E)\) on \(Z_N\) with \(\|E\|\le\delta_u\)
   and use
   \(\|(I+E)^{-1}-I\|\le\delta_u/(1-\delta_u)\).

   For the canonical inverse choice
   \(\theta^\tau=-G_{u,0}^{-1}v^\tau\), decompose
   \[
      \theta^\tau
      =
      -\chi_u^{-1}v^\tau
      -
      \left(G_{u,0}^{-1}-\chi_u^{-1}I_{Z_N}\right)v^\tau .
      \tag{LNT4}
   \]
   Using \((a+b)^+\le a^+ + |b|\), Cauchy--Schwarz, and \((LNT3)\),
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      \sum_j\Omega_{u,j}(\theta^\tau_j)^+
      &\le
      \frac1{\chi_u}\sum_j\Omega_{u,j}(v^\tau_j)^-
      +
      \sum_j\Omega_{u,j}
      \left|
      \left(\left(G_{u,0}^{-1}-\chi_u^{-1}I_{Z_N}\right)v^\tau\right)_j
      \right| \\
      &\le
      \frac1{\chi_u}\sum_j\Omega_{u,j}(v^\tau_j)^-
      +
      \frac{\delta_u}{\chi_u(1-\delta_u)}
      \|\Omega_u\|_2\,\|v^\tau\|_2 .
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{LNT5}
   \]
   Hence \((LNT2)\) implies the canonical inverse bound \((LNS3)\), and
   \cref{cor:canonical-zero-sum-min-chart} proves \((LNO2)\).

   The final assertions are the same balance calculation as in
   \cref{cor:canonical-zero-sum-min-chart}.  Constant row sums are equivalent
   to \(G_u\mathbf 1_N\) being proportional to \(\mathbf 1_N\), and since
   \(G_u\) is symmetric this is equivalent to \(Z_N\) being invariant.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Range-restricted zero-sum inverse certificate]
   \label{cor:range-restricted-zero-sum-min-chart}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:canonical-zero-sum-min-chart}.  Let
   \(\mathcal V_u\subseteq Z_N\cap\mathcal L_{u,0}\) be a set of admissible
   chart-score vectors.  Suppose that, for every \(v\in\mathcal V_u\), we have
   selected a zero-sum right inverse \(P_u(v)\in Z_N\) satisfying
   \[
      G_uP_u(v)=v,
      \qquad
      \left\|P_u(v)-\chi_u^{-1}v\right\|_2
      \le \varepsilon_u\|v\|_2
      \tag{LNU1}
   \]
   for some \(\chi_u>0\) and \(\varepsilon_u\ge0\).  If, for every chart
   \(\tau\), there is a nonnegative off-chart majorant
   \(\zeta^\tau\ge_\tau\mu_u\) such that \(v^\tau=h_\tau(\zeta^\tau)\in
   \mathcal V_u\) and
   \[
      \frac1{\chi_u}\sum_j\Omega_{u,j}(v^\tau_j)^-
      +
      \varepsilon_u\|\Omega_u\|_2\,\|v^\tau\|_2
      \le \Xi_u ,
      \tag{LNU2}
   \]
   then the band-limited residual condition \((LNO2)\) holds.

   This is the form needed for large code panels.  It does not require
   \(G_u\) to be invertible, or close to scalar, on all of \(Z_N\); it only asks
   for a controlled right inverse on the chart-score vectors actually used by
   the residual certificate.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   For a chart \(\tau\), set
   \[
      \theta^\tau=-P_u(v^\tau).
      \tag{LNU3}
   \]
   Then \(\theta^\tau\in Z_N\) and
   \(G_u\theta^\tau=-v^\tau=-h_\tau(\zeta^\tau)\), so the Gram equation in
   \((LNR3)\) holds.  Write
   \(P_u(v^\tau)=\chi_u^{-1}v^\tau+e^\tau\), where
   \(\|e^\tau\|_2\le\varepsilon_u\|v^\tau\|_2\).  Since
   \((a+b)^+\le a^+ + |b|\),
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      \sum_j\Omega_{u,j}(\theta^\tau_j)^+
      &=
      \sum_j\Omega_{u,j}\bigl(-\chi_u^{-1}v^\tau_j-e^\tau_j\bigr)^+ \\
      &\le
      \frac1{\chi_u}\sum_j\Omega_{u,j}(v^\tau_j)^-
      +
      \|\Omega_u\|_2\|e^\tau\|_2 \\
      &\le \Xi_u .
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{LNU4}
   \]
   Hence \((LNR3)\) holds for every chart, and
   \cref{cor:off-chart-majorant-min-chart} proves \((LNO2)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Dual form of the chart-majorant lower tail]
   \label{cor:chart-majorant-lower-tail-dual}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:canonical-zero-sum-min-chart}.  For a chart \(\tau\), a
   nonnegative residual budget \(\mu\), and nonnegative prices
   \(\omega\in\R_+^N\), define
   \[
      \mathfrak L_{u,\tau}(\mu,\omega)
      =
      \inf_{\zeta\ge_\tau\mu}
      \sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\bigl(h_\tau(\zeta)_j\bigr)^- .
      \tag{LNV1}
   \]
   For a nonnegative selector \(s\in\R_+^N\), write
   \[
      s_i(a)=\sum_{j:\ c_j(i)=a}s_j .
      \tag{LNV2}
   \]
   Then
   \[
      \mathfrak L_{u,\tau}(\mu,\omega)
      =
      \sup
      \left\{
         -\sum_{j=1}^Ns_jh_\tau(\mu)_j:
         \begin{array}{l}
            0\le s_j\le\omega_j\quad(j=1,\ldots,N),\\
            s_i(a)\le s_i(\tau_i)\quad(i\in[b],\ a\ne\tau_i)
         \end{array}
      \right\}.
      \tag{LNV3}
   \]
   Thus the optimal lower-tail majorant has an explicit dual obstruction: a
   price-capped submeasure on true codewords for which the chart symbol is at
   least as heavy as every competing symbol in every coordinate.

   In the balanced scalar setting \((LNS4)\)--\((LNS5)\), the scalar lower-tail
   check \((LNS6)\) is equivalent to
   \[
      \mathfrak L_{u,\tau}(\mu_u,\Omega_u)\le \chi_u\Xi_u
      \qquad(\tau\in[q]^b).
      \tag{LNV4}
   \]
   Hence a failed scalar residual certificate returns a concrete
   chart-dominated selector \(s\), not an unspecified bad score table.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   The chart-minimum coordinates of \(\zeta\) do not affect \(h_\tau(\zeta)\),
   so write the off-chart variables as
   \[
      \zeta_{i,a}=\mu_{i,a}+\alpha_{i,a},
      \qquad a\ne\tau_i,\quad \alpha_{i,a}\ge0 .
      \tag{LNV5}
   \]
   Let \(g_{i,a}\in\R^N\) be the column
   \[
      g_{i,a}(j)=\mathbf1_{\{c_j(i)=a\}}-\mathbf1_{\{c_j(i)=\tau_i\}} .
      \tag{LNV6}
   \]
   Then
   \[
      h_\tau(\zeta)
      =
      h_\tau(\mu)+\sum_{i,a\ne\tau_i}\alpha_{i,a}g_{i,a}.
      \tag{LNV7}
   \]
   Introducing variables \(t_j\ge0\) for the negative parts, the primal LP in
   \((LNV1)\) is
   \[
      \min\sum_j\omega_jt_j
      \quad\text{subject to}\quad
      t+h_\tau(\mu)+\sum_{i,a\ne\tau_i}\alpha_{i,a}g_{i,a}\ge0,
      \quad t\ge0,\quad\alpha\ge0 .
      \tag{LNV8}
   \]
   Its dual has a nonnegative multiplier \(s_j\) for the displayed lower-bound
   constraints.  The variables \(t_j\ge0\) impose \(s_j\le\omega_j\), while
   the variables \(\alpha_{i,a}\ge0\) impose
   \[
      \sum_js_jg_{i,a}(j)\le0,
      \tag{LNV9}
   \]
   which is exactly \(s_i(a)\le s_i(\tau_i)\).  The dual objective is
   \(-\sum_js_jh_\tau(\mu)_j\).  Linear-programming duality gives \((LNV3)\).
   Finally, in the scalar balanced setting, \((LNS6)\) asks precisely for a
   majorant whose objective in \((LNV1)\) is at most \(\chi_u\Xi_u\), proving
   \((LNV4)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Penalized chart-majorant dual]
   \label{cor:penalized-chart-majorant-dual}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:chart-majorant-lower-tail-dual}.  For \(\rho\ge0\), define
   \[
      \mathfrak P_{u,\tau}(\mu,\omega,\rho)
      =
      \inf_{\zeta\ge_\tau\mu}
      \left\{
         \sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\bigl(h_\tau(\zeta)_j\bigr)^-
         +
         \rho\|h_\tau(\zeta)\|_2
      \right\}.
      \tag{LNW1}
   \]
   Then
   \[
      \mathfrak P_{u,\tau}(\mu,\omega,\rho)
      =
      \sup
      \left\{
         \ip{r-s}{h_\tau(\mu)}:
         \begin{array}{l}
            0\le s_j\le\omega_j\quad(j=1,\ldots,N),\\
            \|r\|_2\le\rho,\\
            (s-r)_i(a)\le (s-r)_i(\tau_i)
            \quad(i\in[b],\ a\ne\tau_i)
         \end{array}
      \right\},
      \tag{LNW2}
   \]
   where \((s-r)_i(a)=\sum_{j:c_j(i)=a}(s_j-r_j)\).

   Consequently, in the range-restricted inverse certificate, if the selected
   right inverse obeys \((LNU1)\) for every feasible chart score
   \(h_\tau(\zeta)\), then \((LNU2)\) follows from the conic chart checks
   \[
      \mathfrak P_{u,\tau}
      \left(
         \mu_u,\frac{\Omega_u}{\chi_u},
         \varepsilon_u\|\Omega_u\|_2
      \right)
      \le \Xi_u
      \qquad(\tau\in[q]^b).
      \tag{LNW3}
   \]

   The perturbation term therefore has a concrete dual meaning: the
   chart-dominated selector in \((LNV3)\) may be blurred by an \(\ell_2\)-bounded
   signed measure \(r\).  When \(\rho=0\), \((LNW2)\) reduces to \((LNV3)\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Use the same notation \(g_{i,a}\) as in \((LNV6)\).  The support-function
   identities
   \[
      \sum_j\omega_jv_j^-=\sup_{0\le s\le\omega}\ip{-s}{v},
      \qquad
      \rho\|v\|_2=\sup_{\|r\|_2\le\rho}\ip{r}{v}
      \tag{LNW4}
   \]
   give
   \[
      \mathfrak P_{u,\tau}(\mu,\omega,\rho)
      =
      \inf_{\alpha\ge0}
      \sup_{\substack{0\le s\le\omega\\ \|r\|_2\le\rho}}
      \left\langle
         r-s,\,
         h_\tau(\mu)+\sum_{i,a\ne\tau_i}\alpha_{i,a}g_{i,a}
      \right\rangle .
      \tag{LNW5}
   \]
   This is a finite convex program with a strictly feasible epigraph form, so
   conic duality applies.  Minimizing over \(\alpha_{i,a}\ge0\) is finite
   exactly when
   \[
      \ip{r-s}{g_{i,a}}\ge0
      \qquad(i\in[b],\ a\ne\tau_i).
      \tag{LNW6}
   \]
   Since
   \[
      \ip{r-s}{g_{i,a}}
      =
      (r-s)_i(a)-(r-s)_i(\tau_i),
      \tag{LNW7}
   \]
   this is the displayed domination condition
   \((s-r)_i(a)\le(s-r)_i(\tau_i)\).  Under these inequalities, the minimizing
   \(\alpha\) is \(0\), and the remaining objective is
   \(\ip{r-s}{h_\tau(\mu)}\), proving \((LNW2)\).

   Substituting
   \(\omega=\Omega_u/\chi_u\) and
   \(\rho=\varepsilon_u\|\Omega_u\|_2\) in \((LNW1)\) is exactly the left side
   of \((LNU2)\).  Thus \((LNW3)\) supplies the majorants required by
   \cref{cor:range-restricted-zero-sum-min-chart}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Uniform residual budgets and soft chart shadows]
   \label{cor:uniform-residual-chart-shadow}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:chart-majorant-lower-tail-dual}.  Let
   \(\nu\in\R_+^b\) and set
   \[
      \mu^\nu_{i,a}=\nu_i
      \qquad(i\in[b],\ a\in[q]).
      \tag{LNX1}
   \]
   For a selector \(s\in\R_+^N\), write \(S(s)=\sum_j s_j\).  Then
   \[
      h_\tau(\mu^\nu)_j
      =
      \sum_{i=1}^b
      \nu_i\left(1-q\,\mathbf1_{\{c_j(i)=\tau_i\}}\right),
      \tag{LNX2}
   \]
   and
   \[
      \mathfrak L_{u,\tau}(\mu^\nu,\omega)
      =
      \sup
      \left\{
         \sum_{i=1}^b\nu_i\bigl(qs_i(\tau_i)-S(s)\bigr):
         \begin{array}{l}
            0\le s_j\le\omega_j\quad(j=1,\ldots,N),\\
            s_i(a)\le s_i(\tau_i)\quad(i\in[b],\ a\ne\tau_i)
         \end{array}
      \right\}.
      \tag{LNX3}
   \]
   Therefore, in the balanced scalar setting \((LNS4)\)--\((LNS5)\), the
   band-limited residual condition \((LNO2)\) is implied by the soft
   chart-shadow bounds
   \[
      \sup_{\substack{0\le s\le\Omega_u\\
             s_i(a)\le s_i(\tau_i)}}
      \sum_{i=1}^b\nu_i\bigl(qs_i(\tau_i)-S(s)\bigr)
      \le
      \chi_u\Xi_u
      \qquad(\tau\in[q]^b),
      \tag{LNX4}
   \]
   Moreover, if \(\mu^\nu\) is residual-Hall valid in the sense of \((LNO1)\),
   then the residual-budget compiler applies.

   The quantity in \((LNX4)\) is a weighted list-recovery shadow: after choosing
   a price-capped submeasure of codewords, every coordinate is biased toward the
   chart symbol \(\tau_i\), and the objective measures the total excess over
   uniform coordinate mass.  This is the finite combinatorial theorem left by
   the diagonal model.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   For one coordinate \(i\), the definition of \(h_\tau\) gives
   \[
      \sum_{a\in[q]}\nu_i
      \left(
         \mathbf1_{\{c_j(i)=a\}}
         -
         \mathbf1_{\{c_j(i)=\tau_i\}}
      \right)
      =
      \nu_i\left(1-q\,\mathbf1_{\{c_j(i)=\tau_i\}}\right),
      \tag{LNX5}
   \]
   proving \((LNX2)\).  Substituting \((LNX2)\) in the dual objective of
   \((LNV3)\) yields
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      -\sum_js_jh_\tau(\mu^\nu)_j
      &=
      \sum_i\nu_i
      \left(
         q\sum_{j:c_j(i)=\tau_i}s_j-\sum_js_j
      \right) \\
      &=
      \sum_i\nu_i\bigl(qs_i(\tau_i)-S(s)\bigr),
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{LNX6}
   \]
   which proves \((LNX3)\).  If \((LNX4)\) holds, then
   \(\mathfrak L_{u,\tau}(\mu^\nu,\Omega_u)\le\chi_u\Xi_u\) for every chart.
   By \cref{cor:chart-majorant-lower-tail-dual}, this is exactly the scalar
   lower-tail check \((LNS6)\).  Hence
   \cref{cor:canonical-zero-sum-min-chart} proves \((LNO2)\).  The final
   sentence follows by combining this with
   \cref{cor:band-limited-residual-budget-compiler}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Posterior plurality form of soft chart shadows]
   \label{cor:posterior-plurality-chart-shadow}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:uniform-residual-chart-shadow}.  For a nonzero selector
   \(s\in\R_+^N\), define the selector posterior on coordinate \(i\) by
   \[
      \pi_i^s(a)=\frac{s_i(a)}{S(s)},
      \qquad
      S(s)=\sum_j s_j,
      \tag{LNY1}
   \]
   and put
   \[
      \Delta_\nu(s)
      =
      \sum_{i=1}^b\nu_i
      \left(q\max_{a\in[q]}\pi_i^s(a)-1\right).
      \tag{LNY2}
   \]
   Then the soft chart-shadow family \((LNX4)\) is equivalent to the single
   posterior-plurality bound
   \[
      \sup_{0\le s\le\Omega_u}
      S(s)\Delta_\nu(s)
      \le
      \chi_u\Xi_u ,
      \tag{LNY3}
   \]
   with the convention that the term is \(0\) when \(S(s)=0\).

   Moreover, let
   \[
      V_\nu=\sum_{i=1}^b\nu_i,
      \qquad
      \mathcal E_\nu(s)
      =
      \sum_{i=1}^b\nu_i
      \left(
         \sum_{a\in[q]}\pi_i^s(a)^2-\frac1q
      \right).
      \tag{LNY4}
   \]
   Then
   \[
      \Delta_\nu(s)
      \le
      \sqrt{q(q-1)V_\nu\,\mathcal E_\nu(s)} .
      \tag{LNY5}
   \]
   Thus \((LNX4)\), and hence \((LNO2)\) in the balanced scalar setting, follows
   from the collision-energy shadow bound
   \[
      \sup_{\substack{0\le s\le\Omega_u\\ S(s)>0}}
      S(s)\sqrt{q(q-1)V_\nu\,\mathcal E_\nu(s)}
      \le
      \chi_u\Xi_u .
      \tag{LNY6}
   \]

   Finally, if
   \[
      A^\nu_{j,k}
      =
      \sum_{i=1}^b\nu_i\,\mathbf1_{\{c_j(i)=c_k(i)\}},
      \qquad
      B^\nu=A^\nu-\frac{V_\nu}{q}\mathbf1_N\mathbf1_N^\top,
      \tag{LNY7}
   \]
   then
   \[
      \mathcal E_\nu(s)
      =
      \frac1{S(s)^2}
      s^\top B^\nu s .
      \tag{LNY8}
   \]
   Equivalently, the sufficient collision-energy condition \((LNY6)\) is the
   box-restricted quadratic-form bound
   \[
      \sup_{0\le s\le\Omega_u}s^\top B^\nu s
      \le
      \frac{(\chi_u\Xi_u)^2}{q(q-1)V_\nu}.
      \tag{LNY9}
   \]
   Hence the chart-shadow theorem can be attacked as a restricted weighted
   second-moment statement for all price-capped selector measures \(s\le
   \Omega_u\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Fix \(s\ne0\).  If a chart \(\tau\) satisfies the domination constraints in
   \((LNX4)\), then \(\pi_i^s(\tau_i)=\max_a\pi_i^s(a)\) for every \(i\), and
   the objective in \((LNX4)\) equals \(S(s)\Delta_\nu(s)\).  Conversely, for
   any selector \(s\), choosing \(\tau_i\in\arg\max_a\pi_i^s(a)\) makes the
   chart constraints feasible and gives the same value.  Taking suprema proves
   the equivalence with \((LNY3)\).

   For a probability vector \(p\) on \([q]\),
   \[
      \max_ap_a-\frac1q
      \le
      \sqrt{\frac{q-1}{q}}
      \left(\sum_a\left(p_a-\frac1q\right)^2\right)^{1/2}.
      \tag{LNY10}
   \]
   This is sharp for one raised coordinate and all others equal.  Multiplying
   by \(q\), applying it to \(p=\pi_i^s\), and using Cauchy's inequality over
   the weights \(\nu_i\) gives
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      \Delta_\nu(s)
      &\le
      \sqrt{q(q-1)}
      \sum_i\nu_i
      \left(
         \sum_a\left(\pi_i^s(a)-\frac1q\right)^2
      \right)^{1/2} \\
      &\le
      \sqrt{q(q-1)V_\nu
      \sum_i\nu_i
      \left(
         \sum_a\pi_i^s(a)^2-\frac1q
      \right)} ,
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{LNY11}
   \]
   which is \((LNY5)\).  Substituting this bound in \((LNY3)\) proves
   \((LNY6)\).

   The pair form follows by expanding
   \[
      \sum_a\pi_i^s(a)^2
      =
      \frac1{S(s)^2}
      \sum_{j,k:\ c_j(i)=c_k(i)}s_js_k
      \tag{LNY12}
   \]
   and summing over \(i\) with weights \(\nu_i\).  This proves \((LNY8)\), and
   substituting \((LNY8)\) into \((LNY6)\) gives \((LNY9)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Positive-overlap tail certificate for chart shadows]
   \label{cor:positive-overlap-chart-shadow-tail}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:posterior-plurality-chart-shadow}, and write
   \[
      b^\nu_{j,k}=A^\nu_{j,k}-\frac{V_\nu}{q}
      \qquad(j,k\in[N]).
      \tag{LNZ1}
   \]
   For nonnegative prices \(\omega\in\R_+^N\), define the weighted positive
   overlap tail
   \[
      \mathcal C_{\nu,\omega}(t)
      =
      \sum_{j,k=1}^N
      \omega_j\omega_k\,\mathbf1_{\{b^\nu_{j,k}\ge t\}}
      \qquad(t\ge0).
      \tag{LNZ2}
   \]
   If
   \[
      \int_0^\infty \mathcal C_{\nu,\Omega_u}(t)\,dt
      \le
      \frac{(\chi_u\Xi_u)^2}{q(q-1)V_\nu},
      \tag{LNZ3}
   \]
   then the box-restricted quadratic condition \((LNY9)\) holds, hence the
   soft chart-shadow bounds \((LNX4)\) hold in the balanced scalar setting.

   A Laplace sufficient condition is the following: for any \(\eta>0\), if
   \[
      \sum_{j,k=1}^N
      \Omega_{u,j}\Omega_{u,k}
      \mathbf1_{\{b^\nu_{j,k}\ge0\}}
      \exp\!\left(\eta b^\nu_{j,k}\right)
      \le
      \frac{\eta(\chi_u\Xi_u)^2}{q(q-1)V_\nu},
      \tag{LNZ4}
   \]
   then \((LNZ3)\) holds.

   Thus the uniform-budget chart-shadow theorem can be reduced to a weighted
   pair-enumerator estimate: under the internal-gap prices \(\Omega_u\), pairs
   of true codewords with above-random coordinate overlap must have only
   polylogarithmic total tail mass.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   For any selector \(0\le s\le\Omega_u\),
   \[
      s^\top B^\nu s
      =
      \sum_{j,k}s_js_k b^\nu_{j,k}
      \le
      \sum_{j,k}s_js_k(b^\nu_{j,k})_+ .
      \tag{LNZ5}
   \]
   Since all coefficients \(s_js_k\) are nonnegative and \(s\le\Omega_u\),
   layer cake gives
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      \sum_{j,k}s_js_k(b^\nu_{j,k})_+
      &=
      \int_0^\infty
      \sum_{j,k}s_js_k\,\mathbf1_{\{b^\nu_{j,k}\ge t\}}\,dt \\
      &\le
      \int_0^\infty \mathcal C_{\nu,\Omega_u}(t)\,dt .
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{LNZ6}
   \]
   Therefore \((LNZ3)\) implies \((LNY9)\), and
   \cref{cor:posterior-plurality-chart-shadow} gives the chart-shadow
   conclusion.

   For the Laplace form, Markov's inequality gives
   \[
      \mathcal C_{\nu,\Omega_u}(t)
      \le
      e^{-\eta t}
      \sum_{j,k}
      \Omega_{u,j}\Omega_{u,k}
      \mathbf1_{\{b^\nu_{j,k}\ge0\}}
      \exp\!\left(\eta b^\nu_{j,k}\right).
      \tag{LNZ7}
   \]
   Integrating over \(t\ge0\) proves that \((LNZ4)\) implies \((LNZ3)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Singleton shadow obstruction and localized residuals]
   \label{cor:singleton-chart-shadow-obstruction}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:chart-majorant-lower-tail-dual}.  For a nonnegative residual budget
   \(\mu\in\R_+^{bq}\) and a codeword \(c_j\), define its off-codeword residual
   mass
   \[
      \operatorname{off}_\mu(j)
      =
      \sum_{i=1}^b
      \sum_{a\ne c_j(i)}\mu_{i,a}.
      \tag{LOA1}
   \]
   If the chart-majorant lower-tail check
   \[
      \mathfrak L_{u,\tau}(\mu,\omega)\le B
      \qquad(\tau\in[q]^b)
      \tag{LOA2}
   \]
   holds for some nonnegative price vector \(\omega\), then necessarily
   \[
      \omega_j\,\operatorname{off}_\mu(j)\le B
      \qquad(j=1,\ldots,N).
      \tag{LOA3}
   \]
   In particular, for the uniform residual budget \(\mu^\nu_{i,a}=\nu_i\),
   \[
      \operatorname{off}_{\mu^\nu}(j)=(q-1)V_\nu,
      \tag{LOA4}
   \]
   so the soft chart-shadow route with bound \(B=\chi_u\Xi_u\) requires
   \[
      \max_j\omega_j
      \le
      \frac{\chi_u\Xi_u}{(q-1)V_\nu}.
      \tag{LOA5}
   \]

   Thus the uniform-budget diagonal model cannot by itself handle unbounded
   internal-gap prices.  Any polylogarithmic proof using the full prices
   \(\Omega_{u,j}=e^{\lambda(M-W_j)}+\Xi_u\) must either truncate the price
   universe and separately prove that no negative coefficient mass reaches the
   discarded tail, or use residual budgets localized around high-price
   codewords so that \(\operatorname{off}_\mu(j)\) decays like \(1/\Omega_{u,j}\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Fix \(j\), and let \(\tau^j_i=c_j(i)\).  In the dual formula \((LNV3)\), take
   the singleton selector \(s=\omega_je_j\).  It is feasible for the chart
   \(\tau^j\), because in every coordinate its histogram is supported on the
   chart symbol.  Moreover,
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      -s_jh_{\tau^j}(\mu)_j
      &=
      -\omega_j
      \sum_{i=1}^b\sum_{a\in[q]}
      \mu_{i,a}
      \left(
         \mathbf1_{\{c_j(i)=a\}}-1
      \right)\\
      &=
      \omega_j
      \sum_i\sum_{a\ne c_j(i)}\mu_{i,a}
      =
      \omega_j\,\operatorname{off}_\mu(j).
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{LOA6}
   \]
   Since \(\mathfrak L_{u,\tau^j}(\mu,\omega)\) is the supremum over all feasible
   selectors, \((LOA2)\) implies \((LOA3)\).  Formula \((LOA4)\) is immediate
   from the definition of the uniform budget, and \((LOA5)\) follows by taking
   \(B=\chi_u\Xi_u\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Uniform full-price chart-shadow barrier]
   \label{cor:uniform-full-price-chart-shadow-barrier}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:singleton-chart-shadow-obstruction}, and use the full
   internal-gap prices
   \[
      \Omega_{u,j}
      =
      \exp\!\bigl(\lambda(M(u)-W(c_j))\bigr)+\Xi_u .
      \tag{LOA7}
   \]
   For the uniform residual budget \(\mu^\nu_{i,a}=\nu_i\), any scalar
   chart-shadow certificate
   \[
      \mathfrak L_{u,\tau}(\mu^\nu,\Omega_u)\le \chi_u\Xi_u
      \qquad(\tau\in[q]^b)
      \tag{LOA8}
   \]
   must satisfy
   \[
      \chi_u\Xi_u
      \ge
      (q-1)V_\nu
      \left(
         \exp\!\bigl(\lambda(M(u)-\min_jW(c_j))\bigr)+\Xi_u
      \right).
      \tag{LOA9}
   \]
   Hence a uniform-budget proof of the full chart-incidence tail is impossible
   at polylogarithmic cost unless the internal score range obeys
   \[
      \lambda(M(u)-\min_jW(c_j))
      \le
      O\!\left(\log\frac{\chi_u\Xi_u}{(q-1)V_\nu}\right).
      \tag{LOA10}
   \]

   Thus the frozen LP/SA target is not the uniform diagonal model
   \((LNX4)\)--\((LNZ4)\) with the full prices.  The target is
   \((LNN2)\) together with a residual budget localized around high-price
   codewords, as in
   \cref{cor:localized-residual-posterior-mismatch,cor:localized-residual-feasibility-dual,cor:source-localized-residual-lp}.
   Equivalently, one may first prove a separate near-leader certificate that
   removes the far internal-gap tail and then apply the uniform chart-shadow
   bound only to the truncated price universe.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Apply \((LOA5)\) with \(B=\chi_u\Xi_u\) and
   \(\omega=\Omega_u\).  Since the maximum price is attained by a lowest-scoring
   true codeword,
   \[
      \max_j\Omega_{u,j}
      =
      \exp\!\bigl(\lambda(M(u)-\min_jW(c_j))\bigr)+\Xi_u ,
   \]
   which gives \((LOA9)\).  Rearranging gives the range condition
   \((LOA10)\).  The final statement is the contrapositive interpretation:
   when the full internal-gap price range is larger than the allowed
   polylogarithmic budget, the singleton chart already violates the uniform
   residual certificate, so any successful proof must localize the residual
   budget or truncate and pay the far score tail separately.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Frozen target and numerical checkpoint]
   \label{rem:frozen-score-band-target}
   We stop the LP/SA route at the finite score-band condition \((LNN2)\) and
   its chart-incidence lower-tail interface
   \((LNP5)\)--\((LNZ4)\).  Later normal forms are useful only as
   implementation views of the same obligation; they should not be treated as
   progress unless they either prove \((LNN2)\) for a concrete low-rate panel or
   expose a barrier like
   \cref{cor:uniform-full-price-chart-shadow-barrier}.

   The direct finite-score diagnostic is correspondingly small.  For the full
   product-simplex relaxation \(P_u=\Delta_q^b\), the nonlinear maximum in
   \((LNN2)\) becomes finite after choosing both a block-minimum chart and a
   block-maximum chart; each chart pair is an ordinary LP.  The script
   \texttt{impl/score\_band\_lp\_stress.py} enumerates these chart pairs for
   toy panels with a dependency-free simplex solver.  It gives zero gap on the
   full binary cube and exposes the expected unit gap when one binary corner is
   deleted.  On balanced random toy panels, however, the bare product-simplex
   relaxation already violates the polylog-budget version of \((LNN2)\):
   with \(\Xi=(\log N)^3\), the worst observed ratios
   \(\text{gap}/\Xi\) were about \(10.0\) for
   \(N=6,b=3,q=2\), \(2.5\) for \(N=8,b=3,q=2\), and \(3.0\) for
   \(N=9,b=2,q=3\).  Thus the remaining theorem cannot be a statement about the
   coordinate simplex alone.  It must use genuine low-rate LP/SA constraints,
   Tanner structure, or another mechanism that removes these missing-chart
   pseudocodewords.
   The same script now fixes a single candidate source and solves the
   corresponding score-band LP.  This exposes a second barrier: local projection
   checks do not help unless they actually remove the offending integral
   pseudowords.  The length-\(3\) even-parity code has four odd words that pass
   every pair projection, and the worst such word has score-band gap \(1/2\) at
   unit prices.  For the binary random toy panels above, all pair projections
   still left integral local pseudowords attaining exactly the same worst
   \(\text{gap}/\Xi\) ratios as the product-simplex search.  The concrete code
   theorem must therefore be a local list-recovery or Tanner expansion
   statement strong enough to exclude the high-price missing charts, not just
   coordinate balance plus low-order projection consistency.
   There is a useful distinction here: on an \(N=8,b=4,q=2\) toy sweep, all
   triple projections eliminated integral local pseudowords, while the
   product-simplex score-band gap remained.  Once the integral obstruction is
   gone, the next numerical target is the fractional local-marginal LP itself,
   not another integral missing-word search.
   The current diagnostic therefore adds both sampled and exact tiny
   local-marginal checks.  The sampled mode uses integral locally consistent
   words, random unary local-marginal vertices, and the vertices obtained by
   optimizing the score tables returned by the fixed-source band LP.  The exact
   mode works directly in the projected unary source coordinates: for each
   check it forms the convex hull of the allowed local assignments, converts
   that tiny hull to facets, intersects these facet systems with the block
   simplexes, and enumerates the resulting projected-source vertices.  This is
   valid because the fixed-source gap \(\Gamma_u(x;\omega)\) is a supremum of
   linear functions of \(x\), hence attains its maximum over the projected
   local-marginal source polytope on a projected-source vertex.

   In the same \(N=8,b=4,q=2\) triple-projection regime, exact
   projected-source sweeps with no integral local pseudowords had
   product-simplex gaps far above budget but fractional local-marginal gaps
   below budget.  A \(64\)-seed exact scan found \(55\) clean seeds, no clean
   over-budget fractional case, and clean maximum
   \(\text{gap}/\Xi\simeq0.918\) at seed \(24\).  That seed checked \(66045\)
   projected active sets and had \(8\) projected-source vertices.  The overall
   exact local-marginal maximum was \(\text{gap}/\Xi\simeq1.17\), but it
   occurred on a seed with an integral local pseudoword.  The previous sampled
   clean maximum seed \(46\) is also exact-clean: projected-source enumeration
   checked \(58905\) active sets, found \(8\) projected-source vertices, and
   gave \(\text{gap}/\Xi\simeq0.906\), while the product-simplex ratio on that
   seed was about \(6.87\).  The earlier
   local-check basis enumerator found \(145\) local vertices and \(37\)
   projected images for the same panel, but the extra projected images are not
   vertices of the unary source polytope and are unnecessary for maximizing the
   convex fixed-source gap.  The convex-hull
   dominance screen isolates why the product-simplex number is too pessimistic
   but also why dominance mass alone is insufficient.  For the worst seed-\(46\)
   source
   \[
      ((1,0),(1/2,1/2),(1/2,1/2),(1/2,1/2))
   \]
   the true-code hull dominates mass \(3/4\), leaving residual
   \(((1,0),(1,0),(1,0),(1,0))\).  Its residual score-band ratio is about
   \(3.62\), so the localized residual charge is
   \((1/4)\cdot3.62\simeq0.906\), matching the exact source gap and closing
   that source; the global product-simplex residual charge would be
   \((1/4)\cdot6.87\simeq1.72\).  However, another local source,
   \[
      ((1/2,1/2),(1/2,1/2),(0,1),(1/2,1/2)),
   \]
   exposes a sharper finite barrier to the residual-dominance proof route.  In
   the clean seed \(3\) exact scan, this source has score-band ratio about
   \(0.750\), with no integral local pseudoword.  The max-mass true-hull
   residual screen nevertheless leaves residual
   \[
      ((1,0),(1,0),(0,1),(0,1))
   \]
   and charges \((1/4)\cdot5.93\simeq1.48\Xi\).  Thus max-mass residual
   dominance can fail even when the exact projected-source target passes.  The
   remaining structural theorem must either bound the projected-source vertices
   directly, or choose the dominated true-code mass through a genuinely
   score-aware minimax rule; a scalar dominance deficit and a mandatory
   max-mass subtraction are not enough.
   Pairwise checks still
   fail exactly: on the \(N=8,b=3,q=2\) pairwise diagnostic, exact enumeration
   has \(8\) projected-source vertices and reproduces the integral/product-simplex
   gap.  On \(N=12,b=4,q=2\) with triple projections, a \(64\)-seed exact scan
   found \(25\) clean seeds, no clean over-budget fractional case, and clean
   maximum \(\text{gap}/\Xi\simeq0.601\) at seed \(4\).  That seed checked
   \(73815\) active sets and had \(9\) projected-source vertices.  The overall
   exact local-marginal maximum was \(\text{gap}/\Xi\simeq1.62\), again on a
   seed with an integral local pseudoword.
   The first larger exact probe shows that all \((b-1)\)-coordinate projection
   checks are still not enough.  For \(N=10,b=5,q=2\), global halfspace
   deduplication reduces the seed-\(3\) projected source enumeration from
   \(66\) raw halfspaces to \(26\) distinct halfspaces and \(65780\) active
   sets.  An \(8\)-seed exact scan had no integral local pseudowords in any
   seed, but it found one clean over-budget fractional source, at seed \(3\).
   That projected source is
   \[
      ((1/2,1/2),(1/2,1/2),(0,1),(1/2,1/2),(1,0))
   \]
   with score-band ratio \(\text{gap}/\Xi\simeq18.36\).  The source is feasible
   in the original local-marginal equality formulation, so this is not an
   artifact of the projected H-representation.  Thus the next finite barrier is
   no longer hypothetical: after integral pseudowords disappear, weak
   local-projection constraints can still leave a genuinely fractional
   projected-source vertex that violates \((LNN2)\).  Any successful low-rate
   code theorem must use stronger Tanner/SA constraints or prove a structural
   exclusion of this fractional pattern.
   The immediate diagnostic points to the former route.  If the same
   \(4\)-coordinate check marginals are required to agree on their complete
   pairwise overlaps, namely the \(3\)-coordinate intersection marginals, then
   this source is infeasible in the local-marginal LP.  Moreover, optimizing
   the exact separating score table over the overlap-consistent relaxation gives
   no positive gap over the true codeword maximum.  This is not yet a proof of
   \((LNN2)\) for the stronger relaxation, but it identifies the missing
   constraint as overlap consistency rather than another score-band normal
   form.
   A direct sampled closure scan supports this diagnosis.  On the same
   \(N=10,b=5,q=2\) ensemble with all \(4\)-coordinate checks, an overlap-only
   \(64\)-seed run with \(128\) random objectives and six closure rounds had
   \(63\) seeds with no integral local pseudoword.  The clean overlap-consistent
   sampled maximum was exactly zero, with no clean over-budget case, and every
   sampled overlap source had zero unary integrality defect.  The only nonzero
   sampled overlap gap was \(0.293\Xi\) on the non-clean seed, where an integral
   local pseudoword remained.  Thus the next exact target is to prove, or find a
   counterexample to, integrality of the projected unary overlap polytope for a
   concrete low-rate Tanner/SA construction; by
   \cref{cor:projected-unary-integrality-reduction}, projected integrality plus
   integral-pseudoword exclusion would prove \((LNN2)\) for that finite panel.
   To remove the sampling ambiguity, the script now also has an exact
   support-oracle projected-hull diagnostic.  It optimizes arbitrary unary
   source objectives over the overlap LP, enumerates the facets of the currently
   found projected source hull, and re-optimizes each facet normal.  If no facet
   is violated, the found hull is exactly the projected unary overlap polytope.
   On the same \(N=10,b=5,q=2\) leave-one-out ensemble, this exact diagnostic
   certified all \(64\) seeds.  The \(63\) clean seeds had only integral
   projected vertices, no integral pseudowords, and exact score-band gap zero.
   The only nonzero exact overlap gap was again the non-clean seed with one
   integral pseudoword, with ratio \(0.293\).  For the previous fractional
   obstruction seed \(3\), the certified overlap hull has \(10\) projected
   vertices, all true codewords, so the \(18.36\Xi\) unary-glued obstruction is
   eliminated exactly by overlap consistency.  A larger
   \(N=12,b=6,q=2\) leave-one-out sweep certified all \(64\) seeds, all clean:
   no fractional projected vertices and no integral pseudowords were found
   (maximum projected source count \(12\), maximum facet count \(46\)).  This is
   not a proof, but it makes the remaining theorem sharply construction
   specific: prove projected-unary integrality and integral-pseudoword exclusion
   for the leave-one-out overlap/Tanner panel, or find a certified fractional
   projected vertex in that exact model.  \Cref{cor:two-deletion-injective-overlap-closure}
   gives a first positive theorem in that exact model: if the chosen low-rate
   panel has minimum distance at least \(3\), then the leave-one-out overlap
   lift is already the true codeword hull, so the local score-band gap is zero.
   By \cref{cor:polylog-cost-two-deletion-injective-panel}, imposing this
   distance condition costs only a polylogarithmic ambient-size slack for fixed
   alphabet.  Thus the low-rate code separator itself is no longer a
   subpolynomial-loss source in the leave-one-out overlap model; any remaining
   overhead must come from the score-tail truncation or routing/tree layer, not
   from projected local pseudowords.
   The qualification is necessary: unrestricted overlap consistency does not
   force unary integrality.  Even in the binary case, the \(b=3\) panel
   \(\{001,100,010\}\) has the all-half projected unary vertex under
   pair-overlap consistency.  A ternary \(b=4\) random panel similarly has a feasible
   overlap-consistent projected source with unary integrality defect \(4/3\).
   The viable route is therefore construction-specific overlap structure plus
   an integral-pseudoword exclusion theorem, not a blanket local-marginal
   integrality fact.

   The tilted-overlap diagnostic is equally simple.  Generate a balanced
   \(q\)-ary panel, draw independent centered Gaussian symbol scores, set
   \(\lambda\simeq\sqrt{2\log N/b}\), form
   \(\Omega_j=e^{\lambda(M-W_j)}\), and measure the weighted positive-overlap
   tail in \((LNZ4)\), separating diagonal and off-diagonal pairs.  The script
   \texttt{impl/chart\_tail\_stress.py} implements exactly this check.  On
   balanced random panels with \(N=512\), \(b=32\), \(q=8\), eight seeds gave
   mean \(\max_j\Omega_j\approx5.8\cdot10^8\) and diagonal share
   \(0.99999\) for the full tail, while the off-diagonal normalized tail stayed
   near a constant.  Clipping prices at \((\log N)^3\) kept the off-diagonal
   tail essentially unchanged.  The same run tested the single shared
   posterior residual of
   \cref{cor:single-posterior-residual-barrier}: the mean full-price singleton
   lower bound was still about \(1.2\cdot10^{10}\), and the aggregate
   self-selector mismatch was about \(9.1\cdot10^9\), even though clipping
   reduced the corresponding singleton cost to about \(6.8\cdot10^3\).
   This supports the barrier diagnosis: the first obstruction is the
   singleton/diagonal full-price term, not an unexplained random-code pair tail,
   and one global posterior residual does not remove it.  The script also tests
   the tempting exact-anchor truncation of
   \cref{cor:exact-anchor-truncation-barrier}.  To reduce the remaining
   posterior singleton cost to the clipped polylog budget, the balanced random
   panels needed about \(74\) anchors out of \(128\), \(172\) out of \(256\),
   and \(361\) out of \(512\).  Thus exact anchoring of the largest prices is
   not a near-leader list; it is almost the entire far-below-leader tail.  The
   clipped near-leader set itself was much smaller: about \(23\), \(34\), and
   \(64\) codewords at those three sizes, consistent with
   \cref{lem:gaussian-clipped-near-leader-size}.  However, the complementary
   far tail carried more than \(0.9996\) of the Boltzmann price mass in all
   three runs.  The next proof attempt should therefore prove directly that
   residual or negative coefficient mass avoids that far tail, or prove that
   such a tail-avoidance theorem is impossible for the chosen code family.
   \Cref{lem:necessary-boltzmann-tail-decay} makes this quantitative: in the
   \(512\)-word run, a polylogarithmic Boltzmann tail budget allows only about
   \(6.7\cdot10^{-4}\) total negative coefficient mass at the \(90\)th
   percentile score gap and about \(2.7\cdot10^{-6}\) at the maximum gap.
   \Cref{lem:finite-range-boltzmann-threshold} gives the matching finite-window
   threshold.  In the same run, normalized toy coefficient profiles
   \(b_j\propto e^{-\alpha(M-W_j)}\) had mean Boltzmann budgets about
   \(4.4\cdot10^6\), \(2.7\cdot10^4\), \(1.3\cdot10^2\), and \(6.7\) at
   \(\alpha/\lambda=0,1/2,1,3/2\), and the mean ratio needed to meet the
   \(\log^3N\) cap was \(0.90\).  This is a diagnostic only, but it says the
   missing theorem must create nearly \(\lambda\)-tilted coefficient decay,
   with any subcritical exponent paid explicitly out of the finite score range.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Posterior mismatch form for localized residuals]
   \label{cor:localized-residual-posterior-mismatch}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:chart-majorant-lower-tail-dual}.  Let \(\mu\in\R_+^{bq}\) be any
   residual budget, and put
   \[
      m_i^\mu=\sum_{a\in[q]}\mu_{i,a}.
      \tag{LOB1}
   \]
   For a nonzero selector \(s\in\R_+^N\), define
   \[
      \pi_i^s(a)=\frac{s_i(a)}{S(s)},
      \qquad S(s)=\sum_j s_j,
      \tag{LOB2}
   \]
   and
   \[
      \Delta_\mu(s)
      =
      \sum_{i=1}^b
      \left(
         m_i^\mu\max_{a\in[q]}\pi_i^s(a)
         -
         \sum_{a\in[q]}\mu_{i,a}\pi_i^s(a)
      \right).
      \tag{LOB3}
   \]
   Then the full chart-majorant family
   \[
      \mathfrak L_{u,\tau}(\mu,\omega)\le B
      \qquad(\tau\in[q]^b)
      \tag{LOB4}
   \]
   is equivalent to
   \[
      \sup_{0\le s\le\omega}S(s)\Delta_\mu(s)\le B,
      \tag{LOB5}
   \]
   with the convention that the term is \(0\) when \(S(s)=0\).

   Equivalently, for coordinates with \(m_i^\mu>0\), let
   \(r_i^\mu(a)=\mu_{i,a}/m_i^\mu\).  Then
   \[
      \Delta_\mu(s)
      =
      \sum_{i:m_i^\mu>0}
      m_i^\mu
      \left(
         \max_a\pi_i^s(a)-\sum_a r_i^\mu(a)\pi_i^s(a)
      \right).
      \tag{LOB6}
   \]
   Thus a residual budget is cheap exactly when its coordinate distributions
   place mass on the symbols favored by every high-price selector.  Uniform
   budgets make \(r_i^\mu\) uniform and recover
   \cref{cor:posterior-plurality-chart-shadow}; localized or anchor-fiber
   budgets can instead make \(r_i^\mu\) follow the high-price posterior and
   avoid the singleton obstruction of
   \cref{cor:singleton-chart-shadow-obstruction}.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   For a fixed chart \(\tau\), the dual objective in \((LNV3)\) is
   \[
      -\sum_js_jh_\tau(\mu)_j
      =
      \sum_{i=1}^b
      \left(
         m_i^\mu s_i(\tau_i)-\sum_a\mu_{i,a}s_i(a)
      \right).
      \tag{LOB7}
   \]
   If \(s\) is feasible for \(\tau\), then \(s_i(\tau_i)=\max_a s_i(a)\) for
   each coordinate after changing \(\tau_i\) within the set of maximizers if
   necessary.  Conversely, for every selector \(s\), choosing
   \(\tau_i\in\arg\max_a s_i(a)\) makes the chart domination constraints
   feasible.  Therefore maximizing over all charts and feasible selectors gives
   \[
      \sup_\tau\mathfrak L_{u,\tau}(\mu,\omega)
      =
      \sup_{0\le s\le\omega}
      \sum_i
      \left(
         m_i^\mu\max_a s_i(a)-\sum_a\mu_{i,a}s_i(a)
      \right).
      \tag{LOB8}
   \]
   Dividing by \(S(s)\) for nonzero \(s\) gives \((LOB5)\), and \((LOB6)\) is
   just the normalization of \(\mu\) inside each coordinate block.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Single posterior residual barrier]
   \label{cor:single-posterior-residual-barrier}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:localized-residual-posterior-mismatch}.  Fix nonnegative prices
   \(\omega\), let \(S=\sum_j\omega_j>0\), and consider the shared
   posterior-matched residual budget
   \[
      \mu^\omega_{i,a}
      =
      \nu_i\frac{\sum_{k:c_k(i)=a}\omega_k}{S},
      \qquad
      V_\nu=\sum_i\nu_i .
      \tag{LOB9}
   \]
   If the chart-majorant check
   \[
      \mathfrak L_{u,\tau}(\mu^\omega,\omega)\le B
      \qquad(\tau\in[q]^b)
      \tag{LOB10}
   \]
   holds, then
   \[
      B\ge
      \max_j
      \omega_j
      \sum_{i=1}^b
      \nu_i
      \left(
         1-
         \frac{\sum_{k:c_k(i)=c_j(i)}\omega_k}{S}
      \right).
      \tag{LOB11}
   \]
   Moreover, the \(\omega\)-average of the off-codeword residual in
   \((LOB11)\) is exactly
   \[
      \frac1S\sum_j\omega_j
      \sum_i\nu_i
      \left(
         1-
         \frac{\sum_{k:c_k(i)=c_j(i)}\omega_k}{S}
      \right)
      =
      V_\nu\left(1-\frac1q\right)
      -
      \frac1{S^2}\sum_{j,k}\omega_j\omega_k b^\nu_{j,k},
      \tag{LOB12}
   \]
   where \(b^\nu_{j,k}=A^\nu_{j,k}-V_\nu/q\) is the centered overlap from
   \((LNZ1)\).

   Thus matching one residual budget to the global Boltzmann posterior does not
   by itself remove the singleton obstruction.  It is cheap only if every
   high-price codeword sees almost all residual mass on its own symbols, or if
   the price-weighted overlap energy almost saturates the random-overlap
   deficit on the high-price support.  The remaining viable localized route is
   therefore genuinely anchor/source dependent, as in
   \cref{cor:localized-residual-feasibility-dual,cor:source-localized-residual-lp},
   or else it must first truncate the far internal-gap prices by a separate
   near-leader theorem.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Apply the singleton obstruction \((LOA3)\) to the budget
   \(\mu^\omega\).  Its off-codeword mass at \(c_j\) is
   \[
      \operatorname{off}_{\mu^\omega}(j)
      =
      \sum_i\nu_i
      \left(
         1-
         \frac{\sum_{k:c_k(i)=c_j(i)}\omega_k}{S}
      \right),
   \]
   which proves \((LOB11)\).

   For the average identity, expand
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      \frac1S\sum_j\omega_j\operatorname{off}_{\mu^\omega}(j)
      &=
      V_\nu
      -
      \frac1{S^2}
      \sum_{j,k}\omega_j\omega_k
      \sum_i\nu_i\mathbf1_{\{c_j(i)=c_k(i)\}}\\
      &=
      V_\nu
      -
      \frac1{S^2}\sum_{j,k}\omega_j\omega_kA^\nu_{j,k}\\
      &=
      V_\nu\left(1-\frac1q\right)
      -
      \frac1{S^2}\sum_{j,k}\omega_j\omega_kb^\nu_{j,k}.
   \end{aligned}
   \]
   The final interpretation follows because a polylogarithmic budget \(B\)
   forces the maximum in \((LOB11)\) to be polylogarithmic despite the full
   internal-gap prices.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact-anchor truncation barrier]
   \label{cor:exact-anchor-truncation-barrier}
   In the setting of
   \cref{cor:single-posterior-residual-barrier}, suppose a set
   \(A\subseteq[N]\) of codewords is handled by exact source-local anchors, so
   singleton selectors supported on \(A\) have zero residual mismatch.  Let
   \(\mu^{\rm rem}\) be any residual budget used for the unanchored codewords.
   If the remaining chart-majorant check has budget \(B\), then every
   unanchored codeword obeys
   \[
      \omega_j\,\operatorname{off}_{\mu^{\rm rem}}(j)\le B
      \qquad(j\notin A).
      \tag{LOB13}
   \]
   Consequently, for any lower bounds
   \(a_j\le\operatorname{off}_{\mu^{\rm rem}}(j)\), the exact-anchor set must
   contain the whole high-price tail
   \[
      \{j:\ \omega_j a_j>B\}\subseteq A .
      \tag{LOB14}
   \]

   With the full internal-gap prices
   \(\omega_j=\exp(\lambda(M-W(c_j)))+\Xi\), this is a far-below-leader tail,
   not a near-leader list.  Exact anchoring therefore removes the singleton
   obstruction only after another theorem has already shown that the residual or
   negative coefficient mass ignores this far tail.  A proof that merely
   ``anchors the large prices'' is paying for the wrong side of the score
   distribution.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Apply the singleton obstruction \((LOA3)\) to the residual budget used on the
   unanchored part.  Exact anchors eliminate the singleton cost only for
   \(j\in A\); for every \(j\notin A\), the same feasible singleton selector
   gives \((LOB13)\).  If \(a_j\le\operatorname{off}_{\mu^{\rm rem}}(j)\) and
   \(\omega_j a_j>B\), then \((LOB13)\) is impossible unless \(j\) was placed
   in \(A\), proving \((LOB14)\).  The last statement is the definition of the
   full internal-gap prices: \(\omega_j\) is largest when \(W(c_j)\) is far
   below the local maximum \(M\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Gaussian clipped near-leader list size]
   \label{lem:gaussian-clipped-near-leader-size}
   Let \(W_1,\ldots,W_N\) be independent \(N(0,\sigma^2)\) variables, put
   \(M=\max_jW_j\), \(L=\log N\), and
   \[
      \lambda_N=\frac{\sqrt{2L}}{\sigma}.
      \tag{LOB15}
   \]
   For \(\Delta\ge0\), define the \(\Delta\)-near-leader list
   \[
      \mathcal L_\Delta=\{j:\ M-W_j\le\Delta\}.
      \tag{LOB16}
   \]
   Then, for all sufficiently large \(N\),
   \[
      \E|\mathcal L_\Delta|
      \le
      2(\log N)^2\exp(\lambda_N\Delta).
      \tag{LOB17}
   \]
   In particular, if a clipped price cap is \(K=\log^A N\) and
   \(\Delta=(\log K)/\lambda_N\), then
   \[
      \E|\mathcal L_\Delta|\le 2\log^{A+2}N .
      \tag{LOB18}
   \]

   Thus, in the independent Gaussian score model, clipping
   \(e^{\lambda_N(M-W_j)}\) at a polylogarithmic cap leaves only a
   polylogarithmic near-leader list.  The obstruction isolated above is not the
   size of the clipped list; it is proving that the LP/SA negative coefficients
   or residual budget do not see the complementary far-below-leader tail.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Write
   \[
      t_N=\sqrt{2L}-\frac{2\log L}{\sqrt{2L}},
      \qquad m_N=\sigma t_N .
      \tag{LOB19}
   \]
   The Gaussian Mills lower bound gives, for all large \(N\),
   \[
      \Pr[W_1\ge m_N]
      \ge
      \frac{1}{2t_N}\exp(-t_N^2/2)
      \ge
      \frac{L^{3/2}}{N}.
      \tag{LOB20}
   \]
   Hence
   \[
      \Pr[M<m_N]
      \le
      \left(1-\frac{L^{3/2}}{N}\right)^N
      \le e^{-L^{3/2}}.
      \tag{LOB21}
   \]
   On the event \(M\ge m_N\),
   \[
      |\mathcal L_\Delta|
      \le
      e^{\lambda_N\Delta-\lambda_NM}
      \sum_{j=1}^Ne^{\lambda_NW_j}
      \le
      e^{\lambda_N\Delta-\lambda_Nm_N}
      \sum_{j=1}^Ne^{\lambda_NW_j}.
      \tag{LOB22}
   \]
   Taking expectations and using
   \(\E e^{\lambda_NW_1}=e^{\lambda_N^2\sigma^2/2}=e^L=N\), while
   \(\lambda_Nm_N=2L-2\log L\), gives
   \[
      \E\bigl[|\mathcal L_\Delta|\mathbf1_{\{M\ge m_N\}}\bigr]
      \le
      e^{\lambda_N\Delta}L^2 .
      \tag{LOB23}
   \]
   The bad event contributes at most \(Ne^{-L^{3/2}}\), which is at most
   \(e^{\lambda_N\Delta}L^2\) for all large \(N\).  This proves \((LOB17)\).
   Substituting \(\lambda_N\Delta=\log K=A\log\log N\) gives \((LOB18)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Necessary Boltzmann tail decay]
   \label{lem:necessary-boltzmann-tail-decay}
   Let \(g_j\ge0\), \(b_j\ge0\), and \(\lambda,\Xi>0\).  If
   \[
      \sum_j b_j e^{\lambda g_j}\le \Xi ,
      \tag{LOB24}
   \]
   then the cumulative tail
   \[
      A(s)=\sum_{j:g_j\ge s}b_j
      \tag{LOB25}
   \]
   obeys
   \[
      A(s)\le \Xi e^{-\lambda s}
      \qquad(s\ge0).
      \tag{LOB26}
   \]
   In particular, if the near-leader price cap is \(K=e^{\lambda\Delta}\), then
   for every \(r\ge0\),
   \[
      A(\Delta+r)\le \frac{\Xi}{K}e^{-\lambda r}.
      \tag{LOB27}
   \]

   Applied to the LP/SA negative-tail certificate, this is a necessary
   condition, not another sufficient reformulation: once prices are clipped at a
   polylogarithmic cap, any negative coefficient mass that remains deeper than
   the clipped window must decay exponentially at rate \(\lambda\) in the
   additional gap.  Thus the unresolved theorem is exactly a tail-avoidance
   theorem for the coefficients or residual sources.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   For every \(s\ge0\),
   \[
      \sum_jb_je^{\lambda g_j}
      \ge
      \sum_{j:g_j\ge s}b_je^{\lambda g_j}
      \ge
      e^{\lambda s}A(s).
   \]
   Combining this with \((LOB24)\) gives \((LOB26)\).  Taking
   \(s=\Delta+r\) and \(K=e^{\lambda\Delta}\) gives \((LOB27)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finite-range Boltzmann tail threshold]
   \label{lem:finite-range-boltzmann-threshold}
   Let \(0\le g_j\le G\), \(b_j\ge0\), and define
   \(A(s)=\sum_{j:g_j\ge s}b_j\).  Then
   \[
      \sum_j b_je^{\lambda g_j}
      =
      A(0)+\lambda\int_0^G e^{\lambda s}A(s)\,ds .
      \tag{LOB28}
   \]
   Consequently, if \(\sum_jb_j\le1\) and
   \[
      A(s)\le C e^{-\alpha s}
      \qquad(0\le s\le G),
      \tag{LOB29}
   \]
   then
   \[
      \sum_j b_je^{\lambda g_j}
      \le
      1+\lambda C\,\Psi_{\lambda,\alpha}(G),
      \tag{LOB30}
   \]
   where
   \[
      \Psi_{\lambda,\alpha}(G)=
      \begin{cases}
      \dfrac{1-e^{-(\alpha-\lambda)G}}{\alpha-\lambda},
         & \alpha>\lambda,\\[1.2ex]
      G, & \alpha=\lambda,\\[0.8ex]
      \dfrac{e^{(\lambda-\alpha)G}-1}{\lambda-\alpha},
         & \alpha<\lambda.
      \end{cases}
      \tag{LOB31}
   \]

   Thus the slope \(\lambda\) is the critical finite-window threshold for the
   frozen negative-tail target.  Supercritical decay \(\alpha>\lambda\) gives a
   range-free budget, critical decay \(\alpha=\lambda\) pays only the score
   window length \(G\), and subcritical decay \(\alpha<\lambda\) is viable only
   if the finite score range supplies the missing factor
   \(e^{(\lambda-\alpha)G}\).  Combined with
   \cref{lem:necessary-boltzmann-tail-decay}, this is the exact proof-or-barrier
   shape for the coefficient tail: any successful LP/SA theorem must either
   prove this near-\(\lambda\) cumulative decay or identify a structural reason
   why the relevant coefficients never enter the far score window.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   For each \(j\),
   \[
      e^{\lambda g_j}
      =
      1+\lambda\int_0^{g_j}e^{\lambda s}\,ds .
      \tag{LOB32}
   \]
   Multiplying by \(b_j\), summing over the finite family, and exchanging the
   sum with the integral gives \((LOB28)\).  Under \((LOB29)\),
   \[
      \lambda\int_0^G e^{\lambda s}A(s)\,ds
      \le
      \lambda C\int_0^G e^{(\lambda-\alpha)s}\,ds ,
      \tag{LOB33}
   \]
   and the three cases in \((LOB31)\) are exactly this elementary integral.
   The additive \(1\) in \((LOB30)\) is the assumption \(A(0)=\sum_jb_j\le1\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Finite dual for localized residual feasibility]
   \label{cor:localized-residual-feasibility-dual}
   Work at a branch-and-bound node \(u\), with relaxation \(P_u\) and true
   codewords \(c_1,\ldots,c_N\).  For a nonnegative score table \(y\), write
   its residual-Hall gap as
   \[
      \mathcal H_u(y)
      =
      \sup_{z\in P_u}\ip{y}{z}
      -
      \max_{j\in[N]}\ip{y}{\iota(c_j)} .
      \tag{LOC1}
   \]
   For a selector \(0\le s\le\omega\), define its posterior-mismatch direction
   \(D_s\in\R_+^{bq}\) by
   \[
      D_s(i,a)=\max_{\alpha\in[q]}s_i(\alpha)-s_i(a).
      \tag{LOC2}
   \]
   Then, for every residual budget \(\mu\ge0\),
   \[
      \ip{D_s}{\mu}=S(s)\Delta_\mu(s).
      \tag{LOC3}
   \]

   Let \(\mathcal Y\subset\R_+^{bq}\) be a finite family of Hall score tables and
   let \(\mathcal S\subseteq\{s\in\R_+^N:0\le s\le\omega\}\) be a finite family
   of chart selectors.  There exists a residual budget \(\mu\ge0\) satisfying
   \[
      \ip{y}{\mu}\ge\mathcal H_u(y)
      \qquad(y\in\mathcal Y),
      \tag{LOC4}
   \]
   and
   \[
      \ip{D_s}{\mu}\le B
      \qquad(s\in\mathcal S)
      \tag{LOC5}
   \]
   if and only if every pair of nonnegative multipliers
   \((\alpha_y)_{y\in\mathcal Y}\) and
   \((\beta_s)_{s\in\mathcal S}\) obeying the coordinatewise domination
   \[
      \sum_{y\in\mathcal Y}\alpha_y y
      \le
      \sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\beta_sD_s
      \tag{LOC6}
   \]
   also obeys
   \[
      \sum_{y\in\mathcal Y}\alpha_y\mathcal H_u(y)
      \le
      B\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\beta_s .
      \tag{LOC7}
   \]

   Hence the localized residual theorem has an exact finite obstruction.  If the
   restricted residual LP is infeasible, preprocessing obtains a nonnegative
   mixture of genuine relaxation gaps whose score table is dominated by a
   mixture of posterior-mismatch directions, but whose Hall value is larger than
   the allowed chart budget.  Conversely, ruling out all such dominated mixtures
   gives a residual budget that is simultaneously Hall-valid on
   \(\mathcal Y\) and chart-cheap on \(\mathcal S\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Formula \((LOC3)\) is just the linearized form of
   \((LOB5)\):
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      S(s)\Delta_\mu(s)
      &=
      \sum_i
      \left(
         m_i^\mu\max_a s_i(a)-\sum_a\mu_{i,a}s_i(a)
      \right)\\
      &=
      \sum_{i,a}\mu_{i,a}
      \left(\max_\alpha s_i(\alpha)-s_i(a)\right).
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{LOC8}
   \]

   The feasibility problem \((LOC4)\)--\((LOC5)\), together with \(\mu\ge0\), is
   the finite linear system
   \[
      -\ip{y}{\mu}\le-\mathcal H_u(y),
      \qquad
      \ip{D_s}{\mu}\le B,
      \qquad
      -\mu_{i,a}\le0 .
      \tag{LOC9}
   \]
   By Farkas' lemma, it is infeasible if and only if there are nonnegative
   multipliers \(\alpha_y,\beta_s,\gamma_{i,a}\) such that
   \[
      -\sum_y\alpha_yy+\sum_s\beta_sD_s-\gamma=0
      \tag{LOC10}
   \]
   and
   \[
      -\sum_y\alpha_y\mathcal H_u(y)+B\sum_s\beta_s<0.
      \tag{LOC11}
   \]
   Eliminating \(\gamma\ge0\), the equality \((LOC10)\) is exactly the
   coordinatewise domination \((LOC6)\).  The strict inequality
   \((LOC11)\) is the negation of \((LOC7)\).  This proves the equivalence.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Source-level localized residual LP]
   \label{cor:source-localized-residual-lp}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:localized-residual-feasibility-dual}, and put
   \[
      K_u=\operatorname{conv}\{\iota(c_j):j\in[N]\}.
      \tag{LOD1}
   \]
   Let \(\mathcal Z\subseteq P_u\) be a finite set of relaxation sources and let
   \(\mathcal S\subseteq\{s\in\R_+^N:0\le s\le\omega\}\) be a finite selector
   family.  Define the best shared localized residual budget
   \(\mathsf B_u(\mathcal Z,\mathcal S)\) as the optimum of
   \[
   \begin{array}{ll}
      \text{\rm minimize} & B\\[1mm]
      \text{\rm over} & B\in\R,\ \mu\in\R_+^{bq},\
                        x_z\in K_u\ (z\in\mathcal Z)\\[1mm]
      \text{\rm subject to}
         & z-x_z\le\mu\qquad(z\in\mathcal Z),\\[1mm]
         & \ip{D_s}{\mu}\le B\qquad(s\in\mathcal S),
   \end{array}
      \tag{LOD2}
   \]
   where \(D_s\) is the posterior-mismatch direction from \((LOC2)\).

   Then finite LP duality gives the exact formula
   \[
      \mathsf B_u(\mathcal Z,\mathcal S)
      =
      \sup_{\substack{\beta\in\Delta(\mathcal S),\ y_z\in\R_+^{bq}\\
             \sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}y_z\le D_\beta}}
      \sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}
      \left(
         \ip{y_z}{z}
         -
         \max_{j\in[N]}\ip{y_z}{\iota(c_j)}
      \right),
      \qquad
      D_\beta=\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\beta_sD_s .
      \tag{LOD3}
   \]

   Consequently, a budget \(B\) is sufficient for the finite source/selector
   system if and only if every nonnegative source-local score assignment
   \(z\mapsto y_z\), whose aggregate score table is dominated by a convex
   combination of posterior-mismatch directions, has total source-local Hall
   gap at most \(B\).  If \(\mathcal Z\) contains all vertices of \(P_u\), then
   any feasible solution of \((LOD2)\) is residual-Hall valid for every
   \(z\in P_u\); if, in addition, \(\mathcal S\) is the full finite selector
   family used by the chart verifier, the same \(\mu\) is chart-cheap on that
   family by \((LOC3)\).

   This is the compact normal form for the localized-residual theorem: prove
   that chart-mismatch directions have small one-sided distance to the true
   codeword convex hull, uniformly over all shared source assignments.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   The program \((LOD2)\) is feasible by taking \(\mu\) large enough and
   \(x_z\in K_u\) arbitrarily, and its optimum is bounded below by \(0\).  Use
   nonnegative multipliers \(\beta_s\) for the constraints
   \(\ip{D_s}{\mu}-B\le0\), and \(y_z\in\R_+^{bq}\) for the constraints
   \(z-x_z-\mu\le0\).  The Lagrangian is
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      L
      &=
      B+\sum_s\beta_s(\ip{D_s}{\mu}-B)
      +\sum_z\ip{y_z}{z-x_z-\mu} \\
      &=
      B\left(1-\sum_s\beta_s\right)
      +
      \left\langle
         \sum_s\beta_sD_s-\sum_zy_z,\mu
      \right\rangle
      +
      \sum_z\left(\ip{y_z}{z}-\ip{y_z}{x_z}\right).
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{LOD4}
   \]
   Minimizing over the free scalar \(B\) forces
   \(\sum_s\beta_s=1\).  Minimizing over \(\mu\ge0\) is finite exactly when
   \[
      \sum_zy_z\le\sum_s\beta_sD_s .
      \tag{LOD5}
   \]
   Finally, for each \(z\),
   \[
      \inf_{x_z\in K_u}-\ip{y_z}{x_z}
      =
      -\max_{x\in K_u}\ip{y_z}{x}
      =
      -\max_{j\in[N]}\ip{y_z}{\iota(c_j)} .
      \tag{LOD6}
   \]
   Substituting these conditions into the dual gives \((LOD3)\), and strong
   duality holds because \((LOD2)\) is an ordinary finite LP with finite optimum.

   If \(\mathcal Z\) contains every vertex of \(P_u\), take any
   \(z=\sum_v\lambda_vv\in P_u\), choose the corresponding feasible witnesses
   \(x_v\in K_u\), and set \(x=\sum_v\lambda_vx_v\in K_u\).  Since
   \(v-x_v\le\mu\) for every vertex \(v\),
   \[
      z-x=\sum_v\lambda_v(v-x_v)\le\mu .
      \tag{LOD7}
   \]
   Hence the residual-Hall witness condition of
   \cref{cor:residual-hall-verifier} holds for all of \(P_u\).  The chart-cost
   statement is exactly \((LOC3)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Shared-envelope distance form]
   \label{cor:shared-envelope-distance-form}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:source-localized-residual-lp}.  For a nonnegative coordinate weight
   \(D\in\R_+^{bq}\), define
   \[
      \mathsf d_u(\mathcal Z;D)
      =
      \inf_{\substack{\mu\in\R_+^{bq},\ x_z\in K_u\\
                      z-x_z\le\mu\ (z\in\mathcal Z)}}
      \ip{D}{\mu}.
      \tag{LOE1}
   \]
   Then
   \[
      \mathsf d_u(\mathcal Z;D)
      =
      \inf_{x_z\in K_u}
      \sum_{i=1}^b\sum_{a\in[q]}
      D_{i,a}
      \left(
         \max_{z\in\mathcal Z}(z_{i,a}-x_z(i,a))
      \right)_+ ,
      \tag{LOE2}
   \]
   and finite LP duality gives
   \[
      \mathsf d_u(\mathcal Z;D)
      =
      \sup_{\substack{y_z\in\R_+^{bq}\\
                      \sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}y_z\le D}}
      \sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}
      \left(
         \ip{y_z}{z}
         -
         \max_{j\in[N]}\ip{y_z}{\iota(c_j)}
      \right).
      \tag{LOE3}
   \]
   Consequently, for the finite selector family \(\mathcal S\),
   \[
      \mathsf B_u(\mathcal Z,\mathcal S)
      =
      \max_{\beta\in\Delta(\mathcal S)}
      \mathsf d_u(\mathcal Z;D_\beta),
      \qquad
      D_\beta=\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\beta_sD_s .
      \tag{LOE4}
   \]

   Thus the localized residual problem may be stated without Hall score tables:
   every convex combination of posterior-mismatch directions must have small
   shared positive-envelope distance from the exposed relaxation sources to the
   true codeword convex hull.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   For fixed witnesses \(x_z\), the least feasible \(\mu\) in \((LOE1)\) is
   coordinatewise
   \[
      \mu_{i,a}
      =
      \left(
         \max_{z\in\mathcal Z}(z_{i,a}-x_z(i,a))
      \right)_+ ,
      \tag{LOE5}
   \]
   because \(D\ge0\).  This proves \((LOE2)\).

   The dual formula \((LOE3)\) is the fixed-\(D\) version of the Lagrange-dual
   calculation in \cref{cor:source-localized-residual-lp}: remove the epigraph
   variable \(B\) and replace the condition
   \(\sum_zy_z\le\sum_s\beta_sD_s\) by \(\sum_zy_z\le D\).  Strong duality
   again holds because this is a finite LP with finite optimum.

   Finally, substituting \(D=D_\beta\) in \((LOE3)\) and maximizing over
   \(\beta\in\Delta(\mathcal S)\) gives exactly the dual expression
   \((LOD3)\) for \(\mathsf B_u(\mathcal Z,\mathcal S)\).  This proves
   \((LOE4)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Anchor-fiber LP/SA certificate compiler]
   \label{cor:anchor-fiber-lp-sa-compiler}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:anchor-fiber-internal-tail-certificate} and
   \cref{cor:conditional-gaussian-projection-certificate}.  Fix
   \(\lambda>0\) and a mesh \(\delta>0\).  Suppose that every branch node
   \(u\) satisfies the following finite certificates.

   First, for every \(h\in E_u\),
   \[
      \sum_j a_u(h)_j^-\le1,
      \qquad
      M(u)\kappa_u(h)\le R_u .
      \tag{LMU1}
   \]
   Second, for some \(C_u,\eta_u>0\), every dyadic level \(k\ge0\), every
   selector \(r\in\mathcal R_u(k\delta)\), and every anchor \(c\in C_u\),
   \[
      \sup_{z\in P_{u,c}}
      \ip{-A_uG_u^+r}{z-\iota(c)}
      \le
      C_u e^{-(\lambda+\eta_u)k\delta}.
      \tag{LMU2}
   \]
   Finally the orthogonal residual term obeys
   \[
      e^{\lambda R_u}
      \left(
         1+\frac{e^{\lambda\delta}C_u}{1-e^{-\eta_u\delta}}
      \right)
      \exp\!\left(
         \lambda\omega_u^\perp
         +\frac{\lambda^2(r_u^\perp)^2}{2}
      \right)
      \le A_\lambda .
      \tag{LMU3}
   \]
   Then the conditional tilted-excess bound \((LPT2)\) holds with this
   \(A_\lambda\).  Consequently, at the Gaussian tilt \(\lambda=T/b\), if
   \(A_\lambda=\log^{O(1)}n\) and the per-node relaxation solve is
   polylogarithmic, the LP/SA threshold reporter has only polylogarithmic
   expected overhead.

   Thus a fixed-level LP or Sherali--Adams proof can be made completely local:
   verify scalar balance and negative-mass normalization in \((LMU1)\), solve
   the anchor-fiber separation LPs in \((LMU2)\), and bound the orthogonal
   residual in \((LMU3)\).  No global pseudocodeword-spectrum statement remains
   hidden inside the branch-and-bound analysis.

   The selector LPs in \((LMU2)\) may be replaced by the singleton influence
   tail \((LMV2)\) of
   \cref{cor:singleton-down-influence-certificate}.  This is often the more
   realistic route for a code proof: prove that each low-scoring true
   codeword has small down-influence on every anchor fiber, and sum those
   influences over score shells.

   Even the dyadic tail is stronger than necessary.  The one-line weighted
   condition \((LMW1)\) of
   \cref{cor:singleton-boltzmann-influence-certificate} directly implies the
   Boltzmann negative-tail certificate; it is the natural form if the code
   proof works by a tilted or planted-distribution moment calculation.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   By \cref{cor:anchor-fiber-internal-tail-certificate}, \((LMU2)\) implies
   the dyadic cumulative tail condition \((LMR10)\).  Then
   \cref{cor:cumulative-internal-tail-certificate}, using \((LMU1)\), gives
   \[
      \mathcal Z_{u,\lambda}(w)
      \le
      e^{\lambda R_u}
      \left(
         1+\frac{e^{\lambda\delta}C_u}{1-e^{-\eta_u\delta}}
      \right).
      \tag{LMU4}
   \]
   Multiplying by the orthogonal residual factor and applying \((LMU3)\)
   proves the Boltzmann certificate \((LMQ3)\).  Hence
   \cref{cor:boltzmann-negative-tail-certificate} gives the conditional
   tilted-excess bound.  The final overhead statement is exactly
   \cref{cor:conditional-tilted-excess-certificate}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Well-conditioned Gram coefficient bounds]
   \label{cor:well-conditioned-gram-coefficients}
   Continue with the notation of
   \cref{cor:gram-projection-certificate}.  Suppose the nonzero spectrum of
   the codeword overlap Gram matrix satisfies
   \[
      G_u\succeq \sigma_u I
      \quad\text{on }\operatorname{range}(G_u)
      \tag{LPEO1}
   \]
   for some \(\sigma_u>0\).  Then, for every \(h\in E_u\),
   \[
      \|a_u(h)\|_2
      \le
      \frac{\|v_u(h)\|_2}{\sigma_u},
      \qquad
      \|\Pi_u h\|_2
      \le
      \frac{\|v_u(h)\|_2}{\sqrt{\sigma_u}},
      \tag{LPEO2}
   \]
   and, if \(a_u(h)\) has support at most \(s_u(h)\),
   \[
      \sum_j a_u(h)_j^-
      \le
      \|a_u(h)\|_1
      \le
      \sqrt{s_u(h)}\,\frac{\|v_u(h)\|_2}{\sigma_u}.
      \tag{LPEO3}
   \]
   Thus a low-rate code proof may certify the shifted coefficient target by
   bounding three purely geometric quantities: scalar leakage
   \(\kappa_u(h)\), excess overlap norm \(\|v_u(h)\|_2\), and coefficient
   support \(s_u(h)\), together with the orthogonal residual geometry in
   \((LPB4)\)--\((LPB5)\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Since \(v_u(h)\in\operatorname{range}(G_u)\), the spectral assumption gives
   \(\|G_u^+v_u(h)\|_2\le \|v_u(h)\|_2/\sigma_u\).  This proves the first
   inequality in \((LPEO2)\).  Also,
   \[
      \|\Pi_u h\|_2^2
      =
      v_u(h)^\top G_u^+v_u(h)
      \le
      \frac{\|v_u(h)\|_2^2}{\sigma_u},
   \]
   using \((LPB4)\), proving the second inequality in \((LPEO2)\).  Finally,
   the negative coefficient mass is at most \(\|a_u(h)\|_1\), and Cauchy's
   inequality on the support of \(a_u(h)\) gives \((LPEO3)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[LP and Sherali--Adams decoder target]
   \label{rem:lp-sa-soft-decoder-target}
   \Cref{cor:sharp-lp-soft-decoder} identifies the exact theorem needed from a
   convex or iterative code decoder.  It is not enough to find one good
   codeword.  The relaxation must give a branch-and-bound upper certificate
   whose excess over the best true codeword in every surviving subproblem is
   only
   \[
      O(\sqrt{\log\log n})
   \]
   in unnormalized Gaussian score.  Equivalently, the normalized score gap is
   \(O(\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})\), which is the largest loss whose Gaussian
   tail inflation remains polylogarithmic.

   This makes low-rate Tanner or expander codes a plausible structured-panel
   target.  Take \(q=\log^{O(1)}n\) and
   \(b=\Theta(\log n/\log\log n)\), so a fixed-level local LP or
   Sherali--Adams relaxation has \(\log^{O(1)}n\) variables and constraints.
   The missing self-contained theorem is a Gaussian pseudocodeword-spectrum
   bound: with high probability over the panel scores, every subproblem reached
   by the certified branch-and-bound search satisfies \((LPS1)\) with
   \(\Gamma=O(\sqrt{\log\log n})\).  If such a bound holds, the decoder becomes
   one of the finite proposal laws allowed by
   \cref{lem:proposal-law-filter-separator}: its reported codewords are verified
   deterministic columns, and failed LP nodes are discarded by certificate
   rather than retained in the index.

   The same MAP oracle could later be used for perturb-and-MAP sampling, but
   that would need a separate domination theorem for the perturbations.  The
   clean proof route is the certified threshold reporter above: prove the
   Gaussian LP/SA sharpness bound first, then feed the output-sensitive decoded
   panel into the existing generated-cover and shared-panel separators.

   \Cref{cor:anchored-lp-width-certificate} gives a concrete sufficient form
   of the pseudocodeword theorem.  It is enough to anchor every fractional
   pseudocodeword to a true codeword in the same branch subcode so that the
   excess directions have Gaussian width \(O(\sqrt{\log\log n})\), with
   summable concentration losses.  This is the place where level-two or
   level-three Sherali--Adams could matter: if the relaxation forces every
   pseudocodeword to decompose around nearby true codewords with only small
   pair-overlap excess, then the anchored width is the right quantity to bound.
   The union term in \((LPC4)\) is also a warning.  If one insists on certifying
   a full polynomial-size prefix universe with constant-radius excess sets,
   \((LPC4)\) gives a \(\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})\) loss, which is too large.
   A successful low-rate code proof must therefore either prove the
   \(O(\sqrt{\log\log n})\) sharpness directly on the near-threshold node
   process, make the anchored excess radius shrink, or restrict preprocessing
   to a build-certified node universe with summable failure budget.

   The near-threshold alternative is made precise by
   \cref{cor:false-survivor-lp-accounting}.  Uniform sharpness over every
   possible prefix is stronger than needed.  A node with a real codeword within
   \(O(\sqrt{\log\log n})\) of the threshold is already paid for by the ordinary
   lowered-threshold list.  Only nodes whose true maximum is lower must be
   controlled by a relaxation-gap tail.  Thus the natural low-rate code theorem
   is the joint estimate \((LPF7)\): anchored pseudocodeword excess should be
   unlikely exactly on subproblems whose real codeword maximum has fallen below
   the relevant slack level.  This is a sharper target than a full union bound
   over the prefix universe and matches the extreme-value nature of the
   decoder.

   \Cref{cor:exponential-false-survivor-certificate} is the cleanest current
   form of that target.  Instead of proving a high-probability LP gap bound for
   every prefix, it asks for one tilted moment bound: below the ordinary
   \(T-\gamma\) true-codeword frontier, the aggregate mass of
   \(M(u)+X_u(w)\)-crossings must be comparable to the true \(T\)-tail list.
   A natural proof would use the Gaussian tilt \(\lambda\simeq T/b\) and show
   that a high anchored pseudocodeword excess under the no-true-codeword
   conditioning behaves like a planted low-rate decoding problem, rather than
   like an independent extra codebook.  This is now the precise LP/SA analogue
   of the smooth-decoder theorem needed for a polylogarithmic terminal panel.

   \Cref{cor:conditional-tilted-excess-certificate} isolates the most local
   sufficient form.  The code theorem no longer has to count prefixes directly:
   at the Gaussian tilt \(\lambda=T/b\), it is enough to prove the conditional
   moment bound
   \[
      \E[\exp(\lambda X_u)\mid W(c),\,c\in C_u]\le\log^{O(1)}n
   \]
   for every branch subproblem that the certified decoder may expose.  The
   ordinary true-codeword maximum is then paid by the exponential-moment
   identity \(\sum_u e^{\lambda M(u)}\le(H+1)\sum_c e^{\lambda W(c)}\).  This
   makes the remaining LP/SA obstacle very specific: high pseudocodeword excess
   must not acquire more than polylogarithmic tilted moment after conditioning
   on the real codeword score process inside the same subproblem.

   \Cref{cor:conditional-gaussian-projection-certificate} turns that obstacle
   into a geometric decomposition of the anchored excess set.  After the true
   codeword scores are revealed, only two quantities remain: the support
   function of the excess set projected onto the real-codeword span, and the
   Gaussian width/radius of its orthogonal projection.  This is the first point
   where an actual Tanner/SA proof can aim at local polytope geometry: level-2
   or level-3 constraints should make fractional excess nearly explainable by
   nearby true codewords, shrinking the orthogonal radius, while low-rate
   overlap should keep the projected bias from growing under the Gaussian tilt.

   \Cref{cor:false-survivor-projection-certificate} is the sharper target for
   this last sentence.  The projected bias need not be uniformly small on every
   formal prefix.  It only has to be small after weighting by
   \(\exp(\lambda(M(u)-T))\) on nodes whose true maximum is already below the
