   threshold frontier.  This matches the branch-and-bound process: nodes with
   a near-threshold real codeword are paid by the ordinary lowered list, and
   only false survivors need pseudocodeword control.

   \Cref{cor:gram-projection-certificate} makes the Tanner/SA obligation
   finite and checkable.  The projected bias is the support function of the
   excess-overlap vectors \(v_u(h)\) through the inverse codeword-overlap Gram
   matrix \(G_u^+\), while the remaining width and radius are those of the
   orthogonal residual \(h-A_uG_u^+v_u(h)\).  Thus a useful low-rate code
   theorem does not have to discuss arbitrary Gaussian projections: it must
   prove that local LP or constant-level SA pseudocodewords have controlled
   overlap coefficients and small orthogonal residuals under the tilted
   false-survivor weighting.

   \Cref{cor:shifted-overlap-coefficient-certificate} further separates the
   projected part into two interpretable failure modes.  On a false-survivor
   node, take the shift \(\Theta=T-\gamma\).  Positive coefficient mass above
   the shift cannot help, because every real codeword score is already below
   the frontier.  What remains is scalar leakage
   \((T-\gamma)\kappa_u(h)\) and negative coefficient mass multiplied by the
   score gaps \(T-\gamma-W(c_j)\).  In a good low-rate relaxation, anchored
   pseudocodeword excesses should have negligible scalar leakage and should not
   place large negative coefficients on many real codewords far below the
   frontier.

   \Cref{cor:balance-witness-scalar-leakage} shows that scalar leakage is not
   an independent obstruction for ordinary q-ary LP relaxations.  Every
   coordinate simplex constraint supplies a balance witness \(e_i\).  If a
   coordinate witness lies in the local codeword span, then \(\kappa_u(h)=0\)
   exactly.  If it is only close to that span, the leakage is paid by the
   orthogonal residual \(r_u^\perp\), which is already present in the Gaussian
   projection certificate.  Thus the real projected-bias problem is the
   negative coefficient mass against below-frontier score gaps, not an
   additional scalar shift defect.

   \Cref{cor:frontier-gap-negative-coefficients} removes another artificial
   loss.  If the negative coefficient mass is at most one, the gap from the
   true subcode maximum \(M(u)\) to the false-survivor frontier \(T-\gamma\) is
   paid exactly by the factor \(\exp(\lambda(M(u)-T))\) already present in the
   false-survivor moment.  The remaining gap term is internal:
   \(M(u)-W(c_j)\).  Thus the low-rate code theorem should control
   pseudocodeword coefficients only against score differences inside the same
   subproblem, rather than against the absolute threshold deficit.

   \Cref{cor:direct-coefficient-projection-certificate} gives a cleaner
   anchor-free variant of the same idea.  Instead of comparing a relaxation point
   to a leader or to an explicit convex witness, represent its projection onto
   the true-codeword span by coefficients \(b\) with \(A_ub=\Pi_u z\).  True
   codewords and true convex combinations can choose nonnegative coefficients,
   so they have no negative tail.  The sufficient LP/SA theorem becomes: every
   relaxation point admits a score-span coefficient representation whose
   negative mass has polylogarithmic Boltzmann tail under the internal gaps
   \(M(u)-W(c_j)\), while the orthogonal width of \(P_u\) remains
   \(O(\sqrt{b\log q})\).  This avoids both the score-leader overcharge and the
   need to materialize a convex-hull witness.

   \Cref{cor:negative-coefficient-tail-dual} makes the negative-tail part
   finite-dimensional: the minimum weighted negative coefficient mass is dual to
   maximizing a score-span separator \(y\) over \(P_u\), under clipped constraints
   \(-\omega_j\le\ip{y}{\iota(c_j)}\le0\) on every true codeword.  With the
   combined price \(\omega^\lambda+\Xi_u\mathbf1\), one LP check gives a single
   coefficient representation with both small total negative mass and small
   Boltzmann negative tail.  \Cref{cor:coefficient-scalar-leakage-witness}
   handles the remaining scalar term by the coordinate-block balance witness,
   paying only the orthogonal residual when the witness is not exactly in the
   local span.

   \Cref{cor:near-optimal-score-gap-tail-verifier} turns the same check into a
   more standard LP-decoding statement.  After subtracting block minima, a signed
   clipped separator becomes a nonnegative score table whose true codeword
   deficits are bounded by the same prices \(\omega_j\).  Therefore it is enough
   to prove that every such near-optimal score band has relaxation optimum only
   polylogarithmically above the best true codeword.  This is a sharper
   code-theoretic target than controlling arbitrary signed pseudocodeword
   objectives.

   \Cref{cor:finite-score-band-lp-sa-compiler} packages this into the actual
   overhead criterion.  At each exposed branch node, use the combined prices
   \(\Omega_j=e^{\lambda(M-W_j)}+\Xi\).  If every
   \(\Omega\)-near-optimal nonnegative score band has LP/SA gap at most \(\Xi\),
   and the coordinate-balance witness pays scalar leakage, then the conditional
   tilted-excess moment is already polylogarithmic after multiplying by the
   orthogonal Gaussian-width factor.  This is now the narrowest local code
   theorem needed by the LP/SA route.

   \Cref{cor:band-limited-residual-budget-compiler} gives an even more
   geometric sufficient form.  It is enough to find a one-sided residual budget
   \(\mu_u\) that Hall-covers every relaxation point by the true codeword convex
   hull, and whose mass \(\ip{R}{\mu_u}\) is at most \(\Xi\) for every
   \(\Omega\)-near-optimal score band \(R\).  This turns the LP/SA target into a
   residual localization theorem: fractional mass may remain, but it must avoid
   all score bands that are competitive with the current true-codeword frontier.
   \Cref{cor:min-chart-band-residual-verifier} removes the remaining informal
   quantifier in this statement: the worst competitive score band is found by a
   finite block-minimum chart LP.  Thus a failed residual localization proof
   returns an actual chart and score-span table, not just an abstract
   pseudocodeword-spectrum obstruction.
   \Cref{cor:min-chart-deficit-transport-dual} gives the matching positive
   certificate: for every chart, the block-centered residual must be neutralized
   by free upward moves away from chart minima plus a zero-total signed
   combination of true codewords whose positive part has small near-leader
   price.  Equivalently, it must solve the finite Gram system
   \(h_\tau(\mu)+h_\tau(\alpha)+G_u\theta=0\).  This is the finite transport
   form of the remaining code theorem.
   \Cref{cor:off-chart-majorant-min-chart} absorbs the upward variables into
   one off-chart majorant \(\zeta\ge_\tau\mu\), leaving the even cleaner target
   \(h_\tau(\zeta)+G_u\theta=0\) with cheap positive \(\theta\)-mass.
   \Cref{cor:canonical-zero-sum-min-chart} records the canonical inverse form:
   solve this equation in the zero-sum coefficient subspace, and in the
   balanced diagonal model it is enough to bound the \(\Omega\)-weighted
   lower tail of the chart-incidence score \(h_\tau(\zeta)\).
   \Cref{cor:perturbed-scalar-zero-sum-min-chart} makes this target stable
   under the Gram errors expected for finite balanced code panels: it suffices
   to add an explicit spectral-error term
   \(\delta_u\|\Omega_u\|_2\|h_\tau(\zeta)\|_2/(\chi_u(1-\delta_u))\).
   \Cref{cor:range-restricted-zero-sum-min-chart} removes the unnecessary
   full-rank idealization: for large panels, it is enough to build a
   scalar-like right inverse only on the selected chart-score vectors.
   \Cref{cor:chart-majorant-lower-tail-dual} then optimizes the majorant
   \(\zeta\) itself.  Its dual obstruction is a price-capped selector whose
   coordinate histograms are dominated by the chart symbols.  Thus the
   remaining random-code/Tanner-code theorem has a concrete list-recovery
   shape: rule out heavy chart-dominated shadows under the internal-gap prices.
   \Cref{cor:penalized-chart-majorant-dual} folds the restricted-inverse error
   term into the same obstruction by allowing an \(\ell_2\)-bounded signed blur
   of the price-capped selector.  In the uniform residual-budget model,
   \cref{cor:uniform-residual-chart-shadow} reduces the diagonal obstruction to
   the soft chart excess
   \(\sum_i\nu_i(qs_i(\tau_i)-\sum_js_j)\), the exact weighted list-recovery
   quantity that must be polylogarithmically bounded.
   \Cref{cor:posterior-plurality-chart-shadow} removes the chart notation from
   this target: every price-capped selector induces coordinate posteriors
   \(\pi_i^s\), and the obstruction is their weighted plurality bias.  A
   Cauchy step bounds that bias by the centered overlap quadratic form
   \(s^\top B^\nu s\).  Thus the random-code theorem can be stated as a
   box-restricted second-moment bound for all \(0\le s\le\Omega_u\).
   \Cref{cor:positive-overlap-chart-shadow-tail} weakens this further to a
   weighted positive-overlap pair tail, or equivalently a tilted pair
   enumerator under the same internal-gap prices.
   \Cref{cor:singleton-chart-shadow-obstruction} records the matching warning:
   with full internal-gap prices, a uniform residual budget already fails on
   singleton selectors unless all prices are bounded.  The residual theorem
   therefore has to become localized, with off-codeword residual mass decaying
   around high-price codewords, or else the far internal-gap tail must be
   removed by a separate near-leader certificate.
   \Cref{cor:localized-residual-posterior-mismatch} gives the exact localized
   replacement: the obstruction is the mismatch between the coordinate
   distribution of the residual budget and the posterior induced by the
   price-capped selector.  This is the form in which anchor-fiber mobility
   bounds should be plugged into the residual theorem.
   \Cref{cor:localized-residual-feasibility-dual} then turns that plug-in step
   into one finite LP dual: a failed localized residual budget produces a Hall
   gap mixture dominated coordinatewise by chart-mismatch directions.  Thus the
   next theorem can be stated positively as ruling out those dominated mixtures,
   rather than as a global Gaussian pseudocodeword-spectrum assertion.
   \Cref{cor:source-localized-residual-lp} gives the corresponding source-level
   normal form: one shared residual budget is enough exactly when every
   chart-dominated aggregate of source-local Hall gaps has small value.  This is
   the current cleanest finite target for a Tanner, SA, or list-recovery proof.
   \Cref{cor:shared-envelope-distance-form} removes the score tables from that
   target: for each convex combination of chart-mismatch directions, project the
   exposed relaxation sources to the true codeword hull while keeping the
   coordinatewise positive envelope small in that direction.

   \Cref{cor:leader-shift-near-leader-certificate} gives the clean terminal
   version of this idea when scalar leakage is killed exactly, or otherwise
   bounded with the true local maximum \(M(u)\).  Shift at \(M(u)\), not at the
   external frontier \(T-\gamma\).  Then the branch tree is still charged by
   the ordinary true-codeword exponential moment
   \(\sum_u e^{\lambda M(u)}\), while the projected pseudocodeword term is
   only the negative coefficient mass against internal near-leader gaps.  In
   particular, exact balance plus the condition that negative coefficients are
   supported on codewords within \(O(\sqrt{\log\log n})\) unnormalized score of
   the local leader would close the projected-bias part of the LP/SA theorem
   up to the already separated orthogonal width and radius terms.  This is the
   most concrete current coding-theoretic target.

   \Cref{cor:boltzmann-negative-tail-certificate} is a softer and probably
   more realistic version of the same target.  The low-rate code theorem need
   not prove literal zero negative mass below the near-leader window.  It is
   enough to prove that the weighted partition function
   \[
      \sup_{h\in E_u}
      e^{\lambda M(u)\kappa_u(h)}
      \left(
         1+\sum_j a_u(h)_j^- e^{\lambda(M(u)-W(c_j))}
      \right)
   \]
   is polylogarithmic at the Gaussian tilt \(\lambda=T/b\), after the
   orthogonal width/radius factors are included.  This turns the remaining
   coding statement from a brittle support property into an internal
   negative-tail estimate: far-below-leader codewords may receive negative
   coefficient mass, but only in proportion to their exponential score gap.

   \Cref{cor:cumulative-internal-tail-certificate} rewrites this estimate in
   the form a code proof can realistically certify.  For each anchored excess
   \(h\), let \(A_{u,h}(s)\) be the negative coefficient mass on true
   codewords lying at least \(s\) below the local leader.  It is enough that
   \(A_{u,h}(s)\) decay slightly faster than \(e^{-\lambda s}\) at the
   Gaussian tilt, or equivalently that a dyadic shell sum of these cumulative
   tails be polylogarithmic.  This is the current sharp target: prove an
   exponential internal-tail decay theorem for negative Gram coefficients of
   low-rate LP/SA pseudocodeword excesses, together with the already separated
   scalar-leakage and orthogonal-residual bounds.

   \Cref{cor:support-function-internal-tail-certificate} removes one more
   layer of coefficient bookkeeping.  The cumulative tail \(A_{u,h}(s)\) is
   exactly the support function of the anchored excess set in directions
   \(-A_uG_u^+r\), where \(r\) ranges over fractional selectors of true
   codewords at least \(s\) below the leader.  Thus the low-rate theorem can be
   stated as a separation theorem for the LP/SA relaxation: down-score
   selectors should have exponentially small support over anchored excesses.
   A failure is not vague; it returns an explicit selector \(r\) and objective
   direction for the local relaxation.

   \Cref{cor:anchor-fiber-internal-tail-certificate} makes this separation
   fully finite.  Once the anchor map is fixed, the support check decomposes
   over fibers \(P_{u,c}\): for each below-leader selector \(r\) and each
   anchor \(c\), solve the LP with objective
   \(-A_uG_u^+r\) over the fiber relaxation and compare against the anchored
   codeword \(c\).  Thus a failure of the negative-tail theorem is an explicit
   fractional point in one anchor fiber, not a global pseudocodeword mystery.

   \Cref{cor:anchor-fiber-lp-sa-compiler} packages the preceding reductions
   into the checklist form needed for an actual Tanner or Sherali--Adams proof:
   scalar balance and negative-mass normalization, anchor-fiber separation LPs,
   and an orthogonal residual bound.  Once these local checks have
   polylogarithmic slack at the Gaussian tilt, the branch-and-bound overhead
   follows from the existing false-survivor accounting automatically.

   \Cref{cor:singleton-down-influence-certificate} simplifies the most
   expensive line in that checklist.  The selector \(r\) need not be handled as
   an arbitrary point of a high-dimensional cube: by subadditivity of support
   functions, it suffices to bound the singleton down-influences
   \(I_{u,c,j}\) and prove their cumulative exponential decay over true
   codewords below the local leader.  This is a smaller and more code-like
   theorem target.

   \Cref{cor:singleton-boltzmann-influence-certificate} is the corresponding
   tilted-moment form.  It asks only for the weighted sum
   \(\sum_j e^{\lambda(M-W(c_j))}I_{u,c,j}\) to be polylogarithmic on every
   anchor fiber.  This is probably the cleanest statement for an LP/SA proof
   based on Gaussian tilting: the hard object is a singleton influence
   partition function, not a family of selector LPs.

   \Cref{cor:simplex-envelope-influence-compiler} translates this influence
   partition function into ordinary \(q\)-ary code geometry.  For product-simplex
   relaxations, \(I_{u,c,j}\) is bounded by the coordinate envelope of the
   inverse-Gram objective \(-A_uG_u^+e_j\) around the anchor \(c\).  Therefore
   the remaining theorem can be attacked by distance or overlap shells: prove
   that the envelope decays with separation from \(c\), and prove a planted
   tilted enumerator bound for the corresponding score shells.

   \Cref{cor:mobility-envelope-influence-compiler} records the more plausible
   contracted-fiber form.  The full product-simplex envelope usually leaves a
   diagonal inverse-Gram contribution for every true codeword overlapping the
   anchor, which is too large once it is multiplied by the Boltzmann gap weights.
   A successful singleton-influence proof should therefore show that the
   anchor-fiber relaxation has small off-anchor mobility on the dangerous
   coordinates, or else return to the aggregate selector support-function
   condition where cancellations between many codewords are still visible.

   \Cref{cor:aggregate-mobility-selector-certificate} makes the second option
   finite.  Instead of bounding each singleton column of \(G_u^+\), it bounds
   the support of the aggregate selector objective \(-A_uG_u^+\theta\) through
   the same mobility constraints.  This is strictly the safer theorem target:
   low-rate code geometry may cancel the dangerous inverse-Gram directions only
   after the below-leader selector has been aggregated.

   \Cref{cor:box-dual-mobility-certificate} dualizes the remaining selector box.
   The obstruction is now a mobility multiplier pattern \(\beta\) on off-anchor
   coordinate-symbols, and the required estimate is a positive-part enumerator
   over true codewords with Boltzmann weights.  This is closer to a planted
   decoding theorem: every dangerous fractional movement pattern must have small
   tilted positive correlation with the low-scoring codeword population.

   \Cref{cor:laplace-tail-mobility-enumerator} puts this last condition in the
   most conventional probabilistic form.  For each mobility pattern \(\beta\),
   one may prove either a tail bound for the weighted population with
   \(L_{u,c,\beta}(j)\ge t\), or a Laplace bound for
   \(\sum_jw_j\exp(\nu L_{u,c,\beta}(j))\).  This is the current clean proof
   target for low-rate Tanner/SA panels: under the planted Boltzmann weights,
   every certified off-anchor movement pattern should have only polylogarithmic
   positive tail.

   \Cref{cor:balanced-gram-mobility-scores} removes the last notational
   ambiguity from that target.  Each mobility pattern is an ambient direction
   \(d_\beta\) whose entries sum to zero in every coordinate block, and the
   scalar score is
   \(L_\beta(j)=-(G_u^+A_u^\top d_\beta)_j\).  Thus the remaining theorem is a
   one-sided Laplace or negative-part estimate for inverse-Gram coefficients of
   balanced directions under the Boltzmann tilt.  This is the form in which a
   low-rate Tanner, level-2 SA, or list-recovery proof should be attempted.

   \Cref{cor:score-leader-anchoring} removes a diagonal nuisance from that
   target.  Instead of assigning fractional points to arbitrary anchor codewords,
   one may anchor the whole node at its current score leader.  The conditional
   certificates are unchanged, because the leader is measurable after the true
   codeword scores in the node are revealed.  The important consequence is that
   the anchor's self-column has Boltzmann weight one, not
   \(e^{\lambda(M-W(c))}\) for a possibly low-scoring anchor.

   \Cref{cor:diagonal-preconditioned-leader-mobility} then isolates the random
   code-like part of the problem.  After expanding \(G_u^+\) around the diagonal
   preconditioner \(b^{-1}I\), the leader-anchored mobility certificate splits
   into the explicit self-mobility budget \(B_\beta/b\), an off-anchor planted
   enumerator for \((\zeta_\beta(j))^-\), and a residual term measuring how
   far the inverse overlap Gram is from \(b^{-1}I\) on balanced directions.  This
   is the sharpened target for random-code, Tanner, or list-recovery panels.

   \Cref{cor:coordinate-overlap-load-closure} turns the off-anchor enumerator
   into an even more concrete weighted list-recovery load.  Since
   \(\zeta_\beta(j)\) can be negative only when \(c_j\) agrees with the score
   leader on still-mobile coordinates, it is enough to bound the Boltzmann mass
   of codewords sharing each leader coordinate.  The residual target is now
   explicit: small leader-coordinate overlap loads on mobile coordinates, plus
   a small inverse-Gram preconditioning error on balanced directions.

   \Cref{cor:convex-residual-mobility-certificate} records the cleaner version
   for an actual LP/SA theorem.  The score-leader bound is useful for diagnosing
   which overlaps are dangerous, but it measures displacement from the leader and
   can therefore charge ordinary low-scoring true codewords.  The convex-residual
   certificate first compares each LP point to a point of the true codeword
   convex hull.  Integral codewords then have zero residual, and the remaining
   theorem is a transported balanced-direction tail bound for only the genuinely
   fractional mass.  This is the right target for a sharp LP, constant-level
   Sherali--Adams, or iterative-decoding proof.

   \Cref{cor:residual-hall-verifier} makes that target finite.  A proposed
   residual budget \(\mu\) is valid exactly when every nonnegative symbol-score
   objective has relaxation advantage over true codewords at most
   \(\ip{y}{\mu}\).  A failure returns the score table \(y\) and fractional point
   \(z\) witnessing the pseudocodeword obstruction.  Thus the convex-hull
   residual step can be certified by code maximization and relaxation
   maximization oracles, rather than by explicitly materializing
   \(\operatorname{conv}(C_u)\).

   \Cref{cor:priced-residual-gap-duality} gives the sharper objective-wise
   version.  Instead of fixing a coordinate budget \(\mu\) in advance, give
   positive residual mass a price \(r\).  The exact minimum priced distance to
   the true convex hull is dual to a clipped nonnegative score-table gap
   \(0\le y\le r\).  For an inverse-Gram selector direction this means the
   separator searches only the score tables that are actually visible to that
   direction, reducing the overcharge from a single global residual envelope.

   \Cref{cor:well-conditioned-gram-coefficients} gives the first elementary
   path to such a theorem.  If the local subcode has a well-conditioned overlap
   Gram matrix, then overlap vectors \(v_u(h)\) with small norm and sparse
   coefficient support automatically have small projected radius and small
   negative coefficient mass.  The remaining, genuinely coding-theoretic
   statement is that level-2 or level-3 local constraints force precisely this
   form of sparse, low-leakage overlap for every false-surviving fractional
   pseudocodeword.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Sampled structured-panel compiler]
   \label{prop:sampled-structured-panel}
   Fix a terminal localized ANN subproblem of size \(m\), approximation \(c\),
   and target exponent \(\rho=\rho_c\).  Let \(L_m=\log^{A_c}m\).  A random
   sampled panel \(\mathcal P\) consists of a finite label set \(\mathcal L\),
   data predicates \(A_g(x)\in\{0,1\}\), and, for every promised query \(q\),
   a probability law \(\pi_q\) on \(\mathcal L\) from which the query can sample in
   \(d\log^{O_c(1)}m\) time per trial.  Suppose that
   \[
      \E_{\mathcal P}\sum_{x\in P}\sum_{g\in\mathcal L}A_g(x)
      \le m^{1+\rho}L_m ,
      \tag{SP1}
   \]
   and, for every promised query \(q\),
   \[
      \E_{\mathcal P}
      \sum_{\substack{x\in P\\ \|x-q\|>cr}}
      \sum_{g\in\mathcal L}\pi_q(g)A_g(x)
      \le m^\rho L_m .
      \tag{SP2}
   \]
   Finally assume that every near pair \((p,q)\), \(\|p-q\|\le r\), satisfies
   the one-sample hit condition
   \[
      \E_{\mathcal P}
      \sum_{g\in\mathcal L}\pi_q(g)A_g(p)
      \ge L_m^{-1}.
      \tag{SP3}
   \]
   Then \(O(L_m)\) independent sampled panels give a terminal ANN data
   structure with query work
   \[
      d\,m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m
   \]
   and space
   \[
      dm+m^{1+\rho}\log^{O_c(1)}m .
   \]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
   Store \(B=\lceil C L_m\rceil\) independent panels.  In each panel, put
   every point \(x\) in every bucket \(g\) with \(A_g(x)=1\).  The expected
   stored point-bucket incidences are bounded by \(B m^{1+\rho}L_m\), which is
   \(m^{1+\rho}\log^{O_c(1)}m\); the raw coordinates add \(dm\).

   On query \(q\), draw one label \(g\sim\pi_q\) from each panel, scan the
   corresponding bucket, and verify all reported points in the original metric.
   By \((SP2)\), the expected number of invalid scanned points per panel is at
   most \(m^\rho L_m\), and the sampling overhead is
   \(d\log^{O_c(1)}m\).  Multiplying by \(B\) gives the displayed query bound
   after increasing the polylogarithmic exponent.

   If \(p\) is a true near neighbor of \(q\), the probability that one random
   panel and one label sample hit a bucket containing \(p\) is at least
   \(L_m^{-1}\) by \((SP3)\).  Hence all \(B\) independent trials miss \(p\)
   with probability at most \((1-L_m^{-1})^B\le e^{-C}\).  Taking \(C\) large
   gives constant success probability, and verification prevents false
   positives.  The capped-expectation convention from the preliminaries gives
   the stated capped resources after the usual constant-factor loss.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Gibbs sampled product-panel certificate]
   \label{cor:gibbs-sampled-product-panel}
   Fix the terminal setting of \cref{prop:sampled-structured-panel}.  A random
   product panel has labels
   \(\mathcal C=\prod_{j=1}^h\mathcal C_j\), data scores
   \[
      S_P(x,c)=\sum_{j=1}^h\psi_j(x,c_j),
      \qquad
      S_Q(q,c)=\sum_{j=1}^h\phi_j(q,c_j),
   \]
   and stores \(x\) in bucket \(c\) when \(S_P(x,c)\ge\theta_P\).  For a
   promised query \(q\), the query samples one label from the Gibbs law
   \[
      \pi_q(c)=\frac{e^{\beta S_Q(q,c)}}{Z_Q(q)},
      \qquad
      Z_Q(q)=\sum_{a\in\mathcal C}e^{\beta S_Q(q,a)}.
   \]
   Assume this law can be sampled in \(d\log^{O_c(1)}m\) time.  Suppose that
   for some \(\alpha,\beta>0\),
   \[
      \E
      \sum_{x\in P}
      e^{-\alpha\theta_P}
      \sum_{c\in\mathcal C}e^{\alpha S_P(x,c)}
      \le m^{1+\rho}L_m,
      \tag{GS1}
   \]
   and, for every promised query \(q\),
   \[
      \E
      \sum_{\substack{x\in P\\ \|x-q\|>cr}}
      \frac{
         e^{-\alpha\theta_P}
         \sum_{c\in\mathcal C}
         e^{\alpha S_P(x,c)+\beta S_Q(q,c)}
      }{Z_Q(q)}
      \le m^\rho L_m .
      \tag{GS2}
   \]
   Finally assume that every near pair \((p,q)\), \(\|p-q\|\le r\), satisfies
   \[
      \E
      \frac{
         \sum_{c\in\mathcal C:\,S_P(p,c)\ge\theta_P}
         e^{\beta S_Q(q,c)}
      }{Z_Q(q)}
      \ge L_m^{-1}.
      \tag{GS3}
   \]
   Then \(O(L_m)\) independent Gibbs sampled product panels give the terminal
   ANN bounds of \cref{prop:sampled-structured-panel}.

   If the labels are a full product and
   \(Z_j^Q(q),Z_j^P(x),Z_j^{PQ}(x,q)\) are as in
   \cref{lem:product-panel-tensorization}, then
   \[
      Z_Q(q)=\prod_jZ_j^Q(q),
      \qquad
      \sum_{c\in\mathcal C}e^{\alpha S_P(x,c)}
      =\prod_jZ_j^P(x),
   \]
   and
   \[
      \frac{
         \sum_c e^{\alpha S_P(x,c)+\beta S_Q(q,c)}
      }{Z_Q(q)}
      =
      \prod_j\frac{Z_j^{PQ}(x,q)}{Z_j^Q(q)}.
      \tag{GS4}
   \]
   Thus \((GS1)\) and \((GS2)\) factor block-by-block.  If
   \(\theta_P=\sum_j\theta_{P,j}\), then the near condition is implied by
   \[
      \prod_j
      \E\left[
      \frac{
         \sum_{a\in\mathcal C_j:\,\psi_j(p,a)\ge\theta_{P,j}}
         e^{\beta\phi_j(q,a)}
      }{Z_j^Q(q)}
      \right]
      \ge L_m^{-1}
      \tag{GS5}
   \]
   whenever the block panels are independent.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   For a realized panel, set the sampled-panel label set to
   \(\mathcal L=\mathcal C\), put
   \(A_c(x)=\mathbf 1\{S_P(x,c)\ge\theta_P\}\), and use the displayed Gibbs
   law \(\pi_q\).  The storage condition \((SP1)\) follows from
   \[
      A_c(x)\le e^{\alpha(S_P(x,c)-\theta_P)}
   \]
   and \((GS1)\).  For far sampled co-load,
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      \sum_c\pi_q(c)A_c(x)
      &\le
      \frac{
         e^{-\alpha\theta_P}
         \sum_c e^{\alpha S_P(x,c)+\beta S_Q(q,c)}
      }{Z_Q(q)} ,
   \end{aligned}
   \]
   so \((SP2)\) follows from \((GS2)\).  The near sampled mass condition
   \((SP3)\) is exactly \((GS3)\).  Therefore
   \cref{prop:sampled-structured-panel} applies.

   The factor identities in \((GS4)\) follow by expanding the additive product
   scores and summing independently over the coordinates \(c_j\).  Finally, on
   the block event
   \(\psi_j(p,c_j)\ge\theta_{P,j}\) for every \(j\), the full label satisfies
   \(S_P(p,c)\ge\theta_P\).  Since the Gibbs law and the random panel factor
   across independent blocks, the expected Gibbs mass of this sufficient event
   is the product in \((GS5)\), which proves the last claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Gibbs sampled product-panel rate bookkeeping]
   \label{cor:gibbs-sampled-rate-bookkeeping}
   Work in the full-product setting of
   \cref{cor:gibbs-sampled-product-panel}, and assume the number of blocks is
   \(h\le\log^{O_c(1)}m\).  The query Gibbs sampler is the product sampler
   obtained from the one-block laws proportional to
   \(e^{\beta\phi_j(q,a)}\), and its sampling time is
   \(d\log^{O_c(1)}m\).  For data points, far pairs, and near pairs define
   \[
      \mathfrak s_j(x)=
      \E\!\left[e^{-\alpha\theta_{P,j}}Z_j^P(x)\right],
   \]
   \[
      \mathfrak f_j(x,q)=
      \E\!\left[
         e^{-\alpha\theta_{P,j}}
         \frac{Z_j^{PQ}(x,q)}{Z_j^Q(q)}
      \right],
   \]
   and
   \[
      \mathfrak h_j(p,q)=
      \E\!\left[
      \frac{
         \sum_{a\in\mathcal C_j:\,\psi_j(p,a)\ge\theta_{P,j}}
         e^{\beta\phi_j(q,a)}
      }{Z_j^Q(q)}
      \right].
   \]
   If
   \[
      \prod_{j=1}^h\mathfrak s_j(x)
      \le m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m
      \qquad\text{for every data point }x,
      \tag{GR1}
   \]
   \[
      \prod_{j=1}^h\mathfrak f_j(x,q)
      \le m^{-(1-\rho)}\log^{O_c(1)}m
      \qquad
      \text{whenever }\|x-q\|>cr,
      \tag{GR2}
   \]
   and
   \[
      \prod_{j=1}^h\mathfrak h_j(p,q)
      \ge \log^{-O_c(1)}m
      \qquad
      \text{whenever }\|p-q\|\le r,
      \tag{GR3}
   \]
   then the Gibbs sampled product panel satisfies the terminal ANN bounds of
   \cref{prop:sampled-structured-panel}.

   Equivalently, it is enough to prove one-block log-rate bounds
   \[
      \mathfrak s_j(x)\le m^{v_j},\qquad
      \mathfrak f_j(x,q)\le m^{-w_j},\qquad
      \mathfrak h_j(p,q)\ge e^{-b_j},
   \]
   with
   \[
      \sum_jv_j\le\rho+O_c\!\left(\frac{\log\log m}{\log m}\right),
      \qquad
      \sum_jw_j\ge1-\rho-O_c\!\left(\frac{\log\log m}{\log m}\right),
   \]
   and
   \[
      \sum_jb_j=O_c(\log\log m).
   \]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Since the product sampler chooses block symbols independently with
   probabilities proportional to \(e^{\beta\phi_j(q,a)}\), its law on
   \(\mathcal C\) is exactly the Gibbs law in
   \cref{cor:gibbs-sampled-product-panel}.  For a fixed data point \(x\),
   independence and \((GS4)\) give
   \[
      \E e^{-\alpha\theta_P}
      \sum_{c\in\mathcal C}e^{\alpha S_P(x,c)}
      =
      \prod_j\mathfrak s_j(x).
   \]
   Summing over \(x\in P\) and applying \((GR1)\) gives \((GS1)\).  For a
   fixed far pair \((x,q)\), the mixed/query partition ratio factors as
   \[
      \E\,
      \frac{
         e^{-\alpha\theta_P}
         \sum_c e^{\alpha S_P(x,c)+\beta S_Q(q,c)}
      }{Z_Q(q)}
      =
      \prod_j\mathfrak f_j(x,q).
   \]
   Summing over the at most \(m\) far points and using \((GR2)\) gives
   \((GS2)\).  Finally, \((GR3)\) is exactly the sufficient product lower bound
   \((GS5)\) for the near Gibbs mass condition \((GS3)\).  Hence
   \cref{cor:gibbs-sampled-product-panel} applies.

   The log-rate form is obtained by multiplying the one-block bounds and using
   \(m^{O_c((\log\log m)/\log m)}=\log^{O_c(1)}m\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Tilted moment lower bound for Gibbs near mass]
   \label{lem:gibbs-near-moment-lower-bound}
   Fix one block of a Gibbs sampled product panel, one query \(q\), and one
   near point \(p\).  Let
   \[
      \Pi_q(a)=\frac{e^{\beta\phi(q,a)}}{Z^Q(q)}
   \]
   be the block query Gibbs law on the block labels, and let
   \(\psi(p,a)\) be the block data storage score.  For \(\gamma>0\) put
   \[
      M_\gamma(p,q)
      =
      e^{-\gamma\theta_P}
      \sum_a\Pi_q(a)e^{\gamma\psi(p,a)}
      =
      \frac{
         e^{-\gamma\theta_P}
         \sum_a e^{\gamma\psi(p,a)+\beta\phi(q,a)}
      }{Z^Q(q)} .
   \]
   Then, for every realized block,
   \[
      \Pi_q\{\psi(p,a)\ge\theta_P\}
      \ge
      \frac{(M_\gamma(p,q)-1)_+^2}{M_{2\gamma}(p,q)}.
      \tag{GM1}
   \]
   Consequently, in the notation of
   \cref{cor:gibbs-sampled-rate-bookkeeping},
   \[
      \mathfrak h_j(p,q)
      \ge
      \E\left[
      \frac{(M_{j,\gamma}(p,q)-1)_+^2}{M_{j,2\gamma}(p,q)}
      \right],
      \tag{GM2}
   \]
   where \(M_{j,\gamma}\) is the corresponding block quantity.  In
   particular, the near-rate condition \((GR3)\) follows if the product over
   blocks of the right-hand side of \((GM2)\) is at least
   \(\log^{-O_c(1)}m\).  A simpler sufficient deterministic margin is
   \[
      M_{j,\gamma}(p,q)\ge 1+\delta_j,
      \qquad
      M_{j,2\gamma}(p,q)\le U_j
   \]
   on an event of probability \(1-\varepsilon_j\), which gives
   \[
      \mathfrak h_j(p,q)
      \ge
      (1-\varepsilon_j)\frac{\delta_j^2}{U_j}.
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Let \(Y=e^{\gamma(\psi(p,A)-\theta_P)}\), where
   \(A\sim\Pi_q\).  Then \(\E Y=M_\gamma(p,q)\) and
   \(\E Y^2=M_{2\gamma}(p,q)\).  Since
   \[
      \E(Y-1)_+\ge(\E Y-1)_+,
   \]
   and since \((Y-1)_+\le Y\mathbf 1_{\{Y\ge1\}}\), Cauchy's inequality gives
   \[
      (M_\gamma-1)_+^2
      \le
      \left(\E Y\mathbf 1_{\{Y\ge1\}}\right)^2
      \le
      \E Y^2\cdot \Pr[Y\ge1].
   \]
   The event \(Y\ge1\) is exactly
   \(\{\psi(p,A)\ge\theta_P\}\), proving \((GM1)\).  Averaging \((GM1)\) over
   the random block gives \((GM2)\).  The product and deterministic-margin
   statements are immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Critical tilted-Gaussian sampled spectrum]
   \label{lem:critical-tilted-gaussian-sampled-spectrum}
   Fix \(c>1\), and put
   \[
      a_0=1-\frac1{c^2},
      \qquad
      \rho=\frac1{2c^2-1}.
   \]
   Let \(m\ge2\), \(L=\log m\), and choose a storage threshold \(T\) and query
   tilt \(\beta\) by
   \[
      T^2=2(1-\rho)L,
      \qquad
      \beta=\frac{T}{a_0}.
   \]
   Consider the ideal continuous Gaussian filter family with base label
   \(G\sim N(0,I_d)\), label intensity \(m\), and storage predicate
   \[
      A_G(x)=\mathbf 1\{\ip{G}{x}\ge T\}
      \qquad(x\in\mathbb S^{d-1}).
   \]
   For a query \(q\), sample the filter label from the exponentially tilted
   law \(G_q\sim N(\beta q,I_d)\).  Then the following spectrum bounds hold.
   For every data point \(x\),
   \[
      m\,\Pr[\ip{G}{x}\ge T]\le m^\rho.
      \tag{TG1}
   \]
   For every far pair with \(\ip{x}{q}\le0\),
   \[
      \Pr[\ip{G_q}{x}\ge T]\le m^{-(1-\rho)}.
      \tag{TG2}
   \]
   For every near pair with \(\ip{p}{q}\ge a_0\),
   \[
      \Pr[\ip{G_q}{p}\ge T]\ge\frac12.
      \tag{TG3}
   \]
   Thus the ideal sampled Gaussian spectrum has storage rate \(\rho\), sampled
   far-separation rate \(1-\rho\), and constant near sampled mass at the
   critical Euclidean normalization.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   For a unit vector \(x\), \(\ip{G}{x}\sim N(0,1)\).  The elementary Gaussian
   tail bound gives
   \[
      m\,\Pr[\ip{G}{x}\ge T]
      \le m e^{-T^2/2}
      =
      m^\rho,
   \]
   proving \((TG1)\).

   If \(\ip{x}{q}\le0\), then
   \(\ip{G_q}{x}\sim N(\beta\ip{x}{q},1)\) has mean at most zero, so
   \[
      \Pr[\ip{G_q}{x}\ge T]\le e^{-T^2/2}=m^{-(1-\rho)},
   \]
   which is \((TG2)\).  If \(\ip{p}{q}\ge a_0\), then
   \(\ip{G_q}{p}\sim N(\beta\ip{p}{q},1)\) has mean at least
   \(\beta a_0=T\).  Therefore
   \[
      \Pr[\ip{G_q}{p}\ge T]\ge \Pr[N(T,1)\ge T]=\frac12,
   \]
   proving \((TG3)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the tilted-Gaussian spectrum supplies]
   \label{rem:tilted-gaussian-spectrum}
   \Cref{lem:critical-tilted-gaussian-sampled-spectrum} is not by itself a
   finite index: a literal continuous filter family has no stored bucket for a
   newly sampled \(G_q\).  Its role is to identify the exact spectrum that a
   structured code, lattice, trellis, or product panel should emulate.  A
   compact panel that realizes this Gaussian quadrature and supports sampling
   from the query tilt would plug into
   \cref{cor:gibbs-sampled-rate-bookkeeping}.  The calculation also explains
   why sampling is potentially easier than reporting here: at the critical
   normalization the query does not need to enumerate the
   \(m^\rho\) active filters.  One tilted sample already lands in a near
   filter with constant probability, while its expected far bucket size is
   \(m^\rho\).
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Naive Gaussian-label quadrature barrier]
   \label{lem:naive-gaussian-quadrature-barrier}
   In the setting of
   \cref{lem:critical-tilted-gaussian-sampled-spectrum}, let
   \(M=m^\nu\) independent base labels \(G_1,\ldots,G_M\sim N(0,I_d)\) be used
   as an ordinary Monte Carlo discretization of the query tilt.  More generally
   take a threshold \(T^2=2\tau\log m\) and the near-critical tilt
   \(\beta=T/a_0\).  For a fixed query \(q\), the Monte Carlo estimator of the
   tilted partition function
   \[
      Z_q=\E e^{\beta\ip{G}{q}}=e^{\beta^2/2}
   \]
   is
   \[
      \widehat Z_q=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M e^{\beta\ip{G_i}{q}},
   \]
   and its relative variance is
   \[
      \frac{\operatorname{Var}\widehat Z_q}{Z_q^2}
      =
      \frac{e^{\beta^2}-1}{M}
      =
      m^{2\tau/a_0^2-\nu+o(1)}.
      \tag{NQ1}
   \]
   Hence bounded-relative-variance Monte Carlo quadrature requires
   \[
      \nu\ge \frac{2\tau}{a_0^2}-o(1).
      \tag{NQ2}
   \]
   On the other hand, the ANN storage and sampled far-load powers force
   \[
      \nu\le\tau+\rho+o(1),
      \qquad
      \tau\ge1-\rho-o(1).
      \tag{NQ3}
   \]
   These three inequalities are incompatible for every fixed \(c>1\).
   Consequently the ideal tilted-Gaussian sampler cannot be materialized by a
   plain iid Gaussian label pool whose correctness is proved by ordinary
   self-normalized Monte Carlo concentration; the finite construction must use
   additional structure, such as a code, lattice, trellis, or deterministic
   quadrature.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Since \(\ip{G}{q}\sim N(0,1)\),
   \[
      \E e^{\beta\ip{G}{q}}=e^{\beta^2/2},
      \qquad
      \E e^{2\beta\ip{G}{q}}=e^{2\beta^2}.
   \]
   Thus
   \[
      \frac{\operatorname{Var}\widehat Z_q}{Z_q^2}
      =
      \frac1M
      \frac{e^{2\beta^2}-e^{\beta^2}}{e^{\beta^2}}
      =
      \frac{e^{\beta^2}-1}{M}.
   \]
   Since \(\beta^2=2\tau\log m/a_0^2\), this is \((NQ1)\), and \((NQ2)\)
   follows.

   The expected number of stored labels for one point is
   \[
      M\Pr[N(0,1)\ge T]=m^{\nu-\tau+o(1)},
   \]
   so keeping the per-point storage within \(m^{\rho+o(1)}\) gives
   \(\nu\le\tau+\rho+o(1)\).  For a far point with correlation zero to the
   query, the continuous tilted law leaves its score distributed as \(N(0,1)\).
   Thus a sampled far bucket has probability \(m^{-\tau+o(1)}\), and summing
   over \(m\) far points gives the target \(m^\rho\) only if
   \(\tau\ge1-\rho-o(1)\).  This proves \((NQ3)\).

   It remains to check incompatibility.  Write \(C=c^2>1\).  Then
   \(a_0=(C-1)/C\) and \(\rho=1/(2C-1)\).  At the smallest possible
   \(\tau=1-\rho\),
   \[
      \frac{2\tau}{a_0^2}-(\tau+\rho)
      =
      \frac{2C^2+3C-1}{(C-1)(2C-1)}
      >0.
   \]
   The left-hand side is increasing in \(\tau\), so the gap remains positive
   for every \(\tau\ge1-\rho\).  Thus \((NQ2)\) and \((NQ3)\) cannot both hold.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Weighted Gaussian quadrature panel verifier]
   \label{cor:weighted-gaussian-quadrature-panel}
   Fix a terminal spherical instance of size \(m\) at the critical parameters
   of \cref{lem:critical-tilted-gaussian-sampled-spectrum}.  Let \(L_m\) be a
   sufficiently large power of \(\log m\).  A retained weighted quadrature
   panel consists of labels \(g\in\mathcal L\subset\mathbb R^d\), positive
   weights \(w_g\), a storage threshold \(T\), and a query tilt \(\beta\).
   Store \(x\) in bucket \(g\) when
   \[
      \ip{g}{x}\ge T.
   \]
   On query \(q\), sample one label from
   \[
      \pi_q(g)=
      \frac{w_g e^{\beta\ip{g}{q}}}
           {\sum_{h\in\mathcal L}w_h e^{\beta\ip{h}{q}}},
      \tag{WQ0}
   \]
   assuming this sampling operation is supported in \(d\log^{O_c(1)}m\) time.

   If the retained panel satisfies
   \[
      \sum_{x\in P}
      |\{g\in\mathcal L:\ip{g}{x}\ge T\}|
      \le m^{1+\rho}L_m,
      \tag{WQ1}
   \]
   \[
      \sum_{\substack{x\in P\\ \|x-q\|>cr}}
      \sum_{\substack{g\in\mathcal L\\ \ip{g}{x}\ge T}}
      \pi_q(g)
      \le m^\rho L_m
      \qquad\text{for every promised query }q,
      \tag{WQ2}
   \]
   and
   \[
      \sum_{\substack{g\in\mathcal L\\ \ip{g}{p}\ge T}}
      \pi_q(g)
      \ge L_m^{-1}
      \qquad
      \text{whenever }\|p-q\|\le r,
      \tag{WQ3}
   \]
   then \(O(L_m)\) independent retained panels give the terminal ANN bounds of
   \cref{prop:sampled-structured-panel}.

   The same statement holds for labels drawn from a structured code, lattice,
   trellis, or product panel after replacing \(\ip{g}{x}\) by the certified
   data score and \(\ip{g}{q}\) by the certified query score.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   This is \cref{prop:sampled-structured-panel} with
   \(A_g(x)=\mathbf 1\{\ip{g}{x}\ge T\}\) and the query sampling law
   \((WQ0)\).  The storage, far sampled co-load, and near sampled mass
   hypotheses are exactly \((SP1)\), \((SP2)\), and \((SP3)\).  The final
   sentence is only a change of notation for the same sampled-panel compiler.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Bucket-quotient weighted quadrature]
   \label{cor:bucket-quotient-quadrature}
   Fix the terminal setting of \cref{prop:sampled-structured-panel}.  Let
   \(\mathcal L\) be any finite or compact label family with base weights
   \(w_g\), data predicates \(A_g(x)\in\{0,1\}\), and positive query scores
   \(R_q(g)\).  Partition the labels into bucket classes \(b\in\mathcal B\) by
   the stored point set
   \[
      C_b=\{x\in P:A_g(x)=1\},
      \qquad g\in b.
   \]
   For a query \(q\), define the aggregate tilted bucket weight
   \[
      W_q(b)=\sum_{g\in b}w_gR_q(g),
      \qquad
      \Pi_q(b)=\frac{W_q(b)}{\sum_{a\in\mathcal B}W_q(a)} .
   \]
   The same definition applies with integrals when a bucket class contains a
   continuum of labels.  Suppose that the query can sample \(b\sim\Pi_q\) in
   \(d\log^{O_c(1)}m\) time, and that
   \[
      \sum_{b\in\mathcal B}|C_b|\le m^{1+\rho}L_m,
      \tag{BQ1}
   \]
   \[
      \sum_{\substack{x\in P\\\|x-q\|>cr}}
      \sum_{b:x\in C_b}\Pi_q(b)
      \le m^\rho L_m
      \qquad\text{for every promised query }q,
      \tag{BQ2}
   \]
   and
   \[
      \sum_{b:p\in C_b}\Pi_q(b)
      \ge L_m^{-1}
      \qquad\text{whenever }\|p-q\|\le r.
      \tag{BQ3}
   \]
   Then \(O(L_m)\) independent quotient panels give the terminal ANN bounds of
   \cref{prop:sampled-structured-panel}.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Store one bucket \(C_b\) per bucket class \(b\).  Use the sampled-panel label
   set \(\mathcal B\), predicate
   \[
      A_b(x)=\mathbf 1\{x\in C_b\},
   \]
   and query law \(\Pi_q\).  The three displayed assumptions are exactly
   \((SP1)\), \((SP2)\), and \((SP3)\) for this quotient panel.  Therefore
   \cref{prop:sampled-structured-panel} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the quotient buys]
   \label{rem:bucket-quotient}
   \Cref{cor:bucket-quotient-quadrature} separates two entropies that were
   conflated in \cref{cor:weighted-gaussian-quadrature-panel}.  A trellis,
   code, lattice coset, or continuous Gaussian rule may have many internal
   labels, but the index stores point copies only for distinct bucket sets.
   Query time then depends on whether the decoder can compute or sample the
   aggregate weights \(W_q(b)\) without enumerating all labels in the bucket
   class.  Thus a structured decoder can win in either of two ways: by keeping
   the number of distinct stored buckets small, or by representing many labels
   with one bucket and sampling their total tilted mass directly.  The
   remaining certification is still the same three quantities: bucket storage,
   far sampled co-load, and near sampled mass.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Random sparse buckets do not quotient-compress]
   \label{lem:random-sparse-bucket-no-quotient}
   Let \(\mathcal L\) be a hidden label set and let \(P\) have size \(m\).
   For each \(g\in\mathcal L\), form a random stored bucket
   \(C_g\subseteq P\) by including each point independently with probability
   \(s_m\le1/2\), independently over \(g\).  If
   \[
      m s_m\to\infty,
      \qquad
      \log|\mathcal L|=o(ms_m),
      \tag{RBQ1}
   \]
   then, with probability \(1-o(1)\), all buckets \(C_g\) are distinct.
   Consequently quotienting only by identical stored point sets gives no
   asymptotic storage compression in this sparse random model.

   In particular, in the ANN sparse-storage scale
   \(s_m=m^{\rho-1+o(1)}\) with any fixed \(\rho>0\), every polynomial-size
   hidden label family has distinct random buckets with high probability.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   For two labels \(g\ne h\),
   \[
      \Pr[C_g=C_h]
      =
      (s_m^2+(1-s_m)^2)^m
      =
      (1-2s_m(1-s_m))^m
      \le e^{-m s_m},
   \]
   because \(s_m\le1/2\).  The union bound over pairs gives
   \[
      \Pr[\exists g\ne h:C_g=C_h]
      \le
      |\mathcal L|^2e^{-m s_m}
      =
      \exp\{-m s_m+o(ms_m)\}=o(1).
   \]
   The final statement is the special case \(ms_m=m^{\rho+o(1)}\) and
   \(\log|\mathcal L|=O(\log m)=o(m^\rho)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What this storage barrier says]
   \label{rem:random-sparse-bucket-no-quotient}
   \Cref{lem:random-sparse-bucket-no-quotient} is deliberately simple, but it
   rules out a common false hope.  If a code, lattice, or trellis behaves like
   independent sparse filters on the retained data set, then identical-bucket
   quotienting almost never merges hidden labels.  A useful quotient sampler
   must therefore create shared bucket identities by design--for example
   through a canonical child map, a residue/coset bucket, a leader bucket, or a
   responsibility-thinned aggregate law.  Accidental equality of random stored
   subsets is not the compression mechanism.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Compressed aggregate sampler]
   \label{lem:compressed-aggregate-sampler}
   Let a finite acyclic directed graph have source \(s\), terminal states
   \(\mathcal T\), and edges \(e=(u,v)\).  A label is a path from \(s\) to a
   terminal \(t\), and each terminal has a bucket class \(b(t)\in\mathcal B\).
   Suppose the tilted weight of a path factors as
   \[
      \prod_{e\in\pi}r_e(q),
      \qquad r_e(q)>0.
   \]
   For a query \(q\), define suffix partition functions by the backward
   recursion
   \[
      H_q(t)=1\quad(t\in\mathcal T),
      \qquad
      H_q(u)=\sum_{(u,v)}r_{(u,v)}(q)H_q(v)
   \]
   at nonterminal states.  Then a top-down walk that, at state \(u\), chooses
   the edge \((u,v)\) with probability
   \[
      \frac{r_{(u,v)}(q)H_q(v)}{H_q(u)}
   \]
   outputs a terminal bucket \(b\) with probability proportional to the
   aggregate tilted weight of all labels ending in that bucket:
   \[
      \Pr[b(t)=b]
      =
      \frac{
         \sum_{\pi:s\leadsto t,\ b(t)=b}\prod_{e\in\pi}r_e(q)
      }{
         \sum_{\pi:s\leadsto t}\prod_{e\in\pi}r_e(q)
      } .
   \]
   The preprocessing may attach to each bucket class \(b\) its stored point set
   \(C_b\).  If the graph partition functions and the sampled path can be
   computed in \(d\log^{O_c(1)}m\) time, and the induced bucket law satisfies
   \((BQ1)\)--\((BQ3)\), then the terminal ANN bounds of
   \cref{prop:sampled-structured-panel} follow.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   For any state \(u\), the quantity \(H_q(u)\) is exactly the total tilted
   weight of all suffix paths from \(u\) to a terminal.  Therefore the displayed
   transition probabilities are normalized and sample a path with probability
   equal to its tilted weight divided by \(H_q(s)\).  Summing over all sampled
   paths whose terminal has bucket class \(b\) gives the displayed bucket
   probability.  The final statement is precisely
   \cref{cor:bucket-quotient-quadrature}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[BCJR trellis quotient sampler]
   \label{cor:bcjr-trellis-quotient-sampler}
   Let a code or quotient label family be represented by a layered acyclic
   trellis
   \[
      V_0\to V_1\to\cdots\to V_h,
   \]
   with source \(s\in V_0\).  Each edge \(e\in E_i\) from \(V_{i-1}\) to
   \(V_i\) carries a symbol \(a(e)\) and a positive query weight
   \(r_e(q)\).  Assume retained labels are the source-to-terminal paths
   \(\pi\), with tilted weight
   \[
      W_q(\pi)=\prod_{e\in\pi}r_e(q),
      \tag{BTS1}
   \]
   and that every terminal \(t\) maps to a stored bucket class \(b(t)\).
   Then the usual backward trellis recursion
   \[
      H_q(t)=1\quad(t\in V_h),\qquad
      H_q(u)=\sum_{(u,v)}r_{(u,v)}(q)H_q(v)
      \tag{BTS2}
   \]
   samples bucket \(b\) with probability
   \[
      \frac{
         \sum_{t\in V_h:\ b(t)=b}\sum_{\pi:s\leadsto t}W_q(\pi)
      }{
         \sum_{t\in V_h}\sum_{\pi:s\leadsto t}W_q(\pi)
      },
      \tag{BTS3}
   \]
   in arithmetic work \(O(|E|)\).

   In particular, convolutional or tail-biting trellises, recursive
   Barnes--Wall/Barnes--Sloane state graphs, and any polar, Tanner, or
   Construction-A residue decoder that exposes an exact acyclic sum-product
   state graph automatically implement the aggregate-query part of
   \cref{cor:bucket-quotient-quadrature}.  What remains is not a decoding
   theorem about nearest raw codewords; it is the bucket spectrum
   \((BQ1)\)--\((BQ3)\) for the induced quotient law.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   This is \cref{lem:compressed-aggregate-sampler} with the trellis layers as
   the acyclic graph.  The recursion \((BTS2)\) is exactly the BCJR backward
   partition function, and the top-down transition probabilities of
   \cref{lem:compressed-aggregate-sampler} sample each path with probability
   proportional to \((BTS1)\).  Summing sampled paths by terminal bucket gives
   \((BTS3)\).  Each edge contributes once to the backward pass and at most once
   to the sampled forward path, so the arithmetic work is linear in the trellis
   size.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Marked trellis spectrum verifier]
   \label{lem:marked-trellis-spectrum-verifier}
   Work with a layered acyclic trellis as in
   \cref{cor:bcjr-trellis-quotient-sampler}.  Let \(\mathcal P\) be its
   source-to-terminal paths, and let
   \[
      W_q(\pi)=\prod_{e\in\pi}r_e(q),
      \qquad
      Z_q=\sum_{\pi\in\mathcal P}W_q(\pi).
   \]
   Suppose that each point \(x\in P\) has an additive trellis storage score
   \[
      S_x(\pi)=\sum_{e\in\pi}\phi_e(x),
      \tag{MTS1}
   \]
   and that the raw hidden path stores \(x\) when \(S_x(\pi)\ge T\).  Let
   \[
      C_\pi=\{x\in P:S_x(\pi)\ge T\},
   \]
   and quotient paths by equality of \(C_\pi\).  For a query \(q\), define the
   marked partition function
   \[
      Z_{q,x}^{\ge T}
      =
      \sum_{\pi\in\mathcal P:\ S_x(\pi)\ge T}W_q(\pi).
      \tag{MTS2}
   \]
   Then the induced quotient bucket law satisfies the exact identities
   \[
      \sum_{b:x\in C_b}\Pi_q(b)
      =
      \frac{Z_{q,x}^{\ge T}}{Z_q}
      \qquad(x\in P),
      \tag{MTS3}
   \]
   and therefore the sampled far-load and near-mass conditions \((BQ2)\) and
   \((BQ3)\) are exactly
   \[
      \sum_{\substack{x\in P\\ \|x-q\|>cr}}
      \frac{Z_{q,x}^{\ge T}}{Z_q}
      \le m^\rho L_m,
      \tag{MTS4}
   \]
   and
   \[
      \frac{Z_{q,p}^{\ge T}}{Z_q}
      \ge L_m^{-1}
      \qquad(\|p-q\|\le r).
      \tag{MTS5}
   \]
   The raw incidence bound
   \[
      \sum_{x\in P}
      |\{\pi\in\mathcal P:S_x(\pi)\ge T\}|
      \le m^{1+\rho}L_m
      \tag{MTS6}
   \]
   is a sufficient, but not necessary, condition for the quotient storage
   bound \((BQ1)\).

   If all scores \(\phi_e(x)\) lie in a lattice \(\delta\mathbb Z\) and the
   attainable score range has \(M_x\) bins, then \(Z_{q,x}^{\ge T}\) is
   computable exactly by the marked forward recursion
   \[
      F_0(s,0)=1,\qquad
      F_i(v,t)=
      \sum_{(u,v)\in E_i}r_{(u,v)}(q)
      F_{i-1}\bigl(u,t-\phi_{(u,v)}(x)\bigr),
      \tag{MTS7}
   \]
   followed by
   \[
      Z_{q,x}^{\ge T}
      =
      \sum_{v\in V_h}\sum_{t\ge T}F_h(v,t),
      \tag{MTS8}
   \]
   in \(O(|E|M_x)\) arithmetic operations for that \(x\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The quotient bucket probability is obtained by summing path weights over
   all paths in the bucket class:
   \[
      \Pi_q(b)
      =
      \frac{\sum_{\pi:C_\pi=C_b}W_q(\pi)}
           {\sum_{\pi\in\mathcal P}W_q(\pi)} .
   \]
   Therefore
   \[
      \sum_{b:x\in C_b}\Pi_q(b)
      =
      \frac{\sum_{\pi:x\in C_\pi}W_q(\pi)}{Z_q}
      =
      \frac{Z_{q,x}^{\ge T}}{Z_q},
   \]
   which proves \((MTS3)\).  Summing \((MTS3)\) over invalid far points gives
   \((MTS4)\), and applying it to the true near point gives \((MTS5)\).

   For storage, the quotient stores one copy of \(x\) for each distinct bucket
   \(C_b\) containing \(x\).  This is at most the number of hidden paths whose
   raw bucket contains \(x\).  Summing over \(x\) gives \((MTS6)\Rightarrow
   (BQ1)\).

   Finally, \((MTS7)\) is the ordinary forward dynamic program with an extra
   score coordinate.  By induction on the layer, \(F_i(v,t)\) is the total
   \(W_q\)-weight of prefixes ending at \(v\) with storage score \(t\) for
   point \(x\).  Summing terminal states and score bins \(t\ge T\) gives
   \((MTS8)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the trellis verifier leaves open]
   \label{rem:marked-trellis-spectrum-target}
   \Cref{lem:marked-trellis-spectrum-verifier} is the concrete calculation to
   run for a Construction-A residue trellis, a low-state convolutional code, or
   a recursive lattice state graph.  The query side and the sampled near/far
   spectrum are transfer-matrix quantities.  The remaining storage question is
   separate: either the raw incidence bound \((MTS6)\) already fits, or the
   construction must prove a genuine canonicalization theorem for the distinct
   bucket sets \(C_\pi\).  By
   \cref{lem:random-sparse-bucket-no-quotient}, random-looking sparse bucket
   sets will not provide that compression by accidental equality.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Finite-state trellis rate test]
   \label{cor:finite-state-trellis-rate-test}
   Consider the additive trellis setting of
   \cref{lem:marked-trellis-spectrum-verifier}, but suppose the trellis is
   homogeneous of depth
   \[
      h=\lceil\kappa\log m\rceil
   \]
   on a fixed state set \(S\).  Let the source vector be \(e_s\) and let
   \(\mathbf 1\) denote the all-terminal vector.  For a query \(q\), define
   the tilted transition matrix
   \[
      A_q(u,v)=\sum_{e:u\to v}r_e(q),
   \]
   and for a point \(x\) define the marked matrices
   \[
      A_{q,x}(\theta)(u,v)
      =
      \sum_{e:u\to v}r_e(q)e^{\theta\phi_e(x)},
      \qquad
      B_x(\theta)(u,v)
      =
      \sum_{e:u\to v}e^{\theta\phi_e(x)} .
   \]
   Assume these matrices are Perron--Frobenius regular uniformly over the
   relevant \(q,x,\theta\), in the sense that their boundary partition
   functions differ from the corresponding spectral-radius powers by factors
   absorbed into the displayed polylogarithmic slack.  Write
   \[
      \Lambda_q=\log\lambda(A_q),
      \qquad
      \Lambda_{q,x}(\theta)=\log\lambda(A_{q,x}(\theta)),
      \qquad
      \Gamma_x(\theta)=\log\lambda(B_x(\theta)).
   \]
   Use storage threshold \(T=ht\), and suppose the following three scalar
   conditions hold with a polylogarithmic slack \(L_m\):
   \[
      \sup_{x\in P}
      \inf_{\theta\ge0}\{\Gamma_x(\theta)-\theta t\}
      \le
      \frac{\rho}{\kappa}+O\!\left(\frac{\log L_m}{\log m}\right),
      \tag{FST1}
   \]
   \[
      \inf_{\substack{q\ {\rm promised}\\ x\ {\rm invalid\ for}\ q}}
      \sup_{\theta\ge0}
      \{\theta t-\Lambda_{q,x}(\theta)+\Lambda_q\}
      \ge
      \frac{1-\rho}{\kappa}
      -O\!\left(\frac{\log L_m}{\log m}\right),
      \tag{FST2}
   \]
   and, for every near witness \(\|p-q\|\le r\),
   \[
      \frac{Z_{q,p}^{\ge ht}}{e_s^TA_q^h\mathbf 1}
      \ge L_m^{-1},
      \tag{FST3}
   \]
   where \(Z_{q,p}^{\ge ht}\) is the marked path partition function from
   \((MTS2)\).
   Then the raw-incidence trellis panel satisfies \((BQ1)\)--\((BQ3)\).

   A convenient sufficient condition for \((FST3)\) is a uniform tilted
   law-of-large-numbers gap:
   \[
      \left.
      \frac{d}{d\theta}\Lambda_{q,p}(\theta)
      \right|_{\theta=0}
      \ge t+\delta
      \tag{FST4}
   \]
   for some fixed \(\delta>0\), with the same primitive finite-state
   regularity; then the ratio in \((FST3)\) is \(1-e^{-\Omega_{\delta}(h)}\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   The raw number of hidden paths storing a fixed point \(x\) is
   \[
      N_x(ht)=|\{\pi:S_x(\pi)\ge ht\}|.
   \]
   By Chernoff and Perron--Frobenius regularity,
   \[
      N_x(ht)
      \le
      \inf_{\theta\ge0}
      e^{-\theta ht}e_s^TB_x(\theta)^h\mathbf 1
      \le
      \exp\left\{
         h\inf_{\theta\ge0}(\Gamma_x(\theta)-\theta t)
      \right\}L_m^{O(1)}.
   \]
   Using \(h=\kappa\log m+O(1)\), condition \((FST1)\) gives
   \(N_x(ht)\le m^\rho L_m\) up to a fixed enlargement of \(L_m\).  Summing
   over \(m\) points proves the raw incidence bound \((MTS6)\), hence
   \((BQ1)\).

   For an invalid point \(x\) and query \(q\), the same Chernoff bound applied
   to the marked tilted partition gives
   \[
      \frac{Z_{q,x}^{\ge ht}}{Z_q}
      \le
      \inf_{\theta\ge0}
      \exp\left\{
         -\theta ht
         +h\Lambda_{q,x}(\theta)
         -h\Lambda_q
      \right\}L_m^{O(1)}.
   \]
   Condition \((FST2)\) makes this at most
   \(m^{-(1-\rho)}L_m\), after increasing the polylogarithmic factor.  Summing
   over the at most \(m\) invalid points and using \((MTS4)\) proves
   \((BQ2)\).

   Condition \((FST3)\) is exactly \((MTS5)\), which is \((BQ3)\).  Finally,
   under \((FST4)\), the tilted path law induced by \(A_q\) is a primitive
   finite-state Markov chain with additive functional \(S_p(\pi)\) of mean at
   least \(t+\delta\) per step.  The standard finite-state Chernoff bound for
   the lower tail gives
   \[
      \Pr_q[S_p(\pi)<ht]\le e^{-\Omega_\delta(h)},
   \]
   which proves the displayed sufficient condition for \((FST3)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[How to use the finite-state test]
   \label{rem:finite-state-trellis-test-use}
   \Cref{cor:finite-state-trellis-rate-test} is the scalar audit for a concrete
   Construction-A residue trellis or convolutional sampler.  One chooses the
   modulus, scale, local state graph, query edge weights, and threshold \(t\),
   then computes three spectral curves:
   the raw storage entropy \(\inf_\theta(\Gamma_x(\theta)-\theta t)\), the
   far sampled separation exponent
   \(\sup_\theta(\theta t-\Lambda_{q,x}(\theta)+\Lambda_q)\), and the near
   tilted mean \(\Lambda'_{q,p}(0)\).  If these curves miss
   \((FST1)\)--\((FST4)\), the construction has a genuine spectrum barrier.  If
   they pass but raw storage is too large, then the only remaining issue is a
   designed bucket canonicalization theorem; by
   \cref{lem:random-sparse-bucket-no-quotient}, random sparse bucket equality
   will not supply that theorem.  The information screen in
   \cref{cor:randomized-aggregate-sampler-information-screen} gives the
   complementary charge test: exact BCJR sampling of hidden paths is useful
   only when the certified bucket charge is the quotient or responsibility
   charge, not the full raw path entropy.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Full-entropy raw trellis paths fail the charge test]
   \label{cor:raw-trellis-path-information-barrier}
   Let a homogeneous code or lattice trellis be used in the Gaussian near-block
   setting of \cref{lem:gaussian-information-charge-contraction}.  Let \(\Pi\)
   be the path sampled from the exact query law, and assume the construction is
   transitive and equivariant so that \(\Pi\) is marginally uniform on
   \(\exp\{rR+o(r)\}\) hidden paths.  Suppose further that the retained index
   charges each hidden path as an ordinary raw bucket, so the fixed-path
   far-tail threshold for the path score \(\Phi_\pi(U)\) has rate
   \(C_\pi\ge R-o(1)\).  If the near channel has any fixed noise
   \(\chi<1\), then no law-of-large-numbers proof can place these raw
   fixed-path thresholds below the selected near means
   \[
      r^{-1}\E[\Phi_\Pi(U)\mid \Pi=\pi]
   \]
   uniformly over successful paths \(\pi\).

   Consequently an exact BCJR, polar, convolutional, Construction-A, or
   recursive-lattice sampler does not by itself discharge the finite-state
   test at full raw path charge.  A successful trellis proof must lower the
   charged object to a quotient bucket, responsibility law, or Fano/list-work
   prefix charge, or else verify a genuinely different far spectrum whose
   fixed-transcript rate is below the conditional information budget.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Apply
   \cref{cor:randomized-aggregate-sampler-information-screen} with
   \(T=\Pi\).  Transitivity makes
   \(i_\pi=r^{-1}D(P_{U\mid \Pi=\pi}\|P_U)\) independent of \(\pi\), and the
   Gaussian contraction gives
   \[
      i_\pi\le \chi^2 R+o(1).
   \]
   Since \(\chi<1\), the raw path charge \(C_\pi\ge R-o(1)\) is eventually
   larger than \(i_\pi\).  The information-charge survivor test then forbids
   the fixed-path far threshold from lying below the selected near mean.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Marked trellis responsibility verifier]
   \label{lem:marked-trellis-responsibility-verifier}
   Work in the marked trellis setting of
   \cref{lem:marked-trellis-spectrum-verifier}, but allow a designed bucket
   map \(\lambda:\mathcal P\to\Lambda\) in place of equality of raw stored
   sets.  For a query \(q\), put
   \[
      Z_{q,\ell}
      =
      \sum_{\pi:\lambda(\pi)=\ell}W_q(\pi),
      \qquad
      \Pi_q(\ell)=\frac{Z_{q,\ell}}{Z_q},
   \]
   and define the bucket-marked partition function
   \[
      Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}
      =
      \sum_{\substack{\pi:\lambda(\pi)=\ell\\ S_x(\pi)\ge T}}W_q(\pi).
      \tag{MTR1}
   \]
   The exact hidden responsibility of \(x\) inside a sampled bucket \(\ell\) is
   \[
      r_{q,x,\ell}
      =
      \begin{cases}
      Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}/Z_{q,\ell},& Z_{q,\ell}>0,\\
      0,& Z_{q,\ell}=0 .
      \end{cases}
      \tag{MTR2}
   \]
   Suppose that, after sampling \(\ell\sim\Pi_q\), an output-sensitive reporter
   emits \(x\) with conditional probability \(\theta_{q,x,\ell}\) satisfying
   \[
      r_{q,x,\ell}\le\theta_{q,x,\ell}
      \le\min\{1,K r_{q,x,\ell}\}
      \tag{MTR3}
   \]
   for all promised query/load pairs.  Then every promised query satisfies
   \[
      \sum_{\substack{x\in P\\ \|x-q\|>cr}}
      \sum_{\ell\in\Lambda}\Pi_q(\ell)\theta_{q,x,\ell}
      \le
      K
      \sum_{\substack{x\in P\\ \|x-q\|>cr}}
      \frac{Z_{q,x}^{\ge T}}{Z_q},
      \tag{MTR4}
   \]
   and every near pair \((p,q)\) satisfies
   \[
      \sum_{\ell\in\Lambda}\Pi_q(\ell)\theta_{q,p,\ell}
      \ge
      \frac{Z_{q,p}^{\ge T}}{Z_q}.
      \tag{MTR5}
   \]

   If the scores lie in \(\delta\mathbb Z\) and the bucket map is
   terminal-measurable, \(\lambda(\pi)=\lambda(t)\) for the terminal \(t\) of
   \(\pi\), then \(Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}\) is computed by the marked recursion
   \((MTS7)\) with the final sum restricted to terminals \(t\) with
   \(\lambda(t)=\ell\).  Thus a code or lattice trellis with
   \(K\le\log^{O_c(1)}m\), polylogarithmic sampled reporter work, and the
   marked bounds \((MTS4)\)--\((MTS5)\) supplies the sampled far-load and
   near-hit parts of the terminal ANN certificate without scanning whole
   quotient buckets.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Apply \cref{lem:responsibility-thinned-quotient} to the hidden path family
   \(\mathcal T=\mathcal P\), quotient map \(\lambda\), hidden law
   \(\pi_q(\pi)=W_q(\pi)/Z_q\), and predicate
   \(U_x(\pi)=\mathbf 1\{S_x(\pi)\ge T\}\).  For this specialization,
   \[
      h_{q,x,\ell}
      =
      \sum_{\pi:\lambda(\pi)=\ell}\pi_q(\pi)U_x(\pi)
      =
      \frac{Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}}{Z_q},
   \]
   while
   \[
      \Pi_q(\ell)=Z_{q,\ell}/Z_q.
   \]
   Therefore the conditional responsibility
   \(h_{q,x,\ell}/\Pi_q(\ell)\) is exactly \((MTR2)\).  The hypotheses
   \((MTR3)\) are the hypotheses \((RTQ0)\), so \((MTR4)\)--\((MTR5)\) are
   \((RTQ1)\)--\((RTQ2)\) after summing
   \(Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}\) over \(\ell\).  The final recursion statement is
   the proof of \((MTS7)\)--\((MTS8)\) with the terminal sum restricted to the
   chosen bucket.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Full bucket scans require large marked responsibility]
   \label{cor:full-bucket-scan-responsibility-barrier}
   In the setting of \cref{lem:marked-trellis-responsibility-verifier}, suppose
   the query scans every point that appears in the sampled quotient bucket:
   \[
      \theta_{q,x,\ell}
      =
      \mathbf 1\{Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}>0\}.
   \]
   Then the polylogarithmic responsibility condition \((MTR3)\) with constant
   \(K\) holds if and only if every emitted query/load triple satisfies
   \[
      \frac{Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}}{Z_{q,\ell}}\ge\frac1K.
      \tag{FBR1}
   \]
   More generally, the pointwise overcharge of full scanning relative to the
   hidden marked spectrum is exactly
   \[
      \frac{\Pi_q(\ell)}
           {Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}/Z_q}
      =
      \frac{Z_{q,\ell}}{Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}}
      =
      r_{q,x,\ell}^{-1}.
      \tag{FBR2}
   \]
   Thus a quotient bucket containing points with superpolylogarithmically small
   marked responsibility cannot be certified by ordinary union scanning; it
   needs responsibility-thinned reporting or a finer bucket map.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   For full scanning, the lower inequality in \((MTR3)\) is automatic whenever
   \(\theta_{q,x,\ell}=1\), because then \(r_{q,x,\ell}>0\).  The upper
   inequality is
   \[
      1\le K r_{q,x,\ell},
   \]
   which is exactly \((FBR1)\).  The overcharge identity \((FBR2)\) is the
   ratio between the full-scan contribution
   \(\Pi_q(\ell)=Z_{q,\ell}/Z_q\) and the hidden marked contribution
   \(Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}/Z_q\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Heavy-responsibility reporting is the concrete escape]
   \label{cor:heavy-responsibility-trellis-reporter}
   Work in the setting of
   \cref{lem:marked-trellis-responsibility-verifier}.  Fix \(K\ge1\).  Suppose
   that, after a query samples \(\ell\sim\Pi_q\) (so \(Z_{q,\ell}>0\)), a
   reporter lists a candidate set \(H(q,\ell)\) containing every point with
   \[
      r_{q,x,\ell}
      =
      \frac{Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}}{Z_{q,\ell}}
      \ge K^{-1},
      \tag{HRT1}
   \]
   and that the reporter then computes the exact marked ratio for the listed
   candidates and emits exactly those satisfying \((HRT1)\).  Then every
   promised query \(q\) has emitted far load
   \[
      \sum_{\substack{x\in P\\ \|x-q\|>cr}}
      \sum_{\ell}\Pi_q(\ell)\mathbf 1\{x\ {\rm emitted\ from}\ \ell\}
      \le
      K
      \sum_{\substack{x\in P\\ \|x-q\|>cr}}
      \frac{Z_{q,x}^{\ge T}}{Z_q}.
      \tag{HRT2}
   \]
   Moreover, if every near pair \(\|p-q\|\le r\) has heavy responsibility mass
   \[
      \sum_{\ell:\ r_{q,p,\ell}\ge K^{-1}}\Pi_q(\ell)\ge \eta,
      \tag{HRT3}
   \]
   then the query emits \(p\) with probability at least \(\eta\).

   Consequently, when \(K,\eta^{-1}\le\log^{O_c(1)}m\), the marked far
   spectrum \((MTS4)\)--\((MTS5)\) gives the desired sampled far-load and
   near-hit bounds without scanning whole quotient buckets, provided the
   heavy-responsibility candidate lister itself has polylogarithmic overhead
   plus output-sensitive work.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   If \(x\) is emitted from \(\ell\), then \(r_{q,x,\ell}\ge K^{-1}\).  Hence
   \[
      \Pi_q(\ell)\mathbf 1\{x\ {\rm emitted\ from}\ \ell\}
      \le
      K\Pi_q(\ell)r_{q,x,\ell}
      =
      K\frac{Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}}{Z_q}.
   \]
   Summing over invalid far points and over \(\ell\) proves \((HRT2)\), since
   \(\sum_\ell Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}=Z_{q,x}^{\ge T}\).
   The near statement is immediate from the assumed completeness of
   \(H(q,\ell)\) on the heavy set: whenever a sampled bucket satisfies
   \(r_{q,p,\ell}\ge K^{-1}\), the exact filter emits \(p\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Marked spectrum plus a heavy lister closes the trellis branch]
   \label{cor:marked-heavy-lister-closes-trellis}
   Work in the setting of
   \cref{lem:marked-trellis-responsibility-verifier}.  Let \(L_m\ge1\).  Assume
   the marked spectrum satisfies, for every promised query \(q\),
   \[
      \sum_{\substack{x\in P\\ \|x-q\|>cr}}
      \frac{Z_{q,x}^{\ge T}}{Z_q}
      \le m^\rho L_m,
      \tag{MHL1}
   \]
   and, for every near witness \(\|p-q\|\le r\),
   \[
      \frac{Z_{q,p}^{\ge T}}{Z_q}\ge L_m^{-1}.
      \tag{MHL2}
   \]
   Suppose that after sampling \(\ell\sim\Pi_q\), the query has a
   polylogarithmic-overhead, output-sensitive lister containing every point
   with
   \[
      r_{q,x,\ell}
      =
      \frac{Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}}{Z_{q,\ell}}
      \ge (2L_m)^{-1},
      \tag{MHL3}
   \]
   followed by exact ratio filtering at the same threshold.  Then one sampled
   panel emits far points in expected number at most \(2m^\rho L_m^2\), and
   emits every near witness with probability at least \((2L_m)^{-1}\).
   Hence \(O(L_m\log m)\) independent panels give the terminal sampled ANN
   bounds with only a polylogarithmic loss whenever \(L_m=\log^{O_c(1)}m\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Apply \cref{cor:heavy-responsibility-trellis-reporter} with
   \(K=2L_m\).  The far-load bound \((HRT2)\), together with \((MHL1)\), gives
   the expected far output bound \(2m^\rho L_m^2\).

   For the near point \(p\), draw \(\ell\sim\Pi_q\) and put
   \(R_\ell=r_{q,p,\ell}\).  Then \(0\le R_\ell\le1\) and
   \[
      \E_{\ell\sim\Pi_q}R_\ell
      =
      \frac{Z_{q,p}^{\ge T}}{Z_q}
      \ge L_m^{-1}.
   \]
   With \(\tau=(2L_m)^{-1}\),
   \[
      \E R_\ell
      \le
      \tau+\Pr[R_\ell\ge\tau],
   \]
   because light buckets contribute less than \(\tau\) and every bucket
   contributes at most one.  Therefore
   \[
      \Pr[R_\ell\ge(2L_m)^{-1}]
      \ge L_m^{-1}-(2L_m)^{-1}
      =
      (2L_m)^{-1}.
   \]
   The heavy lister emits \(p\) on all such sampled buckets.  Repeating
   \(O(L_m\log m)\) times gives high constant success probability for each
   promised query, while multiplying the far output by only the same
   polylogarithmic factor.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Conditional hidden-path sampling implements heavy reporting]
   \label{cor:conditional-hidden-sampling-heavy-lister}
   Work in the setting of
   \cref{lem:marked-trellis-responsibility-verifier}.  After sampling a bucket
   \(\ell\sim\Pi_q\), suppose the query can draw independent hidden paths from
   the conditional law
   \[
      \Pr_q[\pi\mid \ell]
      =
      \frac{W_q(\pi)}{Z_{q,\ell}}
      \mathbf 1\{\lambda(\pi)=\ell\},
      \tag{CHS1}
   \]
   and can enumerate the raw subbucket
   \(C_\pi=\{x:S_x(\pi)\ge T\}\).  Let \(\tau\in(0,1]\), draw \(N\) such
   conditional paths, scan the union of their raw subbuckets, and then emit
   exactly the scanned points with
   \[
      \frac{Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}}{Z_{q,\ell}}\ge\tau
      \tag{CHS2}
   \]
   by exact marked-ratio filtering.  Then, for every fixed
   \((q,\ell,x)\),
   \[
      \Pr[x\ {\rm is\ scanned}\mid q,\ell]
      =
      1-(1-r_{q,x,\ell})^N.
      \tag{CHS3}
   \]
   Consequently every point with \(r_{q,x,\ell}\ge\tau\) is scanned with
   probability at least \(1-e^{-N\tau}\), while every emitted far point is
   charged by
   \[
      \Pi_q(\ell)\mathbf 1\{x\ {\rm emitted\ from}\ \ell\}
      \le
      \tau^{-1}\frac{Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}}{Z_q}.
      \tag{CHS4}
   \]

   If the marked spectrum \((MHL1)\)--\((MHL2)\) holds and
   \(\tau=(2L_m)^{-1}\), then with
   \(N=\lceil \tau^{-1}\log2\rceil\) one sampled panel emits every near witness
   with probability at least \((4L_m)^{-1}\), and has expected emitted far load
   at most \(2m^\rho L_m^2\).

   The corresponding raw-scan work is
   \[
      N\,
      \E_{\ell\sim\Pi_q}
      \E_{\pi\sim\Pr_q[\cdot\mid\ell]}
      |C_\pi|
      =
      N\sum_{x\in P}\frac{Z_{q,x}^{\ge T}}{Z_q},
      \tag{CHS5}
   \]
   plus the conditional-path sampling and exact-filtering overhead.  Thus this
   compiler is polylogarithmic over the sampled ANN budget whenever the
   conditional sampler, raw-subbucket enumeration, and exact ratio filter have
   polylogarithmic overhead and the all-resident marked raw-scan load in
   \((CHS5)\) is \(m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Under the conditional law \((CHS1)\),
   \[
      \Pr_q[x\in C_\pi\mid\ell]
      =
      \frac{1}{Z_{q,\ell}}
      \sum_{\substack{\pi:\lambda(\pi)=\ell\\S_x(\pi)\ge T}}W_q(\pi)
      =
      r_{q,x,\ell}.
   \]
   The \(N\) conditional path samples are independent, so the probability that
   none of their raw subbuckets contains \(x\) is
   \((1-r_{q,x,\ell})^N\).  This proves \((CHS3)\), and the lower bound
   \(1-e^{-N\tau}\) follows when \(r_{q,x,\ell}\ge\tau\).

   Exact filtering emits only points with \(r_{q,x,\ell}\ge\tau\).  Therefore
   \[
      \Pi_q(\ell)\mathbf 1\{x\ {\rm emitted\ from}\ \ell\}
      \le
      \tau^{-1}\Pi_q(\ell)r_{q,x,\ell}
      =
      \tau^{-1}\frac{Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}}{Z_q},
   \]
   proving \((CHS4)\).

   For the near witness \(p\), \cref{cor:marked-heavy-lister-closes-trellis}
   proves that the sampled mass of buckets with
   \(r_{q,p,\ell}\ge(2L_m)^{-1}=\tau\) is at least \((2L_m)^{-1}\).  On those
   buckets, \(N=\lceil\tau^{-1}\log2\rceil\) scans \(p\) with probability at
   least \(1/2\).  Thus one panel emits \(p\) with probability at least
   \((4L_m)^{-1}\).  Summing \((CHS4)\) over invalid far points and all
   buckets, and using \((MHL1)\), gives the far emitted load
   \(\tau^{-1}m^\rho L_m=2m^\rho L_m^2\).

   Finally,
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      \E_{\ell}\E_{\pi\mid\ell}|C_\pi|
      &=
      \sum_{\ell}\Pi_q(\ell)
      \sum_{\pi:\lambda(\pi)=\ell}
      \frac{W_q(\pi)}{Z_{q,\ell}}
      \sum_{x\in P}\mathbf 1\{S_x(\pi)\ge T\}  \\
      &=
      \sum_{x\in P}
      \sum_{\ell}\frac{1}{Z_q}
      \sum_{\substack{\pi:\lambda(\pi)=\ell\\S_x(\pi)\ge T}}W_q(\pi)
      =
      \sum_{x\in P}\frac{Z_{q,x}^{\ge T}}{Z_q}.
   \end{aligned}
   \]
   Multiplying by \(N\) proves \((CHS5)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Random sparse aggregate buckets overcharge full scans]
   \label{lem:random-sparse-aggregate-responsibility-barrier}
   Let one quotient bucket aggregate \(H\) hidden labels with equal conditional
   query weight.  For each point \(x\in P\), \(|P|=m\), and each hidden label
   \(a\), let \(U_x(a)\) be independent Bernoulli\((s)\).  Put
   \[
      N_x=\sum_{a=1}^H U_x(a),
      \qquad
      r_x=\frac{N_x}{H}.
   \]
   The hidden marked load of this aggregate bucket is
   \(\sum_x r_x\), while ordinary union scanning emits
   \(\sum_x\mathbf 1\{N_x>0\}\) points.  Their expectations are
   \[
      \E\sum_x r_x=ms,
      \qquad
      \E\sum_x\mathbf 1\{N_x>0\}
      =
      m\bigl(1-(1-s)^H\bigr).
      \tag{RSR1}
   \]
   Therefore the expected full-scan overcharge relative to the hidden marked
   spectrum is
   \[
      \frac{1-(1-s)^H}{s}
      \ge c\,\min\{H,s^{-1}\}
      \tag{RSR2}
   \]
   for a universal constant \(c>0\) whenever \(0<s\le1/2\).

   In the ANN sparse scale \(s=m^{\rho-1+o(1)}\), any forced aggregate class
   of size \(H=\log^{\omega(1)}m\) has superpolylogarithmic expected overcharge
   under ordinary union scanning.  If \(H=\log^{O(1)}m\), the overcharge is only
   polylogarithmic but the aggregate class is too small to provide more than
   polylogarithmic hidden-label compression.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The identity for the hidden marked load follows from
   \[
      \E r_x=H^{-1}\sum_{a=1}^H\E U_x(a)=s.
   \]
   A point is scanned by the union bucket exactly when at least one hidden label
   contains it, so
   \[
      \Pr[N_x>0]=1-(1-s)^H,
   \]
   proving \((RSR1)\).

   If \(Hs\le1\), then
   \[
      1-(1-s)^H\ge \frac12Hs
   \]
   for \(s\le1/2\), giving overcharge at least \(H/2\).  If \(Hs>1\), then
   \(1-(1-s)^H\ge1-e^{-1}\), giving overcharge at least
   \((1-e^{-1})s^{-1}\).  This proves \((RSR2)\).  Substituting
   \(s=m^{\rho-1+o(1)}\) gives the final claims.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Random sparse heavy responsibilities have a binomial screen]
   \label{lem:random-sparse-heavy-responsibility-screen}
   In the random aggregate model of
   \cref{lem:random-sparse-aggregate-responsibility-barrier}, fix a threshold
   \(s<\tau<1\), and let
   \[
      d(a\Vert b)
      =
      a\log\frac ab+(1-a)\log\frac{1-a}{1-b}
   \]
   be the binary relative entropy.  Then the expected number of far passenger
   points whose marked responsibility is at least \(\tau\) is at most
   \[
      m\exp\{-H d(\tau\Vert s)\}.
      \tag{RHB1}
   \]
   If a distinguished near point has independent hidden memberships with
   probability \(u>\tau\), so that
   \(N_p\sim{\rm Binomial}(H,u)\), then it fails to be \(\tau\)-heavy with
   probability at most
   \[
      \Pr[N_p/H<\tau]\le \exp\{-H d(\tau\Vert u)\}.
      \tag{RHB2}
   \]

   In particular, at the ANN far scale \(s=m^{\rho-1+o(1)}\), with
   \(\tau=K^{-1}\) and \(K=\log^{O(1)}m\),
   \[
      H\ge
      \left(\frac{1+\epsilon}{1-\rho}+o(1)\right)K
      \tag{RHB3}
   \]
   makes the expected number of far \(\tau\)-heavy passengers \(o(1)\).  Thus
   the sparse random aggregate is statistically compatible with
   \cref{cor:heavy-responsibility-trellis-reporter}; the missing ingredient is
   an output-sensitive way to find the \(\tau\)-heavy points without scanning
   all \(m\) residents.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   For every far point, \(N_x\sim{\rm Binomial}(H,s)\).  Chernoff's bound gives
   \[
      \Pr[N_x/H\ge\tau]\le e^{-H d(\tau\Vert s)}.
   \]
   Summing this probability over the \(m\) resident points proves \((RHB1)\).
   The lower-tail Chernoff bound for \(N_p\sim{\rm Binomial}(H,u)\) gives
   \((RHB2)\).

   For the displayed ANN specialization,
   \[
      d(K^{-1}\Vert s)
      =
      K^{-1}\log\frac{K^{-1}}s
      +(1-K^{-1})\log\frac{1-K^{-1}}{1-s}
      =
      \frac{(1-\rho)\log m-\log K-O(1)}{K}+o(K^{-1}).
   \]
   Substituting \((RHB3)\) into \(m\exp\{-H d(K^{-1}\Vert s)\}\) gives
   \(m^{-\epsilon+o(1)}\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Trellis target for codes and lattices]
   \label{rem:trellis-quotient-target}
   \Cref{lem:compressed-aggregate-sampler} is the sampled analogue of the
   Fano/list-decoding DAG certificates earlier in the paper.  A code or lattice
   construction need not expose its labels as an explicit list.  It may expose
   a compact state graph whose path weights are the query reliabilities, whose
   terminals map to stored buckets, and whose dynamic program samples the
   quotient bucket law.  The remaining theorem for such a trellis is then only
