   the spectrum certificate \((BQ1)\)--\((BQ3)\) plus the graph-size/query-time
   bound for evaluating \(H_q\).  \Cref{lem:marked-trellis-spectrum-verifier}
   makes the additive-score case explicit: \((BQ2)\) and \((BQ3)\) are marked
   transfer-matrix ratios, while \((BQ1)\) is either a raw incidence bound or a
   genuine distinct-bucket canonicalization theorem.  \Cref{cor:bcjr-trellis-quotient-sampler}
   records the standard BCJR/sum-product instance of this target: exact
   partition-function decoding is already the right query algorithm whenever
   the retained code or lattice quotient has a compact acyclic state graph, but
   \cref{cor:randomized-aggregate-sampler-information-screen} still requires
   the charged transcript to be the quotient bucket or responsibility object
   rather than a full-entropy hidden path.
   \Cref{lem:marked-trellis-responsibility-verifier} is the responsibility
   version of the same calculation: the quantity a reporter must approximate
   for point \(x\) in sampled bucket \(\ell\) is exactly the marked partition
   ratio \(Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}/Z_{q,\ell}\).
   \Cref{cor:full-bucket-scan-responsibility-barrier} records the matching
   obstruction to ordinary union scanning: its pointwise overcharge is the
   inverse of this marked responsibility.
   \Cref{cor:heavy-responsibility-trellis-reporter} is the corresponding
   positive target: a code or lattice decoder only has to list the points whose
   bucket-local marked posterior is at least inverse-polylogarithmic, and the
   exact ratio filter charges the remaining far load to the marked spectrum.
   \Cref{cor:marked-heavy-lister-closes-trellis} removes the last separate
   near-heavy hypothesis: once the marked near mass is inverse-polylogarithmic,
   at least inverse-polylogarithmic sampled bucket mass has the witness above
   the matching responsibility threshold.
   \Cref{cor:conditional-hidden-sampling-heavy-lister} gives one direct
   implementation path for such a lister: sample a few hidden paths conditional
   on the already-sampled quotient bucket and scan only their raw subbuckets.
   This succeeds for heavy residents with probability proportional to their
   marked responsibility, while its work is exactly the conditional raw-scan
   load \(\sum_x Z_{q,x}^{\ge T}/Z_q\) times the inverse responsibility
   threshold.
   \Cref{lem:random-sparse-aggregate-responsibility-barrier} shows that this is
   not a pathological edge case: aggregating \(H\) independent sparse hidden
   filters into one bucket inflates union-scan load by
   \(\Theta(\min\{H,s^{-1}\})\) in expectation.
   \Cref{lem:random-sparse-heavy-responsibility-screen} explains why this does
   not rule out responsibility thresholding: with an inverse-polylogarithmic
   threshold, only a binomial large-deviation set of far passengers is heavy.
   The problem is algorithmic and structural--finding those heavy residents by
   code, lattice, or list-recovery machinery--rather than another tail bound
   for ordinary union scans.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Which coding and lattice tools can address the responsibility target]
   \label{rem:code-lattice-responsibility-audit}
   The responsibility normal form now fixes the role of deeper coding and
   lattice constructions.  They are useful only if they implement the heavy
   lister in \cref{cor:heavy-responsibility-trellis-reporter}, or prove that
   the near mass \((HRT3)\) is absent for the proposed family.

   For a Construction-A or Construction-D block,
   \cref{lem:construction-a-theta-quotient} turns the lattice partition
   function into residue-code theta reliabilities.  The heavy test is therefore
   the soft list-recovery inequality
   \[
      \log Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}
      \ge
      \log Z_{q,\ell}-\log K,
   \]
   not a nearest-lattice-point condition.  Koetter--Vardy, expander-code,
   folded-Reed--Solomon, or polar-style list recovery can help exactly when
   those residue reliabilities give an output-sensitive list of data signatures
   passing this inequality.

   GMD and Chase decoders are the high-margin special case.  The certificates
   in \cref{lem:reliability-erasure-sweep},
   \cref{cor:gmd-block-certificate}, and
   \cref{cor:chase-gmd-block-certificate} are valuable when the sampled bucket
   makes one symbol per coordinate dominant, or when a polylogarithmic branch
   set covers the low-confidence coordinates.  They do not solve a diffuse
   posterior bucket: if the mass in \((HRT3)\) is spread over
   superpolylogarithmically many low-responsibility points, a GMD list is simply
   the wrong object.

   Ordered-statistics and information-set decoding are the most concrete
   fallback for linear residue codes.  By
   \cref{lem:min-entropy-information-set} and
   \cref{cor:osd-superset-block-reporter}, the candidate count is controlled by
   \[
      \exp\bigl(\beta\Delta(q,\Theta)+\Lambda_*(q)\bigr),
   \]
   where \(\Lambda_*(q)\) is the minimum soft entropy of an information set.
   Thus an OSD-based Construction-A panel has a clean pass/fail test: after
   translating \((HRT1)\) to its residue-score threshold, the minimum
   information-set entropy must be \(O(\log\log m)\) at the critical
   threshold, while the marked spectrum still satisfies \((MTS4)\)--\((MTS5)\).

   Tanner, LDPC, polar, BCJR, and recursive Barnes--Wall/Barnes--Sloane
   decoders supply compact partition-function or threshold-enumeration
   algorithms.  That is not yet enough.  Sum-product computes bucket weights
   and local beliefs; the ANN index needs a reverse, point-indexed heavy
   posterior list over the resident data.  A trellis path sampler, a
   discrete-Gaussian lattice sampler, or a nearest-cell decoder that returns
   only hidden labels is therefore blocked by the information-charge and
   full-scan barriers above unless it is coupled to this heavy-responsibility
   data lister.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[OSD compiler for heavy-responsibility residents]
   \label{cor:osd-heavy-responsibility-compiler}
   Work in the setting of
   \cref{cor:marked-heavy-lister-closes-trellis}, and fix one sampled
   query-bucket pair \((q,\ell)\).  Suppose the resident points have signatures
   \(c(x)\) in a linear code \(\mathcal C\le\mathbb F^h\), with resident
   lookup lists for each codeword.  Let coordinate scores
   \(\omega_i^{q,\ell}(a)\) define
   \[
      S_{q,\ell}(c)=\sum_{i=1}^h\omega_i^{q,\ell}(c_i).
   \]
   Assume there is a threshold \(\Theta_{q,\ell}\) such that every heavy
   resident satisfies the score test
   \[
      \frac{Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}}{Z_{q,\ell}}\ge(2L_m)^{-1}
      \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
      S_{q,\ell}(c(x))\ge\Theta_{q,\ell}.
      \tag{OHR1}
   \]
   For a fixed \(\beta>0\), define
   \[
      M_{q,\ell}=\sum_i\max_{a\in\mathbb F}\omega_i^{q,\ell}(a),
   \]
   and let \(\Lambda_*(q,\ell)\) be the minimum information-set entropy from
   \cref{lem:min-entropy-information-set} for these scores.  If
   \[
      \beta\bigl(M_{q,\ell}-\Theta_{q,\ell}\bigr)
      +\Lambda_*(q,\ell)
      \le \log W_m,
      \tag{OHR2}
   \]
   and if \(R_{q,\ell}\) denotes the total resident lookup size of the
   codewords listed by this OSD call, then ordered-statistics decoding lists a
   superset of all \((2L_m)^{-1}\)-heavy residents in work
   \[
      \log^{O(1)}m+W_m+O(R_{q,\ell}),
   \]
   after which exact evaluation of \(Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}/Z_{q,\ell}\) on the
   candidates gives the heavy lister required by
   \cref{cor:marked-heavy-lister-closes-trellis}.  Consequently, if
   \(L_m=\log^{O_c(1)}m\), the marked spectrum \((MHL1)\)--\((MHL2)\) holds,
   and
   \[
      \E_{\ell\sim\Pi_q}\bigl[W_m+R_{q,\ell}\bigr]
      \le m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m
      \tag{OHR3}
   \]
   for every promised query, then the trellis/code/lattice panel gives the
   sampled ANN bounds with only polylogarithmic overhead.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Run the OSD reporter of \cref{cor:osd-superset-block-reporter} on the code
   \(\mathcal C\), the scores \(\omega_i^{q,\ell}\), and threshold
   \(\Theta_{q,\ell}\).  Its candidate-codeword bound \((OSD1)\) is exactly
   \[
      \exp\{\beta(M_{q,\ell}-\Theta_{q,\ell})+\Lambda_*(q,\ell)\}
      \le W_m,
   \]
   by \((OHR2)\).  Thus it lists every codeword \(c\in\mathcal C\) with
   \(S_{q,\ell}(c)\ge\Theta_{q,\ell}\) within the displayed work bound.
   By \((OHR1)\), every heavy resident has such a codeword signature, so
   expanding the resident lookup lists gives a candidate set containing every
   heavy resident, with the displayed additional cost \(R_{q,\ell}\).  Exact
   marked-ratio filtering removes false positives and leaves precisely the
   lister assumed in \cref{cor:marked-heavy-lister-closes-trellis}.  Applying
   that corollary gives the far-output and near-hit bounds, while \((OHR3)\)
   charges the OSD and resident-expansion work to the same
   \(m^\rho\operatorname{polylog}m\) query budget.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Tilted weight feasibility is linear]
   \label{lem:tilted-weight-linear-feasibility}
   Fix a finite retained label set \(\mathcal L\) and storage predicate
   \(A_g(x)\in\{0,1\}\).  Let \(\mathcal Q\) be a finite set of promised
   queries and let \(\mathcal N\subseteq P\times\mathcal Q\) be a finite set
   of near-pair witnesses.  For a label \(g\) and query \(q\), write
   \[
      R_q(g)=e^{\beta S_Q(q,g)},
      \qquad
      F_q(g)=\sum_{\substack{x\in P\\\|x-q\|>cr}}A_g(x),
   \]
   and fix targets \(B>0\), \(h>0\).  There are nonnegative weights
   \((w_g)_{g\in\mathcal L}\), \(\sum_gw_g=1\), whose tilted query law
   \[
      \pi_q(g)=\frac{w_gR_q(g)}{\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L}w_\ell R_q(\ell)}
   \]
   satisfies
   \[
      \sum_g\pi_q(g)F_q(g)\le B
      \qquad(q\in\mathcal Q)
      \tag{TW1}
   \]
   and
   \[
      \sum_g\pi_q(g)A_g(p)\ge h
      \qquad((p,q)\in\mathcal N)
      \tag{TW2}
   \]
   if and only if the same weights satisfy the homogeneous linear inequalities
   \[
      \sum_gw_gR_q(g)\bigl(F_q(g)-B\bigr)\le0
      \qquad(q\in\mathcal Q),
      \tag{TW3}
   \]
   and
   \[
      \sum_gw_gR_q(g)\bigl(h-A_g(p)\bigr)\le0
      \qquad((p,q)\in\mathcal N).
      \tag{TW4}
   \]
   Equivalently, the finite retained pool fails to admit such weights iff
   there exist nonnegative dual prices
   \(\lambda_q\) for \(q\in\mathcal Q\) and
   \(\mu_{p,q}\) for \((p,q)\in\mathcal N\), not all zero, such that every
   retained label \(g\in\mathcal L\) has strictly positive reduced obstruction
   \[
      \sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}
      \lambda_qR_q(g)\bigl(F_q(g)-B\bigr)
      +
      \sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal N}
      \mu_{p,q}R_q(g)\bigl(h-A_g(p)\bigr)
      >0.
      \tag{TW5}
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   For any \(q\), the denominator
   \(\sum_gw_gR_q(g)\) is positive because the weights have total mass one and
   \(R_q(g)>0\).  Multiplying \((TW1)\) by this denominator gives \((TW3)\),
   and multiplying \((TW2)\) by the same denominator gives \((TW4)\).  This
   proves the first equivalence.

   Let \(a_g\in\mathbb R^{|\mathcal Q|+|\mathcal N|}\) be the column whose
   coordinates are the left-hand coefficients in \((TW3)\) and \((TW4)\).  The
   linear feasibility problem asks whether
   \[
      \operatorname{conv}\{a_g:g\in\mathcal L\}
   \]
   intersects the nonpositive orthant.  By the finite separating hyperplane
   theorem, equivalently Farkas' lemma, this intersection is empty iff there is
   a nonnegative separating vector, not identically zero, whose inner product
   with every column \(a_g\) is strictly positive.  Writing the coordinates of
   that separating vector as \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) gives \((TW5)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Continuous Gaussian weights have finite test witnesses]
   \label{lem:continuous-gaussian-finite-witness}
   Work in the critical spherical normalization of
   \cref{lem:critical-tilted-gaussian-sampled-spectrum}.  Thus
   \(a_0=1-1/c^2\), \(\rho=1/(2c^2-1)\),
   \(T^2=2(1-\rho)\log m\), and \(\beta=T/a_0\).  Let
   \(P\subset\mathbb S^{d-1}\) have \(|P|=m\).  Let
   \(\mathcal Q\subset\mathbb S^{d-1}\) be a finite set of promised queries
   such that every invalid point for \(q\) has \(\ip{x}{q}\le0\), and let
   \(\mathcal N\subseteq P\times\mathcal Q\) be a finite set of near witnesses
   with \(\ip{p}{q}\ge a_0\).  For a Gaussian label \(g\in\R^d\), put
   \[
      A_g(x)=\mathbf 1\{\ip{g}{x}\ge T\},
      \qquad
      R_q(g)=e^{\beta\ip{g}{q}},
   \]
   and
   \[
      F_q(g)=
      \sum_{\substack{x\in P\\ x\text{ invalid for }q}}A_g(x).
   \]
   Then there are labels \(g_1,\ldots,g_s\in\R^d\) and nonnegative weights
   \(w_1,\ldots,w_s\), with
   \[
      s\le |\mathcal Q|+|\mathcal N|+1,
      \qquad
      \sum_iw_i=1,
   \]
   such that the tilted laws
   \[
      \pi_q(i)=
      \frac{w_iR_q(g_i)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^sw_\ell R_q(g_\ell)}
   \]
   satisfy
   \[
      \sum_i\pi_q(i)F_q(g_i)\le 2m^\rho
      \qquad(q\in\mathcal Q),
      \tag{CG1}
   \]
   and
   \[
      \sum_i\pi_q(i)A_{g_i}(p)\ge\frac13
      \qquad((p,q)\in\mathcal N).
      \tag{CG2}
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Let \(G\sim N(0,I_d)\), and let \(\gamma_q\) be the tilted law with density
   proportional to \(R_q(g)\) with respect to the law of \(G\).  Equivalently,
   \(G_q\sim N(\beta q,I_d)\).  By
   \cref{lem:critical-tilted-gaussian-sampled-spectrum}, for every
   \(q\in\mathcal Q\),
   \[
      \E_{\gamma_q}F_q(G)
      \le
      m\cdot m^{-(1-\rho)}
      =
      m^\rho,
   \]
   and, for every \((p,q)\in\mathcal N\),
   \[
      \E_{\gamma_q}A_G(p)\ge\frac12 .
   \]
   If \(Z_q=\E R_q(G)\), then the corresponding homogeneous coordinates from
   \cref{lem:tilted-weight-linear-feasibility} have expectations
   \[
      \E R_q(G)\bigl(F_q(G)-2m^\rho\bigr)
      =
      Z_q\bigl(\E_{\gamma_q}F_q(G)-2m^\rho\bigr)
      \le
      -Z_qm^\rho,
   \]
   and
   \[
      \E R_q(G)\left(\frac13-A_G(p)\right)
      =
      Z_q\left(\frac13-\E_{\gamma_q}A_G(p)\right)
      \le
      -\frac{Z_q}{6}.
   \]
   All these finitely many random variables are integrable, because
   \(F_q(G)\le m\) and \(R_q(G)\) is lognormal.  Therefore a sufficiently long
   finite iid sample \(G_1,\ldots,G_N\) has, with positive probability, all
   empirical averages of the displayed homogeneous coordinates nonpositive.
   Fix such a sample.  Its empirical column average lies in the convex hull of
   the sampled columns in
   \(\R^{|\mathcal Q|+|\mathcal N|}\).  Caratheodory's theorem represents the
   same average as a convex combination of at most
   \(|\mathcal Q|+|\mathcal N|+1\) sampled columns.  Applying
   \cref{lem:tilted-weight-linear-feasibility} to these labels and weights
   gives \((CG1)\) and \((CG2)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the finite witness lemma does not solve]
   \label{rem:continuous-witness-caveat}
   \Cref{lem:continuous-gaussian-finite-witness} says that the ideal Gaussian
   label universe has no tilted-weight dual obstruction on any finite test
   set.  Equivalently, if a Farkas certificate of the form \((TW5)\) exists,
   it is caused by restricting the labels to a proposed code, lattice, trellis,
   or stored panel, not by the Gaussian spectrum itself.

   This is only an offline separation statement.  It does not give the charged
   ANN index: the number of finite tests may be enormous, the selected labels
   need not have a compact decoder or sampler, and the unweighted bucket
   incidences in \((WQ1)\) are not controlled for the full all-query problem.
   Thus the remaining code/lattice theorem is precisely a low-storage,
   query-decodable quadrature theorem for the continuous tilted Gaussian
   calculation, with polylogarithmic rather than \(m^{o(1)}\) slack.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Small-signature Gaussian quadrature compiler]
   \label{cor:small-signature-gaussian-quadrature}
   Work in the setting of
   \cref{lem:continuous-gaussian-finite-witness}.  Let
   \(D=|\mathcal Q|+|\mathcal N|+1\), and suppose
   \[
      D\le m^\rho L_m
   \]
   for a polylogarithmic factor \(L_m\).  Then there is a retained weighted
   Gaussian panel with at most \(D\) labels such that
   \[
      \sum_{x\in P}
      |\{g:\ip{g}{x}\ge T\}|
      \le m^{1+\rho}L_m,
      \tag{SQ1}
   \]
   and, for every \(q\in\mathcal Q\),
   \[
      \sum_{\substack{x\in P\\ x\text{ invalid for }q}}
      \sum_{\substack{g\\\ip{g}{x}\ge T}}\pi_q(g)
      \le 2m^\rho,
      \tag{SQ2}
   \]
   while every \((p,q)\in\mathcal N\) satisfies
   \[
      \sum_{\substack{g\\\ip{g}{p}\ge T}}\pi_q(g)
      \ge\frac13 .
      \tag{SQ3}
   \]
   The query can sample from \(\pi_q(g)\propto w_g e^{\beta\ip{g}{q}}\) by a
   direct scan over the retained labels in \(O(d\,m^\rho L_m)\) arithmetic
   operations.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Apply \cref{lem:continuous-gaussian-finite-witness} and keep the
   \(s\le D\) labels supplied there, after discarding any zero-weight labels.
   The far and near conditions are exactly \((CG1)\) and \((CG2)\).  For
   storage, each retained label stores at most all \(m\) data points, so the
   total number of point-label incidences is at most
   \(ms\le mD\le m^{1+\rho}L_m\).  Finally, direct sampling computes all \(s\)
   tilted weights \(w_g e^{\beta\ip{g}{q}}\), forms their prefix sums, and
   draws one label; since \(s\le m^\rho L_m\), this is within the stated work.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Las Vegas small-signature Gaussian builder]
   \label{prop:las-vegas-small-signature-gaussian}
   In the setting of
   \cref{cor:small-signature-gaussian-quadrature}, the retained weighted
   Gaussian panel can be found by an uncharged Las Vegas preprocessing
   procedure using only Gaussian sampling and finite linear feasibility solves.
   More explicitly, for a finite candidate batch
   \(G_1,\ldots,G_N\sim N(0,I_d)\), solve the linear system
   \((TW3)\)--\((TW4)\) of
   \cref{lem:tilted-weight-linear-feasibility} on this batch with targets
   \(B=2m^\rho\) and \(h=1/3\).  Whenever the system is feasible, replace the
   feasible weight vector by a basic feasible solution and retain only its
   positive-weight labels.  The returned support has size at most
   \(D=|\mathcal Q|+|\mathcal N|+1\) and satisfies \((SQ1)\)--\((SQ3)\).

   A concrete Las Vegas schedule is to run rounds \(R=1,2,\ldots\); in round
   \(R\), independently sample and test one batch of each size
   \(1,\ldots,R\).  This procedure halts with probability one, and after it
   halts the query sampler is the direct \(O(d\,m^\rho L_m)\)-time sampler of
   \cref{cor:small-signature-gaussian-quadrature}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
   By \cref{lem:continuous-gaussian-finite-witness}, there is some finite
   Gaussian batch size \(N_0\) for which the sampled columns have positive
   probability of containing a feasible convex combination for the homogeneous
   inequalities \((TW3)\)--\((TW4)\) with \(B=2m^\rho\) and \(h=1/3\).  The
   finite LP above detects exactly this event by
   \cref{lem:tilted-weight-linear-feasibility}.  In the round-robin schedule,
   the size-\(N_0\) experiment is repeated independently once in every round
   \(R\ge N_0\), so a feasible batch is eventually found with probability one.

   For a feasible batch, the feasible region is a polytope in the simplex cut
   out by \(|\mathcal Q|+|\mathcal N|\) homogeneous linear inequalities.  A
   basic feasible point has support size at most
   \(|\mathcal Q|+|\mathcal N|+1=D\).  Applying
   \cref{lem:tilted-weight-linear-feasibility} to this basic solution gives
   the tilted far-load and near-mass inequalities \((SQ2)\) and \((SQ3)\).
   Since at most \(D\) labels are retained and \(D\le m^\rho L_m\), the
   storage bound \((SQ1)\) follows exactly as in
   \cref{cor:small-signature-gaussian-quadrature}.  The direct sampler scans
   these retained labels and is therefore within the same
   \(O(d\,m^\rho L_m)\) arithmetic bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Finite-envelope Gaussian quadrature builder]
   \label{prop:finite-envelope-gaussian-quadrature}
   Work in the critical spherical normalization of
   \cref{lem:critical-tilted-gaussian-sampled-spectrum}.  Let
   \(\mathcal Q\) be a possibly continuous promised query domain, let
   \(\sigma:\mathcal Q\to\Sigma\) be a finite signature map, and for each
   \(\sigma_0\in\Sigma\) let \(N_{\sigma_0}\subseteq P\) contain every data
   point that can be a near witness for a query of that signature.  For a
   Gaussian label \(g\), put
   \[
      A_g(x)=\mathbf 1\{\ip{g}{x}\ge T\},
      \qquad
      R_q(g)=e^{\beta\ip{g}{q}},
   \]
   and let
   \[
      F_q(g)=
      \sum_{\substack{x\in P\\ \|x-q\|>cr}}A_g(x)
   \]
   be the invalid bucket load of \(g\) for \(q\).  Fix targets \(B>0\) and
   \(h>0\).  Suppose preprocessing certifies integrable signed envelope
   functions \(C_{\sigma_0}(g)\) and \(D_{\sigma_0,p}(g)\) such that, for all
   labels \(g\),
   \[
      C_{\sigma_0}(g)
      \ge
      R_q(g)\bigl(F_q(g)-B\bigr)
      \qquad(\sigma(q)=\sigma_0),
      \tag{FE1}
   \]
   and
   \[
      D_{\sigma_0,p}(g)
      \ge
      R_q(g)\bigl(h-A_g(p)\bigr)
      \qquad
      (\sigma(q)=\sigma_0,\ \|p-q\|\le r),
      \tag{FE2}
   \]
   while the base Gaussian law \(G\sim N(0,I_d)\) has strict slack
   \[
      \E C_{\sigma_0}(G)<0,
      \qquad
      \E D_{\sigma_0,p}(G)<0.
      \tag{FE3}
   \]
   Let
   \[
      D_0=|\Sigma|+\sum_{\sigma_0\in\Sigma}|N_{\sigma_0}|+1 .
   \]
   Then uncharged Las Vegas preprocessing can find a retained weighted
   Gaussian panel with at most \(D_0\) labels such that, for every promised
   query \(q\),
   \[
      \sum_{\substack{x\in P\\ \|x-q\|>cr}}
      \sum_{\substack{g\\ A_g(x)=1}}\pi_q(g)
      \le B ,
      \tag{FE4}
   \]
   and every near pair \(p,q\) satisfies
   \[
      \sum_{g:\ A_g(p)=1}\pi_q(g)\ge h ,
      \tag{FE5}
   \]
   where \(\pi_q(g)\propto w_gR_q(g)\) is the retained tilted sampling law.
   The stored incidences are at most \(mD_0\), and direct sampling costs
   \(O(dD_0)\) arithmetic operations.  In particular, if
   \(D_0\le m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m\), \(B\le m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m\), and
   \(h\ge\log^{-O_c(1)}m\), then this retained panel satisfies the sampled
   terminal ANN requirements of \cref{prop:sampled-structured-panel}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
   For a finite sampled batch \(G_1,\ldots,G_N\), solve the linear feasibility
   problem
   \[
      \sum_iw_i C_{\sigma_0}(G_i)\le0,
      \qquad
      \sum_iw_iD_{\sigma_0,p}(G_i)\le0,
      \qquad
      w_i\ge0,\quad \sum_iw_i=1 .
      \tag{FE6}
   \]
   Since all envelope functions are integrable and have strictly negative
   expectations, the empirical averages of all coordinates in \((FE6)\) are
   simultaneously negative with positive probability for all sufficiently
   large \(N\).  Thus a round-robin Las Vegas schedule over increasing batch
   sizes eventually finds a feasible batch with probability one.

   Replace any feasible solution by a basic feasible solution.  There are
   \(|\Sigma|+\sum_{\sigma_0}|N_{\sigma_0}|\) inequality constraints in
   \((FE6)\), so a basic feasible solution has support size at most \(D_0\).
   Retain only those positive-weight labels.

   Fix a promised query \(q\) with signature \(\sigma_0\).  From \((FE1)\) and
   \((FE6)\),
   \[
      \sum_gw_gR_q(g)\bigl(F_q(g)-B\bigr)
      \le
      \sum_gw_gC_{\sigma_0}(g)
      \le0 .
   \]
   Dividing by \(\sum_gw_gR_q(g)>0\) gives \((FE4)\).  If
   \(\|p-q\|\le r\), then \(p\in N_{\sigma_0}\), and \((FE2)\)--\((FE6)\)
   similarly give
   \[
      \sum_gw_gR_q(g)\bigl(h-A_g(p)\bigr)\le0 .
   \]
   Dividing by the same tilted partition function proves \((FE5)\).

   The storage bound is trivial because each retained label stores at most all
   \(m\) points.  Direct sampling scans the retained labels, evaluates
   \(w_gR_q(g)\), and samples from the resulting prefix sums.  The final
   sampled-panel statement is exactly
   \cref{prop:sampled-structured-panel} with the displayed storage, sampled
   far-load, and near-mass bounds.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Signature entropy is the charged obstruction]
   \label{rem:signature-entropy-obstruction}
   \Cref{cor:small-signature-gaussian-quadrature} is deliberately finite.  It
   shows that once the continuum of promised queries and near witnesses is
   compressed to \(m^\rho\polylog m\) exact signatures, storage and sampling no
   longer require a sophisticated lattice decoder: a direct retained weighted
   panel already fits the terminal \(m^\rho\) budget.  For the full ANN problem
   the signature family is not known to be this small.  A code, lattice,
   trellis, or list-recovery construction should therefore be judged by the
   entropy of the exact certificates it represents: if it exposes too many
   query/witness signatures, then Caratheodory support alone blows up storage;
   if it represents them compactly and samples without scanning more than
   \(m^\rho\polylog m\) labels, the Gaussian quadrature part is already
   certified.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Metric nets are not the right signatures]
   \label{rem:metric-net-signature-barrier}
   The small-signature condition should not be interpreted as a standard net
   over query directions.  At the critical parameters,
   \[
      \beta=\frac{T}{a_0}=\Theta_c(\sqrt{\log m}).
   \]
   For a critical near pair with \(\ip{p}{q}=a_0\), the ideal tilted label
   satisfies
   \[
      \Pr[\ip{G_q}{p}\ge T]=\frac12.
   \]
   If a representative query \(q'\) has
   \(\ip{p}{q'}\le a_0-\Delta\), then
   \[
      \Pr[\ip{G_{q'}}{p}\ge T]
      =
      \Pr[N(0,1)\ge \beta\Delta].
   \]
   Thus a purely metric representative argument that must preserve the
   constant near mass for every possible critical witness needs
   \(\Delta=O(1/\beta)\), hence angular mesh \(O(1/\sqrt{\log m})\) up to
   constants.  A spherical net at that mesh in dimension \(d\) has size at
   least
   \[
      (c_0\sqrt{\log m})^{d-1}.
   \]
   In the usual terminal dimension \(d=\Theta(\log m)\), this is
   \(m^{\Theta(\log\log m)}\), far above the
   \(m^\rho\polylog m\) budget in
   \cref{cor:small-signature-gaussian-quadrature}.  Hence the desired
   signatures cannot be ordinary metric cells.  They must be reliability,
   rank-prefix, code, lattice, or trellis states whose entropy is tied to the
   active certificate rather than to a uniform cover of the sphere.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Lattice Gaussian panels as sampled decoders]
   \label{rem:lattice-gaussian-panels}
   \Cref{prop:sampled-structured-panel} is the sampler analogue of the
   threshold-reporter interface in
   \cref{lem:soft-list-recovery-reporter}.  It matches the coding-theoretic
   view even more literally: labels \(g\) may be codewords, lattice points,
   coset representatives, or states of a finite trellis, and the query samples
   a likely label instead of listing every active label.  A typical target is a
   discrete Gaussian or Gibbs law
   \[
      \pi_q(g)\propto
      \exp\!\left(-\tau\|Pq-g\|^2\right)
   \]
   on a structured code or lattice in the projected block.  Randomized nearest
   plane, sampling decoders, and lattice Gaussian samplers
   \cite{Kle00,LLS11,GPV08,Pei10} are relevant
   because they supply exactly this kind of law for decodable lattices; product
   filters and lattice sieving already exploit the same idea at the level of
   implicit filter families~\cite{BDGL16,GNR10}.

   This avoids the black-box weakness of ordinary lattice CVP or ANN.  The
   theorem does not ask the lattice decoder to return the nearest center, and
   it does not require an additive Gumbel optimizer over the data points.  It
   asks for the three directly checkable spectrum quantities \((SP1)\)--\((SP3)\):
   stored redundancy, far sampled co-load, and near sampled mass.  In
   particular, middle-density near sets are not an all-reporting obstruction:
   many valid buckets improve the sampling mass in \((SP3)\) without forcing
   the query to enumerate all of them.  This is the formal version of the
   empirical lesson that redundancy is the useful part of \(k\)-means
   multi-assignment, while Lloyd convergence itself is not a proof object.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Construction-A theta quotient]
   \label{lem:construction-a-theta-quotient}
   Let \(p\ge2\), let \(\Sigma=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\), and choose representatives
   \(\iota(a)\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) for \(a\in\Sigma\).  For a code
   \(C\subseteq\Sigma^b\), put
   \[
      \Lambda(C,p)
      =
      \{\iota(c)+pz:\ c\in C,\ z\in\mathbb Z^b\}\subseteq\mathbb R^b .
   \]
   Fix a center \(y\in\mathbb R^b\) and inverse temperature \(\tau>0\).  For
   \(a\in\Sigma\) define the one-coordinate theta weight
   \[
      \Theta_a(y_i)
      =
      \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}
      \exp\!\left(
         -\frac{\tau}{2}(y_i-\iota(a)-pk)^2
      \right),
   \]
   and for \(c\in C\) put
   \[
      \Omega_y(c)=\sum_{i=1}^b\log\Theta_{c_i}(y_i).
   \]
   Then the lattice discrete-Gaussian partition function factors through the
   residue code:
   \[
      \sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda(C,p)}
      \exp\!\left(-\frac{\tau}{2}\|y-\lambda\|^2\right)
      =
      \sum_{c\in C}\exp(\Omega_y(c)).
      \tag{CA1}
   \]
   Moreover exact sampling from the left-hand law is obtained by first sampling
   \(c\in C\) with probability proportional to \(\exp(\Omega_y(c))\), and then,
   independently over coordinates, sampling \(K_i\in\mathbb Z\) with
   \[
      \Pr[K_i=k\mid c]
      =
      \frac{
         \exp\!\left(
            -\frac{\tau}{2}(y_i-\iota(c_i)-pk)^2
         \right)}
      {\Theta_{c_i}(y_i)}
   \]
   and outputting \(\lambda_i=\iota(c_i)+pK_i\).

   The score form used in the product-panel certificates is the same identity:
   for
   \[
      S_y(\lambda)=\ip{y}{\lambda}-\frac12\|\lambda\|^2,
   \]
   the law proportional to \(\exp(\beta S_y(\lambda))\) is the
   \(\tau=\beta\) instance above, multiplied by the query-only factor
   \(\exp(\beta\|y\|^2/2)\).  Finally, if
   \[
      M_a(y_i)=
      \max_{k\in\mathbb Z}
      \left\{-\frac{\tau}{2}(y_i-\iota(a)-pk)^2\right\},
      \qquad
      M_y(c)=\sum_iM_{c_i}(y_i),
   \]
   then every lattice point with
   \(-\tau\|y-\lambda\|^2/2\ge\Theta\) has residue \(c=\lambda\bmod p\)
   satisfying \(M_y(c)\ge\Theta\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Expanding the lattice sum by residue class gives
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      \sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda(C,p)}
      e^{-\tau\|y-\lambda\|^2/2}
      &=
      \sum_{c\in C}
      \sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^b}
      \prod_{i=1}^b
      e^{-\tau(y_i-\iota(c_i)-pz_i)^2/2}  \\
      &=
      \sum_{c\in C}\prod_{i=1}^b\Theta_{c_i}(y_i)
      =
      \sum_{c\in C}e^{\Omega_y(c)} ,
   \end{aligned}
   \]
   proving \((CA1)\).  The displayed conditional sampler is exactly the same
   factorization normalized first over residues and then over the independent
   integer coordinates.  The score identity follows from
   \[
      \beta S_y(\lambda)
      =
      \frac{\beta}{2}\|y\|^2
      -
      \frac{\beta}{2}\|y-\lambda\|^2 .
   \]
   For the threshold statement, each coordinate contribution of a lattice point
   with residue \(c_i\) is at most \(M_{c_i}(y_i)\), so its total score is at
   most \(M_y(c)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Construction-A reduces lattice sampling to soft list recovery]
   \label{rem:construction-a-soft-decoding}
   \Cref{lem:construction-a-theta-quotient} is the most direct way to use
   Construction-A or Construction-D ideas here.  A lattice decoder does not have
   to search over all integer lifts first.  It can compute the theta
   reliabilities \(\log\Theta_a(y_i)\), run a soft decoder or partition-function
   recursion for the residue code \(C\), and then sample the one-dimensional
   integer lifts independently.  For threshold reporting, the max-residue scores
   \(M_a(y_i)\) give a certified soft list-recovery superset of residues that
   could contain any close lattice point; a standard sphere decoder can then
   enumerate the remaining integer lifts inside each reported residue.

   This matches the list-decoding literature more closely than a black-box CVP
   formulation.  Euclidean Reed--Solomon and Barnes--Sloane decoders use
   Koetter--Vardy style soft information exactly in this sense, while random and
   nested Construction-A list-decoding results describe the achievable list-size
   spectrum for the residue/lattice ensemble~\cite{MP20,ZV21}.  Expander-based
   list-recovery results are relevant as possible outer-code engines because
   the residue problem is now an ordinary soft list-recovery or partition
   problem on symbol reliabilities~\cite{ST25}.  The remaining ANN theorem is
   still the same one: after choosing rotations, moduli, scalings, and bucket
   thresholds, the retained Construction-A panel must satisfy the storage,
   far sampled co-load, and near sampled-mass certificates of
   \cref{cor:weighted-gaussian-quadrature-panel} or
   \cref{cor:bucket-quotient-quadrature}.  The theta quotient only removes an
   unnecessary lattice-search layer.
\end{remark}

\begin{assumption}[Flat structured spherical-code decoder]
   \label{asm:flat-spherical-code-decoder}
   Fix a localized terminal spherical gap with \(m\) resident points.  There is
   a distribution over finite structured code panels \(\mathcal G\).  Each
   \(g\in\mathcal G\) has a data predicate \(A_g(x)\), a query predicate
   \(B_g(q)\), and a bucket storing the points with \(A_g(x)=1\).  For every
   realized panel, the query decoder lists exactly
   \[
      \mathsf L(q)=\{g\in\mathcal G:B_g(q)=1\}
   \]
   in work \(d\log^{O_c(1)}m+O(|\mathsf L(q)|)\).  For every data set and
   every promised query, the panel distribution satisfies
   \[
      \E|\mathsf L(q)|\le m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m,
      \qquad
      \E\sum_{x\in P}\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}A_g(x)
      \le m^{1+\rho}\log^{O_c(1)}m,
   \]
   and the far co-load bound
   \[
      \E\sum_{\substack{x\in P\\ \|x-q\|>cr}}
      \sum_{g\in\mathcal G}A_g(x)B_g(q)
      \le m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m .
   \]
   Finally, if \(p\) is a true near neighbor of \(q\), then one panel hits it
   with inverse-polylogarithmic probability:
   \[
      \Pr_{\mathcal G}\!\left[
         \exists g\in\mathcal G:\ A_g(p)B_g(q)=1
      \right]\ge \log^{-O_c(1)}m .
   \]
\end{assumption}

\begin{proposition}[Flat code decoder gives a terminal spherical engine]
   \label{prop:flat-spherical-code-terminal}
   Under \cref{asm:flat-spherical-code-decoder}, a terminal localized
   spherical instance of size \(m\) has a data structure with query work
   \[
      d\,m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m
   \]
   and space
   \[
      dm+m^{1+\rho}\log^{O_c(1)}m .
   \]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
   Store \(B=\log^{O_c(1)}m\) independent panels, where the exponent is large
   enough that \(B\) independent near-hit trials succeed with constant
   probability.  In each panel, put every data point \(x\) in every bucket
   \(g\) with \(A_g(x)=1\).  The expected total bucket storage is
   \(m^{1+\rho}\log^{O_c(1)}m\), plus the raw \(dm\) coordinates used for final
   metric verification.

   On query \(q\), decode \(\mathsf L(q)\) in every panel, scan all listed
   buckets, and verify candidate distances in the original metric.  The
   expected decoder work over all panels is
   \(d\,m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m\), after increasing the polylogarithmic exponent
   to absorb \(B\).  The far co-load bound gives the same expected order for
   invalid candidates.  If \(p\) is a true near neighbor, the independent panels
   miss every bucket containing \(p\) with probability at most
   \((1-\log^{-O_c(1)}m)^B\), which is at most a fixed constant strictly below
   one for the chosen \(B\).  The standard capped-expectation convention from the
   preliminaries turns the expected work and storage bounds into the displayed
   capped resources after another constant-factor loss in success probability.
   Any reported point is verified, so the structure never returns a false
   answer.
\end{proof}

The flat-code target is a possible replacement for the terminal score tree, not
another proof of it.  A random Gaussian filter family has the desired spectrum
but no compact decoder.  Existing structured-code work gives pieces of the
right picture: spherical-code hashing analyzes angular nearest-neighbor
partitions induced by polytopes, root lattices, and spherical codes, while
polar-code nearest-neighbor search uses list decoding to multiprobe a
high-dimensional binary LSH space~\cite{Laa20,TH23}.  The missing theorem for
our purposes is the simultaneous combination of random-like cap spectrum,
Euclidean soft scores, and output-sensitive list enumeration at the critical
large-deviation scale.  Construction-A lattices, group-orbit spherical codes,
or concatenated/list-recoverable codes are useful candidates precisely because
they would turn the branching score tree into one decoding problem with the
resource conditions stated in \cref{asm:flat-spherical-code-decoder}.

\begin{lemma}[Finite sampled-cover dual]
   \label{lem:finite-sampled-cover-dual}
   Fix one query state $q$, a finite retained family of certified children
   $\mathcal C$, and a finite unresolved near-point set $N_q\subseteq P$.  For
   each child $C$, let $a_C(q)\in\{0,1\}$ be its activation indicator, let
   $Q_C\ge0$ be its certified query price, and let $\sigma_C\in[0,1]$ be its
   certified success credit.  Given route-mass targets $h_p\ge0$ for
   $p\in N_q$ and a query-price budget $L_q$, consider the sampled-cover
   feasibility problem
   \[
   \begin{array}{ll}
   \text{\rm find} & \pi_C\ge0\qquad(C\in\mathcal C)\\[0.3em]
   \text{\rm subject to}
      & \pi_C=0\qquad(a_C(q)=0),\\[0.4em]
      & \displaystyle \sum_C\pi_C\le1,\\[0.8em]
      & \displaystyle \sum_C\pi_CQ_C\le L_q,\\[0.8em]
      & \displaystyle
        \sum_{C:p\in P_C}\pi_C\sigma_C\ge h_p
        \qquad(p\in N_q).
   \end{array}
   \tag{$\mathsf S_q$}
   \]
   If $\mathsf S_q$ is infeasible, then there are route-demand prices
   $\beta_p\ge0$ $(p\in N_q)$, a query-work price $\lambda\ge0$, and a
   normalization price $\mu\ge0$ such that
   \[
      \sum_{p\in N_q}\beta_ph_p>\lambda L_q+\mu,
      \tag{SD1}
   \]
   while every active child has nonpositive sampled reduced gain,
   \[
      \sigma_C\sum_{p\in P_C\cap N_q}\beta_p
      \le
      \lambda Q_C+\mu
      \qquad(C:a_C(q)=1).
      \tag{SD2}
   \]
   Conversely, the existence of such prices certifies infeasibility of
   $\mathsf S_q$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The converse is immediate: if $\pi$ were feasible, then multiplying the
   route constraints by $\beta_p$ and summing gives
   \[
      \sum_p\beta_ph_p
      \le
      \sum_C\pi_C\sigma_C\sum_{p\in P_C\cap N_q}\beta_p
      \le
      \lambda\sum_C\pi_CQ_C+\mu\sum_C\pi_C
      \le
      \lambda L_q+\mu,
   \]
   contradicting \((SD1)\).

   For the forward implication, apply the finite-dimensional separating
   hyperplane theorem, equivalently Farkas' lemma, to the polyhedron
   $\mathsf S_q$.  Since all constraints are linear and the variables are
   restricted to active children by setting inactive variables to zero,
   infeasibility is exactly the existence of nonnegative multipliers for the
   lower-bound route constraints and upper-bound budget constraints such that
   the resulting linear combination has a strictly positive right-hand side
   but a nonpositive coefficient on every active variable.  Written with
   multipliers $(\beta,\lambda,\mu)$, those two conditions are precisely
   \((SD1)\) and \((SD2)\).
\end{proof}

Thus a finite sampled decoder has the same column-generation interpretation as
the all-listing cover, but with a different obstruction.  A bad query assigns
prices to unresolved near points and asks for one active child whose certified
success credit times its priced point mass beats its query price and the unit
normalization price.  If every surplus sampled dual certificate has such a
positive-gain child in the candidate universe, unbounded preprocessing can add
that child and repeat until the sampled route-mass LP is feasible.

\begin{lemma}[Finite existential sampled-cover dual]
   \label{lem:finite-existential-sampled-cover-dual}
   Fix one query state \(q\), a finite retained family of certified children
   \(\mathcal C\), and a finite unresolved near set
   \(N_q\subseteq P\). Assume \(N_q\ne\emptyset\).  Given a target \(h_0>0\)
   and query-price budget \(L_q\), consider the feasibility problem
   \[
   \begin{array}{ll}
   \text{\rm find} & \pi_C\ge0\qquad(C\in\mathcal C)\\[0.3em]
   \text{\rm subject to}
      & \pi_C=0\qquad(a_C(q)=0),\\[0.4em]
      & \displaystyle \sum_C\pi_C\le1,\\[0.8em]
      & \displaystyle \sum_C\pi_CQ_C\le L_q,\\[0.8em]
      & \displaystyle
        \sum_{C:\ P_C\cap N_q\ne\emptyset}\pi_C\sigma_C\ge h_0 .
   \end{array}
   \tag{$\mathsf E_q$}
   \]
   If \(\mathsf E_q\) is infeasible, then there are prices
   \(\lambda,\mu\ge0\) such that
   \[
      h_0>\lambda L_q+\mu,
      \tag{ED1}
   \]
   while every active child has nonpositive existential reduced gain,
   \[
      \sigma_C\mathbf 1\{P_C\cap N_q\ne\emptyset\}
      \le
      \lambda Q_C+\mu
      \qquad(C:a_C(q)=1).
      \tag{ED2}
   \]
   Conversely, such prices certify infeasibility of \(\mathsf E_q\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The converse is immediate: multiplying the price and normalization
   constraints by \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\), respectively, and using \((ED2)\)
   gives, for any feasible \(\pi\),
   \[
      \sum_{C:\ P_C\cap N_q\ne\emptyset}\pi_C\sigma_C
      \le
      \lambda\sum_C\pi_CQ_C+\mu\sum_C\pi_C
      \le
      \lambda L_q+\mu
      <
      h_0,
   \]
   contradicting the route-mass constraint.

   For the forward implication, apply the same Farkas separation as in
   \cref{lem:finite-sampled-cover-dual}.  The infeasibility certificate has
   nonnegative multipliers \((\beta,\lambda,\mu)\), where \(\beta\) prices the
   single existential lower-bound constraint.  Since its right-hand side is
   \(h_0>0\), any separating certificate has \(\beta>0\); divide by \(\beta\).
   The resulting normalized inequalities are exactly \((ED1)\) and \((ED2)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finite sampled-route verifier]
   \label{lem:finite-sampled-route-verifier}
   Fix a finite retained family of certified children $\mathcal C$, a target
   set $E\subseteq P$, a residual block $U_0\subseteq E$, and a query domain
   $\Omega$.  For $q\in\Omega$, define the unresolved near set
   \[
      N(q)=\{p\in E\setminus U_0:\|p-q\|\le r\},
   \]
   and the sampled-route signature
   \[
      \tau(q)=
      \left(
         (a_C(q))_{C\in\mathcal C},
         (\mathbf 1\{p\in N(q)\})_{p\in E\setminus U_0}
      \right).
   \]
   Let $\Sigma$ be any finite set of signatures containing
   $\{\tau(q):q\in\Omega\}$.  For each $\tau\in\Sigma$, let
   $A_\tau\subseteq\mathcal C$ be its active-child set and
   $N_\tau\subseteq E\setminus U_0$ its unresolved near-point set.  Suppose
   that, for every $\tau\in\Sigma$, the sampled-cover feasibility problem
   \(\mathsf S_\tau\) from \cref{lem:finite-sampled-cover-dual} is feasible
   with route targets $h_p=h_0$ for all $p\in N_\tau$ and query-price budget
   $L$, using activation indicators $\mathbf 1\{C\in A_\tau\}$.

   Store one feasible sampling vector $\pi^\tau$ for every realized signature,
   and suppose the query decoder computes $\tau(q)$ and samples from
   $\pi^{\tau(q)}$ in work $D(q)$.  Then the hypotheses of
   \cref{lem:sampled-priced-cover} hold uniformly over $\Omega$: every near
   pair with $q\in\Omega$, $p\in E\setminus U_0$, and $\|p-q\|\le r$ receives
   route mass at least $h_0$, and the expected sampled child price is at most
   $L$.  Hence $B$ independent sampled child invocations give failure
   probability at most $\exp(-Bh_0)$ and expected work
   $O(B(D(q)+L))$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Fix $q\in\Omega$ and write $\tau=\tau(q)$.  By construction, the active
   coordinates and unresolved near-point coordinates in $\tau$ agree with the
   actual query.  The stored vector $\pi^\tau$ is feasible for
   \(\mathsf S_\tau\), so it is supported only on active children,
   has $\sum_C\pi^\tau_CQ_C\le L$, and for every
   $p\in N(q)=N_\tau$ satisfies
   \[
      \sum_{C:p\in P_C}\pi^\tau_C\sigma_C\ge h_0 .
   \]
   These are exactly the support, expected-price, and route-mass hypotheses of
   \cref{lem:sampled-priced-cover}.  Applying that lemma gives the stated
   success and work bounds.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finite existential sampled-route verifier]
   \label{lem:finite-existential-sampled-route-verifier}
   Work in the setting of \cref{lem:finite-sampled-route-verifier}, but for
   each finite signature \(\tau\) with \(N_\tau\ne\emptyset\) require only the
   existential feasibility problem \(\mathsf E_\tau\) from
   \cref{lem:finite-existential-sampled-cover-dual}, with active set
   \(A_\tau\), unresolved near set \(N_\tau\), target \(h_0\), and query-price
   budget \(L\).  Store one feasible sampler \(\pi^\tau\) for every realized
   nonempty signature, and suppose the query decoder computes \(\tau(q)\) and
   samples from \(\pi^{\tau(q)}\) in work \(D(q)\).

   Then every query with \(N(q)\ne\emptyset\) receives near-set route mass at
   least \(h_0\).  Hence \(B\) independent sampled child invocations fail to
   return any verified \(cr\)-neighbor with probability at most
   \(\exp(-Bh_0)\), and have expected work \(O(B(D(q)+L))\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Fix \(q\in\Omega\) with \(N(q)\ne\emptyset\), and put
   \(\tau=\tau(q)\).  The signature records both the active-child pattern and
   the exact unresolved near set, so \(N_\tau=N(q)\) and \(A_\tau\) is the
   actual active set.  The stored sampler is feasible for
   \(\mathsf E_\tau\), hence it is supported on active children, has expected
   child price at most \(L\), and satisfies
   \[
      \sum_{C:\ P_C\cap N(q)\ne\emptyset}\pi^\tau_C\sigma_C\ge h_0 .
   \]
   Apply \cref{lem:existential-sampled-priced-cover}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Two-child existential sampler]\label{lem:two-child-existential-sampler}
   Fix one finite signature with active child family
   \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal C\), nonempty unresolved near set \(N\),
   certified prices \(Q_C\ge0\), success credits \(\sigma_C\in[0,1]\), and
   target \(0<h_0\le1\).  Suppose the existential feasibility problem
   \(\mathsf E\) is feasible:
   \[
      \pi_C=0\quad(C\notin\mathcal A),\qquad
      \sum_C\pi_C\le1,\qquad
      \sum_C\pi_CQ_C\le L,
   \]
   and
   \[
      \sum_{C:\ P_C\cap N\ne\emptyset}\pi_C\sigma_C\ge h_0 .
   \]
   Then there are two not-necessarily-distinct active useful children
   \(C_1,C_2\), where \(P_{C_i}\cap N\ne\emptyset\), and weights
   \(\theta_1,\theta_2\ge0\) with
   \[
      \theta_1+\theta_2\le1,\qquad
      \theta_1Q_{C_1}+\theta_2Q_{C_2}\le L,
   \]
   and
   \[
      \theta_1\sigma_{C_1}+\theta_2\sigma_{C_2}\ge h_0 .
   \]
   Moreover, for
   \[
      K\ge\left\lceil 4h_0^{-1}\right\rceil ,
   \]
   there are integers \(k_1,k_2\ge0\) with \(k_1+k_2\le K\) such that the
   uniform sampler on \(K\) records, consisting of \(k_i\) copies of \(C_i\)
   and \(K-k_1-k_2\) no-op records, has expected child price at most \(L\) and
   near-set route mass at least \(h_0/2\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Delete all probability mass on non-useful children and move it to a no-op
   record.  This cannot increase expected price and does not decrease the
   existential route mass.  Now consider the linear program that maximizes
   \[
      \sum_{C:\ P_C\cap N\ne\emptyset}\pi_C\sigma_C
   \]
   over useful active children under
   \(\sum_C\pi_C\le1\), \(\sum_C\pi_CQ_C\le L\), and \(\pi_C\ge0\).  It has a
   feasible solution of value at least \(h_0\), so an optimal extreme point also
   has value at least \(h_0\).  Since the LP has only the two nontrivial
   resource inequalities, every basic feasible solution has at most two
   positive variables.  These positive variables are the desired
   \(C_1,C_2\), with weights \(\theta_1,\theta_2\); if the support has only
   one child, duplicate it and put the second weight equal to zero.

   For the integer sampler, set \(k_i=\lfloor K\theta_i\rfloor\).  Then
   \(k_1+k_2\le K\), and rounding down only decreases expected price:
   \[
      \frac{k_1Q_{C_1}+k_2Q_{C_2}}{K}
      \le
      \theta_1Q_{C_1}+\theta_2Q_{C_2}
      \le L .
   \]
   Since \(\sigma_{C_i}\le1\),
   \[
      \frac{k_1\sigma_{C_1}+k_2\sigma_{C_2}}{K}
      \ge
      \theta_1\sigma_{C_1}+\theta_2\sigma_{C_2}-\frac2K
      \ge
      h_0/2 .
   \]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Activation-pattern sampled-route verifier]
   \label{lem:activation-sampled-route-verifier}
   Work in the setting of \cref{lem:finite-sampled-route-verifier}, but group
   queries only by their active-child pattern
   \[
      a(q)=(a_C(q))_{C\in\mathcal C}.
   \]
   Let \(\mathcal A_\Omega\) be any finite set of activation patterns
   containing all patterns realized on \(\Omega\).  For
   \(a\in\mathcal A_\Omega\), write
   \[
      \Omega_a=\{q\in\Omega:a(q)=a\},
      \qquad
      N_a=
      \{p\in E\setminus U_0:\exists q\in\Omega_a,\ \|p-q\|\le r\}.
   \]
   Suppose that, for every realized activation pattern \(a\), the
   sampled-cover feasibility problem \(\mathsf S_a\) is feasible with active
   set \(A_a=\{C:a_C=1\}\), unresolved set \(N_a\), route targets
   \(h_p=h_0\), and query-price budget \(L\).  Store one feasible sampler
   \(\pi^a\) for each realized activation pattern, and suppose the query
   decoder computes \(a(q)\) and samples from \(\pi^{a(q)}\) in work \(D(q)\).

   Then the hypotheses of \cref{lem:sampled-priced-cover} hold uniformly over
   \(\Omega\) with route mass at least \(h_0\) and expected sampled child price
   at most \(L\).  In particular, the query-time signature need not include
   the exact unresolved near set \(N(q)\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Fix a query \(q\in\Omega\), put \(a=a(q)\), and let
   \(p\in E\setminus U_0\) satisfy \(\|p-q\|\le r\).  By definition,
   \(q\in\Omega_a\), hence \(p\in N_a\).  The stored vector \(\pi^a\) is
   feasible for \(\mathsf S_a\), so it is supported on active children for
   this same pattern, has expected child price at most \(L\), and satisfies
   \[
      \sum_{C:p\in P_C}\pi^a_C\sigma_C\ge h_0 .
   \]
   These are exactly the support, expected-price, and route-mass requirements
   of \cref{lem:sampled-priced-cover}.  Applying that compiler gives the
   claimed uniform guarantee.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Sampled-route cohort materialization]
   \label{lem:sampled-route-cohort}
   Fix one sampled-route signature with active child family
   $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal C$, unresolved near set $N$, certified prices
   $Q_C\ge0$, success credits $\sigma_C\in[0,1]$, and target \(h_0>0\).
   Suppose the sampled feasibility problem has a solution $\pi$ satisfying
   \[
      \pi_C=0\quad(C\notin\mathcal A),\qquad
      \sum_C\pi_C\le1,\qquad
      \sum_C\pi_CQ_C\le L,
   \]
   and
   \[
      \sum_{C:p\in P_C}\pi_C\sigma_C\ge h_0
      \qquad(p\in N).
   \]
   If
   \[
      K\ge
      \max\left\{
         1,\,
         \left\lceil 8h_0^{-1}\log(4\max\{|N|,1\})\right\rceil
      \right\},
   \]
   then there is a multiset \(M=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_K)\) of records, each either an
   active child or a no-op record \(\bot\), such that
   \[
      \frac1K\sum_{t:Y_t\ne\bot} Q_{Y_t}\le4L
   \]
   and, for every \(p\in N\),
   \[
      \frac1K\sum_{t:Y_t\ne\bot,\ p\in P_{Y_t}}\sigma_{Y_t}
      \ge\frac{h_0}{2}.
   \]
   Consequently the real-valued sampler $\pi$ can be replaced, for this
   signature, by the uniform sampler on \(M\), losing only a constant factor in
   expected child price and route mass; sampling \(\bot\) simply performs no
   child invocation.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Add a no-op record \(\bot\) with price \(Q_\bot=0\), success credit
   \(\sigma_\bot=0\), and no resident points, and put
   \[
      \pi_\bot=1-\sum_C\pi_C .
   \]
   Draw \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_K\) independently from this probability distribution on
   \(\mathcal A\cup\{\bot\}\).  If \(L=0\), the average price is zero almost
   surely because the prices are nonnegative.  Otherwise the expected average
   price is at most \(L\), so Markov's inequality gives
   \[
      \Pr\left[\frac1K\sum_{t=1}^KQ_{Y_t}>4L\right]\le\frac14 .
   \]

   Fix \(p\in N\), and put
   \[
      X_t=\sigma_{Y_t}\mathbf 1\{Y_t\ne\bot,\ p\in P_{Y_t}\}\in[0,1],
      \qquad \mu_p=\E X_t\ge h_0 .
   \]
   We use the elementary one-sided bound
   \[
      \Pr\left[\sum_{t=1}^KX_t\le\frac{K\mu_p}{2}\right]
      \le e^{-K\mu_p/8}.
   \]
   Indeed, for \(0\le X\le1\) and \(\lambda=1\),
   convexity of \(e^{-\lambda x}\) on \([0,1]\) gives
   \(e^{-X}\le1-(1-e^{-1})X\), hence
   \[
      \E e^{-\sum_tX_t}
      \le
      \exp\bigl(-K\mu_p(1-e^{-1})\bigr).
   \]
   Markov's inequality applied to \(e^{-\sum_tX_t}\) yields
   \[
      \Pr\left[\sum_tX_t\le\frac{K\mu_p}{2}\right]
      \le
      \exp\bigl(K\mu_p/2-K\mu_p(1-e^{-1})\bigr)
      \le e^{-K\mu_p/8}.
   \]
   Since \(h_0\le\mu_p\), the event
   \(\frac1K\sum_tX_t<h_0/2\) is contained in the displayed lower-tail event,
   and therefore has probability at most \(e^{-Kh_0/8}\).

   A union bound over \(p\in N\) shows that all route inequalities fail with
   probability at most
   \[
      |N|e^{-Kh_0/8}\le\frac14
   \]
   when \(N\ne\emptyset\), and with probability zero when \(N=\emptyset\).
   With positive probability, both the price bound and all route bounds hold.
   Any sampled multiset realizing this event is the required cohort.  Sampling
   uniformly from the cohort has expected price equal to its average price and
   route mass equal to the displayed averages.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Activation-cohort sampled compiler]
   \label{lem:activation-cohort-sampled-compiler}
   Work in the setting of
   \cref{lem:activation-sampled-route-verifier}, with target \(h_0>0\).
   Suppose every realized activation pattern \(a\) has a feasible sampled LP
   \(\mathsf S_a\) with active set \(A_a\), unresolved union \(N_a\), route
   targets \(h_p=h_0\), and query-price budget \(L\).  For each such pattern
   choose
   \[
      K_a\ge
      \max\left\{
         1,\,
         \left\lceil 8h_0^{-1}\log(4\max\{|N_a|,1\})\right\rceil
      \right\}.
   \]
   Then preprocessing can store, for every realized activation pattern \(a\),
   a cohort \(M_a\) of \(K_a\) records, each either an active child
   \(C\in A_a\) or a no-op record, such that the uniform sampler on \(M_a\)
   has expected child price at most \(4L\) and gives every
   \(p\in N_a\) route mass at least \(h_0/2\).

   Consequently, if the query decoder computes \(a(q)\) and locates
   \(M_{a(q)}\) in work \(D(q)\), then \(B\) independent uniform draws from
   this cohort followed by verification fail on any unresolved near pair with
   probability at most
   \[
      \exp(-Bh_0/2),
   \]
   and have expected query work
   \[
      O\bigl(D(q)+B(L+1)\bigr).
   \]
   The sampler metadata is
   \[
      \sum_{a}K_a
   \]
   child/no-op records plus the activation-pattern decoder.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   For each realized activation pattern \(a\), take a feasible LP solution
   \(\pi^a\) for \(\mathsf S_a\), and apply
   \cref{lem:sampled-route-cohort} with active family \(A_a\), unresolved set
   \(N_a\), and the same \(h_0,L\).  This gives a cohort \(M_a\) whose uniform
   distribution is supported on active children and no-op records, has expected
   child price at most \(4L\), and gives route mass at least \(h_0/2\) to every
   point in \(N_a\).

   Now fix \(q\in\Omega\), set \(a=a(q)\), and let
   \(p\in E\setminus U_0\) satisfy \(\|p-q\|\le r\).  Then \(p\in N_a\) by the
   definition of the activation-pattern near union.  A single sampled trial
   from \(M_a\) therefore chooses a child containing \(p\) and succeeds inside
   it with probability at least \(h_0/2\), with no-op records contributing
   zero.  Independent trials fail with probability at most
   \((1-h_0/2)^B\le e^{-Bh_0/2}\).  The expected child price in one trial is at
   most \(4L\).  The activation pattern and cohort address are computed once,
   and each additional draw from the stored cohort costs constant work before
   the selected child invocation.  Linearity of expectation gives
   \(O(D(q)+B(L+1))\), with the constant \(4\) absorbed in the
   \(O(\cdot)\) notation.  The metadata bound is exactly one stored record per
   cohort entry.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Activation-cohort resource certificate]
   \label{cor:activation-cohort-resources}
   In the setting of \cref{lem:activation-cohort-sampled-compiler}, let
   \(\mathcal A_\Omega\) be the set of realized activation patterns and let
   \(M_{\rm dec}\) be the retained metadata used to decode the pattern and
   address its cohort.  If \(N_a\subseteq P\) for every \(a\), then the cohorts
   may be chosen so that their total number of stored records is
   \[
      M_{\rm coh}
      =
      \sum_{a\in\mathcal A_\Omega}K_a
      \le
      |\mathcal A_\Omega|
      \left(1+8h_0^{-1}\log(4m)\right).
   \]
   For any \(0<\delta<1\), with
   \[
      B=\left\lceil 2h_0^{-1}\log(1/\delta)\right\rceil ,
   \]
   the retained activation-cohort sampler fails on any unresolved near pair
   with probability at most \(\delta\), has expected query work
   \[
      O\!\left(D(q)+h_0^{-1}\log(1/\delta)(L+1)\right),
   \]
   and uses storage
   \[
      \sum_{C\in\mathcal C}S_C+M_{\rm dec}+M_{\rm coh}.
   \]
   Thus, in a local node with target price \(F_4(m,R)\), this route has only
   polylogarithmic overhead whenever
   \[
      h_0^{-1}\le \log^{O_c(1)}m,\qquad
      L\le F_4(m,R)\log^{O_c(1)}m,\qquad
      D(q)\le F_4(m,R)\log^{O_c(1)}m,
   \]
   and
   \[
      \sum_CS_C+M_{\rm dec}
      +|\mathcal A_\Omega|h_0^{-1}\log m
      \le
      mF_4(m,R)\log^{O_c(1)}m .
   \]
   The construction of the LP solutions, the enumeration of activation
   patterns, and the search for good cohorts are preprocessing tasks and are
   not charged to these retained resources.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Since \(N_a\subseteq P\), the definition of \(K_a\) in
   \cref{lem:activation-cohort-sampled-compiler} gives
   \(K_a\le1+8h_0^{-1}\log(4m)\) after increasing constants.  Summing over
   realized patterns gives the metadata bound.  The failure and work bounds
   are the bounds of \cref{lem:activation-cohort-sampled-compiler} with the
   displayed value of \(B\), because
   \[
      \exp(-Bh_0/2)\le\delta .
   \]
   The storage expression counts each retained child subindex once, plus the
   pattern decoder and the integer cohort records.  The final polylogarithmic
   statement is the same set of inequalities with
   \(h_0^{-1},L,D(q)\), and the cohort metadata bounded by the indicated
   local budgets.
\end{proof}

For ball, cap, affine-score, and Lipschitz-score filters with finitely many
retained predicates, the active-child part of the signature is controlled by
the same arrangement machinery as in \cref{lem:finite-activation-patterns}; the
near-set part adds the arrangement of the balls $\Ball(p,r)$ for
$p\in E\setminus U_0$.  The verifier is useful when this combined signature
class is small enough to store or can be sampled from implicitly.  Otherwise it
still serves as a finite offline certificate and dual diagnostic, but its table
size must be charged to the retained index.
\Cref{lem:activation-sampled-route-verifier} gives a stricter but cleaner
alternative: certify, for each activation pattern, the union of all near points
that can occur under that pattern.  Then query-time decoding never needs the
exact near set or the ball-arrangement cell; it only needs the ordinary
activation pattern.  This is useful when the larger pattern-level LP is
feasible, because it moves the remaining metadata issue from near-set
signatures to the already-present activation decoder.
\Cref{lem:sampled-route-cohort} gives the corresponding integer
materialization: for inverse-polylogarithmic \(h_0\), each feasible signature
needs only a polylogarithmic cohort of child identifiers to implement its
sampler, provided the signature itself is stored or decodable.
\Cref{lem:two-child-existential-sampler} is sharper for exact existential
signatures: because there is only one route-mass constraint, the sampler can
be supported on two useful children plus no-op records, and an integer
materialization uses only \(O(h_0^{-1})\) records with no \(\log |N|\) factor.
This applies only when the exact unresolved near-set signature is available;
the activation-only verifier still needs the stronger per-witness union
certificate above.
\Cref{lem:activation-cohort-sampled-compiler} packages the activation-only
case as a concrete retained object: one small cohort per activation pattern,
with no real-valued sampler and no near-set coordinate at query time.
\Cref{cor:activation-cohort-resources} spells out the remaining retained
resource condition: inverse-polylogarithmic route mass makes each cohort small,
so the only possible metadata bottleneck is the number and decodability of
activation patterns, not the offline LP or cohort search.

\begin{lemma}[Certified cover with residual scan]\label{lem:cover-residual-scan}
   In the setting of \cref{lem:certified-cover-compiler}, suppose the stored
   filters cover only $P\setminus U_0$, where $U_0\subseteq P$ is a residual
   block that every query scans directly.  If
   \[
      \sum_{i\in I(q)} |P_i|^\rho\Psi(R_i)\le L
      \qquad\text{for every query }q,
   \]
   and $|U_0|\le L_0$, then the node is routing-correct and contributes query
   work
   \[
      O((L+L_0)\polylog n)
   \]
   and storage
   \[
      O((S_0+|U_0|)\polylog n),
   \]
   where $S_0=\sum_i |P_i|^{1+\rho}\Psi(R_i)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Let $\|p-q\|\le r$.  If $p\in U_0$, the always-scanned residual block
   verifies it directly.  Otherwise $p$ lies in some stored filter, and the
   proof of \cref{lem:certified-cover-compiler} shows that the query activates
   a child containing $p$.  The displayed work and storage bounds add the
   residual scan and residual storage to the certified-cover accounting.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Guard-restricted cover compiler]\label{lem:guard-restricted-cover}
   Work in one node with resident set $P$, $|P|=m$, and define the resident
   guard density
   \[
      g(q)=\frac1m\bigl|\{x\in P:\|x-q\|\le cr\}\bigr|.
   \]
   Fix a threshold $\gamma>0$.  Suppose a residual cover as in
   \cref{lem:cover-residual-scan} is routing-correct for every near pair, but
   its active-power certificate is required only on the low-guard domain
   \[
      \Omega_{\rm low}=\{q:g(q)<\gamma\}.
   \]
   Thus, for every $q\in\Omega_{\rm low}$,
   \[
      \sum_{i\in I(q)} |P_i|^\rho\Psi(R_i)\le L,
      \qquad |U_0|\le L_0 .
   \]
   There is a capped query procedure with work
   \[
      O((\gamma^{-1}+L+L_0)\polylog n)
   \]
   and the same storage as the residual cover, such that every near pair is
   found with constant probability.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   First sample
   \[
      T=\left\lceil \gamma^{-1}\log 4\right\rceil
   \]
   resident points uniformly and verify them in the original metric.  If any
   sampled point is within distance $cr$ of the query, return it.  If not, run
   the cover decoder with a cap: enumerate active filters, but abort this query
   copy before recursing if the accumulated active power would exceed $L$.
   Always scan the residual block $U_0$ before recursing into the enumerated
   filters.

   If $q\notin\Omega_{\rm low}$, then $g(q)\ge\gamma$, so the guard misses all
   valid points with probability at most
   \[
      (1-\gamma)^T\le e^{-\gamma T}\le\frac14 .
   \]
   Hence this high-guard query succeeds with probability at least $3/4$ before
   any cover work is needed; if the guard misses, aborting is harmless for
   constant-success ANN.

   If $q\in\Omega_{\rm low}$ and $\|p-q\|\le r$, then the low-guard
   active-power certificate implies that the capped decoder does not abort and
   lists every active filter.  If $p\in U_0$, the residual scan finds it.
   Otherwise, routing correctness puts $p$ in a listed child, and the recursive
   or terminal subroutine finds a valid answer.  The work bound is the guard
   sample size plus the capped active-power and residual costs.  Storage is
   unchanged.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Low-guard shadow compiler]\label{lem:low-guard-shadow}
   Work in one node with resident set $P$, guard density $g$, and low-guard
   domain $\Omega_{\rm low}=\{q:g(q)<\gamma\}$ as in
   \cref{lem:guard-restricted-cover}.  Define the low-guard shadow of the
   resident set
   \[
      E_\gamma
      =
      \{p\in P:\exists q\in\Omega_{\rm low}\text{ with }\|p-q\|\le r\}.
   \]
   Suppose the residual cover is required to route only low-guard near pairs:
   for every $q\in\Omega_{\rm low}$ and every $p\in P$ with $\|p-q\|\le r$,
   either $p\in U_0$ or some active stored filter contains $p$.  For
   compiler-compatible ball or Lipschitz-score filters, it is enough to cover
   the exposed set $E_\gamma\setminus U_0$, because the query slack then
   activates every filter containing such a near point.  Assume that the
   active-power certificate
   \[
      \sum_{i\in I(q)} |P_i|^\rho\Psi(R_i)\le L
   \]
   is imposed only for $q\in\Omega_{\rm low}$, and that
   $|U_0|\le L_0$.  Then the same capped query procedure as in
   \cref{lem:guard-restricted-cover} has work
   \[
      O((\gamma^{-1}+L+L_0)\polylog n)
   \]
   and finds a valid answer for every near pair with constant probability.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   If $q\notin\Omega_{\rm low}$, the resident guard succeeds with probability
   at least $3/4$, exactly as in \cref{lem:guard-restricted-cover}.  On this
   event no recursive cover is used, so points outside $E_\gamma$ need not be
   stored in any child.

   If $q\in\Omega_{\rm low}$ and $\|p-q\|\le r$, then $p\in E_\gamma$ by
   definition.  The low-guard routing condition says that $p$ is either in the
   residual scan or in an active listed child.  The active-power certificate
   prevents the capped decoder from aborting on such a query, so the residual
   scan or recursive call finds a valid answer.  The work bound is unchanged.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Middle-density singleton obstruction]
   \label{lem:middle-density-singleton-obstruction}
   Fix $\rho<1/2$ and any polylogarithmic factor $L(m)$.  There are
   bounded-diameter nodes and low-guard queries for which retaining every
   exposed point as a certified singleton child has active power polynomially
   larger than $F_4(m,R)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Let
   \[
      s=\left\lfloor \frac{m^{1-\rho}}{2L(m)}\right\rfloor .
   \]
   Put $s$ data points in an arbitrarily small ball around a query point $q$,
   and put the remaining points at distance greater than $cr$ from $q$ but
   still inside a parent ball of radius $R=O_c(r)$.  Then
   \[
      g(q)=\frac1m|\{x:\|x-q\|\le cr\}|
      \le \frac{m^{-\rho}}{2L(m)},
   \]
   so $q$ lies in the low-guard domain for threshold
   $\gamma=m^{-\rho}/L(m)$.

   A singleton child has certified radius $0$ and weight
   $1^\rho\Psi(0)=1$.  If every exposed singleton within distance $r$ of $q$
   is activated, the active power at $q$ is at least $s$.  Since
   $R=O_c(r)$, $F_4(m,R)=\Theta_c(m^\rho)$.  Thus
   \[
      \frac{s}{F_4(m,R)}
      \ge
      m^{1-2\rho}\log^{-O_c(1)}m,
   \]
   which is polynomially large when $\rho<1/2$.
\end{proof}

Consequently, the low-guard refinement is not by itself a sparse range-reporting
theorem.  Free preprocessing can enumerate singleton proposals and exact
residual covers, but the retained index still needs a selective activation rule,
a route-value allocation, or a posterior/rank-prefix reporter that avoids
listing every valid point in the middle-density regime
$m^\rho\ll |P\cap\Ball(q,cr)|\ll m^{1-\rho}$.

\begin{lemma}[Budgeted pure-alternative sampling]
   \label{lem:budgeted-pure-alternative-sampling}
   Fix one query $q$ in a node.  Let $A(q)$ be a finite candidate set that a
   query sampler can draw from, and let $V(q)\subseteq A(q)$ be a set of pure
   terminal alternatives: every element of $V(q)$ carries a representative
   point within distance $cr$ of $q$.  If the sampler returns independent
   uniform elements of $A(q)$, then after $B$ samples and verification the
   failure probability is at most
   \[
      \left(1-\frac{|V(q)|}{|A(q)|}\right)^B
      \le
      \exp\!\left(-B\frac{|V(q)|}{|A(q)|}\right).
   \]
   In particular, if the sampler is supported on pure alternatives
   $(A(q)=V(q))$, one sample succeeds whenever $V(q)\ne\emptyset$, independent
   of $|V(q)|$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   A sampled alternative in $V(q)$ returns a representative within distance
   $cr$ of $q$, and verification accepts it.  The samples are independent, so
   the miss probability is exactly the probability that none of them falls in
   $V(q)$, giving the displayed bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Weighted terminal-sampler compiler]
   \label{lem:weighted-terminal-sampler}
   Fix a query $q$ and a nonempty finite active family of terminal groups
   $\mathcal G(q)$.  Each group $g$ has a nonempty finite candidate set
   $A_g(q)$, a positive sampling weight $b_g$, and an $O(1)$-time sampler for
   the uniform distribution on $A_g(q)$.  Let $V_g(q)\subseteq A_g(q)$ be the
   pure alternatives in group $g$, meaning that every sampled element of
   $V_g(q)$ carries a representative within distance $cr$ of $q$.  One
   terminal trial chooses a group with probability proportional to $b_g$ and
   then samples uniformly inside that group.  Put
   \[
      h(q)=
      \frac{\sum_{g\in\mathcal G(q)}
         b_g\,|V_g(q)|/|A_g(q)|}
           {\sum_{g\in\mathcal G(q)}b_g}.
   \]
   Then $B$ independent terminal trials followed by verification fail with
   probability at most $\exp(-Bh(q))$.  In particular, if
   $h(q)\ge h_0$, then $O(h_0^{-1})$ trials give constant success probability,
   independent of the total number of pure alternatives.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   A single trial lands in a pure alternative with probability exactly $h(q)$.
   Such a trial returns a representative within distance $cr$ of $q$, and
   verification accepts it.  The trials are independent, so the miss
   probability is $(1-h(q))^B\le e^{-Bh(q)}$.
\end{proof}

Thus the obstruction in
\cref{lem:middle-density-singleton-obstruction} is specifically an
all-reporting obstruction.  Middle-density terminal alternatives are harmless
if the query can sample from a pure active family, or from a candidate family
whose pure fraction is inverse-polylogarithmic.  The weighted form
\cref{lem:weighted-terminal-sampler} is the terminal analogue of the saturated
value-delivery formulation below: a large number of parallel valid alternatives
should contribute sampling mass, not active listing cost.  It is also the
reason the structured posterior target asks for output-sensitive rank-prefix
sampling/reporting rather than an explicit list of all near singletons.
\Cref{lem:sampled-priced-cover} gives the corresponding recursive local
compiler: the query may sample active children from a certified distribution
and pay only the expected sampled child price, provided the true near point
receives inverse-polylogarithmic route mass.

This also gives a safe way to use an empirical cover such as $k$-means without
claiming that Lloyd's objective proves anything. At a node, store an arbitrary
certified cover together with a capped decoder. On query $q$, the decoder either
lists every active filter while certifying
\[
   \sum_{i\in I(q)} |P_i|^\rho\Psi(R_i)\le L,
\]
or aborts before spending more than the chosen cap. In the first case the query
searches the listed filters and is correct by the compiler. In the second case
the query ignores the cover and runs the baseline score-and-ball node. Thus a
heuristic cover can only improve benign instances; the worst-case theorem is
still carried by the baseline unless one proves a uniform power-stabbing bound.
The open theoretical problem is therefore not to analyze Lloyd's algorithm
directly, but to construct covers that pass this certificate recursively.

\begin{assumption}[Decodable contracting power cover]\label{asm:power-cover}
   Fix $c>1$, $\rho=\rho_c$, and a parameter $\eta>0$. In every bounded-diameter
   localized node with $m$ resident points in a certified ball of radius $R$,
   either the node is terminal, or preprocessing constructs a query-decodable
   certified cover $(P_i,o_i,R_i)_{i\in I}$ with the following properties.
   \begin{itemize}
      \item Cover and radius decrease:
      \[
         \bigcup_iP_i=P,
         \qquad
         R_i\le R\sqrt{1-\eta^2}.
      \]
      \item For every query $q$, the decoder lists every filter whose inflated
      ball contains $q$,
      \[
         I(q)\supseteq\{i:\|q-o_i\|\le R_i+r\},
      \]
      in time
      \[
         d\,F_4(m,R)\log^{O_c(1)}m
      \]
      plus the listed-output cost.
      \item Unless the resident guard density at $q$ is at least
      $m^{-\rho}\log^{-O_c(1)}m$, the listed filters satisfy the power-stabbing
      contraction
      \[
         \sum_{i\in I(q)} |P_i|^\rho\Psi(R_i)
         \le
         (1-\kappa\eta^2)F_4(m,R)
      \]
      for a constant $\kappa=\kappa(c)>0$.
      \item The stored cover satisfies the storage bound
      \[
         \sum_i |P_i|^{1+\rho}\Psi(R_i)
         \le
         mF_4(m,R) .
      \]
   \end{itemize}
\end{assumption}

\begin{proposition}[Conditional power-cover endpoint]\label{prop:power-cover-polylog}
   If \cref{asm:power-cover} holds uniformly for
   \[
      \eta=\Theta_c\!\left(\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}\right),
   \]
   and terminal nodes are handled by resident scans or by
   \cref{thm:smooth-product-terminal}, then worst-case Euclidean ANN has
   \[
      Q(n,d)=d\,n^{\rho_c}\log^{O_c(1)}n,
      \qquad
      S(n,d)=dn+n^{1+\rho_c}\log^{O_c(1)}n .
   \]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
   Work after the bounded-diameter localization, so $R_0/r=\log^{O_c(1)}n$.
   At every reached node, first sample a resident guard of size
   $m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m$ and verify its points. If the guard-density
   alternative in \cref{asm:power-cover} holds, the guard succeeds with
   constant probability after increasing the logarithmic constant.

   Otherwise decode the active cover filters and recurse into all listed
   children. If $\|p-q\|\le r$ and $p\in P_i$, then
   $\|q-o_i\|\le r+R_i$, so the child containing $p$ is listed. Thus, on the
   non-guard branch, routing is deterministic; no independent success loss is
   paid at each geometric level.

   Each recursive cover edge decreases radius by at least
   $\sqrt{1-\eta^2}$, so a lineage has length
   \[
      H=O_c\!\left(\eta^{-2}\log\frac{R_0}{r}\right)
      =
      \log^{O_c(1)}n
   \]
   for the displayed choice of $\eta$. Let $T(m,R)$ be the expected query work
   from a node, normalized by the local potential. The decoding, guard, and
   terminal costs contribute $dF_4(m,R)\log^{O_c(1)}n$. The active-child
   power-stabbing contraction gives
   \[
      \sum_{i\in I(q)}F_4(|P_i|,R_i)
      \le
      (1-\kappa\eta^2)F_4(m,R).
   \]
   Unrolling the recurrence over the radius levels therefore gives
   \[
      T(m,R)\le d\,\eta^{-2}F_4(m,R)\log^{O_c(1)}n
      =
      d\,F_4(m,R)\log^{O_c(1)}n .
   \]
   At the root, $F_4(n,R_0)=n^{\rho_c}\log^{O_c(1)}n$.

   The storage recurrence uses the last bullet of \cref{asm:power-cover}. Since
   every child radius decreases, summing over the $H=\log^{O_c(1)}n$ radius
   levels and the polylogarithmic localization copies gives
   $dn+n^{1+\rho_c}\log^{O_c(1)}n$. Standard truncation and a constant number of
   independent guard samples give the stated capped bounds.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Balanced fanout obstruction]\label{lem:balanced-fanout-obstruction}
   Consider one node with $m$ points and radius $R$. Suppose that, for some
   query $q$, the active certified cover contains $K\ge2$ disjoint children
   of equal size $m/K$, and each has radius at least
   $R\sqrt{1-\eta^2}$ up to lower-order terms. Then its active recursive
   power satisfies
   \[
      \sum_{i=1}^K |P_i|^\rho\Psi(R_i)
      \ge
      K^{1-\rho}\left(1-O(\eta^2)\right)F_4(m,R).
   \]
   In particular, for every fixed $\rho<1$ and sufficiently small $\eta$, such
   a balanced active fanout violates the contraction required in
   \cref{asm:power-cover}.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The equal-size assumption gives
   \[
      \sum_{i=1}^K |P_i|^\rho\Psi(R_i)
      \ge
      K\left(\frac mK\right)^\rho
      \min_i\frac{\Psi(R_i)}{\Psi(R)}\Psi(R).
   \]
   Since $R_i\ge R\sqrt{1-\eta^2}$ and
   $\Psi(R)=1+(R/r)^4$, we have
   \[
      \frac{\Psi(R_i)}{\Psi(R)}
      \ge
      1-O(\eta^2)
   \]
   uniformly for $R\ge r$. The displayed lower bound follows. Because
   $K^{1-\rho}>1$ for $K\ge2$ and $\rho<1$, this is larger than
   $(1-\kappa\eta^2)F_4(m,R)$ for all sufficiently small $\eta$.
\end{proof}

This lemma explains both why $k$-means works and why it is not the most
theory-native objective. Lloyd's algorithm minimizes an average squared
reconstruction error,
\[
   \sum_x \min_i\|x-o_i\|^2,
\]
whereas ANN routing cares about the inflated-ball stabbing sums above. A large
cluster with a slightly better mean can be bad because its inflated ball is hit
by many queries; a boundary point may need replication even if its squared
error to the nearest center is small.

The corresponding replacement for $k$-means is a power-stabbing cover problem:
choose centers, radii, and overlapping assignments to minimize a Lagrangian such
as
\[
   \max_{q\in\mathcal Q}
   \sum_{i:\|q-o_i\|\le R_i+r}|P_i|^\rho\Psi(R_i)
   +
   \lambda
   \sum_i |P_i|^{1+\rho}\Psi(R_i),
\]
subject to covering the data, or the analogous sampled-near-pair objective when
only a bounded number of active filters is probed. Multi-assignment is then not
an ad hoc repair but the intended filtering mechanism: spend overlap on points
whose near-neighbor queries otherwise escape their closest cell.

There is a particularly clean finite surrogate for the replication part. Fix a
pool of candidate certified filters and a query rule $I(q)$, and let
$\mathcal E$ be a multiset of sampled near pairs $(x,q)$. For a set $A$ of
chosen memberships $(x,i)$, define the covered near-pair weight
\[
   \operatorname{Cov}(A)
   =
   \sum_{(x,q)\in\mathcal E} w_{x,q}\,
   \mathbf 1\{\exists i\in I(q):(x,i)\in A\}.
\]

\begin{lemma}[Greedy near-pair cover]\label{lem:greedy-near-pair-cover}
   With the candidate filters and query rule fixed, $\operatorname{Cov}$ is a
   monotone submodular set function of the selected memberships. Consequently,
   if every membership has unit storage cost, the greedy rule that repeatedly
   adds the membership with largest marginal gain achieves at least a
   $(1-e^{-1})$ fraction of the best coverage achievable with the same number
   of memberships.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Monotonicity is immediate. For submodularity, compare two membership sets
   $A\subseteq B$ and one additional membership $e=(x,i)$. The marginal gain of
   adding $e$ is exactly the total weight of sampled pairs $(x,q)$ with
   $i\in I(q)$ that are not already covered. Since $B$ covers every pair covered
   by $A$, the uncovered set under $B$ is smaller, so the marginal gain under
   $B$ is at most the marginal gain under $A$.

   Let $O$ be an optimal set of $B_0$ memberships and let $A_t$ be the greedy
   set after $t$ steps. By submodularity, the total marginal contribution of the
   elements of $O$ relative to $A_t$ is at least
   $\operatorname{Cov}(O)-\operatorname{Cov}(A_t)$. Hence some element of $O$
   has marginal gain at least
   $(\operatorname{Cov}(O)-\operatorname{Cov}(A_t))/B_0$, and the greedy step
   gains at least as much. Thus
   \[
