      \operatorname{Cov}(O)-\operatorname{Cov}(A_{t+1})
      \le
      \left(1-\frac1{B_0}\right)
      \bigl(\operatorname{Cov}(O)-\operatorname{Cov}(A_t)\bigr).
   \]
   Iterating for $B_0$ steps gives
   $\operatorname{Cov}(A_{B_0})\ge(1-(1-1/B_0)^{B_0})\operatorname{Cov}(O)
   \ge(1-e^{-1})\operatorname{Cov}(O)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Cost-sensitive near-pair cover]\label{lem:cost-sensitive-near-pair-cover}
   In the setting of \cref{lem:greedy-near-pair-cover}, assign every admissible
   membership $e$ a fixed positive cost $c_e$, and write
   $c(A)=\sum_{e\in A}c_e$. Let $O_B$ be the best membership set of cost at most
   $B$, after discarding memberships with $c_e>B$. Run density greedy: at step
   $t$, choose an unused membership maximizing
   \[
      \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(A_t\cup\{e\})-\operatorname{Cov}(A_t)}{c_e}
   \]
   among memberships of positive marginal gain. If the greedy procedure exhausts
   all positive marginal gains before reaching cost $B$, then it is optimal for
   budget $B$. Otherwise, if $A^+$ is the greedy set just after the first step
   with $c(A^+)\ge B$, then
   \[
      \operatorname{Cov}(A^+)\ge (1-e^{-1})\operatorname{Cov}(O_B).
   \]
   Thus allowing one extra membership gives the same approximation as the
   unit-cost greedy rule. Under the strict budget $B$, the better of the
   pre-overflow greedy set and the best single affordable membership gives at
   least
   \[
      \frac12(1-e^{-1})\operatorname{Cov}(O_B).
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Put $f=\operatorname{Cov}$. At a greedy set $A_t$, submodularity and
   monotonicity give
   \[
      f(O_B)-f(A_t)
      \le
      f(A_t\cup O_B)-f(A_t)
      \le
      \sum_{e\in O_B}\bigl(f(A_t\cup\{e\})-f(A_t)\bigr).
   \]
   If the greedy procedure stops because no positive marginal gain remains,
   then every superset has the same coverage value, so the current set is
   optimal. Assume from now on that the first overflow step exists.

   Since $c(O_B)\le B$, some membership in $O_B$ has marginal density at least
   $(f(O_B)-f(A_t))/B$. The greedy membership $e_t$ has at least this density,
   so, writing $a_t=c_{e_t}$,
   \[
      f(O_B)-f(A_{t+1})
      \le
      \left(1-\frac{a_t}{B}\right)(f(O_B)-f(A_t))
      \le
      e^{-a_t/B}(f(O_B)-f(A_t)).
   \]
   Iterating until the first overflow gives
   \[
      f(A^+)\ge
      \left(1-\exp(-c(A^+)/B)\right)f(O_B)
      \ge
      (1-e^{-1})f(O_B).
   \]

   For the strict-budget statement, let $A$ be the pre-overflow set and let $e$
   be the overflowing membership. The one-element set $\{e\}$ is affordable
   because memberships of cost larger than $B$ may be discarded. By
   submodularity, the marginal contribution of $e$ after $A$ is at most
   $f(\{e\})$. Hence
   \[
      f(A^+)\le f(A)+f(\{e\}),
   \]
   so one of $A$ and $\{e\}$ achieves at least half of the one-extra-element
   value.
\end{proof}

This is a sharper diagnostic than a centroid-distance margin rule: an extra
membership only receives credit for near pairs that are still missed by the
current redundancy pattern.  For the recursive proof, however, a uniform
top-$a$ overlap is often the cleaner default.  It gives an exact storage
budget, regular memory layout, and a simple boundary-redundancy knob.  The
greedy lemma is useful when reallocating a fixed candidate pool, but the
quantity it optimizes should be read as an audit of uncovered near-pair
coverage, not as a reason to trust Lloyd's objective.

If one nevertheless pursues an additive ball cover, the theory suggests a
``power-cover Lloyd'' iteration that alternates this coverage or power-cost
assignment step with a center update reducing certified radii and inflated
stabbing.  The update is closer to a one-center or quantile-radius objective
than to the Euclidean mean.  Its assignment score for adding point $x$ to
filter $i$ is the marginal uncovered near-pair weight divided by the marginal
storage and stabbing power
\[
   \Delta_i(x)
   =
   (|P_i|+1)^{1+\rho}
   \Psi\!\left(\max\{R_i,\|x-o_i\|\}\right)
   -
   |P_i|^{1+\rho}\Psi(R_i),
\]
with analogous query-side power penalties when sampled queries already stab
many filters.  The radius term explains what ordinary $k$-means misses: a point
whose inclusion expands a certified ball should be peeled or replicated rather
than allowed to enlarge the query region of an entire cluster.  But this
additive-ball objective is not the preferred final target.  In concentrated
high-dimensional nodes the inflated regions $B(o_i,R_i+r)$ may blanket almost
all plausible queries, and then \cref{lem:balanced-fanout-obstruction} predicts
non-contraction no matter how the memberships are reallocated.  The selective
replacement is the score-filter formulation below.

Concretely, one implementation target is the following certified-cover
analogue of Lloyd iteration.
\begin{enumerate}
   \item Maintain a candidate family of balls $(o_i,R_i)$, initialized for
   example by $k$-means, farthest-point centers, or cap/medoid proposals.
   \item Given the current balls and a sampled near-pair set $\mathcal E$, add
   point--filter memberships by density greedy, using marginal uncovered
   near-pair weight divided by marginal power cost
   \[
      \Delta_i^{\rm store}(x)
      +
      \gamma\,\Delta_i^{\rm stab}(x),
   \]
   where $\Delta_i^{\rm store}$ is the storage increment above and
   $\Delta_i^{\rm stab}$ is the corresponding increase in sampled inflated-ball
   stabbing load.
   \item Recompute each center by minimizing a certified radius or a high
   quantile radius of its assigned points, with outliers allowed to peel into
   singleton or overlapping filters rather than forcing the whole ball to
   expand.
   \item At query time, list the inflated balls containing $q$, but execute the
   cover branch only when the listed power-stabbing sum is below the certified
   cap; otherwise fall back to the baseline score-and-ball node.
\end{enumerate}
Unlike a centroid-margin rule, this objective gives no reward for replicating a
point whose near pairs are already covered. Unlike ordinary $k$-means, it
penalizes the two quantities that enter the recursive proof: the radius
inflation caused by assignments and the number of expensive filters stabbed by
a query. The capped query rule keeps the construction safe as a heuristic
accelerator even before the uniform power-cover theorem is proved.
\Cref{prop:power-cover-polylog} is the exact theorem an additive cover would
have to instantiate. It avoids the branching score-frontier obstruction of
\cref{asm:mixed-continuation-operator}; the missing content is instead a
worst-case decodable cover theorem for the inflated-ball power-stabbing
objective. \Cref{lem:balanced-fanout-obstruction} explains why this is not
ordinary balanced $k$-means: a recursive proof cannot afford a query to stab
several comparable children. It needs either very low stabbing, highly skewed
almost-total splits, randomized thinning as in
\cref{lem:thin-cap-contraction}, or a more selective activation rule than an
inflated ball.

The same point suggests a more selective replacement for $k$-means than another
centroid objective.  The weakness of a certified ball cover is that correctness
forces the query to activate the whole inflated ball $B(o_i,R_i+r)$.  In a
concentrated high-dimensional node these inflated balls can blanket nearly all
plausible queries, so the active fanout is large even when the Voronoi
partition is useful in practice.  A cap filter separates the two roles: a ball
certifies the recursive radius, while a one-sided score inequality certifies
whether a near query must activate the filter.

\begin{lemma}[Cap-slack certified cover]\label{lem:cap-slack-cover}
   Let each filter be specified by
   \[
      (P_i,o_i,R_i,u_i,\theta_i),
      \qquad \|u_i\|=1,
   \]
   with
   \[
      P_i\subseteq \Ball(o_i,R_i)
      \cap \{x:\langle u_i,x\rangle\ge \theta_i\},
      \qquad \bigcup_iP_i=P .
   \]
   On query $q$, list every filter satisfying
   \[
      \langle u_i,q\rangle\ge \theta_i-r .
   \]
   If the listed filters obey
   \[
      \sum_{i:\langle u_i,q\rangle\ge\theta_i-r}
      |P_i|^\rho\Psi(R_i)\le L,
      \qquad
      \sum_i |P_i|^{1+\rho}\Psi(R_i)\le S_0,
   \]
   then the cover compiler of \cref{lem:certified-cover-compiler} applies with
   query work $O(L\polylog n)$ and storage $O(S_0\polylog n)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Let $\|p-q\|\le r$ and choose a filter $i$ with $p\in P_i$.  Since
   $\|u_i\|=1$,
   \[
      \langle u_i,q\rangle
      \ge
      \langle u_i,p\rangle-\|p-q\|
      \ge
      \theta_i-r .
   \]
   Hence the query lists a child containing the near point.  The ball
   certificate $P_i\subseteq\Ball(o_i,R_i)$ supplies the recursive radius
   parameter, and the displayed sums are exactly the active query and storage
   potentials.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Lipschitz-score filter compiler]\label{lem:lipschitz-score-cover}
   Let each filter be specified by a set $P_i$, a certified recursive ball
   $(o_i,R_i)$, a score function $\phi_i:\R^d\to\R$ with Lipschitz constant
   $L_i$, and a threshold $\theta_i$, with
   \[
      P_i\subseteq\Ball(o_i,R_i)\cap\{x:\phi_i(x)\ge\theta_i\},
      \qquad
      \bigcup_iP_i=P .
   \]
   On query $q$, list every filter satisfying
   \[
      \phi_i(q)\ge \theta_i-L_i r .
   \]
   If the listed filters obey
   \[
      \sum_{i:\phi_i(q)\ge\theta_i-L_i r}
      |P_i|^\rho\Psi(R_i)\le L,
      \qquad
      \sum_i |P_i|^{1+\rho}\Psi(R_i)\le S_0,
   \]
   then the cover compiler of \cref{lem:certified-cover-compiler} applies with
   query work $O(L\polylog n)$ and storage $O(S_0\polylog n)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Let $\|p-q\|\le r$ and choose a filter $i$ with $p\in P_i$.  Since
   $\phi_i$ is $L_i$-Lipschitz,
   \[
      \phi_i(q)\ge\phi_i(p)-L_i\|p-q\|\ge\theta_i-L_i r .
   \]
   Thus the query lists a certified child containing the near point.  The
   displayed sums are exactly the active query and storage potentials.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Threshold-tightened score filters]
   \label{lem:threshold-tightening}
   Let $(P_C,o_C,R_C,\phi,L,\theta)$ be a nonempty certified Lipschitz-score
   filter:
   \[
      P_C\subseteq\Ball(o_C,R_C)\cap\{x:\phi(x)\ge\theta\}.
   \]
   Define
   \[
      \theta^\star=\min_{x\in P_C}\phi(x).
   \]
   Replacing $\theta$ by $\theta^\star$ preserves certification and all
   near-pair routing guarantees for this child, keeps its storage weight
   unchanged, and can only decrease its activation predicate:
   \[
      \mathbf 1\{\phi(q)\ge\theta^\star-Lr\}
      \le
      \mathbf 1\{\phi(q)\ge\theta-Lr\}.
   \]
   Consequently, for a fixed finite point set and a fixed score function
   $\phi$, every nonempty retained score filter is dominated by one whose
   threshold is one of the data scores $\{\phi(x):x\in P\}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Since every point of $P_C$ has score at least $\theta$, we have
   $\theta^\star\ge\theta$, and the same point set remains certified.  If
   $p\in P_C$ and $\|p-q\|\le r$, then Lipschitzness gives
   \[
      \phi(q)\ge\phi(p)-Lr\ge\theta^\star-Lr,
   \]
   so tightening the threshold does not lose the query that must route to this
   child.  The point set and certified ball are unchanged, hence the storage
   weight is unchanged.  Because $\theta^\star\ge\theta$, the displayed
   activation inequality holds for every query.  The final claim follows by
   applying the construction to each retained nonempty child.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Radius-tightened score filters]
   \label{lem:radius-tightening}
   Let $(P_C,o_C,R_C,\phi,L,\theta)$ be a nonempty certified Lipschitz-score
   filter.  Define
   \[
      R_C^\star=\max_{x\in P_C}\|x-o_C\|.
   \]
   Replacing $R_C$ by $R_C^\star$ preserves certification and all near-pair
   routing guarantees for this child, leaves its activation predicate
   unchanged, and weakly decreases both active and storage weights:
   \[
      |P_C|^\rho\Psi(R_C^\star)\le |P_C|^\rho\Psi(R_C),
      \qquad
      |P_C|^{1+\rho}\Psi(R_C^\star)\le |P_C|^{1+\rho}\Psi(R_C).
   \]
   Consequently, for a fixed finite point set and a fixed center $o_C$, every
   nonempty retained score filter is dominated by one whose certified radius is
   one of the data distances $\{\|x-o_C\|:x\in P\}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Certification is immediate from the definition of $R_C^\star$:
   $P_C\subseteq\Ball(o_C,R_C^\star)$.  Since $R_C^\star\le R_C$, the radius
   factor $\Psi(R)=1+(R/r)^4$ cannot increase, proving the two displayed
   inequalities.  The score predicate and threshold are unchanged, so the query
   activation rule is unchanged.  Therefore every near query that previously
   activated this child still activates it, and the same point set is searched.
   The final claim follows by applying the construction to each retained
   nonempty child.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finite score-template closure]
   \label{lem:score-template-closure}
   Fix a finite resident set $P$ and a finite family of score-ball templates
   \[
      \mathcal T=\{(o_t,R_t,\phi_t,L_t):t\in T\}.
   \]
   For every template $t$ and every data point $z\in P$, form the parent
   proposal
   \[
      C_{t,z}
      =
      P\cap\Ball(o_t,R_t)\cap
      \{x:\phi_t(x)\ge\phi_t(z)\},
   \]
   with activation predicate
   \[
      a_{t,z}(q)=
      \mathbf 1\{\phi_t(q)\ge\phi_t(z)-L_t r\}.
   \]
   Then every nonempty certified Lipschitz-score child using a template in
   $\mathcal T$ is, after threshold tightening, a certified subchild of one of
   the finitely many parents $C_{t,z}$ and inherits that parent's activation
   predicate.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Let $D$ be a nonempty child using template
   $t=(o_t,R_t,\phi_t,L_t)$:
   \[
      P_D\subseteq
      P\cap\Ball(o_t,R_t)\cap\{x:\phi_t(x)\ge\theta\}.
   \]
   By \cref{lem:threshold-tightening}, we may replace $\theta$ by
   \[
      \theta^\star=\min_{x\in P_D}\phi_t(x).
   \]
   Choose $z\in P_D$ attaining this minimum.  Then
   $\theta^\star=\phi_t(z)$ and
   \[
      P_D\subseteq C_{t,z}.
   \]
   The tightened child and the parent $C_{t,z}$ have the same activation
   predicate
   $\mathbf 1\{\phi_t(q)\ge\phi_t(z)-L_t r\}$ and the same certified radius
   $R_t$.  Since certification is hereditary under taking subsets, $D$ is a
   certified subchild of $C_{t,z}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finite center-score closure]
   \label{lem:center-score-closure}
   Fix a finite resident set $P$ and a finite family of center-score templates
   \[
      \mathcal H=\{(o_h,\phi_h,L_h):h\in H\}.
   \]
   For every template $h$ and every pair of data points $y,z\in P$, form the
   parent proposal
   \[
      C_{h,y,z}
      =
      P\cap\Ball(o_h,\|y-o_h\|)
      \cap\{x:\phi_h(x)\ge\phi_h(z)\},
   \]
   with certified radius $\|y-o_h\|$ and activation predicate
   \[
      a_{h,y,z}(q)=
      \mathbf 1\{\phi_h(q)\ge\phi_h(z)-L_h r\}.
   \]
   Then every nonempty certified Lipschitz-score child using a center-score
   template in $\mathcal H$ is, after threshold and radius tightening, a
   certified subchild of one of the finitely many parents $C_{h,y,z}$ and
   inherits that parent's activation predicate and certified radius.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Let $D$ be a nonempty child using template $(o_h,\phi_h,L_h)$, threshold
   $\theta$, and certified radius $R$.  Apply
   \cref{lem:threshold-tightening} and \cref{lem:radius-tightening}.  Choose
   $z\in P_D$ attaining the minimum score and $y\in P_D$ attaining the maximum
   distance from $o_h$.  The tightened child has threshold $\phi_h(z)$, radius
   $\|y-o_h\|$, and activation predicate $a_{h,y,z}$.  Its point set satisfies
   \[
      P_D\subseteq
      P\cap\Ball(o_h,\|y-o_h\|)
      \cap\{x:\phi_h(x)\ge\phi_h(z)\}
      =
      C_{h,y,z}.
   \]
   Certification is hereditary under taking subsets, so $D$ is a certified
   subchild of this parent.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Shell-normalized cap cover]\label{lem:shell-normalized-cap-cover}
   Fix a center $o$ and a lower shell radius $\sigma>0$.  For
   $\|x-o\|\ge\sigma$, write
   \[
      \widehat x_o=\frac{x-o}{\|x-o\|}.
   \]
   Suppose each filter has a certified recursive ball $(P_i,o_i,R_i)$,
   a unit direction $u_i$, and a threshold $\theta_i$, with
   \[
      P_i\subseteq \Ball(o_i,R_i)
      \cap
      \{x:\|x-o\|\ge\sigma,\ \langle u_i,\widehat x_o\rangle\ge\theta_i\},
      \qquad
      \bigcup_iP_i=P .
   \]
   For a query $q$ with $\|q-o\|\ge\sigma$, list every filter satisfying
   \[
      \langle u_i,\widehat q_o\rangle
      \ge
      \theta_i-\frac{2r}{\sigma}.
   \]
   If the listed filters obey
   \[
      \sum_{i:\langle u_i,\widehat q_o\rangle\ge\theta_i-2r/\sigma}
      |P_i|^\rho\Psi(R_i)\le L,
      \qquad
      \sum_i |P_i|^{1+\rho}\Psi(R_i)\le S_0,
   \]
   then the cover compiler of \cref{lem:certified-cover-compiler} applies with
   query work $O(L\polylog n)$ and storage $O(S_0\polylog n)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   For points outside $\Ball(o,\sigma)$, the normalization map is
   $2/\sigma$-Lipschitz:
   \[
      \left\|
      \frac{x-o}{\|x-o\|}
      -
      \frac{q-o}{\|q-o\|}
      \right\|
      \le
      \frac{2\|x-q\|}{\sigma}.
   \]
   Hence, if $p\in P_i$ and $\|p-q\|\le r$, then
   \[
      \langle u_i,\widehat q_o\rangle
      \ge
      \langle u_i,\widehat p_o\rangle-\frac{2r}{\sigma}
      \ge
      \theta_i-\frac{2r}{\sigma}.
   \]
   Thus the query lists a certified child containing the near point, and the
   work and storage accounting is the same as in
   \cref{lem:certified-cover-compiler}.
\end{proof}

These score-cover lemmas contain both certified ball covers and cap covers.  Taking
$\phi_i(x)=-\|x-o_i\|$ and $\theta_i=-R_i$ gives the ordinary inflated-ball
rule $\|q-o_i\|\le R_i+r$, which is the worst-case-safe interpretation of a
$k$-means cell.  Taking $\phi_i(x)=\langle u_i,x\rangle$ gives
\cref{lem:cap-slack-cover}.  \Cref{lem:shell-normalized-cap-cover} gives the
formal version of the empirical observation that, after local centering and
shelling, Euclidean $k$-means behaves much like an angular quantizer: if the
norms are nearly constant, nearest-center ranking differs from ranking by
linear or normalized-cap scores only by lower-order radial terms.  Thus
$k$-means can initialize the directions, but the certificate should be stated
for overlapping cap or Lipschitz-score filters.
\Cref{lem:threshold-tightening} removes a nuisance continuum from this model:
once a score function and retained point set are fixed, the best safe threshold
is the minimum retained score, so a finite data set contributes only finitely
many threshold choices per score.  \Cref{lem:radius-tightening} does the same
for the certified radius, because score-filter activation is independent of the
radius certificate.  Thus \cref{lem:center-score-closure} is the cleanest
finite closure: a seeded build routine only has to propose center-score
templates; all data-score thresholds, data-distance radii, and retained
subchildren are then generated by finite closure and handled by the existing
atom-safe prefix machinery.

The theory-native alternative to $k$-means is therefore not a different
centroid objective alone.  It is a fixed-overlap score-filter tree: learn
directions or Lipschitz scores whose active sets are selective, store each
point in its top $a$ filters, and recurse only through filters passing the
slack certificate.  Redundancy amplifies a good partition, but it cannot
replace selectivity; the active-power cap is the proof-side test of whether the
learned router is useful at a node.

Thus a theory-native practical alternative is a cap-power or score-power
iteration rather than ordinary Lloyd iteration.  Its simplest filters are
spherical caps after local centering, shell normalization, or whitening, but
\cref{lem:lipschitz-score-cover} also allows learned or anisotropic Lipschitz
scores.  The default assignment is fixed top-$a$ membership by score, with the
threshold $\theta_i$ set to the worst retained score or to a certified peeled
quantile.  If additional adaptive memberships are allowed, they should be
chosen by uncovered near-pair value divided by the marginal increase in
\[
   |P_i|^{1+\rho}\Psi(R_i)
   \quad\text{and}\quad
   \sum_{\text{sampled }q:
      \phi_i(q)\ge\theta_i-L_i r}
      |P_i|^\rho\Psi(R_i),
\]
while the update step should move the score parameters and the certified ball
$(o_i,R_i)$ to reduce query stabbing and child radius.  This objective can beat
plain $k$-means on instances where directional or learned scores are selective
but inflated balls are not: the query probes filters aligned with its score
direction, instead of every cluster whose enclosing ball lies within additive
distance $r$.

A concrete version is the balanced cap-power filter.  In a localized node,
first center, shell, and optionally whiten the data.  Choose directions
$u_1,\ldots,u_K$ and offsets $\theta_i$ so that the retained normalized caps
\[
   P_i=\{x\in P:\langle u_i,\widehat x_o\rangle\ge\theta_i\}
\]
have controlled masses, then attach to each retained cap its certified
recursive ball $(o_i,R_i)$.  A point may be stored in several caps; the
regular default is its top-$a$ caps, with optional greedy additions only when
they buy uncovered near-pair value per marginal storage and stabbing power.
A query lists the caps with
\[
   \langle u_i,\widehat q_o\rangle\ge\theta_i-\frac{2r}{\sigma}
\]
where $\sigma$ is the lower shell radius, or, in the more general Lipschitz case,
$\phi_i(q)\ge\theta_i-L_i r$.  The offsets play the balancing role that
$k$-means cell sizes play in practice, while the cap scores supply the
selectivity that inflated balls lose on concentrated high-dimensional data.
Flat scoring against all $K$ filters can be replaced by a recursive spherical
tree or product-code decoder; the certificate above only concerns the filters
that the decoder actually lists.  Thus ordinary $k$-means becomes an
initializer or fallback, while the proof-aligned object is a balanced
overlapping score cover whose measured quantity is active power, not squared
reconstruction error.

For training such a cover on sampled queries or sampled near pairs, the natural
loss is therefore the empirical active-power loss
\[
   \mathcal L_{\rm act}
   =
   \operatorname*{Quantile}_{q\in\mathcal Q}
   \sum_{i:\phi_i(q)\ge \theta_i-L_i r}
   |P_i|^\rho\Psi(R_i),
\]
together with the storage penalty
\[
   \mathcal L_{\rm store}
   =
   \sum_i |P_i|^{1+\rho}\Psi(R_i)
\]
and a penalty for sampled near pairs that are not covered by an activated
membership.  The quantile can be replaced by a maximum for a worst-query
certificate, or by a high quantile for a practical router with a capped
fallback.  A Lloyd-like implementation would alternate between balancing the
offsets, assigning fixed top-$a$ memberships by score, adding any extra
memberships by the greedy near-pair-cover rule of
\cref{lem:cost-sensitive-near-pair-cover}, and updating the score parameters to
decrease $\mathcal L_{\rm act}+\lambda\mathcal L_{\rm store}$ while recomputing
the certified radii.  Plain $k$-means is the special case that uses the wrong
surrogate loss, namely average squared reconstruction error; the score-power
variant trains directly against the quantity that controls recursive query
work.

The easiest part of this program to make self-contained is the seeding step.
Instead of running Lloyd updates, use a $k$-means++-style residual sampler to
propose cap directions, and then certify every proposed cap by scanning the
node.

\begin{lemma}[Residual cap seeding]\label{lem:residual-cap-seeding}
   Work in one shell around $o$ and write
   $\widehat x_o=(x-o)/\|x-o\|$.  Let $a_x\ge0$ be arbitrary residual weights
   on the current resident set, let $a(P)=\sum_{x\in P}a_x>0$, and sample
   $T$ independent candidate directions by drawing $X_t\in P$ with probability
   $a_x/a(P)$ and setting $u_t=\widehat X_{t,o}$.  Suppose a set
   $A\subseteq P$ satisfies
   \[
      \sum_{x\in A}a_x\ge \alpha a(P)
   \]
   and has shell-normalized diameter at most $\eta$,
   \[
      \|\widehat x_o-\widehat y_o\|\le\eta
      \qquad\text{for all }x,y\in A .
   \]
   Then, with probability at least $1-e^{-\alpha T}$, one sampled direction
   $u_t$ satisfies
   \[
      A\subseteq
      \left\{
         y\in P:\langle u_t,\widehat y_o\rangle\ge1-\frac{\eta^2}{2}
      \right\}.
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Each sample lands in $A$ with probability at least $\alpha$, so the
   probability that no sample lands in $A$ is at most
   $(1-\alpha)^T\le e^{-\alpha T}$.  If $X_t\in A$, then for every $y\in A$,
   \[
      \langle \widehat X_{t,o},\widehat y_o\rangle
      =
      1-\frac12\|\widehat X_{t,o}-\widehat y_o\|^2
      \ge
      1-\frac{\eta^2}{2},
   \]
   which is the displayed cap containment.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Spherical \(D^2\) residual seeding]
   \label{cor:spherical-d2-seeding}
   Work in the same shell and let $U\subseteq P$ be the current uncovered
   residual set.  Given existing candidate directions $V$, define
   \[
      \Delta_V(x)=
      \begin{cases}
         1, & V=\emptyset,\\
         \min_{v\in V}\|\widehat x_o-v\|^2, & V\ne\emptyset,
      \end{cases}
   \]
   and assume $\Delta_V(U)=\sum_{x\in U}\Delta_V(x)>0$.  Draw $T$ independent
   seeds from $U$ with probability proportional to $\Delta_V(x)$.  If
   $A\subseteq U$ satisfies
   \[
      \sum_{x\in A}\Delta_V(x)\ge\alpha\,\Delta_V(U)
   \]
   and has shell-normalized diameter at most $\eta$, then with probability at
   least $1-e^{-\alpha T}$ one sampled direction $u_t$ satisfies
   \[
      A\subseteq
      \left\{
         y\in P:\langle u_t,\widehat y_o\rangle\ge1-\frac{\eta^2}{2}
      \right\}.
   \]
   Moreover, after adding such a seed to $V$, the residual squared distance of
   every $y\in A$ is at most $\eta^2$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Apply \cref{lem:residual-cap-seeding} with residual weights
   $a_x=\Delta_V(x)$ on $U$.  The final claim follows because, if the seed
   lies in $A$, then every $y\in A$ has
   \[
      \min_{v\in V\cup\{u_t\}}\|\widehat y_o-v\|^2
      \le
      \|\widehat y_o-u_t\|^2
      \le \eta^2 .
   \]
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Dual-weighted cap seeding]\label{cor:dual-weighted-cap-seeding}
   Fix point prices $\alpha_x\in[0,1]$, pattern prices $\lambda_a\ge0$, and a
   storage price $\sigma\ge0$, with $\sum_{x\in P}\alpha_x>0$.  Draw seed
   directions from $P$ with probability proportional to $\alpha_x$, and suppose
   a set $A\subseteq P$ has price mass
   \[
      \alpha(A):=\sum_{x\in A}\alpha_x
      \ge \theta\sum_{x\in P}\alpha_x .
   \]
   Assume that every seed $x\in A$ generates an accepted certified parent
   proposal $C_x$ containing $A$.  If, for each such proposal, $k=|A|$ is
   atom-safe and
   \[
      \alpha(A)>
      \Psi(R_{C_x})
      \left(
         \sigma k^{1+\rho}
         +
         k^\rho\sum_a\lambda_a a_{C_x}
      \right),
   \]
   then $T$ independent dual-weighted samples find a positive-gain atom-safe
   subchild with probability at least $1-e^{-\theta T}$.  Exhaustive
   enumeration of all data directions finds one deterministically.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   With probability at least $1-e^{-\theta T}$, one sampled seed lies in $A$.
   For that accepted parent $C_x$, the top-$k$ prefix by point price has price
   at least $\alpha(A)$ because $A\subseteq P_{C_x}$ and $|A|=k$.  The displayed
   inequality is therefore exactly the positive-gain condition in
   \cref{cor:price-density-subchild}.  Exhaustive enumeration includes every
   seed in $A$, so it cannot miss the same certificate.
\end{proof}

Taking $a_x$ to be the squared distance from $\widehat x_o$ to the current
candidate directions gives the spherical analogue of $k$-means++ seeding,
spelled out in \cref{cor:spherical-d2-seeding}.
Taking $a_x$ to be an uncovered near-pair or active-power residual gives the
score-power version.  Taking $a_x$ from the current dual point prices gives the
column-generation version in \cref{cor:dual-weighted-cap-seeding}.  These
statements are deliberately weaker than a Lloyd guarantee: they only say that
any cap carrying a noticeable fraction of the current residual or dual mass is
proposed after logarithmically many samples.  That is the property needed by the
certified-cover route, because the proposed cap is subsequently verified and
used only if its active-power certificate is good.  The remaining worst-case
theorem is therefore not a statement about the convergence of Lloyd's objective;
it is a statement that every tame node exposes enough residual or dual price
mass on certifiable low-stabbing caps, or else the guard or baseline score
process handles the query.

\begin{lemma}[Weak residual-cover compiler]\label{lem:weak-residual-cover}
   Let $P$ be finite with weights $a_x>0$, and let
   $a(U)=\sum_{x\in U}a_x$.  Consider the following abstract residual-cover
   procedure.  At round $t$, with uncovered set $U_t$, draw $T$ independent
   samples from $U_t$ with probabilities $a_x/a(U_t)$, generate the
   corresponding cap or score-filter proposals, and keep only the proposals
   accepted by a deterministic verifier.  Accepted proposals may cover any
   subsets of $U_t$, and covered points are removed before the next round.

   Suppose that for some $\alpha,\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ the following weak
   residual condition holds at every possible round: whenever
   $a(U_t)>\varepsilon a(P)$, there is a set $A_t\subseteq U_t$ with
   \[
      a(A_t)\ge\alpha a(U_t)
   \]
   such that every sample $x\in A_t$ generates an accepted proposal covering
   all of $A_t$.  If
   \[
      H\ge \alpha^{-1}\log\frac1\varepsilon,
      \qquad
      T\ge \alpha^{-1}\log\frac{H}{\delta},
   \]
   then after $H$ rounds the uncovered mass is at most
   $\varepsilon a(P)$ with probability at least $1-\delta$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Fix a round with $a(U_t)>\varepsilon a(P)$.  By the weak residual
   condition, one draw lands in $A_t$ with probability at least $\alpha$.
   Hence the probability that none of the $T$ samples lands in $A_t$ is at most
   \[
      (1-\alpha)^T\le e^{-\alpha T}\le\frac{\delta}{H}.
   \]
   On the complementary event, the verifier accepts a proposal covering all of
   $A_t$, so
   \[
      a(U_{t+1})\le a(U_t)-a(A_t)\le(1-\alpha)a(U_t).
   \]
   A union bound over the $H$ rounds shows that, with probability at least
   $1-\delta$, every nonterminal round decreases residual mass by this factor.
   Therefore either the process has already reached
   $a(U_t)\le\varepsilon a(P)$, or after $H$ successful rounds
   \[
      a(U_H)\le(1-\alpha)^H a(P)
      \le e^{-\alpha H}a(P)
      \le \varepsilon a(P).
   \]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Exhaustive residual-cover compiler]\label{lem:exhaustive-residual-cover}
   In the setting of \cref{lem:weak-residual-cover}, replace the $T$ random
   samples at each round by the exhaustive finite candidate pool generated by
   every point $x\in U_t$.  Under the same weak residual condition, after
   \[
      H\ge \alpha^{-1}\log\frac1\varepsilon
   \]
   rounds the uncovered mass is deterministically at most
   $\varepsilon a(P)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   If $a(U_t)\le\varepsilon a(P)$ there is nothing to prove.  Otherwise the
   weak residual condition gives a set $A_t\subseteq U_t$ with
   $a(A_t)\ge\alpha a(U_t)$ such that every sample point in $A_t$ generates an
   accepted proposal covering $A_t$.  Exhaustive enumeration includes all
   points of $A_t$, hence at least one accepted proposal covering $A_t$ is
   available.  Keeping such a proposal gives
   \[
      a(U_{t+1})\le a(U_t)-a(A_t)\le(1-\alpha)a(U_t).
   \]
   Iterating for $H$ rounds yields
   $a(U_H)\le e^{-\alpha H}a(P)\le\varepsilon a(P)$ unless the process stopped
   earlier.
\end{proof}

Combining \cref{lem:residual-cap-seeding} with
\cref{lem:weak-residual-cover} gives the precise analyzable replacement for
Lloyd iterations.  If every residual with nonnegligible mass contains an
$\alpha$-heavy low-diameter cap whose verified filter has acceptable radius,
storage increment, and marginal active-power increment, then residual sampling
constructs the local cover after
\[
   O\!\left(
      \alpha^{-2}\log\frac1\varepsilon
      \log\frac{\alpha^{-1}\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\delta}
   \right)
\]
verified proposals.  Thus inverse-polylogarithmic weak cap mass gives only
polylogarithmic preprocessing overhead.  The real geometric statement needed
for \cref{asm:power-cover} is now sharper: prove this weak residual condition
for the active-power verifier, not convergence of the Lloyd objective.
\Cref{lem:exhaustive-residual-cover} gives the build-time-heavy variant: the
same weak condition can be certified over the finite pool of all residual data
directions, with no sampling failure and no dependence on Lloyd dynamics.

The same viewpoint separates build time from the theorem's two scarce
resources, index space and query time.  A proposal may be expensive to find and
expensive to certify; if it is not stored, it contributes nothing to either
resource.
In the offline cover route below, preprocessing time is therefore not a
complexity parameter.  It may be superpolynomial in the local node size, may
solve exact integer or fractional programs, and may try many randomized or
learned proposal generators.  The stated ANN bounds count only the certified
children, residual scans, and decoder operations that remain in the final
index.

\begin{lemma}[Offline proposal amplification]\label{lem:offline-amplification}
   Fix deterministic predicates $\mathcal P(L,S)$ certifying that a stored
   cover is routing-correct, has active query power at most $L$ for every
   query in the promised node, and has storage power at most $S$.  Suppose a
   randomized preprocessing routine outputs such a certified cover with
   probability at least $p$, and otherwise either rejects or outputs a cover
   that fails the certificate and is discarded.  After $B$ independent offline
   attempts, keeping the first certified cover succeeds with probability at
   least
   \[
      1-(1-p)^B .
   \]
   Conditional on success, the query and storage bounds are exactly those of
   the single retained certified cover; rejected proposals and failed attempts
   do not affect the index.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The probability that all $B$ independent attempts fail to produce a certified
   cover is at most $(1-p)^B$.  On the complementary event, the data structure
   stores one cover satisfying $\mathcal P(L,S)$.  Query time and storage are
   functions only of this retained cover and its certificate, not of the
   discarded build-time proposals.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Las Vegas offline certification]\label{lem:las-vegas-offline}
   In the setting of \cref{lem:offline-amplification}, suppose the randomized
   preprocessing routine outputs a certified cover with some probability
   $p>0$, and every uncertified output is rejected by the deterministic
   certificate.  If preprocessing time is not charged, the build stage may run
   the routine until the first certified cover appears and then store only that
   cover.  The retained query and storage bounds are exactly the certified
   bounds of one accepted cover, independent of how small $p$ is.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The probability that no certified cover appears in the first $B$ independent
   attempts is $(1-p)^B$, which tends to zero as $B\to\infty$.  Thus the
   repeat-until-certified procedure terminates with probability one, and has
   expected number of attempts $1/p$.  All attempts made before termination are
   discarded preprocessing artifacts.  The final index contains only the first
   accepted certified cover, so its query work and storage are exactly those
   certified for that retained cover.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finite-pool offline optimizer]\label{lem:finite-pool-optimizer}
   Fix a finite proposal pool of certified Lipschitz score filters
   \[
      \mathcal F=\{(M_i,o_i,R_i,\phi_i,\theta_i,L_i):i\in I\},
   \]
   where
   \[
      M_i\subseteq
      P\cap\Ball(o_i,R_i)\cap\{x:\phi_i(x)\ge\theta_i\}
   \]
   is the admissible membership set of filter $i$.  Also fix a deterministic
   verifier which, given a residual block $U_0$ and selected memberships
   $P_i\subseteq M_i$, accepts only if the selected filters cover
   $P\setminus U_0$, the residual size bound holds, and the active query-power
   and storage-power certificates required by \cref{asm:weak-offline-score-cover}
   hold.

   If some choice of $U_0$ and memberships from the pool is accepted by this
   verifier, then unbounded preprocessing can find an accepted choice by
   exhaustive search, or equivalently by an exact finite integer optimization
   over the membership variables.  The query time and index space are those of
   the accepted stored cover only; the size of $\mathcal F$ and the cost of the
   search are preprocessing costs.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The pool is finite, and each point-filter membership is either selected or
   not selected.  Therefore the number of possible residual blocks and selected
   membership patterns is finite.  Exhaustive preprocessing enumerates them,
   runs the deterministic verifier, and keeps the first accepted pattern.  If an
   accepted pattern exists, the enumeration eventually finds one.  Once the
   index is built, the discarded proposals and rejected membership patterns are
   absent from the data structure, so they do not contribute to query work or
   storage.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Offline Pareto compression]\label{cor:offline-pareto-compression}
   In the setting of \cref{lem:finite-pool-optimizer}, suppose the verifier
   also reports the residual size, the active-power vector on the finite
   query-pattern certificate, and the storage power of every accepted retained
   family.  If at least one retained family is accepted, then unbounded
   preprocessing can choose an accepted family minimizing any prescribed
   function of these reported quantities.  In particular, for fixed residual
   and active-power budgets it can choose a minimum-storage accepted cover, or
   for fixed residual and storage budgets it can choose a cover minimizing the
   worst certified active power.

   The proposal pool, failed randomized attempts, rejected children, and the
   search over retained subfamilies are not stored in the final data structure.
   Only the chosen certified family contributes to index space and query time.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   The set of possible retained families and residual blocks is finite.  Run
   the deterministic verifier on every possibility, discard all rejected
   possibilities, and optimize the prescribed objective over the remaining
   finite set.  The final index contains only the selected retained family and
   its decoder.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Offline center-score saturation]
   \label{cor:offline-center-score-saturation}
   Fix a node with resident set $P$ and a finite family of center-score
   templates
   \[
      \mathcal H=\{(o_h,\phi_h,L_h):h\in H\}.
   \]
   Let $\mathcal F(\mathcal H)$ be the finite parent pool obtained by
   \cref{lem:center-score-closure}: for every $h\in H$ and every pair
   $y,z\in P$, include the data-radius, data-threshold parent
   \[
      P\cap\Ball(o_h,\|y-o_h\|)
      \cap\{x:\phi_h(x)\ge\phi_h(z)\}
   \]
   with activation predicate
   $\phi_h(q)\ge\phi_h(z)-L_hr$.  Suppose a deterministic verifier accepts
   some residual block and some certified score-cover whose children use
   templates from $\mathcal H$.

   Then unbounded preprocessing can find an accepted cover using only parents
   from $\mathcal F(\mathcal H)$ and arbitrary retained submemberships of these
   parents, and can choose among all such accepted covers one minimizing any
   prescribed function of the certified residual size, active-power vector, and
   storage power.  If $\mathcal H$ is itself produced by a randomized or learned
   build routine with positive probability of admitting an accepted cover, the
   build stage may repeat the routine until the verifier accepts.  Query time
   and index space are those of the final chosen cover only.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Apply \cref{lem:threshold-tightening} and \cref{lem:radius-tightening} to
   every nonempty child of the accepted score-cover.  By
   \cref{lem:center-score-closure}, each tightened child is a certified
   subchild of some parent in $\mathcal F(\mathcal H)$ and inherits that
   parent's activation predicate and certified radius.  Thus the accepted cover
   can be represented as a residual block together with selected memberships
   inside the finite parent pool $\mathcal F(\mathcal H)$.
   \Cref{lem:finite-pool-optimizer} finds some accepted representation by
   exhaustive preprocessing, and \cref{cor:offline-pareto-compression} chooses
   an accepted representation on the desired certified query-memory frontier.
   If the template family is generated randomly with positive success
   probability, \cref{lem:las-vegas-offline} repeats generation until an
   accepted family is found.  All unsuccessful template families, rejected
   memberships, and nonselected parents are preprocessing artifacts and are not
   stored.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Offline recursive Pareto pricing]
   \label{cor:offline-recursive-pareto-pricing}
   Fix a finite proposal universe at a node.  For each proposed child $C$, let
   $\mathcal P_C$ be a finite list of certified descendant indexes for $P_C$,
   with price pairs $(Q_{C,\pi},S_{C,\pi})$ and decoders
   $\pi\in\mathcal P_C$.  Form the expanded finite universe whose columns are
   pairs $(C,\pi)$, inheriting the membership set and activation predicate of
   $C$ but carrying the prices $(Q_{C,\pi},S_{C,\pi})$.

   If some residual block and some retained subfamily of this expanded universe
   pass the priced cover certificate of \cref{lem:priced-cover-compiler}, then
   unbounded preprocessing can find such a retained subfamily and choose one on
   any prescribed certified query-storage Pareto frontier.  Applying this
   bottom-up over any finite acyclic recursive candidate universe computes the
   exact retained-index Pareto frontier for that universe.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   The expanded universe is finite.  A deterministic verifier checks residual
   routing, the finite activation-pattern form of the priced query constraint
   \[
      \sup_q\sum_{(C,\pi)}a_C(q)Q_{C,\pi},
   \]
   and the storage constraint $\sum_{(C,\pi)}S_{C,\pi}$.  Exhaustive
   preprocessing enumerates retained subfamilies and residual blocks, rejects
   those that fail, and optimizes the requested objective over the accepted
   finite set, exactly as in \cref{cor:offline-pareto-compression}.  For a
   finite acyclic recursive universe, process nodes in reverse topological
   order: terminal nodes provide their certified base price lists, and each
   internal node is handled by the finite expansion above using already
   computed child price lists.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Seed--saturate--certify compiler]
   \label{cor:seed-saturate-certify}
   Fix one node and a finite seed space $\mathcal S$.  Each seed
   $s\in\mathcal S$ generates a finite family of center-score templates
   \(\mathcal H(s)\).  Let $\mathcal B$ be any finite search class of seed
   multisets, and for $B\in\mathcal B$ write
   \[
      \mathcal H_B=\bigcup_{s\in B}\mathcal H(s).
   \]
   From $\mathcal H_B$, form the saturated finite universe obtained by closing
   under all data thresholds and data radii as in
   \cref{cor:offline-center-score-saturation}, optionally intersecting with a
   low-guard shadow, expanding to retained submemberships or atom-safe exposed
   prefixes, and attaching any finite certified descendant price lists as in
   \cref{cor:offline-recursive-pareto-pricing}.  Suppose a deterministic
   verifier accepts some residual block and retained subfamily from one of
   these saturated universes, using either the priced all-listing certificate of
   \cref{lem:priced-cover-compiler} or the sampled-route certificate of
   \cref{lem:sampled-priced-cover} together with
   \cref{lem:finite-sampled-route-verifier}.

   Then unbounded preprocessing can find an accepted retained family and choose
   one minimizing any prescribed certified query-storage objective reported by
   the verifier.  The query work and index space are those of the chosen
   retained family, its residual block, decoder metadata, and descendant
   indexes only; seed families, saturated parent pools, rejected memberships,
   failed sampled-route signatures, and nonselected descendant indexes are
   preprocessing artifacts.

   If instead a randomized seeding routine outputs an acceptable seed multiset
   with positive probability and every unacceptable retained family is rejected
   by the deterministic verifier, preprocessing may repeat the seeding routine
   until certification and again stores only the first accepted retained family.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   The set $\mathcal B$ is finite, and for each $B\in\mathcal B$ all closures
   described in the statement are finite because the resident point set and the
   supplied descendant price lists are finite.  For any fixed $B$,
   \cref{cor:offline-center-score-saturation} reduces the continuous threshold
   and radius choices to the saturated finite center-score universe, while
   \cref{cor:offline-recursive-pareto-pricing} expands each child by its finite
   certified descendant price options.  The finite-pool optimizer and Pareto
   compression, \cref{lem:finite-pool-optimizer} and
   \cref{cor:offline-pareto-compression}, may therefore enumerate all residual
   blocks and retained subfamilies accepted by the deterministic verifier and
   choose the best reported one.  In the sampled case,
   \cref{lem:finite-sampled-route-verifier} is part of that deterministic
   acceptance test, so the stored sampler satisfies the hypotheses of
   \cref{lem:sampled-priced-cover}.  Since all rejected objects are discarded
   before queries are answered, they do not contribute to the retained
   resources.

   For randomized seeding, apply the Las Vegas certification principle of
   \cref{lem:las-vegas-offline}: repeated independent attempts eventually
   produce an acceptable seed multiset almost surely whenever the success
   probability is positive, and the final index contains only the first
   accepted certified family.
\end{proof}

By \cref{lem:guard-restricted-cover}, the finite verifier and the LPs below do
not need to impose active-power constraints on high-guard queries.  For a fixed
guard threshold $\gamma$, take $\mathcal Q$ to be a finite set of constraints
from the low-guard domain $\Omega_{\rm low}=\{q:g(q)<\gamma\}$, or take the
activation-pattern set only over this domain.  High-guard queries are handled
by the resident sample and receive no dual price.  This strictly narrows the
remaining separation theorem: a bad dual certificate prices only low-guard
queries, where no large set of already-valid resident answers is available.
By \cref{lem:low-guard-shadow}, the point side can be narrowed as well.  Let
\[
   E_\gamma=\{p\in P:\exists q\in\Omega_{\rm low},\ \|p-q\|\le r\}.
\]
The finite cover program may cover only $E_\gamma$ up to the residual block,
and the dual point prices $\alpha_x$ may be supported only on $E_\gamma$.
Resident points outside this shadow are solved, whenever they matter, by the
high-guard sample.  Thus the remaining separation theorem is a genuinely
low-density statement: it must defeat dual prices on points that can be near a
low-guard query, not on dense regions already certified by the guard.

\begin{lemma}[Finite-pool fractional dual]\label{lem:finite-pool-dual}
   Fix a finite set $\mathcal Q$ of query constraints and a finite proposal pool
   $\mathcal C$ of certified children.  A child $C\in\mathcal C$ consists of a
   point set $P_C\subseteq P$, a certified radius $R_C$, and an activation rule
   on $\mathcal Q$.  Write
   \[
      a_C(q)=\mathbf 1\{C\text{ is active at }q\},
      \qquad
      w_C=|P_C|^\rho\Psi(R_C),
      \qquad
      s_C=|P_C|^{1+\rho}\Psi(R_C).
   \]
   For budgets $L_q$, $S$, and $L_0$, consider the fractional cover value
   \[
   \begin{array}{ll}
   \text{\rm maximize} & \displaystyle \sum_{x\in P} v_x \\[0.4em]
   \text{\rm subject to}
      & \displaystyle
        v_x\le \sum_{C:x\in P_C} z_C
        \qquad (x\in P),\\[0.8em]
      & 0\le v_x\le1,\qquad z_C\ge0,\\[0.4em]
      & \displaystyle
        \sum_C a_C(q)w_Cz_C\le L_q
        \qquad (q\in\mathcal Q),\\[0.8em]
      & \displaystyle
        \sum_C s_Cz_C\le S .
   \end{array}
   \tag{$\mathsf{P}_{\mathcal Q}$}
   \]
   If $\mathsf{P}_{\mathcal Q}$ has value $< |P|-L_0$, then there exist
   point prices $\alpha_x\in[0,1]$, query prices $\lambda_q\ge0$, and a storage
   price $\sigma\ge0$ such that
   \[
      \sum_{x\in P}\alpha_x
      >
      L_0+\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\lambda_qL_q+\sigma S,
      \tag{D1}
   \]
   while every proposal satisfies
   \[
      \sum_{x\in P_C}\alpha_x
      \le
      \sigma s_C+
      w_C\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q} \lambda_q a_C(q).
      \tag{D2}
   \]
   Conversely, if such prices do not exist, then the fractional pool contains a
   cover of value at least $|P|-L_0$ under the displayed query and storage
   budgets.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The dual of $\mathsf{P}_{\mathcal Q}$ has variables $\alpha_x\ge0$ for the
   constraints $v_x\le\sum_{C:x\in P_C}z_C$, variables $\mu_x\ge0$ for
   $v_x\le1$, query variables $\lambda_q\ge0$, and storage variable
   $\sigma\ge0$.  It is
   \[
   \begin{array}{ll}
   \text{\rm minimize}
      & \displaystyle
        \sum_{x\in P}\mu_x
        +\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\lambda_qL_q+\sigma S\\[0.8em]
   \text{\rm subject to}
      & \alpha_x+\mu_x\ge1
        \qquad (x\in P),\\[0.4em]
      & \displaystyle
        \sum_{x\in P_C}\alpha_x
        \le
        \sigma s_C+
        w_C\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\lambda_q a_C(q)
        \qquad (C\in\mathcal C).
   \end{array}
   \]
   Since the primal is feasible and bounded, strong duality applies.  In an
   optimal dual solution we may assume $0\le\alpha_x\le1$ and
   $\mu_x=1-\alpha_x$.  Therefore the dual objective is
   \[
      |P|-\sum_x\alpha_x+
      \sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\lambda_qL_q+\sigma S .
   \]
   Having primal value below $|P|-L_0$ is exactly the existence of a dual
   feasible solution for which this objective is below $|P|-L_0$, which is
   equivalent to \((D1)\).  The remaining dual constraints are precisely
   \((D2)\).  The converse is the same duality implication read backward.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Shadow finite-pool dual]\label{cor:shadow-finite-pool-dual}
   Fix a target set $E\subseteq P$, a finite low-guard query constraint set
   $\mathcal Q$, and a finite proposal pool whose children are hereditary under
   taking subsets.  Replace every proposal $C$ by the exposed subchild with
   point set $P_C\cap E$, discard empty subchildren, and compute its query and
   storage weights using the exposed cardinality:
   \[
      w_{C,E}=|P_C\cap E|^\rho\Psi(R_C),
      \qquad
      s_{C,E}=|P_C\cap E|^{1+\rho}\Psi(R_C).
   \]
   Consider the fractional cover program that maximizes
   $\sum_{x\in E}v_x$, covers only points of $E$, and uses the active and
   storage weights $w_{C,E},s_{C,E}$.  If its value is below $|E|-L_0$, then
   there are prices $\alpha_x\in[0,1]$ supported on $E$, query prices
   $\lambda_q\ge0$, and a storage price $\sigma\ge0$ such that
   \[
      \sum_{x\in E}\alpha_x
      >
      L_0+\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\lambda_qL_q+\sigma S,
   \]
   while every proposal satisfies
   \[
      \sum_{x\in P_C\cap E}\alpha_x
      \le
      \sigma s_{C,E}
      +
      w_{C,E}\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\lambda_q a_C(q).
   \]
   Conversely, if no such supported price system exists, the exposed pool has a
   fractional cover of $E$ with residual value at most $L_0$ under the displayed
   budgets.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Apply \cref{lem:finite-pool-dual} with ground set $E$ and with the proposal
   pool consisting of the exposed subchildren $P_C\cap E$.  Heredity guarantees
   that each exposed subchild keeps the same radius and activation predicate
   and is still certified.  The displayed inequalities are exactly the dual
   certificate from \cref{lem:finite-pool-dual} after extending the point prices
   by zero on $P\setminus E$.
\end{proof}

The dual gives a concrete way to attack the remaining geometric problem.  A
failure of the finite fractional cover produces a weighted residual set
$\alpha$, a query-load distribution $\lambda$, and a storage price $\sigma$ such
that every certified proposal has less $\alpha$-mass than its charged storage
and query footprint.  Thus the desired local theorem can be phrased without any
reference to Lloyd dynamics: for a rich enough proposal pool, rule out all
price systems satisfying \((D1)\)--\((D2)\), or the shadow-supported version in
\cref{cor:shadow-finite-pool-dual}, then use the offline optimizer and
deterministic verifier to retain only a low-stabbing cover.  In the
guard-restricted route the relevant target set is the low-guard shadow
$E_\gamma$, so dense regions outside $E_\gamma$ never need to be bought by a
dual witness or stored inside an exposed child.

\begin{corollary}[Dual-price proposal separation]\label{cor:dual-price-separation}
   Fix a finite universe $\mathcal C_\star$ of certified candidate children and
   the same finite query constraint set $\mathcal Q$.  For prices
   $(\alpha,\lambda,\sigma)$ define the reduced gain of a child $C$ by
   \[
      \operatorname{gain}_{\alpha,\lambda,\sigma}(C)
      =
      \sum_{x\in P_C}\alpha_x
      -
      \sigma s_C
      -
      w_C\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\lambda_q a_C(q).
   \]
   The full fractional program over $\mathcal C_\star$ has value at least
   $|P|-L_0$ if and only if every price system with
   \[
      \sum_x\alpha_x
      >
      L_0+\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\lambda_qL_q+\sigma S,
      \qquad
      0\le\alpha_x\le1,\quad \lambda_q,\sigma\ge0,
   \]
   has some child $C\in\mathcal C_\star$ with
   \[
      \operatorname{gain}_{\alpha,\lambda,\sigma}(C)>0.
   \]
   Consequently, with unbounded preprocessing, a column-generation routine that
   repeatedly solves the current finite-pool LP and adds any positive-gain child
   from $\mathcal C_\star$ terminates with value at least $|P|-L_0$ whenever the
   full universe satisfies this separation property.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Apply \cref{lem:finite-pool-dual} to the full pool
   $\mathcal C_\star$.  Failure of value at least $|P|-L_0$ is exactly the
   existence of prices satisfying the displayed surplus inequality and
   \(\operatorname{gain}_{\alpha,\lambda,\sigma}(C)\le0\) for every
   $C\in\mathcal C_\star$.  Negating this statement gives the equivalence.

   For the algorithmic statement, $\mathcal C_\star$ is finite.  Each positive
   reduced-gain child violates the current dual certificate, so adding it either
   increases the current pool or the procedure has already reached the target
   value.  The routine therefore terminates after at most $|\mathcal C_\star|$
   additions, and the equivalence rules out termination below value
   $|P|-L_0$ under the separation property.
\end{proof}

This is the proof-aligned analogue of $k$-means++ seeding.  Instead of sampling
from squared-distance residuals, preprocessing may solve the current fractional
cover, read the dual prices, and search the very large proposal universe for a
positive-gain cap, medoid ball, pair-direction filter, or learned score.  The
search may be arbitrarily expensive; the retained index still pays only for the
children that survive the final deterministic certificate.

\begin{lemma}[Finite fractional filter-cover dual]
   \label{lem:finite-filter-cover-dual}
   Fix a finite query constraint set $\mathcal Q$, a finite demand set
   \[
      \mathcal N\subseteq P\times\mathcal Q,
   \]
   and a finite universe $\mathcal F$ of priced filters.  A filter
   $A\in\mathcal F$ has an update side $U_A\subseteq P$, an activation predicate
   $a_A:\mathcal Q\to\{0,1\}$, a certified query price $T_A\ge0$, and a
   certified storage price $S_A\ge0$.  Write
   \[
      c_A(p,q)=\mathbf 1\{p\in U_A\}a_A(q).
   \]
   For budgets $L_q$ and $S$, consider the fractional filter-cover feasibility
   program
   \[
   \begin{array}{ll}
   \text{\rm find} & \lambda_A\ge0 \qquad(A\in\mathcal F)\\[0.4em]
   \text{\rm subject to}
      & \displaystyle
        \sum_{A\in\mathcal F}c_A(p,q)\lambda_A\ge1
        \qquad ((p,q)\in\mathcal N),\\[0.8em]
      & \displaystyle
        \sum_{A\in\mathcal F}a_A(q)T_A\lambda_A\le L_q
        \qquad(q\in\mathcal Q),\\[0.8em]
      & \displaystyle
        \sum_{A\in\mathcal F}S_A\lambda_A\le S .
   \end{array}
   \tag{$\mathsf{FC}_{\mathcal N}$}
   \]
   This program is infeasible if and only if there are demand prices
   $\alpha_{p,q}\ge0$, query prices $\tau_q\ge0$, and a storage price
   $\sigma\ge0$ such that
   \[
      \sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal N}\alpha_{p,q}
      >
      \sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\tau_qL_q+\sigma S,
      \tag{FC-D1}
   \]
   while every filter satisfies
   \[
      \sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal N}\alpha_{p,q}c_A(p,q)
      \le
      S_A\sigma+T_A\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\tau_qa_A(q).
      \tag{FC-D2}
   \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   This is Farkas' lemma applied to the finite system.  Write the coverage
   inequalities as
   \[
      -\sum_A c_A(p,q)\lambda_A\le -1
      \qquad ((p,q)\in\mathcal N),
   \]
   keep the query and storage inequalities in their displayed directions, and
   keep $\lambda_A\ge0$.  A nonnegative multiplier system
   $(\alpha,\tau,\sigma)$ certifies infeasibility exactly when its weighted
   left-hand side is nonnegative on every variable $\lambda_A$ but its weighted
   right-hand side is negative.  Nonnegativity of the $\lambda_A$ coefficient is
   precisely
   \[
      -\sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal N}\alpha_{p,q}c_A(p,q)
      +T_A\sum_q\tau_qa_A(q)+\sigma S_A\ge0,
   \]
   which is \((FC\text{-}D2)\).  Negativity of the right-hand side is
   \[
      -\sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal N}\alpha_{p,q}
      +\sum_q\tau_qL_q+\sigma S<0,
   \]
   which is \((FC\text{-}D1)\).  The converse is the same Farkas certificate read
   backward.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Filter-cover column generation]
   \label{cor:filter-cover-column-generation}
   For prices $(\alpha,\tau,\sigma)$ define the reduced gain of a filter by
   \[
      \operatorname{gain}_{\alpha,\tau,\sigma}(A)
      =
      \sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal N}\alpha_{p,q}c_A(p,q)
      -
      S_A\sigma
      -
      T_A\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\tau_qa_A(q).
   \]
   The full filter-cover program over a finite universe $\mathcal F_\star$ is
   feasible if and only if every price system satisfying \((FC\text{-}D1)\) has
   some filter $A\in\mathcal F_\star$ with positive reduced gain.  Consequently,
   with unbounded preprocessing, a column-generation routine that repeatedly
   solves the current restricted program and adds any positive-gain filter from
   $\mathcal F_\star$ terminates with a feasible cover whenever the full universe
   is feasible.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   By \cref{lem:finite-filter-cover-dual}, infeasibility of the full program is
   exactly the existence of a surplus price system satisfying
   \(\operatorname{gain}_{\alpha,\tau,\sigma}(A)\le0\) for every
   $A\in\mathcal F_\star$.  Negating this statement gives the first claim.
   Since $\mathcal F_\star$ is finite, each positive-gain column either enlarges
   the restricted pool or the current pool is already feasible; thus exhaustive
   column generation terminates after at most $|\mathcal F_\star|$ additions.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Poisson materialization for filter covers]
   \label{lem:poisson-filter-cover-materialization}
   In the setting of \cref{lem:finite-filter-cover-dual}, assume $L_q>0$ for
   every $q\in\mathcal Q$, $S>0$, and the atom bounds
   \[
      a_A(q)T_A\le L_q\qquad(A\in\mathcal F,\ q\in\mathcal Q),
      \qquad
      S_A\le S\qquad(A\in\mathcal F).
   \]
   If $\lambda$ is feasible for \((\mathsf{FC}_{\mathcal N})\) and
   \[
      B\ge
      \max\left\{
         1,\log(4|\mathcal N|),\log(8(|\mathcal Q|+1))
      \right\},
   \]
   then there is an integral retained multiset of filters $\mathcal R$ such that
   every demand is covered,
   \[
      \sum_{A\in\mathcal R}c_A(p,q)\ge1
      \qquad((p,q)\in\mathcal N),
   \]
   and simultaneously
   \[
      \sum_{A\in\mathcal R}a_A(q)T_A\le3BL_q
      \qquad(q\in\mathcal Q),
      \qquad
      \sum_{A\in\mathcal R}S_A\le3BS .
   \]
   Thus a finite fractional near-pair filter cover materializes as an ordinary
   LSF-style retained family with only logarithmic budget inflation.  If each
   retained filter invokes a certified child structure of price $(T_A,S_A)$, then
   querying all active retained filters solves every demand in $\mathcal N$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Independently draw multiplicities
   \[
      M_A\sim{\rm Pois}(B\lambda_A),
   \]
   and keep $M_A$ copies of filter $A$.  For a demand $d=(p,q)$, feasibility gives
   \(\Lambda_d=\sum_Ac_A(p,q)\lambda_A\ge1\), so
   \[
      \Pr[d\text{ is uncovered}]
      =
      \Pr\left[\sum_Ac_A(p,q)M_A=0\right]
      =
      e^{-B\Lambda_d}
      \le e^{-B}.
   \]
   A union bound and the choice of $B$ make the probability of any uncovered
   demand at most $1/4$.

   Fix a query constraint $q$.  Put
   \[
      X_q=\sum_A M_A\,\frac{a_A(q)T_A}{L_q}.
   \]
   The atom bound gives weights in $[0,1]$, and feasibility gives
   $\E X_q\le B$.  For $\theta=\log 2$, the elementary convexity bound
   \(e^{\theta w}-1\le w\) for \(0\le w\le1\) gives
   \[
      \E e^{\theta X_q}
      =
      \exp\left(
         \sum_A B\lambda_A
         \left(e^{\theta a_A(q)T_A/L_q}-1\right)
      \right)
      \le e^B .
   \]
   Hence
   \[
      \Pr[X_q>3B]\le e^{B-3B\log2}\le e^{-B}.
   \]
   The same argument for
   \(X_{\rm store}=\sum_A M_AS_A/S\) gives
   \[
      \Pr[X_{\rm store}>3B]\le e^{-B}.
   \]
   A union bound over all query constraints and the storage constraint has
   failure probability at most $1/4$.  With positive probability no coverage,
   query, or storage event fails.  For such an outcome, the retained multiset has
   the displayed properties.  The final routing statement is immediate: for each
   demand $(p,q)$, some retained active filter contains $p$ on its update side,
   so the certified child queried through that filter contains the true near
   point, and final metric verification accepts any valid answer.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Fractional dense-filter cover]
   \label{def:fractional-dense-filter-cover}
   Work at one resident node with query domain \(\Omega\), resident set
   \(P\), finite query constraints \(\mathcal Q\subseteq\Omega\), and finite
   near-pair demands \(\mathcal N\subseteq P\times\mathcal Q\).  A dense child
   filter is an asymmetric pair
   \[
      D=(U_D,Q_D)
   \]
   together with certified prices \(T_D,S_D\), where \(U_D\subseteq P\) is the
   stored side and \(Q_D\subseteq\Omega\) is the query side.  Its correctness
   certificate is
   \[
      p\in U_D,\quad \|p-q\|\le r
      \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
      q\in Q_D .
      \tag{DFC0}
   \]
   If \(U_D\) lies in a smaller certified ball of radius \(R_D\), the intended
   inductive prices are
   \[
      T_D=|U_D|^{\rho(R_D)}\log^{O_c(1)}n,
      \qquad
      S_D=|U_D|^{1+\rho(R_D)}\log^{O_c(1)}n,
      \tag{DFC1}
   \]
   or any sharper certified descendant prices.  A nonnegative intensity vector
   \((\lambda_D)\) is an \((L,S)\)-fractional dense-filter cover of
   \(\mathcal N\) if
   \[
      \sum_{D:\ p\in U_D,\ q\in Q_D}\lambda_D\ge1
      \qquad ((p,q)\in\mathcal N),
      \tag{DFC2}
   \]
   \[
      \sum_{D:\ q\in Q_D}\lambda_DT_D\le L_q
      \qquad(q\in\mathcal Q),
      \tag{DFC3}
   \]
   and
   \[
      \sum_D\lambda_DS_D\le S .
      \tag{DFC4}
   \]
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}[Dense recursion is a filter cover]
   \label{cor:dense-recursion-filter-cover}
   A fractional dense-filter cover in the sense of
   \cref{def:fractional-dense-filter-cover} is exactly the finite
   filter-cover LP \((\mathsf{FC}_{\mathcal N})\) restricted to the columns
   \[
      A_D=(U_D,a_D,T_D,S_D),
      \qquad
      a_D(q)=\mathbf 1\{q\in Q_D\}.
   \]
   Consequently any feasible dense cover can be Poisson-materialized, under the
   atom bounds of \cref{lem:poisson-filter-cover-materialization}, into an
   ordinary retained overlapping family whose query cost is
   \(O(\log(|\mathcal N|+|\mathcal Q|+2))\,L_q\) and whose storage is
   \(O(\log(|\mathcal N|+|\mathcal Q|+2))\,S\).  Dense overlap therefore never
   creates a separate branching factor; it is already charged by \((DFC3)\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   For the displayed column \(A_D\), the coefficient in
   \((\mathsf{FC}_{\mathcal N})\) is
   \[
      c_{A_D}(p,q)=\mathbf 1\{p\in U_D\}\mathbf 1\{q\in Q_D\}.
   \]
   Thus the coverage, query, and storage constraints of
   \((\mathsf{FC}_{\mathcal N})\) are precisely \((DFC2)\), \((DFC3)\), and
   \((DFC4)\).  Materialization is then
   \cref{lem:poisson-filter-cover-materialization}.  Finally, \((DFC0)\) says
   that whenever the true near point lies in a retained dense child, the query
   side activates that child, so the inductive child certificate is routed to a
   valid witness.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Finite dense/spherical minimax dichotomy]
   \label{cor:finite-dense-spherical-minimax}
   Work in the setting of \cref{lem:finite-filter-cover-dual}.  Let the finite
   filter universe be split as
   \[
      \mathcal F_\star=\mathcal F_{\rm den}\cup\mathcal F_{\rm sph},
   \]
   where \(\mathcal F_{\rm den}\) consists of radius-contracting recursive
   columns and \(\mathcal F_{\rm sph}\) consists of ordinary large-range
   spherical columns.  For prices \((\alpha,\tau,\sigma)\), write
   \[
      G_A(\alpha,\tau,\sigma)
      =
      \sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal N}\alpha_{p,q}c_A(p,q)
      -
      S_A\sigma
      -
      T_A\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\tau_qa_A(q)
   \]
   for the reduced gain of a column.

   Suppose that every nonnegative price system satisfying the surplus
   inequality \((FC\text{-}D1)\) and
   \[
      G_D(\alpha,\tau,\sigma)\le0
      \qquad(D\in\mathcal F_{\rm den})
      \tag{DSM1}
   \]
   has a spherical separator
   \[
      G_Z(\alpha,\tau,\sigma)>0
      \qquad\text{for some }Z\in\mathcal F_{\rm sph}.
      \tag{DSM2}
   \]
   Then the full finite filter-cover LP over
   \(\mathcal F_\star\) is feasible with the stated query and storage budgets.
   Under the atom bounds of \cref{lem:poisson-filter-cover-materialization}, the
   feasible cover materializes with the usual logarithmic inflation.

   Equivalently, to prove local feasibility it is enough to analyze only dual
   residuals on which all dense recursive columns have nonpositive reduced
   gain.  Such a residual must be pseudo-random for the spherical family; if it
   is not, the positive spherical column contradicts the residual certificate.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   If the full LP were infeasible, \cref{lem:finite-filter-cover-dual} would
   give nonnegative prices satisfying \((FC\text{-}D1)\) and
   \[
      G_A(\alpha,\tau,\sigma)\le0
      \qquad(A\in\mathcal F_\star).
   \]
   In particular \((DSM1)\) holds for every dense column.  The assumed
   dense/spherical dichotomy then gives a spherical column \(Z\) satisfying
   \((DSM2)\), contradicting the same dual certificate for
   \(A=Z\in\mathcal F_\star\).  Thus the LP is feasible.  The materialization
   statement is exactly \cref{lem:poisson-filter-cover-materialization}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Proposal-law filter separator]
   \label{lem:proposal-law-filter-separator}
   Work in the setting of \cref{lem:finite-filter-cover-dual}, and let
   \(\mathcal F_\star\) be the full finite filter universe.  Suppose that for
   every surplus price system \((\alpha,\tau,\sigma)\) satisfying
   \((FC\text{-}D1)\) there is a probability law \(\nu\) supported on
   \(\mathcal F_\star\) such that
   \[
      \E_{A\sim\nu}
      \sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal N}\alpha_{p,q}c_A(p,q)
      >
      \E_{A\sim\nu}
      \left(
         S_A\sigma+
         T_A\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\tau_qa_A(q)
      \right).
      \tag{PLS1}
   \]
   Then the full filter-cover LP over \(\mathcal F_\star\) is feasible.  If the
   atom bounds of \cref{lem:poisson-filter-cover-materialization} hold for the
   resulting feasible solution, the cover materializes with the same logarithmic
   query and storage inflation.

   Equivalently, it is enough for the proposal law to certify the marginal
   inequality
   \[
      \sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal N}
         \alpha_{p,q}\Pr_{A\sim\nu}[p\in U_A,\ a_A(q)=1]
      >
      \sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\tau_q
         \E_{A\sim\nu}[T_Aa_A(q)]
      +\sigma\E_{A\sim\nu}S_A .
      \tag{PLS2}
   \]
   In particular, if a finite seed law \(s\sim\nu\) generates filters \(A_s\)
   and satisfies \((PLS1)\), then some deterministic seed \(s\) generates a
   positive reduced-gain filter.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The expectation in \((PLS1)\) is exactly
   \[
      \E_{A\sim\nu}\operatorname{gain}_{\alpha,\tau,\sigma}(A),
   \]
   with reduced gain as in \cref{cor:filter-cover-column-generation}.  If it is
   positive, at least one filter in the support of \(\nu\) has positive reduced
   gain.  Therefore every surplus dual price system exposes a positive-gain
   column, and \cref{cor:filter-cover-column-generation} implies feasibility of
   the full filter-cover LP.  The materialization claim is
   \cref{lem:poisson-filter-cover-materialization}.

   Expanding the two expectations in \((PLS1)\) gives \((PLS2)\).  For a finite
   seed law, if every seed had nonpositive reduced gain, then the average
   reduced gain would be nonpositive, contradicting \((PLS1)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Sampled proposal-law separation]
   \label{lem:sampled-proposal-law-separation}
   Work in the setting of \cref{lem:proposal-law-filter-separator}, and fix one
   surplus price system \((\alpha,\tau,\sigma)\).  Let a seed \(s\sim\nu\)
   generate a certified filter \(A_s\), and write
   \[
      G(s)=\operatorname{gain}_{\alpha,\tau,\sigma}(A_s).
   \]
   Suppose that
   \[
      \E_sG(s)\ge\Gamma>0,
      \qquad
      G(s)_+\le M
      \quad\text{almost surely}.
      \tag{SPL1}
   \]
   Then \(B\) independent build-time samples contain a positive reduced-gain
   filter with probability at least
   \[
      1-\exp\left(-\frac{B\Gamma}{M}\right).
      \tag{SPL2}
   \]
   Thus
   \[
      B\ge \frac{M}{\Gamma}\log\frac1\delta
      \tag{SPL3}
   \]
   suffices to expose a deterministic positive-gain column with probability at
   least \(1-\delta\).

   Consequently a randomized proposal mechanism does not have to be retained in
   the final index.  If the verifier computes \(G(s)\) and accepts only
   positive-gain columns, arbitrary extra preprocessing can amplify a
   positive-margin proposal law into an ordinary deterministic column-generation
   step.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Since \(G=G_+-G_-\), condition \((SPL1)\) gives
   \[
      \E G_+\ge \E G\ge\Gamma .
   \]
   The upper bound \(G_+\le M\) implies
   \[
      \Pr[G>0]\ge\frac{\Gamma}{M}.
   \]
   Hence the probability that \(B\) independent seeds all have nonpositive gain
   is at most
   \[
      \left(1-\frac{\Gamma}{M}\right)^B
      \le
      \exp\left(-\frac{B\Gamma}{M}\right).
   \]
   Whenever a positive seed appears, its certified filter is an ordinary
   positive reduced-gain column for \cref{cor:filter-cover-column-generation}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Benefit-per-price proposal normal form]
   \label{cor:benefit-per-price-proposal}
   Work in the setting of \cref{lem:proposal-law-filter-separator}, and fix one
   surplus price system \((\alpha,\tau,\sigma)\).  For a proposed filter \(A\),
   write its dual benefit and recursive price as
   \[
      B_A=
      \sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal N}\alpha_{p,q}c_A(p,q),
      \qquad
      R_A=
      S_A\sigma+T_A\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\tau_qa_A(q).
      \tag{BPP1}
   \]
   If a proposal law \(\nu\) puts positive probability on a column with
   \(R_A=0\) and \(B_A>0\), then \(\nu\) exposes a positive reduced-gain column
   with positive probability.  Otherwise assume \(\E_\nu R_A>0\) and
   \(B_A=0\) whenever \(R_A=0\).  Let \(\nu^R\) be the \(R\)-size-biased law,
   \[
      \nu^R(A)=\frac{R_A\nu(A)}{\E_\nu R_A}.
      \tag{BPP2}
   \]
   Then
   \[
      \E_\nu(B_A-R_A)>0
      \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
      \E_{A\sim\nu^R}\frac{B_A}{R_A}>1 .
      \tag{BPP3}
   \]
   In particular, a finite proposal panel with positive average reduced gain
   contains a deterministic column with \(B_A/R_A>1\), after discarding zero-price
   zero-benefit columns.  Thus the proof-aligned sampling score is not data mass
   or squared-distance mass by itself; it is dual benefit per certified
   recursive price.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   If \(R_A=0\) and \(B_A>0\), then the reduced gain \(B_A-R_A\) is positive, so
   the first claim is immediate.  In the remaining case,
   \[
      \E_{A\sim\nu^R}\frac{B_A}{R_A}
      =
      \frac{\E_\nu B_A}{\E_\nu R_A}.
   \]
   Since \(\E_\nu R_A>0\), this ratio is larger than one exactly when
   \(\E_\nu B_A>\E_\nu R_A\), which is \(\E_\nu(B_A-R_A)>0\).  For a finite panel,
   if every positive-price column had \(B_A/R_A\le1\) and every zero-price column
   had zero benefit, then the average reduced gain would be nonpositive.  Hence
   positive average reduced gain exposes one deterministic positive-gain column.
\end{proof}

The LP above is the fully fractional version of dense overlap.  A dense ball,
cap, facility bucket, additive-quantization bucket, list-decoder output, or
ordinary spherical LSF bucket is just a column \(A=(U_A,a_A,T_A,S_A)\).  A hard
recursive decomposition asks how many dense children a query may enter.  The
fractional filter cover asks only for the cost-weighted local load
\[
   \sum_A a_A(q)T_A\lambda_A .
\]
Large overlap is harmless when this quantity is small.  If no cheap overlapping
cover exists, the dual prices in \cref{lem:finite-filter-cover-dual} identify the
exact obstruction: demand mass on near pairs, query-local load prices, and a
storage price.  Dense merging is therefore a reduced-gain separation problem,
not a greedy clustering rule.
\Cref{lem:proposal-law-filter-separator} is the corresponding build-time
interface: a randomized geometric routine is useful exactly when its induced
incidence marginals have positive expected reduced gain against the current
dual.  \Cref{lem:sampled-proposal-law-separation} makes the amplification
explicit: a positive-margin seed law can be sampled until the deterministic
verifier finds one positive-gain column.  The routine itself is not stored; the
final fractional LP and rounding charge only retained columns.

The dual also gives the proof-aligned replacement for mass-proportional
seeding.  Against prices \((\alpha,\tau,\sigma)\), the benefit of a proposed
filter is its priced near-pair incidence
\[
   B_A=\sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal N}\alpha_{p,q}c_A(p,q),
\]
while its recursive price is
\[
   R_A=S_A\sigma+T_A\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\tau_qa_A(q).
\]
A proposal is useful exactly when \(B_A-R_A>0\), or in law when
\(\E B_A>\E R_A\).  Thus \(k\)-means++ sampling, additive vector
quantization, range reporting, and list/lattice decoding are analyzable only to
the extent that they approximate this reduced-gain separator.  Sampling by
data mass alone is not an invariant of the proof; the invariant is
cost-normalized priced demand captured per retained filter column, equivalently
the benefit-per-price criterion of
\cref{cor:benefit-per-price-proposal}.

The finite restriction is not a technicality.  A cover written directly for all
queries \(q\in\R^d\) is an analytic guide, but it is not yet a data structure
certificate: the rounding and duality arguments above are finite.  The retained
index must first pass through a finite signature system, an exact near-set
signature, or an equivalent finite transcript whose active-filter pattern and
possible near witnesses are certified.  Thus \(k\)-means++, additive
quantization, range reporting, and list/lattice decoders are acceptable only as
build-time proposal mechanisms for producing finite certified columns; the
proof object remains the reduced-gain separator for that finite universe.

\begin{assumption}[Weighted dense/spherical filter dichotomy]
   \label{asm:weighted-dense-spherical-dichotomy}
   At every recursive node with resident set \(P\), \(|P|=N\), and current
   exponent \(\rho(R)\), let the filter universe contain both:
   \begin{itemize}
      \item radius-contracting dense filters \(D=(U_D,a_D)\), priced by their
      certified descendant costs \(T_D,S_D\);
      \item large-range spherical filters, priced by their terminal scan or
      child costs.
   \end{itemize}
   For every finite low-guard near-pair demand set
   \(\mathcal N\subseteq P\times\mathcal Q\), and for budgets
   \[
      L_q=N^{\rho(R)}\log^{O_c(1)}n,
      \qquad
      S=N^{1+\rho(R)}\log^{O_c(1)}n,
   \]
   every surplus dual price system \((\alpha,\tau,\sigma)\) of
   \cref{lem:finite-filter-cover-dual} exposes a positive-gain column from this
   unified universe.  Equivalently, either the dense recursive filters
   fractionally cover the priced demands within the local budgets, or the dual
   residual is pseudo-random enough that a large-range spherical filter has
   positive reduced gain.
\end{assumption}

This is the clean dense-versus-pseudo-random proof target.  It is strictly
stronger than finding a good \(k\)-means++ distribution and weaker than proving a
hard disjoint dense decomposition: preprocessing may search any proposal family,
but the retained index is accepted only through the finite LP, the reduced-gain
separator, and the materialization certificate above.  Conditional on
\cref{asm:weighted-dense-spherical-dichotomy} and the inductive child prices, the
dense filters, spherical filters, residual scans, and terminal samplers are all
handled by one filter-cover process rather than by separate branching rules.

\begin{lemma}[Weighted spherical reduced-gain test]
   \label{lem:weighted-spherical-reduced-gain}
   Work in a finite spherical terminal node with resident set \(P\), \(|P|=m\),
   finite query set \(\mathcal Q\), and finite near-pair demand set
   \(\mathcal N\subseteq P\times\mathcal Q\).  Let \(\mathcal Z\) be a finite
   family of bucket filters.  For \(z\in\mathcal Z\), write \(U_z\subseteq P\)
   for its update bucket and \(\chi_z(q)\in\{0,1\}\) for its query activation;
   the terminal query and storage prices are both
   \[
      T_z=S_z=|U_z|.
   \]
   Let \(\Pi\) be a probability law on \(\mathcal Z\).  Fix high-correlation
   sets \(H(q)\subseteq P\).  Suppose there are numbers
   \(\pi_1,\pi_2,\pi_u>0\) such that
   \[
      \Pr_{Z\sim\Pi}[p\in U_Z,\ \chi_Z(q)=1]\ge\pi_1
      \qquad((p,q)\in\mathcal N),
      \tag{WS1}
   \]
   \[
      \Pr_{Z\sim\Pi}[x\in U_Z,\ \chi_Z(q)=1]\le\pi_2
      \qquad(q\in\mathcal Q,\ x\notin H(q)),
      \tag{WS2}
   \]
   and
   \[
      \Pr_{Z\sim\Pi}[x\in U_Z]\le\pi_u
      \qquad(x\in P).
      \tag{WS3}
   \]
   For dual prices \(\alpha_{p,q}\ge0\), \(\tau_q\ge0\), and \(\sigma\ge0\), put
   \[
      A_\alpha=\sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal N}\alpha_{p,q},
      \qquad
      T_\tau=\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\tau_q,
   \]
   and define the high-correlation co-load
   \[
      \mathsf D_H(\tau)
      =
      \E_{Z\sim\Pi}
      \sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\tau_q\chi_Z(q)|U_Z\cap H(q)|.
      \tag{WS4}
   \]
   Then
   \[
   \E_{Z\sim\Pi}
