   a genuinely additive nearest-neighbor/MIPS primitive or a different
   structured reporter.

   A more promising diagnostic is facility-style IVF over the same smoothed
   scores.  The accompanying IVF stress script assigns data points to
   \(m^{1-\rho}\)-scale cosine centroid buckets, routes the perturbed center
   \(y\) to the best few centroids, and then exact-reranks by \(A_Y\).  Random
   sampled centers fail for the expected reason: an isolated witness is often
   not represented by a query-visible bucket.  Lloyd or \(k\)-means++-style
   facility centers are much stronger in the planted spherical diagnostic,
   frequently putting the planted score maximizer in the first reported bucket
   with \(O(m^\rho)\) scanned points.  This is still not a proof of
   \cref{asm:smoothed-score-max}, because the diagnostic scores all
   \(m^{1-\rho}\)-scale centroids explicitly and does not prove worst-case
   stability of the facility cover.  It does, however, isolate a concrete
   positive target: a compact centroid decoder whose top few facility buckets
   contain the smoothed score maximizer with inverse-polylogarithmic failure
   probability and \(m^\rho\polylog m\) scan load.

   A follow-up compact-decoder diagnostic,
   \texttt{impl/smoothed\_scoremax\_centroid\_decoder\_stress.py}, stress-tests
   exactly this target instead of changing formulation.  On the same planted
   \(k\)-means++ facility instances with \(m=3000,d=24,c=2\), exact centroid
   scoring still puts the score-maximizer bucket first in all tested trials,
   but a balanced random-projection beam tree over the centroids can miss that
   bucket completely at sublinear work: for one seed, beam \(8\) spent about
   \(0.46C\) centroid-score equivalents, \(C=m^{1-\rho}\), and recovered the
   top bucket in none of the trials; beam \(32\) recovered only about \(74\%\)
   while already spending \(1.24C\).  A flat multiprobe hyperplane decoder shows
   the same tradeoff.  Eight 6-bit tables with 64 probes spend about
   \(0.51C\)--\(0.54C\) and recover only \(28\%\)--\(96\%\) across seeds, while
   128 probes recover all tested trials only after spending about
   \(0.79C\)--\(0.82C\).  Thus the naive compact centroid-search layer is a real
   bottleneck: the facility route remains viable only with a stronger decoder
   that exploits more than ordinary centroid ANN/LSH routing, or with a proof
   that such top-bucket search inherently costs a constant fraction of the
   retained centers in this regime.

   The same diagnostic now includes an exact-neighbor pivot graph over the
   centroids, to separate weak random partitions from local-navigation failure.
   This is a stronger negative control because the centroid graph itself is
   built from exact all-pairs centroid similarities.  With \(172\approx C^{3/4}\)
   query-scored pivots, degree \(16\), and \(256\) graph visits, the graph spends
   about \(0.39C\) centroid-score equivalents on the \(m=3000\) \(k\)-means++
   rows but has only \(0\%\)--\(8.75\%\) additive score-max success; the
   \(90\%\) loss is still about \(4.24\)--\(4.27\) score margins.  Even \(512\)
   graph visits raise success only to \(1.7\%\)--\(30\%\) while spending about
   \(0.61C\).  Thus the obstruction is not just poor tree/hash engineering:
   the score-max bucket can lie outside the query-visible local-navigation basin
   of ordinary centroid proximity graphs until the search is already
   near-dense.

   A separate margin check rules out the easiest explanation for this failure.
   In the same exact-scoring \(m=3000,d=24\) rows, the top centroid is not
   merely tied with the runner-up: the \(10\%\) quantile of the top-minus-second
   centroid score gap, normalized by \(\|y\|\), is \(0.080\)--\(0.159\) across
   the three seeds, and the top-minus-rank-\(32\) gap has \(10\%\) quantile
   \(0.155\)--\(0.233\).  Thus the missing decoder is not just a finer
   tie-breaker.  It must expose the correct high-score basin without first
   enumerating a constant fraction of the retained centers.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Structured decoders after the centroid-search barrier]
   \label{rem:structured-decoder-targets}
   The compact-centroid experiments above are evidence against treating the
   retained buckets as an unstructured set of learned centers searched by a
   generic ANN data structure.  The coding/lattice route should instead replace
   the flat center set by a structured label universe with a native
   threshold/list decoder for the actual score.  The useful interface is already
   the one in \cref{lem:soft-list-recovery-reporter},
   \cref{cor:euclidean-list-decoder-reporter},
   \cref{lem:reliability-erasure-sweep}, and
   \cref{cor:unified-soft-decoded-rate-coverage}: list high-score labels by a
   Fano-biased or soft-decision metric, then verify the reported buckets.

   Four construction families now look worth testing.  First, constrain the
   product-sign label universe by a polar, Reed--Muller, or related outer code
   and use successive-cancellation list decoding to report the top few labels
   under the query bit log-likelihoods~\cite{TV12,TH23}.  This attacks the
   product-sign entropy barrier directly: the outer code can lower tilted
   entropy and storage/far-load while preserving the bitwise near correlation,
   unlike reporting top labels from the full cube.  The immediate experiment is
   to replace the full product-sign panel by a polar/RM subcode and measure
   query-top-\(L\) tilted value, sampled far-load, and rate-coverage feasibility.

   Second, use algebraic or Euclidean soft-decision block decoders as exact
   score reporters.  Koetter--Vardy Reed--Solomon decoding, Barnes--Sloane or
   Barnes--Wall lattice list decoding, and Construction-A/D quotients are useful
   only when the score embeds as a block Euclidean radius or a certified
   coordinatewise soft score~\cite{KV03,GP17,MP20}.  In that case
   \cref{cor:euclidean-list-decoder-reporter} turns the decoder into the right
   threshold reporter without repeated-coordinate discretization.  The
   certificate still has to prove that the target radius/list size and the
   retained spectrum match the \(m^\rho\polylog m\) budget.

   Third, high-rate expander/Tanner/tensor list-recovery codes are better
   viewed as reduced-cost separation engines than as nearest-center
   data structures~\cite{HW15,HRW17,ST25}.  After dyadic discretization of a
   positive coverage score, ordinary list recovery can expose candidate labels
   for the finite rate-coverage verifier; the verifier then filters by exact
   reduced gain.  This is the most plausible way to use deep list-recovery
   theorems against the finite dual obstructions without enumerating the whole
   Cartesian product.

   Finally, lattice sphere enumeration, bounded-distance decoding, Gaussian
   sampling, and nearest-neighbor-aided information-set decoding should not be
   imported as black-box nearest-center oracles~\cite{FP85,SE94,GNR10,Kle00,
   GPV08,MO15}.  Their useful feature is the pruning metric: a stack or
   enumeration decoder subtracts a volume/rate bias from raw likelihood, exactly
   as in \cref{lem:fano-biased-prefix-list}.  A lattice construction is
   therefore promising only if its pruning profile can be certified as a
   budget-stable Fano potential or as a compact quotient sampler in the sense of
   \cref{lem:compressed-aggregate-sampler}.

   The later entropy barriers make this restriction essential rather than
   stylistic.  By \cref{rem:raw-top-one-entropy-barrier}, a symmetric raw
   top-one Gaussian panel charged at full label entropy loses the gap by data
   processing: the data block contains only \(I(A;U)\) nats about the query
   label \(A\), while the far threshold is charged at \(H(A)\).  Thus the
   code/lattice families above should be used as output-sensitive reporters,
   quotient samplers, reduced-cost separators, or Fano-biased prefix decoders,
   not as better nearest-label oracles.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Exact coded product-sign stress test]
   \label{rem:coded-product-sign-stress}
   The first finite test of the preceding route replaces the full product-sign
   cube by an exactly enumerated binary linear code and keeps the same
   threshold storage rule.  For a code \(C\subseteq\{\pm1\}^r\), the query
   reports the top \(L\) codewords by \(\langle s,u(q)\rangle\), while a point
   \(x\) is stored in a reported label when
   \(\Psi_s(x)=\langle s,u(x)\rangle-\sum_a\log\cosh u_a(x)\) exceeds the far
   threshold whose per-reported-label tail is \(m^{\rho-1}/L\).  The script
   \texttt{impl/coded\_product\_sign\_panel\_stress.py} compares Reed--Muller,
   polar-weight, random-linear, and full-cube panels in this exact normal form.

   The \(r=16\) rows are already diagnostic.  With \(m=8192\), \(c=2\),
   \(\sigma=3.5\), near bit correlation \(0.95\), and \(L=8\), \(RM(2,4)\)
   has label exponent \(11/13=0.846\), close to the target \(1-\rho=6/7\),
   and the query decoder is not the bottleneck: the reported list has median
   query mass about \(0.997\) and lower \(5\%\) tilted mass \(0.79\)--\(0.84\).
   Nevertheless the near hit rate is only \(0.107\)--\(0.126\), essentially
   equal to the oracle over all codewords.  The sparse code simply does not
   contain a stored high-score near label often enough at the calibrated far
   threshold.  A random \([16,11]\) code behaves similarly; the polar-weight
   row selection coincides with the same RM panel at this dimension.

   The most promising finite signal is instead the one-label mode.  For the
   same \(RM(2,4)\) panel with \(L=1\), storage is still linear
   (\(0.908\) stored labels per point in the local panel), far load remains at
   the \(m^\rho\) budget, and the top label hits with probability
   \(0.324\)--\(0.436\) while the oracle hit probability is \(0.626\)--\(0.730\).
   The next RM size gives a comparable but weaker constant: \(RM(2,5)\) at
   \(m=2^{19}\), \(L=1\), and the same bit parameters has label exponent
   \(16/19=0.842\), storage \(0.852\) labels per point, and hit probability
   \(0.242\)--\(0.258\); a random \([32,16]\) code is indistinguishable.  At
   bit correlation \(0.99\), the \(RM(2,5)\) hit probability rises to
   \(0.375\)--\(0.425\), close to its oracle \(0.433\)--\(0.450\).

   Thus the coded product-sign experiment does not yet identify a special
   Reed--Muller or polar theorem.  It does show that a sparse
   \(m^{1-\rho}\)-label code can remove the full-cube top-\(k\) entropy
   obstruction and give a constant-probability top-one reporter with only
   linear storage, which could in principle be boosted over independent panels.
   The missing theorem is sharper: prove such a constant uniformly at the
   required bit correlation and growing blocklength, or prove that the observed
   constant decays.  Larger lists do not help in the tested regime, because the
   higher threshold needed to keep the same far load erases the extra query
   mass.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Random-code saddlepoint barrier for sparse product-sign top-one]
   \label{rem:sparse-product-sign-saddlepoint-barrier}
   The constant hit probability in \cref{rem:coded-product-sign-stress} should
   not be mistaken for an asymptotic random-code theorem.  The same script now
   includes an iid-label saddlepoint diagnostic.  Put
   \(b(z)=z-\log\cosh z\), let a sparse panel have \(2^k\) labels in
   \(r\) product-sign bits, and write \(R=k/r\).  For an iid random label set,
   the top query label has per-bit query level approximately
   \(q_R=\sigma\sqrt{2R\log2}\).  The calibrated far threshold has per-bit
   level \(t_R\) determined by the Cramer equation
   \[
      I_0(t_R)=R\log2,\qquad
      I_0(t)=\sup_{\theta\ge0}\{\theta t-\log\E e^{\theta b(Z)}\},
      \quad Z\sim N(0,\sigma^2).
   \]
   If the near/query bit correlation is \(\chi\), then under the usual
   exponential-tilt approximation for the selected label, the near selected
   bit is \(W\sim N(\chi q_R,\sigma^2)\).  Thus a necessary
   random-code top-one condition is
   \[
      \E b(W)\ge t_R,
   \]
   with a positive gap if one wants the hit probability bounded away from zero
   as \(r\to\infty\).

   The diagnostic points the other way.  At the target label exponent for
   \(c=2\), with \(R=1/2\), \(\sigma=3.5\), and bit correlation \(0.95\), the
   Cramer-calibrated median-max gaps for shapes \([32,16]\), \([64,32]\), and
   \([96,48]\) are \(-0.636\), \(-0.563\), and \(-0.549\) per bit; the normal
   hit approximations are \(0.067\), \(0.026\), and \(0.010\).  Even at bit
   correlation \(0.99\), the corresponding gaps are \(-0.586\), \(-0.513\),
   and \(-0.499\).  Sweeping \(\sigma\) on the \([96,48]\) shape does not
   remove the sign: at correlation \(0.95\), \(\sigma=1.0\) still has gap
   \(-0.113\), and larger \(\sigma\) only worsens it.

   This explains the finite experiments.  The exact \(r=16,32\) runs used an
   empirical finite-block threshold; at these small blocklengths the finite
   threshold is noticeably below the Cramer level, so top-one hit rates around
   \(0.2\)--\(0.4\) appear.  Once the far threshold is calibrated at its
   asymptotic rate, iid labels, random linear codes, and the tested
   Reed--Muller panels all point to decay rather than to a clean sparse
   product-sign theorem.  A positive coding/lattice route therefore has to
   exploit additional non-iid geometry--for example a decoder with a Fano
   potential that raises \(\E b(W)\) above \(t_R\), or a genuinely different
   score channel--rather than just replacing the full cube by a random sparse
   subcode.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Ordered-statistics sparse-subset channel]
   \label{rem:sparse-subset-channel-stress}
   The preceding barrier suggests the missing ingredient: the sparse labels
   should not be random codewords.  A direct non-iid alternative is the
   ordered-statistics sparse-subset channel already implicit in
   \cref{lem:information-set-threshold-reporter} and
   \cref{cor:ordered-statistics-information-set}.  Labels are pairs
   \((A,s)\), where \(A\subseteq[r]\), \(|A|=w\), and
   \(s\in\{\pm1\}^A\).  For bit logits \(u\), define the centered log
   probability
   \[
      \Phi_{A,s}(u)
      =
      \sum_{i\in A}s_i u_i
      -\log e_w(2\cosh u_1,\ldots,2\cosh u_r)
      +\log\!\left(2^w\binom{r}{w}\right),
      \tag{OSS0}
   \]
   where \(e_w\) is the elementary symmetric polynomial.  When \(w=r\),
   \((OSS0)\) is exactly the product-sign score.  For \(w<r\), query decoding
   is ordered-statistics decoding: choose the \(w\) largest \(|u_i(q)|\) and
   their signs.  Thus the query-selected label is biased toward reliable
   coordinates, not merely toward a random sparse codeword with a large average
   inner product.

   The diagnostic \texttt{impl/sparse\_subset\_channel\_stress.py} tests this
   exact channel.  It computes the partition function \(e_w\) by dynamic
   programming, calibrates the far threshold by a sampled Cramer transform of
   the fixed-label far score, and measures the near score of the OSD top
   label.  The first rows are qualitatively different from
   \cref{rem:sparse-product-sign-saddlepoint-barrier}.  At bit correlation
   \(0.95\), the narrow controls remain negative:
   \([16,1]\) has saddlepoint gaps \(-0.030,-0.033\) for
   \(\sigma=1,2\), and \([32,2]\) has gaps \(-0.022,-0.022\).  But the
   ordered-statistics regime turns positive: \([32,4]\) has gaps
   \(0.003,0.031\), \([64,4]\) has gaps \(0.015,0.043\), and \([64,8]\) has
   gaps \(0.060,0.119\).  The corresponding sampled-threshold hit estimates
   range from \(0.55\) for the weakest positive row to essentially one for the
   \(64\)-bit rows.

   These numbers are not yet a theorem, because the Cramer threshold is
   estimated from samples and the large-deviation calculation for
   \((OSS0)\) still has to be proved.  They do identify a non-equivalent
   positive target: prove a uniform gap
   \[
      \E\Phi_{A_*(q),s_*(q)}(u(p))>t_{r,w}
   \]
   where \(t_{r,w}\) is the far Cramer level satisfying
      \(I_{r,w}(t_{r,w})=r^{-1}\log(2^w\binom{r}{w})\).  If this gap holds for
   \(r=\Theta(\log m)\) and an appropriate width \(w\), then the OSD reporter
   gives a compact \(m^{1-\rho}\)-label channel with linear expected storage
   and constant one-panel hit probability.  Unlike the random sparse subcode,
   this route exploits reliability ordering and is therefore a genuine
   coding-theoretic construction path rather than a relabeling of the
   product-sign barrier.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Frozen asymptotic form for the sparse-subset channel]
   \label{rem:sparse-subset-asymptotic-normal-form}
   The theorem target behind \cref{rem:sparse-subset-channel-stress} should be
   stated directly as a large-deviation inequality, not as another decoder
   certificate.  Put \(w=\lambda r\), \(0<\lambda<1\), let
   \(\gamma_\sigma=N(0,\sigma^2)\), and define
   \[
      R_\lambda=H(\lambda)+\lambda\log2 .
   \]
   For a probability law \(\nu\) on the real line with finite Gaussian
   exponential moments, define the elementary-symmetric coefficient free
   energy
   \[
      \mathcal F_\lambda(\nu)
      =
      \inf_{\theta>0}
      \left\{
         \int \log(1+2\theta\cosh z)\,d\nu(z)
         -
         \lambda\log\theta
      \right\}.
      \tag{OSS1}
   \]
   The minimizing \(\theta\) is characterized by
   \[
      \lambda
      =
      \int \frac{2\theta\cosh z}{1+2\theta\cosh z}\,d\nu(z).
      \tag{OSS2}
   \]
   Thus, if the empirical law of \(z_1,\ldots,z_r\) tends to \(\nu\), then
   \[
      r^{-1}\log e_{\lambda r}(2\cosh z_1,\ldots,2\cosh z_r)
      \to \mathcal F_\lambda(\nu)
   \]
   at continuity points of the saddle.  The important point is that this is
   the quenched coefficient limit.  Replacing the integral of the logarithm in
   \((OSS1)\) by an annealed \(\log\E(1+2\theta\cosh Z)\) would average away
   exactly the denominator fluctuation that the fixed-label far tail must pay.

   For the canonical far label \(A=\{1,\ldots,\lambda r\}\) and all-positive
   signs, split the empirical laws of the active and inactive coordinates as
   \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_0\).  Sanov plus the coefficient limit gives the
   fixed-label upper-tail rate
   \[
      \mathcal J_{\lambda,\sigma}(t)
      =
      \inf
      \left\{
      \lambda D(\mu_1\|\gamma_\sigma)
      +(1-\lambda)D(\mu_0\|\gamma_\sigma):
      \lambda\!\int z\,d\mu_1(z)
      -
      \mathcal F_\lambda(\lambda\mu_1+(1-\lambda)\mu_0)
      +R_\lambda
      \ge t
      \right\}.
      \tag{OSS3}
   \]
   The storage/far-load threshold for a full signed width-\(\lambda r\) panel
   is therefore the level \(t_{\lambda,\sigma}\) satisfying
   \[
      \mathcal J_{\lambda,\sigma}(t_{\lambda,\sigma})=R_\lambda.
      \tag{OSS4}
   \]
   Equivalently, at exposed upper-tail levels \(\mathcal J\) is the Legendre
   transform of the scalar saddle
   \[
      \Lambda_{\lambda,\sigma}(\beta)
      =
      \beta R_\lambda
      +
      \sup_{\theta>0}
      \Bigg\{
         \beta\lambda\log\theta
         +
         \lambda\log
         \E_{Z\sim\gamma_\sigma}
         \frac{e^{\beta Z}}{(1+2\theta\cosh Z)^\beta}
         +
         (1-\lambda)\log
         \E_{Z\sim\gamma_\sigma}
         \frac{1}{(1+2\theta\cosh Z)^\beta}
      \Bigg\},
      \tag{OSS4a}
   \]
   namely
   \[
      \mathcal J_{\lambda,\sigma}(t)
      =
      \sup_{\beta\ge0}\{\beta t-\Lambda_{\lambda,\sigma}(\beta)\}.
      \tag{OSS4b}
   \]
   For fixed \(\beta>0\), the optimizing \(\theta\) balances the tilted
   denominator occupancy:
   \[
      \lambda
      =
      \lambda\,\E_{\beta,\theta}^{(1)}
      \frac{2\theta\cosh Z}{1+2\theta\cosh Z}
      +(1-\lambda)\,\E_{\beta,\theta}^{(0)}
      \frac{2\theta\cosh Z}{1+2\theta\cosh Z},
      \tag{OSS4c}
   \]
   where \(\E_{\beta,\theta}^{(1)}\) tilts
   \(\gamma_\sigma\) by
   \(e^{\beta Z}(1+2\theta\cosh Z)^{-\beta}\) and
   \(\E_{\beta,\theta}^{(0)}\) tilts it by
   \((1+2\theta\cosh Z)^{-\beta}\).  Thus the numerical target is a
   two-scalar saddle \((\beta,\theta)\), while the proof target remains the
   same Sanov coefficient limit.

   Now let \(Q_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\) be the query logits and
   \(P_i=\chi Q_i+\sigma\sqrt{1-\chi^2}\,E_i\) the near-point logits, with
   \(E_i\sim N(0,1)\) independent.  Let \(z_\lambda\) be defined by
   \(2\Prb[G\ge z_\lambda]=\lambda\) for \(G\sim N(0,1)\).  The OSD top label
   chooses the coordinates with \(|Q_i|\ge\sigma z_\lambda+o(1)\) and their
   signs.  Hence its near score has law-of-large-numbers limit
   \[
      M_{\lambda,\sigma,\chi}
      =
      2\chi\sigma\varphi(z_\lambda)
      -
      \mathcal F_\lambda(\gamma_\sigma)
      +R_\lambda ,
      \tag{OSS5}
   \]
   where \(\varphi\) is the standard normal density.  The denominator in
   \((OSS5)\) is still \(\mathcal F_\lambda(\gamma_\sigma)\), because it uses
   the empirical law of all near logits \(P_i\), not only the selected
   reliability set.

   The frozen sparse-subset theorem is the single strict inequality
   \[
      M_{\lambda,\sigma,\chi}>t_{\lambda,\sigma}.
      \tag{OSS6}
   \]
   If \((OSS6)\) holds with a constant gap and \(r\) is chosen so that
   \(rR_\lambda=(1-\rho)\log m+O(1)\), then a fixed far label is hit with
   probability \(m^{-(1-\rho)+o(1)}\), the expected storage per data point is
   constant, the expected far scan from the query-selected label is
   \(m^{\rho+o(1)}\), and a near pair lands in the query-selected stored label
   with probability tending to one.  Polylogarithmically many independent
   panels then give the desired local terminal reporter.

   The finite stress rows in \cref{rem:sparse-subset-channel-stress} should be
   interpreted through this asymptotic calibration.  Their sampled
   log-moment thresholds probe tails of order \(\exp(-rR_\lambda)\), often far
   below the number of generated far samples, and can therefore be optimistic.
   The positive route is \((OSS6)\) with \(t_{\lambda,\sigma}\) from
   \((OSS4a)\)--\((OSS4b)\), not a finite-block sampled gap by itself.

   This is also the right filter for possible code and lattice replacements.
   A Tanner, polar, Reed--Solomon, Construction-A, or lattice quotient block is
   useful here only if it preserves the reliability-ordered numerator in
   \((OSS5)\) while not increasing the far variational threshold
   \((OSS3)\)--\((OSS4)\).  A random sparse subcode fails precisely because it
   replaces the order statistic in \((OSS5)\) by an ordinary random-code
   extreme average.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Small-width barrier for the sparse-subset channel]
   \label{rem:sparse-subset-small-width-barrier}
   The ordered-statistics gain in \((OSS5)\) is not enough in the
   \(\lambda\downarrow0\) limit.  This rules out the tempting interpretation
   of \cref{rem:sparse-subset-channel-stress} as evidence for taking very
   sparse information sets.

   Let \(\bar\Phi(z)=\Prb[G\ge z]\) for \(G\sim N(0,1)\), let
   \(z_\lambda\) satisfy \(2\bar\Phi(z_\lambda)=\lambda\), and put
   \[
      a_\lambda=\frac{\varphi(z_\lambda)}{\bar\Phi(z_\lambda)}
      =\frac{2\varphi(z_\lambda)}{\lambda}.
   \]
   Then \(a_\lambda^2/2=\log(2/\lambda)+o(\log(1/\lambda))\), and
   \[
      R_\lambda
      =
      \lambda\log(2/\lambda)+\lambda+o(\lambda).
      \tag{OSS7}
   \]
   The saddle in \((OSS1)\) has
   \[
      \theta_\lambda
      =
      \frac{\lambda}{2\E\cosh Z}(1+o(1))
      =
      \frac{\lambda}{2e^{\sigma^2/2}}(1+o(1)),
      \qquad Z\sim N(0,\sigma^2),
   \]
   so
   \[
      \mathcal F_\lambda(\gamma_\sigma)
      =
      R_\lambda+\frac{\lambda\sigma^2}{2}+o(\lambda).
      \tag{OSS8}
   \]
   Therefore the OSD near mean is
   \[
      M_{\lambda,\sigma,\chi}
      =
      \lambda\chi\sigma a_\lambda
      -
      \frac{\lambda\sigma^2}{2}
      +o(\lambda).
      \tag{OSS9}
   \]

   Now fix any \(\chi<1\), and choose \(\eta>0\) with \(\chi+\eta<1\).
   In the far Sanov problem \((OSS3)\), tilt only the active coordinates to
   \(N((\chi+\eta)\sigma a_\lambda,\sigma^2)\) and keep the inactive
   coordinates at \(\gamma_\sigma\).  The entropy cost is
   \[
      \lambda\frac{(\chi+\eta)^2a_\lambda^2}{2}
      =
      ((\chi+\eta)^2+o(1))R_\lambda
      <R_\lambda
      \tag{OSS10}
   \]
   for all small enough \(\lambda\).  The denominator free energy changes only
   by \(o(\lambda a_\lambda)\): the active mixture has mass \(\lambda\), while
   \(\theta_\lambda e^{(\chi+\eta)\sigma a_\lambda}
   =\exp(-\log(1/\lambda)+O_\sigma(\sqrt{\log(1/\lambda)}))=o(1)\).
   Hence this far event has score
   \[
      M_{\lambda,\sigma,\chi}
      +
      \eta\lambda\sigma a_\lambda
      +
      o(\lambda a_\lambda)
   \]
   at rate strictly below \(R_\lambda\).  Consequently the threshold defined
   by \((OSS4)\) obeys
   \[
      t_{\lambda,\sigma}
      \ge
      M_{\lambda,\sigma,\chi}
      +
      \Omega_{\sigma,\chi}\!\left(
         \lambda\sqrt{\log(1/\lambda)}
      \right),
      \qquad \lambda\downarrow0.
      \tag{OSS11}
   \]
   Thus \((OSS6)\) fails throughout the small-width regime for every fixed
   near correlation \(\chi<1\).

   This argument is a genuine barrier, but only to sparse width.  A fixed
   moderate active fraction \(\lambda\) needs a separate obstruction, because
   the denominator occupancy and the active-coordinate large deviation are no
   longer separated by the leading small-\(\lambda\) expansion.  The next
   remark supplies that obstruction.  The small-width calculation also
   explains why finite rows such as \(w=4\) or \(8\) can look positive before
   the \(\exp(-rR_\lambda)\) far threshold is resolved accurately.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Mutual-information barrier for exact OSD sparse subsets]
   \label{rem:sparse-subset-mutual-information-barrier}
   In fact, the exact coordinatewise OSD sparse-subset channel is blocked for
   every fixed \(0<\lambda<1\) and every fixed \(\chi<1\).  The obstruction is
   not the small-\(\lambda\) expansion; it is that the OSD near law itself is
   a far Sanov witness whose cost is strictly below the label entropy.

   Let \((Q,U)\) be centered jointly Gaussian with
   \(\operatorname{Var}Q=\operatorname{Var}U=\sigma^2\) and
   \(\operatorname{Corr}(Q,U)=\chi\).  Let \(z_\lambda\) be as in
   \cref{rem:sparse-subset-asymptotic-normal-form}, and define the ternary
   query decision
   \[
      L(Q)=
      \begin{cases}
         +,& Q\ge \sigma z_\lambda,\\
         -,& Q\le -\sigma z_\lambda,\\
         0,& |Q|<\sigma z_\lambda.
      \end{cases}
   \]
   Then \(\Prb[L=+]=\Prb[L=-]=\lambda/2\), so
   \(H(L)=R_\lambda\).  Write \(\nu_+\) for the law of \(U\) conditioned on
   \(L=+\), and \(\nu_0\) for the law of \(U\) conditioned on \(L=0\).
   In the far variational problem \((OSS3)\), use \(\mu_1=\nu_+\) on the
   active coordinates and \(\mu_0=\nu_0\) on the inactive coordinates.

   This witness has exactly the OSD near numerator:
   \[
      \lambda\int z\,d\nu_+(z)
      =
      \lambda\,\E[U\mid Q\ge\sigma z_\lambda]
      =
      2\chi\sigma\varphi(z_\lambda).
      \tag{OSS12}
   \]
   It also has exactly the typical denominator.  Indeed, for every even
   measurable \(h\),
   \[
      \lambda\int h\,d\nu_+
      +(1-\lambda)\int h\,d\nu_0
      =
      \E h(U),
      \tag{OSS13}
   \]
   because the \(L=-\) conditional law is the reflection of \(\nu_+\).  Since
   the integrand in \((OSS1)\) is an even function of \(z\), \((OSS13)\)
   implies
   \[
      \mathcal F_\lambda(\lambda\nu_++(1-\lambda)\nu_0)
      =
      \mathcal F_\lambda(\gamma_\sigma).
      \tag{OSS14}
   \]
   Combining \((OSS12)\) and \((OSS14)\), this far witness has score
   precisely \(M_{\lambda,\sigma,\chi}\).

   Its Sanov cost is
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
      C_{\lambda,\sigma,\chi}
      &=
      \lambda D(\nu_+\|\gamma_\sigma)
      +(1-\lambda)D(\nu_0\|\gamma_\sigma) \\
      &=
      I(L;U).
   \end{aligned}
      \tag{OSS15}
   \]
   Since \(L\) is a deterministic function of \(Q\), the Markov chain
   \(L\to Q\to U\) and data processing give
   \[
      C_{\lambda,\sigma,\chi}=I(L;U)
      < I(L;Q)=H(L)=R_\lambda
      \tag{OSS16}
   \]
   whenever \(0<\lambda<1\) and \(\chi<1\).  The inequality is strict because
   the Gaussian channel from \(Q\) to \(U\) has nonzero noise, so \(L\) is not
   determined by \(U\).

   Therefore
   \[
      \mathcal J_{\lambda,\sigma}(M_{\lambda,\sigma,\chi})
      \le C_{\lambda,\sigma,\chi}<R_\lambda.
      \tag{OSS17}
   \]
   The far threshold solving \((OSS4)\) cannot be below the near OSD mean:
   \(t_{\lambda,\sigma}\ge M_{\lambda,\sigma,\chi}\).  Thus the strict gap
   \((OSS6)\) is impossible for the exact signed width-\(\lambda r\)
   coordinate-subset panel.

   This closes the raw OSS channel as a positive route.  A useful code or
   lattice construction must change one of the ingredients used above: reduce
   the charged label entropy by quotienting or aggregation, alter the far
   variational problem by a noncoordinate spectrum, or add an external
   Fano/decoder bias that is not equivalent to the ternary query decision
   \(L\).
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Raw top-one entropy barrier for symmetric Gaussian panels]
   \label{rem:raw-top-one-entropy-barrier}
   The preceding obstruction is an instance of a more general rule.  A
   symmetric raw top-one decoder cannot pay the full entropy of its label
   universe and still prove a strict far-threshold gap from a noisy near pair.

   Let \(\mathcal A_r\) be a finite transitive label set, let \(Q_r,U_r\) be a
   near Gaussian block pair, and let \(A=A(Q_r)\in\mathcal A_r\) be a
   deterministic top-one query decision.  Assume \(A\) is uniform on
   \(\mathcal A_r\), write
   \[
      R_r=r^{-1}H(A)=r^{-1}\log|\mathcal A_r|,
   \]
   and let \(\Phi_a(U_r)\) be the storage score for label \(a\).  Let
   \(P_U\) be the far law of \(U_r\).  Suppose symmetry makes
   \[
      m_r=\E[\Phi_A(U_r)\mid A=a],
      \qquad
      c_r=D(P_{U_r\mid A=a}\|P_U)
   \]
   independent of \(a\).  If \(J_r(t)\) is the fixed-label far variational
   rate
   \[
      J_r(t)=
      r^{-1}\inf\{D(\nu\|P_U): \E_\nu\Phi_a(U_r)\ge rt\},
      \tag{RTO1}
   \]
   then the conditional near law itself is an admissible far witness, and
   therefore
   \[
      J_r(m_r/r)\le c_r/r.
      \tag{RTO2}
   \]
   But
   \[
      c_r
      =
      I(A;U_r)
      \le I(A;Q_r)
      =
      H(A),
      \tag{RTO3}
   \]
   by data processing along \(A\to Q_r\to U_r\).  For a nondegenerate noisy
   Gaussian near channel and a nontrivial label decision, the inequality is
   strict:
   \[
      c_r<H(A).
      \tag{RTO4}
   \]
   Consequently a far threshold calibrated at full label entropy,
   \(J_r(t_r)=R_r\), cannot lie below the near top-one mean \(m_r/r\).  In
   particular, any law-of-large-numbers proof that the selected near score is
   typically above the full-entropy far threshold is impossible in this raw
   top-one normal form.

   This explains why the product-sign top-one, sparse random-code top-one, and
   exact OSD sparse-subset attempts all run into the same wall.  The decoder
   may choose an excellent label under \(Q_r\), but after the noisy Gaussian
   channel the data block \(U_r\) contains only \(I(A;U_r)\) nats about that
   label.  Charging storage and far load as if \(H(A)\) nats were recoverable
   leaves a missing information gap.

   The escape routes are now sharply constrained.  A useful code or lattice
   construction must either lower the charged entropy from \(H(A)\) to an
   output-sensitive list, prefix-moment, quotient, or sampler entropy; change
   the far spectrum so that \((RTO1)\) is not the relevant load rate; or add a
   certified Fano/branch-price bias whose retained reporter is charged by the
   biased prefix moment rather than by the raw label universe.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Information-charge test for retained code/lattice reporters]
   \label{lem:information-charge-survivor-test}
   Fix a block of length \(r\).  Let \(Q\) be the query block, let \(U\) be the
   corresponding near data block, and let \(P_U\) be the far data law.  Suppose
   a query-facing reporter exposes a finite transcript or label \(T\), possibly
   by a randomized kernel depending on \(Q\).  For each transcript \(t\), let
   \(\Phi_t(U)\) be the storage or bucket score that the retained index charges
   to that transcript, and define
   the fixed-transcript far rate
   \[
      J_t(a)
      =
      \frac1r
      \inf\left\{
         D(\nu\|P_U):
         \int \Phi_t(u)\,d\nu(u)\ge ra
      \right\}.
      \tag{ICT1}
   \]
   Put
   \[
      m_t=\frac1r\E[\Phi_t(U)\mid T=t],
      \qquad
      i_t=\frac1rD(P_{U\mid T=t}\|P_U).
      \tag{ICT2}
   \]
   If the retained certificate charges transcript \(t\) at far-tail rate
   \(C_t\), so that its threshold must lie at a level \(a_t\) with
   \(J_t(a_t)\ge C_t\), then
   \[
      C_t> i_t
      \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
      a_t\ge m_t .
      \tag{ICT3}
   \]
   Consequently any proof whose near success is a law-of-large-numbers
   comparison between the selected mean \(m_t\) and a fixed-transcript far
   threshold must satisfy the necessary information budget
   \[
      C_t\le i_t+o(1)
      \tag{ICT4}
   \]
   on the successful transcripts.  In a transitive symmetric panel,
   \(i_t=r^{-1}I(T;U)\) for every \(t\), and data processing for the Markov
   chain \(T-Q-U\) gives \(I(T;U)\le I(T;Q)\le H(T)\), with strict inequality
   for a nondegenerate noisy Gaussian near channel whenever \(T\) is not
   already determined by \(U\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The conditional near law \(P_{U\mid T=t}\) is an admissible trial measure in
   \((ICT1)\).  Its score is \(rm_t\) and its cost is \(ri_t\).  Hence
   \(J_t(m_t)\le i_t\).  Since the feasible set in \((ICT1)\) shrinks as the
   required score level \(a\) increases, \(J_t(a)\) is nondecreasing.  If
   \(C_t>i_t\), no threshold level below \(m_t\) can have far rate at least
   \(C_t\); therefore \(a_t\ge m_t\).  The symmetric statement follows by
   averaging \(D(P_{U\mid T=t}\|P_U)\) over \(t\), and the final inequalities
   are data processing for the Markov chain \(T-Q-U\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Gaussian information-charge contraction]
   \label{lem:gaussian-information-charge-contraction}
   In the setting of \cref{lem:information-charge-survivor-test}, assume the
   near block is a Gaussian channel
   \[
      U=\chi Q+\sqrt{1-\chi^2}\,G,
      \qquad
      0\le\chi<1,
      \tag{GIC1}
   \]
   where \(Q,G\) are independent centered Gaussian blocks with the same
   covariance.  Then every finite query transcript \(T\) generated from \(Q\)
   by a Markov kernel satisfies
   \[
      I(T;U)\le \chi^2 I(T;Q)\le\chi^2 H(T).
      \tag{GIC2}
   \]
   Consequently, in any transitive symmetric raw transcript panel with
   transcript entropy rate \(R_T=r^{-1}H(T)\), the selected near law has
   information charge at most
   \[
      i_t\le\chi^2R_T
      \tag{GIC3}
   \]
   for every transcript \(t\).  A fixed-transcript far threshold charged at
   any rate
   \[
      C_t>\chi^2R_T+o(1)
      \tag{GIC4}
   \]
   therefore cannot lie below the selected near mean \(m_t\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Rescale to standard Gaussian measure \(\gamma\).  For each transcript value
   \(t\), let
   \[
      f_t(q)=\frac{\Pr[T=t\mid Q=q]}{\Pr[T=t]},
      \qquad
      \Ent_\gamma(f)=\int f\log f\,d\gamma .
   \]
   Then
   \[
      I(T;Q)=\sum_t\Pr[T=t]\Ent_\gamma(f_t).
      \tag{GIC5}
   \]
   The density of \(U\) conditioned on \(T=t\), relative to its marginal
   Gaussian law, is \(P_\tau f_t\), where \(P_\tau\) is the
   Ornstein--Uhlenbeck semigroup with \(e^{-\tau}=\chi\).  Hence
   \[
      I(T;U)=\sum_t\Pr[T=t]\Ent_\gamma(P_\tau f_t).
      \tag{GIC6}
   \]
   Gaussian entropy contraction for the Ornstein--Uhlenbeck semigroup gives
   \[
      \Ent_\gamma(P_\tau f)\le e^{-2\tau}\Ent_\gamma(f)=\chi^2\Ent_\gamma(f).
      \tag{GIC7}
   \]
   Summing \((GIC7)\) in \((GIC6)\) proves the first inequality in
   \((GIC2)\); the second is \(I(T;Q)\le H(T)\).

   In the transitive symmetric case the number
   \(D(P_{U\mid T=t}\|P_U)\) is independent of \(t\), and its average over
   \(t\) is \(I(T;U)\).  Therefore \(i_t=r^{-1}I(T;U)\le\chi^2R_T\).  The
   final claim is \cref{lem:information-charge-survivor-test}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Randomized aggregate samplers obey the information screen]
   \label{cor:randomized-aggregate-sampler-information-screen}
   Work in the Gaussian near-block setting of
   \cref{lem:gaussian-information-charge-contraction}.  Let \(T\) be the
   transcript sampled by any query kernel: a reported codeword, a BCJR trellis
   path, a Construction-A residue, a discrete-Gaussian lattice point, or a
   bucket identifier.  For each transcript \(t\), let \(C_t\) be the
   fixed-transcript far-tail rate at which the retained certificate charges
   the storage score \(\Phi_t\), and let \(m_t,i_t\) be as in \((ICT2)\).
   Any law-of-large-numbers proof that transcript \(t\) succeeds by putting
   its far threshold below the selected near mean must satisfy
   \[
      C_t\le i_t+o(1).
      \tag{RAS1}
   \]
   Moreover the conditional information available to the sampled transcript is
   bounded on average by
   \[
      \sum_t\Pr[T=t]\,i_t
      =
      \frac1r I(T;U)
      \le
      \chi^2\frac1r I(T;Q)
      \le
      \chi^2\frac1r H(T).
      \tag{RAS2}
   \]
   In particular, in a transitive equivariant raw-path panel whose sampled
   transcript is marginally uniform on \(\exp\{rR+o(r)\}\) hidden paths and
   whose raw buckets are charged at \(C_t\ge R-o(1)\), no such threshold proof
   can succeed for any fixed \(\chi<1\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   The transcriptwise condition \((RAS1)\) is the contrapositive of
   \cref{lem:information-charge-survivor-test}.  Averaging the conditional
   divergences \(D(P_{U\mid T=t}\|P_U)\) over \(t\) gives \(I(T;U)\), and
   \cref{lem:gaussian-information-charge-contraction} gives \((RAS2)\).
   In the transitive equivariant case, \(i_t\) is independent of \(t\), while
   \(H(T)=rR+o(r)\).  Hence \(i_t\le\chi^2R+o(1)\).  Since \(\chi<1\), a raw
   charge \(C_t\ge R-o(1)\) eventually exceeds \(i_t\), and
   \cref{lem:information-charge-survivor-test} prevents the far threshold from
   lying below the selected near mean.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Polylog raw-list entropy barrier]
   \label{cor:polylog-raw-list-entropy-barrier}
   Let \(\mathcal A_r\) be a transitive label set with
   \(r^{-1}\log|\mathcal A_r|\to R>0\), and let
   \(U=\chi Q+\sqrt{1-\chi^2}G\) with fixed \(\chi<1\).  Suppose a raw query
   decoder reports an ordered list
   \[
      A_1(Q),\ldots,A_K(Q)\in\mathcal A_r,
      \qquad
      K=e^{o(r)},
      \tag{RLB1}
   \]
   and assume each reported position is equivariant under the label action, so
   \(A_j\) is uniform and its conditional laws are label-translates.  Assume
   also that each reported position is charged as an ordinary stored label:
   the fixed-label far threshold has rate
   \[
      C_r\ge R-o(1).
      \tag{RLB2}
   \]
   For each fixed position \(j\), condition on \(A_j=a\) and let \(m_{j,a}\)
   be the corresponding selected near mean.  Then the far threshold for that
   label cannot be below \(m_{j,a}\) for all sufficiently large \(r\).  Thus a
   polylogarithmic raw top-list can remove the information barrier only if it
   also changes the charged object--for example by output-sensitive bucket
   responsibility, quotient aggregation, reduced-cost rate coverage, or a
   Fano prefix moment.  Merely replacing top-one by top-\(K\) raw labels gives
   no law-of-large-numbers margin at the full label-entropy threshold.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   For every position \(j\), the transcript \(A_j\) has entropy at most
   \(\log|\mathcal A_r|=rR+o(r)\), and by equivariance it is in fact uniform
   on the labels it can report in the transitive panel.  The conditional
   divergences are independent of the label \(a\).  By
   \cref{lem:gaussian-information-charge-contraction}, that common conditional
   near-law charge is at most
   \[
      \chi^2R+o(1).
   \]
   Since \(\chi<1\) and \(R>0\), the charged far rate \(C_r\ge R-o(1)\) is
   strictly larger than this quantity for all large \(r\).  Applying
   \cref{lem:information-charge-survivor-test} to each reported position proves
   the threshold comparison.  The list length contributes only
   \(r^{-1}\log K=o(1)\), so it cannot close the constant rate gap.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exponential raw-list rate required]
   \label{cor:raw-list-rate-lower-bound}
   Work in the setting of
   \cref{cor:polylog-raw-list-entropy-barrier}, but allow the reported raw
   list length \(K_r\) to be exponential in the block length.  Put
   \[
      L_r=\frac1r\log K_r .
   \]
   Suppose the proof uses the list only through its ordinary union-bound or
   list-work discount: each fixed reported raw label is still charged at a
   fixed-label far-tail rate
   \[
      C_r\ge R-L_r-o(1).
      \tag{RLR1}
   \]
   If the fixed-label far threshold is to lie below the selected near mean for
   the successful reported positions, then necessarily
   \[
      L_r\ge (1-\chi^2)R-o(1).
      \tag{RLR2}
   \]
   Equivalently, a raw codeword list must output
   \[
      K_r\ge \exp\{((1-\chi^2)R-o(1))r\}
      \tag{RLR3}
   \]
   labels before the Gaussian information-charge obstruction can even be
   removed by list-size accounting.

   Thus polynomial block-list decoders such as ordinary SCL, Chase, GMD, or
   bounded-radius lattice enumeration do not rescue a full-rate raw bucket
   panel when \(r=\Theta(\log m)\): their \(r^{O(1)}\) output size is only
   polylogarithmic in \(m\).  An exponential-size list may pass this necessary
   screen, but it spends a genuine constant query-work exponent unless its
   labels are compressed by a quotient, aggregate sampler, or prefix-moment
   certificate.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Fix a reported position whose selected near mean is supposed to beat its
   fixed-label far threshold.  By the contrapositive of
   \cref{lem:information-charge-survivor-test}, this is possible only if
   \(C_r\le i_{j,a}+o(1)\), where \(i_{j,a}\) is the conditional divergence
   rate of the near data block given \(A_j=a\).  The Gaussian contraction
   bound in \cref{lem:gaussian-information-charge-contraction} gives
   \(i_{j,a}\le\chi^2R+o(1)\) for every equivariant raw position.  Combining
   this upper bound with \((RLR1)\) yields
   \[
      R-L_r-o(1)\le \chi^2R+o(1),
   \]
   which is \((RLR2)\).  Exponentiating gives \((RLR3)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Raw-label Fano prices do not change the charge]
   \label{cor:raw-label-fano-price-no-rescue}
   Work in the setting of
   \cref{cor:polylog-raw-list-entropy-barrier}.  Attach to every reported
   position and label a deterministic nonnegative price \(\pi_{j,a}\), and
   replace the storage score by the priced score
   \[
      \widetilde\Phi_{j,a}(U)=\Phi_a(U)-\pi_{j,a}.
      \tag{RFP1}
   \]
   Let \(\widetilde m_{j,a}=r^{-1}\E[\widetilde\Phi_{j,a}(U)\mid A_j=a]\),
   and calibrate the fixed-label far threshold for
   \(\widetilde\Phi_{j,a}\) at the ordinary raw-label rate
   \(C_r\ge R-o(1)\).  Then that far threshold still cannot lie below
   \(\widetilde m_{j,a}\) for all sufficiently large \(r\).

   Thus a Fano or pruning price attached to raw labels is not by itself an
   escape from the Gaussian information barrier.  The price becomes useful only
   when the retained certificate changes the charged object: the charged rate
   must be the prefix/list work moment, quotient bucket entropy, aggregate
   sampler entropy, or rate-coverage load, not the full raw label entropy.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   For the priced score, the conditional near law \(P_{U\mid A_j=a}\) is still
   an admissible far witness, now at mean \(\widetilde m_{j,a}\).  Its
   divergence from the far law is unchanged by subtracting the deterministic
   price.  By the proof of
   \cref{cor:polylog-raw-list-entropy-barrier}, that divergence rate is at
   most \(\chi^2R+o(1)\), which is strictly below \(C_r\ge R-o(1)\).  Applying
   \cref{lem:information-charge-survivor-test} to the priced score gives the
   claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[How a deep code or lattice construction can pass the test]
   \label{rem:code-lattice-survivor-map}
   \Cref{lem:information-charge-survivor-test} is the falsification test for
   code and lattice proposals after \cref{rem:raw-top-one-entropy-barrier}.
   A raw maximum-likelihood or nearest-codeword decoder for a code of size
   \(e^{rR}\) pays \(C_t=R\) when each codeword is stored as an independent
   bucket.  By \cref{lem:gaussian-information-charge-contraction}, the selected
   label has at most \(\chi^2R+o(1)\) information rate after the noisy near
   channel, so algebraic structure alone cannot make the selected near score
   beat the full-rate far threshold.  \Cref{cor:polylog-raw-list-entropy-barrier}
   gives the same conclusion for any equivariant top-\(\polylog m\) raw list:
   the list changes only lower-order query work unless the storage or bucket
   charge is also changed.  \Cref{cor:raw-list-rate-lower-bound} quantifies the
   missing amount: a raw list must have rate at least
   \((1-\chi^2)R\) before ordinary list accounting can erase the contraction
   gap.  Even a deterministic Fano price on the raw labels does not change this
   conclusion by
   \cref{cor:raw-label-fano-price-no-rescue}; the price has to be part of a
   different charged certificate, not a cosmetic shift of the same full-rate
   label score.

   The surviving uses of coding and lattice algorithms are therefore more
   specific.
   Polar, Reed--Muller, Reed--Solomon, Tanner, tensor, or expander codes are
   useful when their list-recovery or soft-decision decoders implement the
   threshold/reduced-cost reporters of
   \cref{lem:soft-list-recovery-reporter},
   \cref{cor:ordinary-list-recovery-positive-coverage}, and
   \cref{cor:unified-soft-decoded-rate-coverage}; the charged quantity is then
   the reported transcript work or reduced-cost bucket class, not the full code
   entropy.  GMD, Chase, and OSD are useful only in the
   \cref{lem:min-entropy-information-set} sense: choose a chart with small
   soft entropy \(\Lambda_*(q)\), enumerate the certified discrepancy ball, and
   exact-filter.  The raw constant-weight OSD channel of
   \cref{rem:sparse-subset-mutual-information-barrier} fails because its
   charge remains \(H(L)\).

   Construction-A/D quotients, Barnes--Wall or Barnes--Sloane recursion, sphere
   enumeration, sequential lattice decoding, and discrete-Gaussian samplers can
   pass only if they expose one of two certificates already isolated in the
   paper.  In the deterministic form, the pruning metric must be a Fano-biased
   prefix score with a certified moment
   \(\sum g_q(u)\exp(\beta U_q(u))\) as in
   \cref{lem:fano-biased-prefix-list}; the branch prices lower \(C_t\) to the
   actual work entropy of the stack.  In the sampled form, the construction
   must compute aggregate bucket weights on a compact state graph as in
   \cref{lem:compressed-aggregate-sampler} and
   \cref{cor:bcjr-trellis-quotient-sampler}, so that the charged object is the
   quotient bucket law rather than the number of hidden lattice or code paths.
   \Cref{cor:randomized-aggregate-sampler-information-screen} shows that
   query randomization itself is not an escape: a sampled hidden path or
   lattice point still carries only \(I(T;U)\le\chi^2 I(T;Q)\) nats through the
   noisy near channel.  Small ordinary quotient classes are not enough; a
   genuine aggregate sampler or responsibility certificate is needed to lower
   the charge below the conditional information budget in \((ICT4)\) and
   \((RAS1)\).
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Audit of deep code and lattice candidates]
   \label{rem:deep-code-lattice-audit}
   The preceding screen leaves only a few genuinely different imports from
   coding and lattice algorithms.

   \begin{itemize}
      \item Algebraic soft-decision and list-recovery codes
      (Reed--Solomon, folded Reed--Solomon, tensor, expander, and related
      outer codes) are useful as \emph{reporters}.  They can implement the
      positive-coverage and reduced-cost separators after dyadic unweighting.
      The theorem to prove is not that the nearest codeword is good; it is that
      the returned soft list has small certified work entropy and that its
      retained buckets pass the storage/far/near spectrum tests.

      \item Polar, Reed--Muller, convolutional, and low-state trellis codes are
      useful as \emph{partition-function samplers}.  If their query likelihood
      factors along an acyclic state graph, BCJR or successive-cancellation
      recursions compute the exact tilted path law.  The natural experiment and
      theorem target is then a transfer-matrix bucket spectrum for
      \((BQ1)\)--\((BQ3)\), not SCL nearest-codeword performance.  Polynomial
      SCL lists remain blocked by \cref{cor:raw-list-rate-lower-bound} unless
      their prefixes are charged by a Fano moment or quotient sampler.

      \item Tanner and LDPC-style constructions are promising only after
      exactness is restored.  Ordinary loopy belief propagation is not a proof
      of the aggregate law in \cref{lem:compressed-aggregate-sampler}.  One must
      either use a genuine trellis or junction tree of polylogarithmic size, or
      prove that the approximate marginals perturb \((BQ1)\)--\((BQ3)\) by only
      polylogarithmic factors.  For a generic random LDPC block the junction-tree
      width is linear, so its raw factor graph is not yet a compact sampler in
      this sense.

      \item Construction-A and Construction-D lattices reduce to residue-code
      soft decisions by \cref{lem:construction-a-theta-quotient}.  This is the
      cleanest lattice route: choose the modulus, scale, rotation, and residue
      code so that theta reliabilities can be summed or sampled compactly, then
      verify the induced storage, far sampled co-load, and near sampled mass.
      Integer-lift enumeration is a local finishing step; it should not be the
      main charged entropy.  By
      \cref{cor:randomized-aggregate-sampler-information-screen}, sampling an
      integer lift or residue from the exact discrete-Gaussian law still does
      not rescue full raw-residue bucket charge; the residue/bucket quotient
      must be the object whose spectrum is certified.

      \item Barnes--Wall, Barnes--Sloane, and other recursive lattices are
      useful if the recursion is retained as a small state graph with aggregate
      terminal buckets.  Their list-decoding theorems help only when the
      recursion supplies either a Fano-biased prefix moment or an exact quotient
      partition function.  A raw bounded-distance list is again just a raw list
      unless the bucket charge is compressed.

      \item Sphere enumeration, sequential lattice decoding, and extreme
      pruning match the deterministic Fano-prefix certificate.  The pruning
      radii must be read as branch prices whose exponential prefix moment is
      certified; nearest-plane or closest-vector success alone does not lower
      the far charge.

      \item Discrete-Gaussian lattice samplers are closest to the continuous
      ideal spectrum of
      \cref{lem:critical-tilted-gaussian-sampled-spectrum}.  They are useful
      only if the sampler is coupled to retained bucket sets with a verified
      quotient spectrum.  Sampling hidden lattice points accurately is not
      enough when many hidden points map to the same expensive stored bucket.
   \end{itemize}

   Thus the next concrete construction to test is a compact exact sampler, not
   another raw decoder: for example a Construction-A residue code with a
   low-state trellis or recursive factorization, analyzed by transfer matrices
   for \((BQ1)\)--\((BQ3)\).  If that spectrum fails, the failure is a real
   storage/far-load barrier rather than a reformulation of the top-list
   obstruction.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Why ordinary ANN does not implement the score-max target]\label{rem:score-max-ordinary-ann}
   One can force the perturbed center $y=Y/t$ to be close to $q$ by taking
   $t$ large. In dimension $D$, if
   \[
      t\ge C(D+\log m)/(a^2r^2),
   \]
   then $\|y-q\|\le ar$ with probability at least $1-m^{-3}$. On that event,
   any true near point is within $(1+a)r$ of $y$, while every invalid point is
   farther than $(c-a)r$ from $y$. Thus an ordinary
   \[
      \kappa(a)=\frac{c-a}{1+a}
   \]
   approximate-nearest-neighbor oracle for query center $y$ would return a
   valid $cr$-neighbor after verification.

   This observation is only a sanity check. Since
   $\rho_{\kappa(a)}=\rho_c+O_c(a)$, keeping the exponent loss polylogarithmic
   requires $a=O_c((\log\log m)/\log m)$. The resulting subproblem is then just
   ANN at approximation $c-O_c(a)$ with essentially the same optimal exponent.
   Hence a black-box ordinary ANN call would make the score-max route circular;
   a proof of \cref{asm:smoothed-score-max} must exploit the smoothed
   maximum-score structure itself.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Why multiplicative ANN does not implement Gumbel-MIPS]\label{rem:gumbel-mips-not-ann}
   The Gumbel primitive needs an additive score guarantee, not a multiplicative
   distance guarantee. If $B\ge\max_x\Gamma_x$, one may lift
   \[
      X_x=\left(x,\sqrt{2(B-\Gamma_x)/t}\right),
      \qquad
      Y'=(y,0),
   \]
   so that minimizing $\|X_x-Y'\|^2$ is equivalent to maximizing
   $A_Y(x)+\Gamma_x$. However, a $c$-ANN answer in the lifted space gives only
   \[
      \|X_I-Y'\|^2
      \le
      c^2\min_x\|X_x-Y'\|^2,
   \]
   which can translate into additive score error
   \[
      \frac t2(c^2-1)\min_x\|X_x-Y'\|^2.
   \]
   Under the smoothing distribution, this minimum can contain the common
   $\|y-q\|^2$ term, of order $d/t$, so the additive score error can be
   $\Theta(d)$ rather than $O(\log\log m)$.

   The obstruction is real even without Gumbel marks. Take $p=q=0$ and
   $x=Lr e_1$ with $L>c$. For $y=q+g$ and $g\sim N(0,I_d/t)$,
   \[
      \|x-y\|^2-\|p-y\|^2=L^2r^2-2Lrg_1.
   \]
   With high probability this is $\Omega(L^2r^2)$, so the Gaussian weight of
   $x$ is polynomially smaller than that of $p$ when $t=\Theta(\log m/r^2)$.
   In high dimension, nevertheless, the shared orthogonal term
   $\|g_\perp\|^2$ can dominate both distances, making
   $\|x-y\|/\|p-y\|$ arbitrarily close to one. A multiplicative ANN oracle may
   then return $x$ with constant probability, which would violate the
   pointwise domination required by \cref{lem:gumbel-additive-domination}.
\end{remark}

A stronger all-listing sufficient form of the same posterior target is captured
by the following assumption.  It is useful as a baseline because it allows an
implicit channel, a signature tree, a multiprobe score index, or a direct
sampled-prefix reporter, but \cref{asm:normalized-likelihood-leader-sampler}
is the lighter sampler target.

\begin{assumption}[Multiscale structured likelihood decoder]\label{asm:multiscale-structured-likelihood}
   Fix $c>1$ and $\rho=\rho_c$. For every bounded-diameter localized node with $m$ resident points there is a structured, output-sensitive posterior decoder over dyadic mass scales
   \[
      \xi\in[1/m,\eta_m],
      \qquad
      \eta_m=m^{-\rho}\log^{A_c}m,
   \]
   with the following properties.
   \begin{itemize}
      \item At scale $\xi$, children are certified subsets $C\subseteq S$ with $\xi/2\le |C|/m\le\xi$, and each stored child has a representative point.
      \item One independent group at one scale can be decoded for a query in $d\log^{O_c(1)}m$ work plus output work.
      \item For every query $q$ and every scale $\xi$, the one-group active-child and stored-child moments satisfy
      \[
         \sum_{C\text{ at scale }\xi}\lambda_q(C)\mu(C)^\rho
         \le
         \xi^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m,
         \qquad
         \sum_{C\text{ at scale }\xi}\sigma(C)\mu(C)^{1+\rho}
         \le
         \xi^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m.
      \]
      \item For every near pair $(p,q)$ in the node, either a uniform resident guard of size $m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m$ finds a valid $cr$-neighbor with constant probability, or the pure multiscale value is inverse-polylogarithmic:
      \[
         \sum_{\xi\le\eta_m}
         \sum_{\substack{C\text{ at scale }\xi\\p\in C,\ C\subseteq\Ball(q,cr)}}
         \lambda_q(C)\mu(C)^{-\rho}
         \ge
         \log^{-O_c(1)}m.
      \]
   \end{itemize}
\end{assumption}

The last bullet is deliberately a pre-amplification value condition. At a fixed
scale $\xi$, value $V_\xi$ only implies hit intensity on the order of
$\xi^\rho V_\xi$ in one independent group; the query algorithm below supplies
$\xi^{-\rho}$ groups at that scale. This is the scale-aware version of the
structured-channel condition and is the reason the assumption does not impose a
coarse lower bound such as $\xi\ge m^{-1/(2c^2)}$.

\begin{proposition}[Conditional multiscale structured endpoint]\label{prop:multiscale-structured-polylog}
   Under \cref{asm:multiscale-structured-likelihood}, worst-case Euclidean ANN has query time
   \[
      Q(n,d)=d\,n^{\rho_c}\log^{O_c(1)}n
   \]
   and space
   \[
      S(n,d)=dn+n^{1+\rho_c}\log^{O_c(1)}n.
   \]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
   Work after bounded-diameter localization. At a node of size $m$, first sample the resident guard from \cref{asm:multiscale-structured-likelihood}. If it fails, apply \cref{lem:dyadic-structured-amplification} with
   \[
      h=\log^{-O_c(1)}m,
      \qquad
      \eta=\eta_m=m^{-\rho}\log^{O_c(1)}m.
   \]
   The smallest dyadic scale is $1/m$, so the total local decoding and active-output work is
   \[
      d\,m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m.
   \]
   With constant probability, the decoder activates a stored child $C$ containing the true near point and satisfying $C\subseteq\Ball(q,cr)$. Returning and verifying the stored representative of $C$ therefore succeeds. The guard case also succeeds by definition.

   The expected number of stored child descriptions over all repeated scales is
   \[
      m^{1+\rho}\log^{O_c(1)}m
   \]
   by \cref{lem:dyadic-structured-amplification}. Adding the original data and the bounded-diameter localization copies gives the displayed space bound. Standard truncation and a constant number of independent copies give capped query bounds with constant success probability.
\end{proof}

For comparison, the coarse finite-channel route is recovered by collapsing the continuum of thresholds to one explicit top-$\xi$ child per outcome. Let $\xi\in(0,1)$ and let $C_j^\xi$ be the top $\lceil \xi m\rceil$ points by posterior ratio $R_j(x)$. If $r_{j,1}\ge\cdots\ge r_{j,m}$ are these ratios, put
\[
   \Delta_j=r_{j,1}^{\beta}-r_{j,\lceil\xi m\rceil+1}^{\beta}.
\]
Store $C_j^\xi$ with Poisson mean
\[
   \Lambda_j=\xi^\rho\mu_j^\beta\Delta_j
\]
and activate each copy with probability $K_q(j)^{s_\beta}$. Then the single top-$\xi$ child dominates the restricted part of the negative moment coming from all thresholds with $\Phi_j(u)\le\xi$. Moreover $\mu_j^\beta\Delta_j\le1$, so the expected number of active top-$\xi$ children in one channel group is at most
\[
   \xi^\rho\sum_jK_q(j)^{s_\beta}
   \le
   \xi^\rho B^\beta .
\]
Thus if $B\le\xi^{-1}\log^{O(1)}m$ and $\beta=O(1/\log m)$, one group has only $O_c(\xi^\rho)$ expected active children. This is precisely where explicit enumeration imposes the coarse scale $\xi=m^{-\rho/(1+\rho)}$: evaluating all $B\simeq\xi^{-1}$ outcomes in $\xi^{-\rho}$ repetitions costs $\xi^{-(1+\rho)}$, so fitting the $m^\rho$ budget forces $\xi\ge m^{-\rho/(1+\rho)}$. This finite specialization is therefore a baseline and diagnostic, not the structured target.

\begin{assumption}[Finite restricted channel]\label{asm:finite-restricted-channel}
   Fix $c>1$ and let
   \[
      \rho=\rho_c,
      \qquad
      \vartheta=\frac{\rho}{1+\rho}=\frac1{2c^2},
      \qquad
      \xi=m^{-\vartheta},
      \qquad
      \beta=\Theta_c(1/\log m).
   \]
   There is a query-decodable finite channel with
   \[
      B\le\xi^{-1}\log^{O_c(1)}m
   \]
   outcomes, evaluable on the node in $dB\log^{O_c(1)}m$ work, such that for every near pair $p,q$ in the node, either a uniformly sampled resident guard block of size $O(\xi^{-1}\log n)$ returns a valid $cr$-neighbor with constant probability, or the restricted top-$\xi$ posterior-superlevel negative moment for $p,q$ is at least $\log^{-O_c(1)}m$.
\end{assumption}

\Cref{thm:continuous-likelihood-balls} proves the geometric part of the posterior approach: likelihood level sets are Euclidean balls, and unless a resident guard succeeds there is constant negative-moment value on children that contain the near point and no invalid point. \Cref{lem:ideal-likelihood-scale-profile} proves that the ideal continuous measure also has the exact dyadic query and storage moments required for $m^\rho$ amplification. What is not yet proved is the structured decoding step in \cref{asm:multiscale-structured-likelihood}: an implicit decoder must materialize stored representatives and preserve that pure value across dyadic mass scales with output-sensitive listing. The finite special case below remains useful as a coarse diagnostic; there the missing statement is balanced, query-decodable compilation with only $B\simeq\xi^{-1}$ outcomes.

The corresponding finite special-case diagnostic is to measure the left-hand side of \cref{asm:finite-restricted-channel}. For a proposed finite channel, let $\tau_j$ be the top-$\xi$ posterior threshold of $R_j(x)$ over the data, and for each planted near pair $(p,q)$ compute
\[
   \mathcal H_\xi(p,q)
   =
   \sum_j
   \mu_j^\beta K_q(j)^{1-\beta}
   \left(R_j(p)^\beta-\tau_j^\beta\right)_+ .
\]
Also compute the resident-guard density
\[
   g(q)=\frac1m|\{x\in S:\|x-q\|\le cr\}|.
\]
The conjecture predicts that the lower quantiles of $g(q)+\mathcal H_\xi(p,q)$ should be at worst inverse-polylogarithmic in $m$, and ideally bounded below by a constant.

\begin{lemma}[Soft-surplus decomposition]\label{lem:soft-surplus-decomposition}
   Let
   \[
      \mathsf A_\beta(p,q)=\sum_j K_p(j)^\beta K_q(j)^{1-\beta}.
   \]
   If \(\mathsf A_\beta(p,q)>0\), define the tilted outcome law
   \[
      W_{p,q}(j)=
      \frac{K_p(j)^\beta K_q(j)^{1-\beta}}{\mathsf A_\beta(p,q)}
   \]
   and the soft posterior surplus
   \[
      \sigma_j(p)=
      \left(1-\left(\frac{\tau_j}{R_j(p)}\right)^\beta\right)_+ .
   \]
   Then
   \[
      \mathcal H_\xi(p,q)
      =
      \mathsf A_\beta(p,q)\,
      \E_{j\sim W_{p,q}}\sigma_j(p).
      \tag{SSD}
   \]
   In particular, if \(j_\star\) maximizes
   \(K_p(j)^\beta K_q(j)^{1-\beta}\), then the fraction of the diagnostic
   value explained by the single tilted winner is
   \[
      \frac{W_{p,q}(j_\star)\sigma_{j_\star}(p)}
           {\E_{j\sim W_{p,q}}\sigma_j(p)}
   \]
   whenever the denominator is nonzero.  For a balanced-softmax channel, this
   tilted winner is the maximum-probability outcome under \(K_z\) with
   \(z=\beta p+(1-\beta)q\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Since \(K_p(j)=\mu_jR_j(p)\), each summand in \(\mathcal H_\xi(p,q)\)
   equals
   \[
      K_p(j)^\beta K_q(j)^{1-\beta}
      \left(1-\left(\frac{\tau_j}{R_j(p)}\right)^\beta\right)_+ .
   \]
   Summing and normalizing by \(\mathsf A_\beta(p,q)\) proves \((SSD)\).
   The final statement is the same softmax interpolation identity used below.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Top-\(k\) tilted backup certificate]
   \label{cor:top-k-tilted-backup}
   In the setting of \cref{lem:soft-surplus-decomposition}, let \(T_k(p,q)\)
   be the \(k\) largest outcomes under the tilted weights
   \(K_p(j)^\beta K_q(j)^{1-\beta}\), and define
   \[
      \theta_k(p,q)=
      \frac{\sum_{j\in T_k(p,q)}W_{p,q}(j)\sigma_j(p)}
           {\E_{j\sim W_{p,q}}\sigma_j(p)}
   \]
   when the denominator is nonzero, and \(\theta_k=0\) otherwise.  If
   \(\mathcal H_\xi(p,q)\ge h\) and \(\theta_k(p,q)\ge\gamma\), then the
   top-\(\xi\) posterior children indexed by \(T_k(p,q)\) carry restricted
   value at least \(\gamma h\).  For a balanced-softmax channel, \(T_k(p,q)\)
   is exactly the set of top \(k\) outcomes under \(K_z\), where
   \(z=\beta p+(1-\beta)q\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   This is \((SSD)\) with the expectation restricted to \(T_k(p,q)\).  The
   balanced-softmax statement follows from the same interpolation identity as
   before.
\end{proof}

The set \(T_k(p,q)\) is not a query-facing object, because it contains the
unknown witness \(p\).  Its role is diagnostic and contractual: it says exactly
what a hidden-label leader reporter must recover.  If a retained reporter can
materialize these \(k\) labels, or labels with comparable restricted value, in
output-sensitive time, then the captured value pays only the \(k\)-label work
rather than the full \(B\)-outcome enumeration cost.  The residual
\((1-\theta_k)\mathcal H_\xi\) is the concrete lower-tail gap left by a
top-\(k\) backup.

\begin{corollary}[Query-visible top-\(k\) backup certificate]
   \label{cor:query-top-k-backup}
   Keep the notation of \cref{lem:soft-surplus-decomposition}.  Let \(Q_k(q)\)
   be the \(k\) largest outcomes under the query law \(K_q\), and put
   \[
      \theta^{\rm qry}_k(p,q)=
      \frac{\sum_{j\in Q_k(q)}W_{p,q}(j)\sigma_j(p)}
           {\E_{j\sim W_{p,q}}\sigma_j(p)}
   \]
   with value \(0\) when the denominator is zero.  If
   \(\mathcal H_\xi(p,q)\ge h\) and
   \(\theta^{\rm qry}_k(p,q)\ge\gamma\), then the query-visible \(k\) labels
   \(Q_k(q)\) carry restricted value at least \(\gamma h\).  Consequently, an
   output-sensitive reporter for the top \(k\) outcomes of \(K_q\), followed by
   the stored top-\(\xi\) posterior children for those outcomes, avoids the
   full \(B\)-outcome enumeration whenever \(\theta^{\rm qry}_k\) has an
   inverse-polylogarithmic lower tail.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
   Restrict the expectation in \((SSD)\) to \(Q_k(q)\).  The set \(Q_k(q)\)
   depends only on the query and the retained finite channel, so reporting it
   is an implementation problem rather than a hidden-witness problem.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Query-to-tilted prefix stability]\label{lem:query-tilted-prefix-stability}
   Let the finite channel have positive probabilities \(K_x(j)\).  For a
   pair \((p,q)\) and exponent \(\beta\in[0,1]\), order the hidden tilted
   labels by
   \[
      W_{p,q}(j)\propto K_p(j)^\beta K_q(j)^{1-\beta}.
   \]
   Let \(Q_k(q)\) be the top \(k\) labels under \(K_q\), and let
   \(g_k(q)\) be the gap between the \(k\)-th and \((k+1)\)-st largest values
   of \(\log K_q(j)\), with \(g_k(q)=+\infty\) if there are at most \(k\)
   labels.  More generally, for \(L\ge k\), let \(g_{k,L}(q)\) be the gap
   between the \(k\)-th and \((L+1)\)-st largest values of \(\log K_q(j)\),
   with \(g_{k,L}(q)=+\infty\) if there are at most \(L\) labels.  Define the
   centered tilt radius
   \[
      \Delta_{p,q}
      =
      \frac{\beta}{2}
      \left(
        \max_j\log\frac{K_p(j)}{K_q(j)}
        -
        \min_j\log\frac{K_p(j)}{K_q(j)}
      \right).
      \tag{QTS}
   \]
   If \(g_k(q)>2\Delta_{p,q}\), then the hidden tilted top \(k\) labels are
   exactly \(Q_k(q)\).  More generally, if \(g_{k,L}(q)>2\Delta_{p,q}\), then
   the hidden tilted top \(k\) labels are contained in \(Q_L(q)\).  Consequently, if
   \(\mathcal H_\xi(p,q)\ge h\) and the hidden tilted top \(k\) labels carry
   a \(\gamma\) fraction of the soft-surplus value, then the query-visible
   labels \(Q_L(q)\) carry at least \(\gamma h\) restricted value.  Conversely,
   if a hidden tilted top-\(k\) label lies outside \(Q_k(q)\), then
   \(g_k(q)\le2\Delta_{p,q}\), and if such a label lies outside \(Q_L(q)\),
   then \(g_{k,L}(q)\le2\Delta_{p,q}\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The tilted ordering is the ordering of
   \[
      \log K_q(j)+\beta\log\frac{K_p(j)}{K_q(j)}
   \]
   because the normalizing constant of \(W_{p,q}\) is independent of \(j\).
   After subtracting the midpoint of the second term's range, the perturbation
   from the query log-probabilities has absolute value at most
   \(\Delta_{p,q}\).  If \(i\in Q_k(q)\) and \(j\notin Q_k(q)\), then
   \[
      \log K_q(i)-\log K_q(j)\ge g_k(q).
   \]
   Under the tilted perturbation this difference can decrease by at most
   \(2\Delta_{p,q}\).  Hence \(g_k(q)>2\Delta_{p,q}\) makes every label in
   \(Q_k(q)\) beat every label outside \(Q_k(q)\) in the hidden tilted order.
   The containment statement is identical: if \(j\notin Q_L(q)\), then every
   one of the \(k\) labels in \(Q_k(q)\) beats \(j\) after the perturbation
   whenever \(g_{k,L}(q)>2\Delta_{p,q}\), so \(j\) cannot be among the hidden
   tilted top \(k\).
   The value statement follows by applying
   \cref{cor:top-k-tilted-backup} and
   \cref{cor:query-top-k-backup} with the containing query label set.  The
   contrapositives give the final claims.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Product-sign top-\(k\) softmax reporter]\label{lem:product-sign-top-k-reporter}
   Let \(B=2^r\).  A product-sign finite channel has labels
   \(s\in\{\pm1\}^r\) and query logits of the additive form
   \[
      L_q(s)=\sum_{a=1}^r s_a u_a(q),
      \qquad
      u_a(q)=\lambda\ip{v_a}{q}+b_a ,
   \]
   where the \(b_a\) are optional bit offsets.  Then the exact top \(k\)
   outcomes of \(K_q(s)\propto\exp L_q(s)\) can be reported after computing
   the \(r\) numbers \(u_a(q)\), using \(O(r\log r+k\log k)\) additional
   arithmetic and \(O(k+r)\) memory.  In particular, when
   \(r=\log B\le\log^{O_c(1)}m\) and \(k=\log^{O_c(1)}m\), this is a
   \(d\log^{O_c(1)}m\)-work reporter for
   \cref{prop:query-top-k-channel-compiler}.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Let \(s^\star_a=\operatorname{sign}u_a(q)\), with a fixed deterministic
   tie rule.  If \(F\subseteq[r]\) is the set of bits flipped away from
   \(s^\star\), then
   \[
      L_q(s^F)=L_q(s^\star)-\sum_{a\in F}2|u_a(q)|.
   \]
   Thus the top \(k\) labels are exactly the \(k\) smallest subset sums of the
   nonnegative weights \(w_a=2|u_a(q)|\).  After sorting the weights, the
   standard best-first subset-sum enumerator starts from the empty subset and,
   for a popped subset whose largest sorted index is \(i\), pushes the two
   children obtained by adding \(i+1\) and by replacing \(i\) with \(i+1\),
   suppressing duplicates.  This heap enumerates subset sums in nondecreasing
   order, so translating each subset back to flipped signs gives the exact
   top \(k\) labels.  Computing the \(u_a(q)\)'s costs \(dr\), sorting costs
   \(O(r\log r)\), and the heap performs \(O(k)\) pushes and pops.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Product-sign posterior-rank score]\label{lem:product-sign-posterior-score}
   For a product-sign channel
   \[
      K_x(s)=
      \prod_{a=1}^r
      \frac{\exp(s_a u_a(x))}{2\cosh u_a(x)},
      \qquad s\in\{\pm1\}^r,
   \]
   define the centered posterior score
   \[
      \Psi_s(x)=
      \sum_{a=1}^r\bigl(s_a u_a(x)-\log\cosh u_a(x)\bigr).
      \tag{PSS}
   \]
   If \(\pi_s\) is any positive reference output mass and
   \(R_s(x)=K_x(s)/\pi_s\), then
   \[
      \log R_s(x)=\Psi_s(x)-\log(2^r\pi_s).
      \tag{PSR}
   \]
   Consequently, for any data node and any \(\eta\), the posterior rank-margin
   event
   \[
      R_s(p)\ge e^\Delta\tau_s
   \]
   is exactly
   \[
      \Psi_s(p)\ge Q_{s,\eta}^{\rm node}+\Delta,
      \tag{PSQ}
   \]
   where \(Q_{s,\eta}^{\rm node}\) is the top-\(\eta\) empirical quantile of
   \(\Psi_s(x)\) over node points.  In particular, the rank-margin event is
   independent of the output-mass imbalance \(\pi_s\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   Expanding the product gives
   \[
      \log K_x(s)=
      \sum_a s_a u_a(x)-\sum_a\log(2\cosh u_a(x))
      =
      \Psi_s(x)-r\log2.
   \]
   Since \(2^r\) is the number of labels, \((PSR)\) follows after subtracting
   \(\log\pi_s\).  The same constant \(-\log(2^r\pi_s)\) appears in
   \(\log R_s(p)\) and in the empirical top-\(\eta\) threshold
   \(\log\tau_s\), so it cancels in the margin comparison.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Fixed-width product-sign containment tail]
   \label{lem:product-sign-containment-tail}
   In the product-sign channel, write
   \(u_x=(u_1(x),\ldots,u_r(x))\).  For \(v\in\R^r\), let
   \(A_1(v)\le\cdots\le A_{2^r}(v)\) be the sorted list of subset sums
   \[
      \sum_{a\in F}2|v_a|,
      \qquad F\subseteq[r].
   \]
   Then the query rank-\(k\) to rank-\((L+1)\) log-probability gap is
   \[
      g_{k,L}(q)=A_{L+1}(u_q)-A_k(u_q),
   \]
   and the centered tilt radius in \((QTS)\) is exactly
   \[
      \Delta_{p,q}=\beta\|u_p-u_q\|_1 .
   \]
   Hence
   \[
      A_{L+1}(u_q)-A_k(u_q)>2\beta\|u_p-u_q\|_1
      \tag{PSG}
   \]
   implies that the hidden tilted top \(k\) labels are contained in the query
   top \(L\) labels.

   Moreover, suppose the bit logits \(u_a(q)\) are independent and
   \(|u_a(q)|\) have densities bounded by \(M\).  If
   \(\|u_p-u_q\|_1\le T\) except on an event of probability \(\varepsilon\),
   then
   \[
      \Prb[T_k(p,q)\not\subseteq Q_L(q)]
      \le
      \varepsilon+C\,2^{2r}M\beta T
      \tag{PST}
   \]
   for a universal constant \(C\).  In particular, for fixed \(r\), Gaussian
   bit directions of nondegenerate variance at \(q\), constant inverse
   temperature, and \(\beta=\Theta_c(1/\log m)\), the containment failure
   probability is \(\log^{-\Omega_c(1)}m\) for every fixed near pair.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The first identity is the same subset-sum ordering as in
   \cref{lem:product-sign-top-k-reporter}: query log-probabilities differ
   only by the flip penalties \(2|u_a(q)|\).  Also
   \[
      \log\frac{K_p(s)}{K_q(s)}
      =
      \sum_{a=1}^r s_a(u_a(p)-u_a(q))+\text{constant}(p,q),
   \]
   so its range over \(s\in\{\pm1\}^r\) is
   \(2\|u_p-u_q\|_1\).  The definition \((QTS)\) gives
   \(\Delta_{p,q}=\beta\|u_p-u_q\|_1\), and \((PSG)\) is exactly the
   containment hypothesis of \cref{lem:query-tilted-prefix-stability}.

   For the probability bound, condition on the event
   \(\|u_p-u_q\|_1\le T\).  If \(A_{L+1}(u_q)-A_k(u_q)\le2\beta T\), then two
   distinct subset sums of the \(2|u_a(q)|\)'s differ by at most \(2\beta T\).
   For a fixed pair of distinct subsets, the difference is
   \(\sum_a c_a|u_a(q)|\), with \(c_a\in\{-2,0,2\}\) and at least one nonzero
   coefficient.  Conditioning on all other coordinates, the remaining
   one-dimensional variable has density \(O(M)\), so this pair falls in an
   interval of length \(O(\beta T)\) with probability \(O(M\beta T)\).  A
   union bound over at most \(2^{2r}\) subset pairs gives \((PST)\).

   In the Gaussian fixed-width case, the absolute bit logits have bounded
   densities, while \(\|u_p-u_q\|_1=O_{c,r}(\sqrt{\log m})\) except with
   probability \(m^{-O_c(1)}\).  Substituting
   \(\beta=\Theta_c(1/\log m)\) gives the stated inverse-polylogarithmic
   failure probability.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Query-top-\(k\) finite-channel compiler]
   \label{prop:query-top-k-channel-compiler}
   Fix a localized node of size \(m\), a scale \(\xi\in[1/m,1]\), and a finite
   channel with \(B\le\xi^{-1}\log^{O_c(1)}m\) outcomes.  For every outcome
   store the top-\(\xi\) posterior child \(C_j^\xi\) with the Poisson intensity
   used in the coarse finite-channel construction above.  Suppose that a
   retained query routine reports \(Q_k(q)\), the top \(k=\log^{O_c(1)}m\)
   outcomes of \(K_q\), in \(d\log^{O_c(1)}m\) time without enumerating all
   \(B\) outcomes.  Suppose also that for every near pair not handled by the
   resident guard,
   \[
      \mathcal H_{\xi,k}^{\rm qry}(p,q)
      :=
      \sum_{j\in Q_k(q)}
      \mu_j^\beta K_q(j)^{1-\beta}
      \left(R_j(p)^\beta-\tau_j^\beta\right)_+
      \ge h_m
      \tag{QTK}
   \]
   with \(h_m=\log^{-O_c(1)}m\).  Then the local finite-channel step can be
   implemented with
   \[
      d\,\xi^{-\rho}h_m^{-1}\log^{O_c(1)}m
   \]
   query work, expected \(k\,\xi^{-\rho}h_m^{-1}\log^{O_c(1)}m\) reported
   children, and \(m^{1+\rho}\log^{O_c(1)}m\) retained child space.  In
   particular, for any \(\xi\ge1/m\) this fits the \(d\,m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m\)
   local query budget after charging recursive calls to the reported children.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
   For a reported outcome \(j\), the Poissonized stored child and query
   activation have expected useful intensity at least
   \[
      \xi^\rho
      \mu_j^\beta K_q(j)^{1-\beta}
      \left(R_j(p)^\beta-\tau_j^\beta\right)_+ .
   \]
   Summing over \(Q_k(q)\) and using \((QTK)\), one group has useful intensity
   at least \(\xi^\rho h_m\).  Therefore
   \(O(\xi^{-\rho}h_m^{-1})\) independent groups give constant probability of
   activating a child containing the true near point and contained in
   \(\Ball(q,cr)\).  The query routine is called once per group and reports
   only \(k\) labels, giving the displayed local work and output count.

   The retained space is unchanged from the explicit finite-channel
   construction: over all repetitions and all \(B\) outcomes,
   \[
      \xi^{-\rho}h_m^{-1}\cdot B\cdot(\xi m)^{1+\rho}
      \le
      m^{1+\rho}\log^{O_c(1)}m ,
   \]
   using \(B\le\xi^{-1}\log^{O_c(1)}m\).  If the recursive child bound is
   \(Q(\xi m)\le d(\xi m)^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m\), then the total recursive work
   from the reported children is
   \[
      k\,\xi^{-\rho}h_m^{-1}\,Q(\xi m)
      \le
      d\,m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m .
   \]
   Since \(\xi\ge1/m\), the nonrecursive reporting work also satisfies
   \(d\,\xi^{-\rho}h_m^{-1}\log^{O_c(1)}m
     \le d\,m^\rho\log^{O_c(1)}m\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Growing product-sign top-\(k\) entropy barrier]
   \label{lem:growing-product-sign-top-k-barrier}
   Fix a product-sign channel and a near pair \(p,q\).  Under the tilted label
   law \(W_{p,q}\), write
   \[
      v_a=\beta u_a(p)+(1-\beta)u_a(q),
      \qquad
      D(v)=\sum_{a=1}^r\log(1+e^{-2|v_a|}).
      \tag{GTK1}
   \]
   For every label set \(Q\subseteq\{\pm1\}^r\),
   \[
      W_{p,q}(Q)\le |Q|e^{-D(v)}
      \tag{GTK2}
   \]
   and the restricted finite-channel value on \(Q\) obeys
   \[
      \mathcal H_{\xi,Q}(p,q)
      :=
      \sum_{s\in Q}\mu_s^\beta K_q(s)^{1-\beta}
      \left(R_s(p)^\beta-\tau_s^\beta\right)_+
      \le W_{p,q}(Q).
      \tag{GTK3}
   \]
   Consequently, if the coordinates \(v_a\) are iid with
   \[
      h=\E\log(1+e^{-2|V|})>0
   \]
   and finite variance, \(r=\lceil\kappa\log m\rceil\), and
   \(|Q|\le\log^C m\), then with probability \(1-o(1)\),
   \[
      \mathcal H_{\xi,Q}(p,q)
      \le m^{-\kappa h+o(1)} .
      \tag{GTK4}
   \]
   In particular, a polylogarithmic top-\(k\) product-sign reporter cannot
   deliver the inverse-polylogarithmic value required by
   \cref{prop:query-top-k-channel-compiler} in any fixed-entropy growing-width
   regime.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
   The tilted product-sign law factorizes:
   \[
      W_{p,q}(s)=
      \prod_{a=1}^r\frac{e^{s_av_a}}{2\cosh v_a}.
   \]
   Its largest atom is obtained by choosing \(s_a=\operatorname{sign}v_a\), and
   equals
   \[
      \prod_a\frac{e^{|v_a|}}{2\cosh v_a}
      =
      \prod_a(1+e^{-2|v_a|})^{-1}
      =
      e^{-D(v)}.
   \]
   Hence any \(Q\) has \(W_{p,q}\)-mass at most \(|Q|e^{-D(v)}\).  For
   \((GTK3)\), use
   \[
      \left(R_s(p)^\beta-\tau_s^\beta\right)_+\le R_s(p)^\beta
   \]
   and \(R_s(p)=K_p(s)/\mu_s\).  Thus
   \[
      \mathcal H_{\xi,Q}(p,q)
      \le
      \sum_{s\in Q}K_p(s)^\beta K_q(s)^{1-\beta}
      =
      \mathsf A_\beta(p,q)W_{p,q}(Q)
      \le W_{p,q}(Q),
   \]
   where the last inequality is Holder's inequality for probability vectors.
