\(A_yK^{\rho_y-1}+\zeta K^{\rho_y}\), covering query-dominated,
storage-dominated, and internally balanced regimes in one rule.  The
support-mass bridge
\cref{cor:support-mass-clipped-hall-shadow-reporter} and
\cref{cor:sampled-support-mass-clipped-hall-shadow-search} further weakens the
proposal requirement: a range-reporting, list-decoding, additive-quantization,
or seeded facility routine may certify only a support size and a one-sided
cut-shadow mass, and the verifier converts any positive coarse surplus into the
exact top-prefix column.  The soft versions
\cref{cor:soft-mass-clipped-hall-shadow-reporter} and
\cref{cor:sampled-soft-mass-clipped-hall-shadow-search} remove even the hard
support requirement: fractional assignment weights certify the same density by
a top-\(K\) rearrangement inequality.  The exact-scale form
\cref{cor:exact-scale-soft-hall-shadow-reporter} and
\cref{cor:sampled-exact-scale-soft-hall-shadow-search} then lets the verifier
optimize over the available prefix cardinalities and charge the exact recursive
price, so clipped and balanced scales become proposal screens rather than
endpoint restrictions.  The routing form
\cref{cor:shadow-routing-exact-scale-soft-reporter} converts any fractional
routing of paid shadow atoms into exact-scale soft records, and
\cref{cor:thresholded-shadow-routing-screen} gives the range-reporting-friendly
version: routed mass \(X\) supported on a degree superlevel \(d_{A,y}\ge\delta\)
contributes the simple certified benefit \(\min\{X,K\delta\}\) at cardinality
\(K\).  The layered form
\cref{cor:layered-thresholded-shadow-routing-screen} allows the same template to
receive many fractional degree-superlevel routes, and
\cref{cor:cardinality-optimized-thresholded-routing-screen} reduces each layer
to the scalar price-density test below or above \(X/\delta\).  The residual
envelope \cref{cor:thresholded-routing-residual-envelope} records the exact
contrapositive: any surviving price-density-winning superlevel is total-mass
limited by the same recursive price.  Finally,
\cref{cor:cumulative-superlevel-hall-shadow-reporter} shows that a reporter need
not construct an explicit routing for one template: a lower bound on the
cumulative mass \(M_A(y,\delta)\) of one degree superlevel is already a
thresholded route certificate, and failure of all such reports is the weak-type
envelope \((CSH5)\).  The price-density and clipped cumulative screens
\cref{cor:cumulative-hall-shadow-price-density-screen} and
\cref{cor:clipped-cumulative-hall-shadow-screen} reduce this to the canonical
test
\[
   \min\left\{\delta,\frac{M_A(y,\delta)}K\right\}
   >
   a\psi_y f_y(K_y^\natural)
\]
near the clipped minimizer \(K_y^\natural\).  The tail-mass version
\cref{cor:tail-mass-cumulative-hall-shadow-screen} removes the explicit
threshold: no surviving residual may have
\[
   M_A^+\!\left(y,\Theta_y\right)>K\Theta_y
\]
at that clipped scale.  The support-limited and cut-center consequences
\cref{cor:support-limited-tail-hall-shadow-screen} and
\cref{cor:support-limited-cut-center-tail-obstruction} convert this tail bound
into a direct Hall-cut accounting statement: if assigned paid shadow at every cut
center is supported on at most \(K_x\) points, then a surviving residual can carry
only \(O(K_x\Theta_x)\) mass through that center.  The support-sensitive version
\cref{cor:support-sensitive-cut-center-tail-obstruction} makes the remaining
large-support branch explicit:
\[
   X_x\le(K_x+s_x)\Theta_x .
\]
With a factor-\(b\) cardinality net, the support-adaptive price obstruction
\cref{cor:support-adaptive-cut-center-price-obstruction} charges the same mass
by
\[
   \psi_x
   \left(A_xs_x^{\rho_x}+\zeta s_x^{1+\rho_x}\right)
\]
up to \(b^{O(1)}\) constants, which is the exact recursive price scale of the
assigned support.
\cref{cor:cut-center-routing-obstruction} records the first obstruction left
when even the cut's own centers cannot route their paid shadow at positive
surplus.  The Hall cut itself can also be assumed marginally closed by
\cref{lem:maximal-hall-cut-marginal-normal-form}; the sharpened normal form
\cref{cor:maximal-no-prefix-hall-cut-normal-form} says that a failed transport
and failed top-prefix repair leave only one inclusion-maximal surplus cut that
also obeys the no-prefix weak-type envelope.  The frontier consequence
\cref{cor:maximal-hall-frontier-expansion} adds the matching outside condition:
any co-load left outside this cut must expose enough novel paid shadow outside
the closed neighborhood \(N(A^\star)\).  Thus the residual is not an uncontrolled
overlap pattern; it is a closed-shadow finite-prefix envelope plus an expanding
outside frontier.  In fact,
\cref{cor:maximal-cut-outside-transport} shows that this outside frontier is
already packable against the novel paid shadow, so the transport failure is
localized to the closed cut.  Finally,
\cref{cor:hall-shadow-finite-prefix-separation} identifies that top-prefix
repair test with the generic finite-prefix separator on the cut-shadow demand
system \(N(A)\), with signatures as the query side and \(r\equiv1\).  Thus
range-reporting, list-decoding, additive-code, and facility proposals can all
target the same certified finite-prefix inequality; once a proposed
container/query-layer/cardinality triple passes the reduced-cost test, the
retained column is again an ordinary Hall-shadow prefix.
\Cref{cor:closed-shadow-query-layer-relaxation} adds that fractional signature
weights are only a search relaxation: if a fractional query layer has positive
closed-shadow prefix value, some certified Boolean layer has positive value as
well.  \Cref{cor:closed-shadow-soft-proposal-hardening} adds the matching
update-side relaxation: soft point memberships and a one-sided lower mass also
harden to the same Boolean layer and top-\(K\) prefix.  The current compact
endpoint is \cref{cor:closed-shadow-soft-proposal-separator-endpoint}: after
maximal Hall localization, one positive certified soft proposal for the closed
shadow is enough.  Its contrapositive residual form,
\cref{cor:closed-shadow-soft-proposal-residual-envelope}, says the exact
remaining dense obstruction is a localized closed Hall cut obeying the universal
normalized soft envelope \((CSSR1)\) for every certified proposal template.
\Cref{cor:closed-shadow-fractional-superlevel-envelope} turns that envelope
into the searchable weak-type form: every fractional signature layer and degree
superlevel must have cumulative paid mass below its recursive query/storage
price density.  \Cref{cor:closed-shadow-dyadic-layer-cake-separator} makes the
finite reporter version explicit: if the dyadic layer-cake mass of one
container/layer beats the sum of its recursive prices, one superlevel is
automatically a valid repair.
\Cref{cor:reported-closed-shadow-layer-cake-separator} further allows one-sided
reported certificates: lower bound the total paid degree, upper bound the
superlevel cardinalities, and keep only a deterministic positive verified
report.  \Cref{cor:reported-closed-shadow-residual-dichotomy} packages the
negative branch: for every finite certified report universe, either one report
repairs the closed cut or all reports satisfy the scalar residual inequality
\((CRR3)\).  \Cref{cor:routed-support-closed-shadow-report} shows that routed
support certificates, including support-price and atom-routing proposals, feed
the same reported layer-cake interface after paying only the dyadic
dynamic-range factor when superlevel sizes are not reported separately.
\Cref{cor:aggregate-routed-support-closed-shadow-panel} gives the matching
panel form: if the aggregate routed paid mass beats the sum of those support
prices, one support report already repairs the cut.
\Cref{cor:reported-support-price-routing-residual} is the scalar optimization
form: in a surviving residual, every partial routed submeasure has mass at most
its reported support price, and every full routing gives the obstruction
\((RPR4)\).  \Cref{cor:reported-marginal-support-law} converts this deterministic
obstruction into a marginal law test: if a facility, additive-quantization,
list-decoding, lattice-decoding, or seeded-clustering proposal law has expected
routed paid mass larger than its marginal reported support price, independent
rounding exposes one deterministic reported routing and hence one ordinary
closed-shadow repair.  Therefore proposal mechanisms may be analyzed through
support probabilities \(\nu_{i,p}\) and one-sided routed-mass certificates; the
retained index still stores only verified deterministic reported supports.
\Cref{cor:certified-one-slot-marginal-support-search} removes the last
coordination artifact from that sufficient condition: any positive aggregate
marginal law contains one positive reported support slot, and a randomized
build-time search only has to sample one certified slot whose conservative
benefit-per-cost surplus is positive.
\Cref{cor:point-coupled-one-slot-support-law} sharpens the certificate for soft
clusters: atoms of the same data point may be coupled to one Bernoulli support
event, so the recursive price is charged to the point support probability
\(\sum_pq_p\), not to a union bound over that point's routed atoms.
\Cref{cor:reported-soft-support-prefix-hardening} then removes the stochastic
support from the retained object: any soft assignment satisfying the exact
cardinality test \((RSH2)\), or the coarse scale test \((RSH3)\), materializes
one deterministic top-\(K\) reported support.
\Cref{cor:reported-soft-support-price-panel} packages this as the scalar
build-facing screen: a soft support report or sampled panel only has to beat the
support-mass price \(\mathsf P_i^{\rm soft}\) in \((RSP3)\), after which the
verifier extracts one deterministic reported prefix.
\Cref{cor:soft-support-no-relaxation-residual} records the exact
contrapositive: a surviving residual is just the top-prefix envelope \((RSN2)\),
and every soft or sampled panel violation contains one ordinary reported prefix
violation.  \Cref{cor:exact-prefix-support-mass-no-layer-cake} records the
sharper exact-prefix route: if the verifier can materialize the top prefix
directly, hard and soft support-mass proposals close at the exact finite-prefix
price, without the reported layer-cake factor \(2bJ\).
\Cref{cor:aggregate-exact-prefix-support-mass-panel} gives the matching finite
and sampled panel form: aggregate surplus over hard and soft exact-prefix
support reports already contains one exact top-prefix repair.
\Cref{cor:optimized-exact-prefix-support-price} sharpens the price further:
hard supports pay
\(s\inf_K\psi(AK^{\rho-1}+\zeta K^\rho)\), and soft supports pay the analogous
\(\inf_K\max\{\mu,K\}\psi(AK^{\rho-1}+\zeta K^\rho)\), so the proposal need not
guess the recursive scale.  \Cref{cor:clipped-optimized-exact-prefix-price}
replaces this discrete infimum by the closed clipped threshold
\(\Theta_i(m)=\psi_i f_i(K_i^\natural(m))\), losing only the retained
cardinality-net factor.  \Cref{cor:clipped-exact-prefix-density-residual}
records the matching obstruction: every searched hard or soft support has
average paid density at most \(\beta_i\Theta_i\) at its own clipped scale.  The
older sufficient forms include
\cref{cor:exact-scale-soft-hall-shadow-separator-endpoint},
\cref{cor:thresholded-shadow-routing-separator-endpoint},
\cref{cor:soft-mass-hall-shadow-separator-endpoint},
\cref{cor:clipped-hall-shadow-separator-endpoint}, and
\cref{cor:balanced-hall-shadow-separator-endpoint}.
\Cref{lem:weighted-spherical-reduced-gain} proves the spherical half of the
dual dichotomy in the exact reduced-gain language: if ordinary spherical buckets
do not violate a surplus dual certificate, then the dual must carry large
query-priced mass on high-correlation buckets.  The guard refinement is now
also priced rather than worst-case: by
\cref{cor:dual-weighted-guard-spherical-reduced-gain}, a spherical obstruction
must have large activation-weighted guard mass, and
\cref{cor:low-guard-contained-spherical-reduced-gain} removes it on the
low-guard domain whenever the high-correlation caps are contained in the
resident \(cr\)-guard balls.  In the corresponding budget-compatible regime,
\cref{cor:contained-high-correlation-local-cover} proves the local filter-cover
LP feasible using spherical buckets alone.  The remaining dense theorem is
therefore narrower:
\cref{lem:high-correlation-dense-slice-separator} intersects
those buckets with the high-correlation cap around the priced query, producing
certified radius-contracting singleton-signature dense slices.  If the
Renyi-priced moment of these slices is below their average captured demand, one
slice has positive reduced gain.  \Cref{cor:spherical-dense-moment-obstruction}
shows that any remaining obstruction must have both large raw high-correlation
co-load and large recursive dense-slice moment; the next geometric step is to
rule out that simultaneous event or to quotient equivalent slices until the
dense moment drops.  \Cref{lem:dense-slice-prefix-separation} sharpens the dense
side further: after sorting dual demand prices inside each high-correlation
slice, every profitable atom-safe subcolumn is witnessed by a prefix, and
therefore any unresolved obstruction must have all price superlevels below the
Renyi density envelope \((DP5)\).  \Cref{lem:dense-slice-quotient-separation}
then gives the exact merge test: grouped singleton slices can be replaced by one
certified dense quotient whenever their de-duplicated primitive demand beats the
quotient query and storage prices.
\Cref{lem:reduced-gain-quotient-refinement} and
\cref{cor:low-spread-quotient-closure} add the radius-contraction screen inside
this same reduced-gain language: any positive quotient whose smaller-radius
refinement has radius-discounted Renyi spread at most
\(\Psi(R)/\Psi(R_\star)\) already contains a positive child quotient.  Hence a
surviving dense/spherical residual is forced to be high-spread under every
certified radius-contracting quotient refinement, not merely hard to find by
seeding.  \Cref{cor:quotient-spread-packing-entropy} converts this residual
spread into an \(R_\star\)-separated packing with Renyi effective support at
least \((\Psi(R)/\Psi(R_\star))^{1/(1-\rho)}\), giving the
spherical/list-decoding side an explicit entropy witness.
\Cref{cor:spread-packing-entropy-energy-screen} gives the matching payment
rule: profile energy must beat the logarithm of the separated-pair count, or
else the offending profile is the dense high-correlation signal.  Finally,
\cref{cor:residual-dense-cover-obstruction} packages the surviving dual
certificate into the explicit inequalities \((RO1)\)--\((RO5)\).  The remaining
geometric theorem is now exactly to rule out those inequalities for a rich enough
quotient universe; by \cref{cor:residual-separator-local-cover}, that residual
separator is already sufficient for local filter-cover feasibility.
\Cref{lem:quotient-packing-reduced-gain} and
\cref{cor:quotient-packing-local-cover} give the operational form of this task:
against every residual dual, construct a distribution over quotients whose
de-duplicated primitive demand exceeds its query/storage price.
\Cref{cor:conic-quotient-packing} removes the normalization: preprocessing may
search over arbitrary nonnegative quotient intensities and verify the signed
linear objective \((CQ1)\).  \Cref{lem:dyadic-quotient-packing} further reduces
proposal generation to a single dyadic price layer, with only the stated
build-time layer factor and exact weighted verification afterward.
\Cref{cor:unweighted-quotient-coverage-screen} turns each such layer into a
plain unweighted quotient-coverage threshold.  The named target is now
\cref{asm:layer-quotient-separator}: after spherical filters, whole slices, and
slice prefixes fail, one dyadic price layer must contain a quotient whose
de-duplicated unweighted coverage beats its query/storage price.
\Cref{lem:captured-demand-dyadic-layer} shows that such a layer can be chosen
from the layers carrying a \(1/O(J)\) fraction of the captured near-pair demand.
\Cref{lem:hinge-quotient-activation} makes the query side canonical: for a
proposed quotient core, keep exactly the query signatures with positive
coverage-minus-load margin and ask whether those margins pay the one-time
storage price.  With logarithmic slack,
\cref{lem:dyadic-query-margin-layer} further reduces this to one uniform
query-margin class, matching the same unweighted search model as the demand
layer.  \Cref{lem:atomized-quotient-reduced-gain} allows the quotient certificate
to use selected point-slice incidences rather than whole primitive slices.
\Cref{lem:atom-deduplication-normal-form} then removes the atom duplicate
factor by keeping one witness slice per covered near pair.
\Cref{lem:pair-support-saturation-atomized} saturates the remaining atom family:
for a fixed certified container and query layer, the whole feasible pair-support
relation dominates every duplicate-free atom certificate.  Finally,
\cref{lem:top-degree-atomized-prefix} shows that within that saturated relation
the best \(k\)-point update side is the degree-sorted prefix.  Thus the
remaining geometric separator can be searched as a
container/query-layer/cardinality problem followed by exact reduced-gain
verification.  If all such prefixes fail,
\cref{cor:saturated-pair-support-envelope} gives the exact residual
saturated degree-superlevel envelope that every certified container must satisfy,
and
\cref{lem:dyadic-atomized-prefix-screen} shows that constant-slack proposal
search only needs dyadic prefix cardinalities before exact verification.
\Cref{lem:saturated-container-packing-separator} makes even the container search
conic: any fractional packing of container/query-layer/prefix records whose
saturated support benefit beats price exposes a single positive reduced-gain
prefix.  \Cref{lem:saturated-query-hinge-normal-form} then makes the query side
canonical for a proposed update core: keep the positive support-minus-load
margins and test whether they pay storage.
\Cref{lem:fractional-query-weight-degree-normal-form} rewrites the same target
as a weighted top-\(k\) support-degree inequality over fractional query weights.
\Cref{lem:layer-cake-query-threshold-separator} then pushes any violation back
to one integral query-threshold layer.
\Cref{lem:fractional-threshold-container-packing} packages this as a conic
container separator: preprocessing may search over fractional query-weighted
container records, but every accepted column is still an ordinary threshold
query layer and top-degree update prefix.
\Cref{cor:fractional-threshold-container-local-cover} makes this directly
sufficient for finite local cover feasibility, and
\cref{lem:threshold-prefix-pareto-pricing} charges each exposed prefix by its
actual descendant Pareto price.
\Cref{lem:pareto-dense-core-layercake} is the most compact version: a smaller
certified child \(U\) is useful exactly when its fractional query-weighted
support beats its true query and storage prices.  Thus the current residual
target is a priced bipartite dense-core separator, with fractional query weights
used only to find integral threshold witnesses.
\Cref{cor:pareto-dense-core-envelope} makes the failure condition explicit:
every certified core must obey the weighted support envelope \((PDCE1)\).
\Cref{lem:pareto-core-hinge-normal-form} converts this envelope to the canonical
positive-margin query side of a proposed core, and
\cref{cor:dyadic-pareto-core-margin-screen} shows that logarithmically many
margin layers suffice for proposal search before exact verification.
\Cref{lem:fractional-pareto-core-packing-separator} then removes the last
integrality from the proposal side: any conic combination of certified cores and
fractional query weights with positive reduced-cost value exposes one ordinary
positive-gain threshold activation.  Equivalently, the dense proposal oracle is
the hinge objective \((FPC2)\), and failure of every such packing is the precise
weighted pseudo-randomness condition left for the spherical residual analysis.
\Cref{lem:weighted-pareto-core-hinge-separator} sharpens this once more by using
the original dual weights \(\alpha_{p,q}\) directly.  The exact core oracle is
now \((WPC2)\); dyadic demand layers are only an unweighted build-time screen,
not a theorem-level source of overhead.
By
\cref{cor:layer-separation-local-cover},
\cref{cor:hinge-container-separator-local-cover}, and
\cref{cor:core-envelope-local-cover}, any one of the concrete separators
already implies local filter-cover feasibility.
\Cref{cor:weighted-pareto-core-law-local-cover} gives the same local-cover
conclusion for an exact weighted core law, a successful separator can now be
verified without dyadic demand unweighting whenever it can optimize the original
dual prices.  \Cref{lem:slice-to-core-domination} supplies the direct bridge
from the spherical obstruction to that core law: dominate the primitive
high-correlation slice incidence profile by certified Pareto cores and pay less
than the captured dual mass.  This recovers the raw dense-slice test as the
singleton-core case and identifies the remaining geometric theorem as a
price-reducing compression or quotienting statement.
\Cref{lem:slice-core-compression-dual} gives the exact dual obstruction when
such compression fails: a pair potential under which every proposed core has
incidence no larger than its Pareto price.
\Cref{asm:compression-dual-separator} and
\cref{cor:compression-dual-local-cover} package this as the current sharp proof
target: no residual filter-cover dual should coexist with such a compression
dual for a sufficiently rich core-record family.
\Cref{lem:compression-dual-hinge-normal-form} optimizes out the record query
weights, and \cref{cor:two-potential-residual-normal-form} gives the exact
counterexample format: a surplus filter-cover potential \(\alpha\) and a
compression potential \(\beta\) must simultaneously satisfy the same
Pareto-core hinge envelopes.  By \cref{cor:balanced-residual-segment}, this
counterexample can be normalized to a fixed captured-mass segment between
\(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), all of which remains core-pseudo-random.
\Cref{asm:one-potential-core-separator} and
\cref{cor:one-potential-local-cover} collapse the remaining dense theorem even
further: it is enough to rule out a single nonnegative potential whose primitive
high-correlation captured mass exceeds the local query/storage price while every
Pareto core obeys its hinge envelope.
\Cref{cor:normalized-one-potential-obstruction} removes the last irrelevant
scale: the obstruction is a unit captured-mass potential whose total
query/storage price is below \(1/\pi_1\).
\Cref{cor:guarded-normalized-residual-segment} adds the spherical guard
information to that same normalized object: after spherical filters fail, the
unit potential also carries activation-weighted high-correlation guard mass
larger than \(\pi_1\kappa/2\).  This rules out the contained low-guard case and
leaves only guard-leaking or guard-heavy residuals for the dense reporter.
\Cref{cor:guard-leakage-residual-dichotomy} makes this sharper in the
budget-compatible regime: the inside-guard contribution is bounded by
\(\eta\pi_1\kappa\), so the residual must charge annular high-correlation
leakage outside \(B(q,cr)\).
\Cref{cor:guard-ball-spherical-fallback} records the complementary
pseudo-random case: if the primitive spherical law already has its far
collision bound outside the true \(cr\)-guard ball, then low-guard local cover
feasibility follows with no dense reporter.  Thus the dense theorem only has to
explain failures of this direct guard-ball far bound.
\Cref{cor:thresholded-annular-collision-residual} turns those failures into a
canonical residual: after thresholding the annulus by the primitive collision
profile \(c_q(x)\), any surviving dual must place constant normalized
activation-weighted mass on the threshold violators.
\Cref{cor:annular-active-collision-residual} weakens this to a single analytic
quantity: local infeasibility forces a lower bound on the weighted far active
collision load \(\sum_q\bar\tau_q\sum_{\|x-q\|>cr}c_q(x)\).  Proving the
matching upper bound under the core hinge envelopes would close this
pseudo-random branch.
\Cref{cor:relative-annular-active-collision-residual} strengthens the same
reduction by thresholding \(c_q(x)\) relative to the query activation \(a_q\).
When \(\beta\max_q a_q|P|\lesssim\pi_1L\), local infeasibility forces the
active-collision lower bound with factor \(\beta\), rather than the absolute
far threshold \(\pi_2\).  This makes the remaining branch a conditional-load
or list-decoding problem instead of an absolute rare-collision problem.
\Cref{cor:far-active-load-spherical-fallback} gives the corresponding
pseudo-random endpoint: a uniform bound
\(\sum_{\|x-q\|>cr}c_q(x)\lesssim\beta\pi_1L\) for every query already rules out
the residual.  The unresolved geometric work is therefore to prove this
aggregate far-load bound for the retained spherical/list-decoding primitive, or
to turn any violation into a positive dense filter-cover column.
\Cref{lem:dyadic-relative-load-superlevel} reduces the latter alternative to a
finite search over relative thresholds: any far-load overflow yields a dyadic
annular superlevel \(A_\beta(q)\) with \(\beta a_q|A_\beta(q)|\) large up to a
logarithmic factor.  This is the concrete range-reporting/list-decoding object
that should replace ad hoc dense clustering in the next geometric lemma.
\Cref{lem:weighted-dyadic-annular-load} and
\cref{cor:dyadic-annular-residual-witness} sharpen this to the actual dual
measure: a surviving infeasible node yields one dyadic level with large
\(\beta\sum_q\bar\tau_q a_q|A_\beta(q)|\), after only logarithmic and tail
losses.  Thus the next separator theorem can be stated as a weighted annular
superlevel reporter: either these conditional-collision superlevels have small
dual load, or one reported superlevel induces a positive paid prefix/core.
\Cref{asm:weighted-annular-scalar-reporter} and
\cref{cor:annular-reporter-local-cover} make this a formal reduction: large
annular false-positive load is useful only if it produces one-sided scalar
superlevel certificates for the real near-pair degree measure
\(d^{\bar\gamma^\theta}\).  This is the current sharp theorem target for
range reporting, list decoding, additive quantization, or any other build-time
proposal oracle.
\Cref{lem:primitive-annular-superlevel-lift} sharpens the target further: the
same lower bound is witnessed as an average over concrete primitive buckets
\(B_{z,\beta}(q)=U_z\cap A_\beta(q)\), and for finite primitive support by at
least one seed \(z\).  Thus the remaining proposal oracle may search a finite
primitive annular panel and only has to turn that panel into the certified
scalar reporter of \cref{cor:primitive-annular-panel-reporter-suffices}.
\Cref{cor:single-seed-annular-query-layer} and
\cref{cor:single-seed-query-layer-reporter-suffices} reduce this once more to a
single seed, one annular collision threshold, and one dyadic query-size layer.
\Cref{def:annular-scalar-reporter-record} and
\cref{cor:single-seed-reporter-proposal-criterion} put the remaining build-time
interface in column-generation form: a randomized \(k\)-means++,
additive-quantization, lattice/list-decoding, or range-reporting panel only has
to produce certified scalar reporter records with positive expected surplus.
Averaging exposes one deterministic retained record, so the annular far points
serve only as proposal evidence and never become cover columns themselves.
\Cref{cor:annular-near-shadow-mass-reporter} makes this still more concrete:
one certified container with enough true near-shadow mass and a size upper bound
already yields the scalar reporter after a dyadic layer-cake loss.  This makes
the next geometric theorem a finite weighted range-reporting/list-recovery
statement rather than an overlapping-cluster selection problem.
\Cref{def:annular-shadow-transport},
\cref{lem:annular-shadow-transport-reporter}, and
\cref{cor:annular-shadow-transport-obstruction} isolate the exact bridge that
is still missing: annular false-positive incidences must be transported into
true near-shadow mass with low congestion.  Such a transport immediately
materializes the scalar reporter; if the LP remains infeasible, every retained
smaller-radius container has a Renyi-affordable congestion lower bound by
\cref{cor:annular-shadow-congestion-lower-bound}.
\Cref{lem:annular-shadow-cut-normal-form} and
\cref{cor:cut-certified-annular-reporter} give the exact cut version of this
statement: either every query sublayer has enough near-shadow neighborhood
capacity, in which case the reporter follows, or some sublayer has annular
demand exceeding its near-shadow cut capacity plus the allowed unshipped tail.
\Cref{cor:half-mass-excess-cut-obstruction} removes the target-mass parameter:
any retained container for which half-mass transport would be affordable must
have a sublayer with excess annular demand
\(\sum_{q\in Y}b_q-C D_W^\theta(Y)>B_{\rm tot}/2\).  Thus the remaining
geometric theorem can be phrased as ruling out a heavy annular query layer whose
every retained smaller-radius container has such a Hall-type half-mass cut
obstruction.  \Cref{lem:cut-recycled-annular-sublayer} converts any such cut
into a dyadic cut-restricted annular layer that keeps a logarithmic fraction of
the weighted annular load and has small true near-shadow capacity inside the
tested container.  This is the current normal form for feeding failed dense
transport back into list recovery, LP range reporting, or the spherical far-load
branch.  \Cref{cor:recycled-sublayer-separator-suffices} records the exact
sufficiency statement: if one affordable retained container rules out all large
recycled layers by a near-shadow lower bound, then the local fractional cover is
already feasible.
\Cref{lem:lagrange-recycled-sublayer-screen} and
\cref{cor:lagrange-recycled-sublayer-separator-suffices} reduce that all-sublayer
condition to a one-parameter positive-part screen over query-wise near-shadow
deficits at each dyadic annular size level.
\Cref{lem:fractional-recycled-layer-dual-normal-form} gives the exact
fractional knapsack dual behind that screen: a positive multiplier with
nonpositive dual value rules out every strict-load fractional recycled layer,
so the geometric separator can be phrased as producing an optimizable scalar
dual certificate rather than checking all sublayers.
\Cref{lem:threshold-recycled-bad-layers} gives the primal normal form for the
same scalar problem: any remaining fractional bad layer can be chosen as a
low-efficiency prefix after sorting queries by
\(s_{W,\theta}(q)/(\Delta'\bar\tau_q)\), with only a boundary level fractional.
This is the range-reporting/list-recovery object that an implementation or a
geometric theorem should search for.
\Cref{cor:threshold-recycled-sublayer-separator-suffices} turns this into the
current sufficient certificate: at every dyadic annular size level, one
affordable retained container must admit a low-efficiency threshold whose
prefix statistic satisfies
\(tL_{\Delta'}(t)-S_{\Delta'}(t)\le(t-2H_m(\Delta)/C)\Lambda\).
\Cref{lem:finite-prefix-recycled-threshold-screen} and
\cref{cor:finite-prefix-recycled-sublayer-separator-suffices} remove the
remaining continuum parameter: the certificate is found, if it exists, by
scanning the sorted efficiency breakpoints, plus the \(A\)-boundary and
terminal low-load cases.
\Cref{lem:load-quantile-recycled-threshold-screen} and
\cref{cor:load-quantile-recycled-sublayer-separator-suffices} reduce this scan
to one weighted quantile: once cumulative low-efficiency load reaches
\(\Lambda\), convexity of the excess curve implies that no later breakpoint can
be better.
\Cref{lem:exact-load-recycled-quantile-screen} and
\cref{cor:exact-load-recycled-sublayer-separator-suffices} express that quantile
without breakpoint overshoot: outside the boundary cases, the certificate is
exactly \(\widehat S_\Lambda\ge A\Lambda\) for the fractional prefix of load
\(\Lambda\).
\Cref{lem:variational-exact-load-recycled-screen} and
\cref{cor:variational-exact-load-recycled-separator-suffices} replace even that
quantile language by a universal exact-load inequality over fractional query
layers.  This is the version a range-reporting/list-recovery theorem should try
to certify directly.
\Cref{lem:exact-load-margin-extension} then recovers the original large-layer
separator with slack: every layer of load \(H>\Lambda\) has capacity at least
\(AH+(a_j-A)(H-\Lambda)\), so the strict recycled-sublayer condition follows.
\Cref{lem:dominated-load-recycled-screen} and
\cref{cor:dominated-load-recycled-separator-suffices} put the same condition in
normalized weak-type form: all probability measures dominated by
\(\ell/\Lambda\) must have mean efficiency at least \(A\).
\Cref{cor:dominated-load-recycled-local-cover-endpoint} is the build-facing
endpoint of this reduction, with the actual annular constants substituted.
\Cref{lem:finite-dominated-load-proposal-game} is the fractional-overlap version
of that endpoint for a finite affordable pool in one congestion stratum: a
proposal law passes all dominated-load tests exactly when there is no
level-weighted dominated residual whose average efficiency is below \(A\) for
every retained record.  This is the clean minimax form of the remaining
range-reporting/list-decoding separator.
\Cref{cor:exact-load-dominated-proposal-obstruction} converts the same minimax
residual into a law over exact-load cohorts: each sampled cohort has load exactly
\(\Lambda\), and extremality leaves at most one fractional query.  This makes the
finite-pool obstruction compatible with cohort materialization and prefix/list
decoding.
\Cref{cor:exact-load-cohort-law-separator} is the corresponding theorem target:
for every law over these cohorts, find one affordable retained record with
expected near-shadow capacity at least \(A\Lambda\).
\Cref{cor:cohort-law-scalar-prefix-normal-form} makes this a scalar prefix
problem: the law over cohorts defines \(d_\eta^\theta(p)\), and failure means
every affordable retained top-\(K\) prefix has \(d_\eta^\theta\)-mass below
\(A\Lambda\).
\Cref{cor:exact-top-prefix-cohort-game} and
\cref{cor:exact-prefix-column-generation} give the cleanest continuation when
preprocessing can solve the exact separator: a finite implicit universe of
materializable top-prefix records is complete under ordinary column generation,
and the accepted records only need surplus \(V_\eta(T)-A\Lambda\ge0\).
\Cref{cor:one-sided-exact-prefix-value-column-generation} gives the verifier
form of the same sharp condition: a reporter may return a hard record with any
certified lower value \(X\le V_\eta(T)\), and \(X\ge A\Lambda\) is already a
valid column-generation step.
\Cref{cor:sublist-closed-exact-prefix-separator} is the finite-container version
of the same statement: for sublist-closed templates, the reduced-gain objective
is exactly \(D_\eta^\theta(W,K)-A\Lambda\), and the retained record is just the
maximizing \(K\)-subset.
\Cref{cor:no-loss-exact-cardinality-net} removes the remaining exact-size
artifact from this version: a dyadic net of \(K\)'s is sufficient at the same
\(A\Lambda\) threshold.
\Cref{cor:average-mass-exact-prefix-screen} is the coarse-mass bridge: a
proposal that only certifies total cohort mass on a support still yields a sharp
top-prefix column whenever \(KM/s\ge A\Lambda\).
\Cref{cor:average-density-exact-prefix-scale-choice} removes the matching-scale
guess from this bridge: a report with \(M\ge A\Lambda\) sets
\(h_*=\lceil A\Lambda s/M\rceil\), rounds to the retained cardinality net, and
keeps the same \(A\Lambda\) threshold.
\Cref{cor:soft-average-density-exact-prefix-scale-choice} extends this to soft
responsibility reports: once \(X\ge A\Lambda\), the mass
\(\mu=\sum_p\pi_p\) determines \(h_*=\lceil A\Lambda\mu/X\rceil\), and the
stored object is again one verified hard prefix.
\Cref{cor:soft-exact-prefix-relaxation-tight} gives the matching obstruction:
the cohort law left by failure of exact prefixes also defeats every soft
responsibility vector, so soft assignment mechanisms need only be analyzed as
search procedures for exact prefixes.
\Cref{cor:finite-soft-exact-prefix-oracle} is the finite minimax version of this
bridge: a generated pool of soft panels closes the dominated-load certificate
exactly when its sharp soft value is nonnegative against every cohort law, and
the proof stores only the induced exact-prefix records.
\Cref{cor:soft-exact-prefix-column-generation} turns that criterion into a
column-generation procedure over hard records, with soft panels used only as
build-time separators against the current minimizing cohort law.
\Cref{cor:exact-prefix-proposal-law-separator} and
\cref{cor:sampled-soft-exact-prefix-separator} put \(k\)-means++,
additive-quantization, list-recovery, or learned proposal panels on this same
no-log track: positive expected exact or one-sided soft surplus is only
build-time evidence, and the stored column is the single verified top prefix.
\Cref{cor:cohort-law-weak-type-superlevel} is the range-reporting version of the
same target: a certified superlevel with height \(\delta\) and size \(h\) closes
the cohort law once \(\delta h\ge A\Lambda\).
\Cref{cor:certified-cohort-law-superlevel-reporter} is the implementation-facing
form: a finite randomized decoder only needs a one-sided certificate
\(X\le\delta h\) and a certified size bound for the retained superlevel; if its
expected certificate reaches \(A\Lambda\), averaging exposes one deterministic
affordable record.
\Cref{cor:certified-cohort-law-mass-reporter} gives the coarser mass interface:
certifying total cohort degree \(V\) in a retained container, height bound \(B\),
and size bound \(K\) is enough after a dyadic \(O(\log(BK/V))\) loss.
\Cref{cor:explicit-cohort-law-mass-envelope} makes this a direct logarithmic
residual envelope: if no proposal closes the game, every retained mass report
has \(V=O(A\Lambda\log(2BK/(A\Lambda)))\).
\Cref{cor:capped-marginal-cohort-law-mass-reporter} adds the corresponding soft
proposal interface: finite capped-list laws are analyzed only through inclusion
marginals, and sublist-closed retained containers accept any responsibility
vector of total mass at most \(K\).
\Cref{cor:finite-capped-marginal-cohort-oracle} turns a generated finite pool of
such panels into an exact matrix game: either a randomized panel law beats every
cohort law at the explicit mass threshold, or one cohort law certifies that all
generated panels are below threshold.
\Cref{cor:logarithmic-top-prefix-cohort-separator} is the final top-prefix
specialization for sublist-closed retained containers: the separator only has to
find a retained top-\(K\) prefix whose cohort degree beats the explicit
logarithmic envelope.
\Cref{cor:cohort-prefix-depth-cancellation} makes the constants transparent:
the factor \(H_m(\Delta)\) cancels from \(4A\Lambda\), so the displayed
top-prefix envelope has no extra dyadic-annulus multiplicative loss.
\Cref{cor:cardinality-net-cohort-prefix-envelope} removes exact-cardinality
search from this target: powers of two are enough, replacing \(K\) by at most
\(2K\) inside the logarithm.
\Cref{cor:finite-prefix-template-separation-game} packages the remaining
build-time target as a finite matrix game over verified prefix records:
positive value gives the dominated-load certificate, while failure of the local
cover leaves one cohort law with negative verified surplus for every generated
record.  This is the precise theoretical replacement for choosing dense
clusters by mass or by a Lloyd/\(k\)-means++ heuristic.
\Cref{cor:prefix-template-column-generation} adds the build-time consequence:
an exact implicit separator over a finite prefix universe is complete by
ordinary column generation, and only the final verified records are charged to
the index.
\Cref{cor:one-sided-prefix-value-column-generation} is the sharper
implementation interface: the oracle only has to certify a current lower bound
on one retained record's value; the LP then reuses that record with its exact
payoff against all later cohort laws.
\Cref{cor:one-sided-proposal-law-prefix-separator} allows the proposed record to
come from a finite randomized batch: if the verified average one-sided surplus
is nonnegative, one support record is a valid deterministic column, while exact
negative reduced gain rules out every such batch.
\Cref{cor:sampled-one-sided-prefix-separator} is the Las Vegas build-time form:
if a sampleable proposal law has nonnegative expected verified surplus, repeated
preprocessing samples eventually expose a deterministic accepted column; no
sampled object is trusted without verification.
\Cref{cor:sampled-soft-prefix-proposal-separator} specializes this to soft
proposal panels: fractional inclusion weights are acceptable proposal evidence,
but preprocessing converts every accepted sample to the exact top-degree prefix
before it enters the retained LP.
\Cref{cor:cardinality-net-cohort-superlevel-reporter} is the corresponding
one-sided reporter interface: a range-reporting, list-decoding, additive
quantization, or seeded-clustering separator may return any certified
threshold-list report whose value beats \(\Theta_C L_b(h)\); it does not have to
solve the top-prefix optimization problem exactly.
\Cref{cor:load-quantile-recycled-obstruction-profile} is the corresponding
residual normal form: outside the \(A\)-boundary and terminal cases, the
remaining obstruction is just strict positivity at that weighted quantile.
\Cref{cor:exact-load-recycled-obstruction-profile} gives the equivalent
capacity form \(\widehat S_\Lambda<A\Lambda\), which is the cleanest target for a
one-sided reporter certificate.
\Cref{cor:variational-exact-load-recycled-obstruction-profile} gives the witness
form: the residual contains one fractional exact-load layer with capacity
strictly below \(A\Lambda\), and the lowest-efficiency prefix is the extremal
choice.
\Cref{cor:dominated-load-recycled-obstruction-profile} is the same witness after
normalization: a dominated probability distribution has average efficiency
strictly below \(A\).
\Cref{cor:finite-prefix-recycled-obstruction-profile} records the precise
failure mode of this finite scan: the total query load is not terminally small,
all positive breakpoints have strict prefix deficit, and the \(A\)-boundary has
either positive deficit or already exceeds the load threshold.  This is the
current finite range-reporting/list-recovery obstruction.
\Cref{lem:integrated-recycled-threshold-obstruction} rewrites that obstruction
as a cumulative excess-load curve whose area above the baseline \(\Lambda\) never
returns to zero.  This is the most compact analytic form of the finite
prefix-screen failure: a reporter must find one retained container for which the
low-efficiency load curve crosses enough below \(\Lambda\) to cancel the initial
\(A\)-boundary shortfall.
\Cref{lem:primitive-hit-kernel-cover-equivalence} gives the matching primal
form: the same theorem is equivalent to fractionally covering the primitive
spherical hit kernel \(r_{p,q}\) by Pareto cores at \(\pi_1\)-scaled query and
storage budgets.  Since \(r_{p,q}\ge\pi_1\) on every demanded pair, such a
hit-kernel cover scales directly to an ordinary near-pair cover with budgets
\((L,S)\), and
\cref{cor:hit-kernel-cover-materialization} rounds it into retained Boolean
core records with only the same logarithmic materialization loss as ordinary
LSF filters.
\Cref{lem:primitive-slice-law-hit-kernel-cover} identifies the baseline case:
if the raw high-correlation primitive slice law has \(\pi_1\)-scaled query and
storage moments, it is already a feasible hit-kernel cover.  The remaining
compression theorem is therefore needed only to replace that raw slice law by
cheaper Pareto cores when the primitive recursive moment is too large.
\Cref{lem:excess-slice-moment-repair} sharpens this once more: the separator
only has to delete and repair a fractional overbudget sublaw of primitive
slices, while the affordable part of the spherical slice law is kept unchanged.
\Cref{lem:finite-repair-dual} gives the matching reduced-gain oracle for this
repair LP, so the build stage can choose a deletion sublaw, solve the finite
repair problem, and search for positive-gain replacement cores exactly as in
ordinary column generation.  \Cref{lem:joint-deletion-repair-dual} optimizes
the deletion sublaw as well:
for fixed dual prices, primitive slices are deleted by the single hinge rule
``saved recursive price exceeds exposed hit value.''  Thus the remaining dense
theorem is not to guess dense clusters, but to rule out the joint
deletion-repair dual obstruction \((JDR1)\)--\((JDR2)\) for a rich enough
Pareto-core family.  \Cref{cor:joint-repair-hit-kernel-cover} makes this
explicit: the corresponding non-strict hinge inequality is sufficient for a
primitive hit-kernel cover.  \Cref{lem:capped-primitive-moment-normal-form}
rewrites that hinge as the capped moment inequality \((CPM1)\).  Thus raw
overbudget primitive slices no longer matter; only slices whose exposed
near-pair value pays their recursive price can contribute to the remaining
obstruction.  \Cref{lem:paid-primitive-sublaw-normal-form} turns this into a
canonical paid sublaw \(\omega\), so the geometric task is to compress paid
overbudget primitive mass rather than all primitive mass.
\Cref{cor:singleton-saturated-paid-law} shows that, once primitive singleton
records are included as build-time columns, this paid law is simply
value-proportional and has total price equal to the primitive captured mass
\(\sum\gamma r\).  \Cref{lem:paid-quotient-reduced-gain} then gives the
corresponding compression test: a core with probability-weighted paid primitive
value larger than its query/storage price has positive reduced gain, with no
duplicate-slice loss.  \Cref{cor:paid-compression-hit-kernel-cover} packages
this as a local-cover theorem: if every surplus singleton-saturated paid law
admits a conic compression into assigned Pareto cores with paid value exceeding
query/storage price, then the primitive hit-kernel cover is feasible.
\Cref{lem:canonical-paid-core-hinge} and
\cref{cor:canonical-paid-core-hit-kernel-cover} simplify the separator further:
for a fixed update core, the best primitive assignment is all visible paid
slices and the best query side is the positive-margin set, so the remaining
search can target only the hinge violation \((CPH4)\).  Finally,
\cref{lem:atomized-paid-core-hinge} and
\cref{cor:atomized-paid-core-hit-kernel-cover} remove the whole-slice
restriction: it is enough for a core to capture hit-kernel-weighted paid atom
mass
\(\bar h_U^\gamma(q)=\sum_{p\in U}\gamma_{p,q}r_{p,q}\), and a violation of
\((APH4)\) already forces the primitive hit-kernel cover.
\Cref{lem:weighted-atomized-prefix-normal-form} and
\cref{cor:weighted-atomized-prefix-envelope} give the prefix residual form of
this target: inside a certified container, sort points by paid degree under an
arbitrary fractional query weighting; if every prefix fails, the degree
superlevels satisfy the explicit envelope \((WAE2)\).
\Cref{asm:paid-atomized-prefix-separator},
\cref{cor:paid-prefix-hit-kernel-cover}, and
\cref{cor:paid-prefix-residual-envelope} package this as the current dense-side
proof target: a successful separator is exactly a violation of one such
container-prefix envelope, and an unsuccessful separator leaves a paid residual
whose every certified container obeys \((PPRE1)\)--\((PPRE2)\).
\Cref{lem:paid-prefix-weak-type} rewrites this residual in weak-type form: high
paid-degree superlevels must be either query-price small or storage-price
massive, and at the query/storage balance scale their density is bounded by
\(C_\rho\psi A_y^\rho\sigma^{1-\rho}\).  This is the current concrete geometric
obstruction to eliminate.
\Cref{lem:forbidden-weak-type-superlevel} and
\cref{cor:weak-type-prefix-hit-kernel-cover} give the exact positive test for
eliminating it: finding a certified superlevel in the forbidden middle regime is
already enough to expose a paid prefix and hence the primitive hit-kernel cover.
Because
preprocessing time is deliberately not a scarce resource,
\cref{lem:finite-pool-optimizer} and
\cref{cor:offline-pareto-compression} allow the build stage to enumerate,
sample, or learn a huge proposal pool and then keep only the certified cover on
the desired query-memory Pareto frontier.  The fractional LP and
pattern-complete rounding remain useful proof devices, but their logarithmic
rounding factor is not inherent to preprocessing: an exact integral certificate
would pay no such index overhead.  With
\cref{cor:offline-center-score-saturation}, even the continuous score-filter
parameters reduce to finite seed data: a proposed center-score family is closed
under all data thresholds, data radii, and retained submemberships before
certification, so the stored cover can be much smaller than the build-time
candidate universe.  \Cref{cor:seed-saturate-certify} makes this the canonical
offline build model: $k$-means++, spherical \(D^2\), dual-weighted, learned, or
exhaustive seeds are saturated and certified first, and only the selected
retained family is charged.  The closed-form $F_4$ charge is also only a
sufficient price certificate: \cref{lem:priced-cover-compiler} and
\cref{cor:offline-recursive-pareto-pricing} allow the offline verifier to price
each candidate child by its actual certified descendant Pareto cost.  This
folds ordinary certified ball recursion, score-filter recursion, residual
scans, and terminal samplers into the same priced cover process, and can only
lower the retained query-memory frontier relative to the surrogate analysis.
The all-reporting obstruction is also separated from the recursive compiler:
\cref{lem:sampled-priced-cover} allows a retained family to be used through a
query sampler, paying expected sampled child price and requiring only
inverse-polylogarithmic route mass on children that contain the true near point.
Thus middle-density singletons and posterior prefixes should be handled as
sampling/value objects whenever listing them would violate active power.
\Cref{lem:finite-sampled-cover-dual} gives the finite obstruction to such a
sampler: a bad query carries route-demand prices on unresolved near points, and
the remaining theorem must find an active child whose priced success mass beats
its query price plus the normalization price.
\Cref{lem:existential-sampled-priced-cover} weakens the sufficient condition to
the actual ANN objective: if the unresolved near set is nonempty, the sampler
only needs inverse-polylogarithmic mass on children that contain at least one
of those near points.  \Cref{lem:finite-existential-sampled-cover-dual} gives
the corresponding one-constraint dual.
\Cref{lem:finite-sampled-route-verifier} turns this into an all-query
certificate by grouping queries according to their activation pattern and
unresolved near set; the cost of storing or implicitly decoding those signatures
is now explicit.
\Cref{lem:finite-existential-sampled-route-verifier} gives the same signature
certificate with existential near-set mass instead of per-witness mass.
\Cref{lem:two-child-existential-sampler} then collapses each exact existential
signature sampler to two useful children plus no-op mass; the \(\log |N|\)
cohort factor is needed only for the stronger per-witness materialization.
\Cref{lem:activation-sampled-route-verifier} gives the clean activation-only
variant: if the route LP is feasible for every activation pattern against the
union of all compatible near points, then the query decoder no longer needs the
near-set coordinate at all.
\Cref{lem:sampled-route-cohort} removes the next fractional artifact: once a
signature LP is feasible, a polylogarithmic cohort of child identifiers
implements its sampler with only constant-factor loss in price and route mass.
\Cref{lem:activation-cohort-sampled-compiler} packages these two reductions
into a directly stored activation-pattern sampler, with no-op records carrying
the leftover subprobability mass.
\Cref{cor:activation-cohort-resources} records the exact query-memory test:
the LP/cohort search may be arbitrarily expensive at build time, but the
retained cohort table and pattern decoder must fit the local storage budget.
\Cref{lem:prefix-list-decoder}, \cref{lem:priority-prefix-list-decoder},
\cref{lem:exponential-list-size}, and \cref{cor:prefix-list-resources} record
the deterministic list-decoding
alternative suggested by the lattice viewpoint: a stack decoder enumerates
exactly the prefixes whose certified upper score can still reach the decoding
threshold, and an exponential-moment certificate turns this into a short-list
and query-work bound.  If the score tree admits such an output-sensitive prefix
enumerator, routing reduces to a list-size theorem followed by ordinary metric
verification.
\Cref{lem:fano-biased-prefix-list} and
\cref{cor:waterfilled-fano-bias} make the sequential-decoding bias explicit:
subtracting a nonnegative branch price from the reliability score preserves
admissibility, can only shrink the exponential list-size moment, and turns an
\(O_c(\log\log n)\) water-filled allocation defect into only a polylogarithmic
threshold loss.  \Cref{cor:robust-fano-allocation-compiler} adds the
multi-witness form: one robust water-filled allocation, tested against all
finite witness mixtures, gives one Fano-biased stack decoder that lists a valid
route for every witness as soon as the raw routes have the corresponding
\(O_c(\log\log n)\) reliability margin.  Thus a code or lattice replacement
should expose Fano-biased threshold reporters, not just nearest-center
reporters.
\Cref{lem:continuation-list-certificate} and
\cref{cor:continuation-as-list-decoding} show that ordinary continuation-mass
pruning is already the \(\beta=1\) case of this certificate; the unresolved
part is to construct an equally tight admissible prefix potential after
geometric recentering and budget-thinned child generation.
\Cref{asm:flat-spherical-code-decoder} and
\cref{prop:flat-spherical-code-terminal} isolate the flatter code/lattice
alternative: replace the terminal score tree by one structured spherical-code
panel whose cap list is output-sensitive, whose point and far-pair loads match
the random Gaussian spectrum, and whose near-pair hit probability is
inverse-polylogarithmic.  This is the theorem a Construction-A lattice,
group-orbit spherical code, or concatenated soft list-recovery construction
would have to prove.  The product-code filtering construction of
Becker--Ducas--Gama--Laarhoven is the closest existing algorithmic template:
it turns an enormous implicit filter family into a decoding problem, so the
missing worst-case statement becomes a prefix-list moment bound and a near-route
hit bound for a structured product panel.  \Cref{lem:soft-list-recovery-reporter}
makes the coding-theoretic interface explicit: any certified soft list-recovery
or lattice enumeration block is enough to supply the threshold reporters used
by the product-panel decoder.  \Cref{cor:euclidean-list-decoder-reporter}
records the direct Euclidean-metric case, where a code or lattice list decoder
already reports the needed soft-score superlevel set.  For non-Euclidean
bounded scores, \cref{lem:hard-list-recovery-lift} gives a self-contained
reduction to ordinary hard list-recovery constraints by repeating each
coordinate across score levels.
\Cref{lem:reliability-erasure-sweep} gives the cheaper GMD special case:
one hard symbol and one confidence per coordinate produce only \(O(h)\)
erasure transcripts, and the weighted-agreement inequality \((GMD)\) is enough
to guarantee that the near route is decoded.
\Cref{lem:soft-score-gmd-margin} turns this into an ordinary soft-score
certificate: top-symbol gaps define the confidences, and any codeword above
the resulting score threshold is included by the same \(O(h)\)-call sweep.
\Cref{cor:gmd-block-certificate} packages the usable block condition for
finite-signature and decoder-DAG rate-coverage certificates.
\Cref{lem:chase-gmd-reporter} and
\cref{cor:chase-gmd-block-certificate} add the polylogarithmic ambiguity
version: branch over a few low-confidence coordinates, promote the guessed
symbols to confidence \(1\), and then use the same GMD sweep.  The branch
product is charged explicitly as decoder work.
\Cref{cor:top-list-chase-completeness} removes the need to branch over the
full alphabet: top lists are complete whenever omitted symbols have enough
score deficit to fall below the reporting threshold.
\Cref{lem:information-set-threshold-reporter} and
\cref{cor:ordered-statistics-information-set} record the complementary OSD
normal form from code and lattice decoding.  A retained systematic chart lists
only high-score information words, extends them through the code or quotient
basis, and exact-filters the resulting candidates.  This can be strictly
cheaper than Chase-GMD when a reliable information set exists, because the
online branch count is the ordered-statistics discrepancy list rather than the
full ambiguity product.
\Cref{rem:sparse-subset-channel-stress} and
\cref{rem:sparse-subset-asymptotic-normal-form} isolate the corresponding
constant-weight signed-subset channel.  This route is now resolved as a
barrier for the raw coordinatewise OSD panel.  The frozen normal form reduces
the question to the quenched coefficient/Sanov far threshold
\((OSS3)\)--\((OSS4)\) and the reliability-ordered near mean \((OSS5)\).
\Cref{rem:sparse-subset-small-width-barrier} rules out the sparse
\(\lambda\downarrow0\) limit, and
\cref{rem:sparse-subset-mutual-information-barrier} rules out every fixed
\(0<\lambda<1\): the OSD near law itself is a far Sanov witness of cost
\(I(L;U)<H(L)=R_\lambda\), so the far threshold cannot lie below the near
mean.  A positive code/lattice theorem must therefore change the charged
label entropy, the far spectrum, or the decoder bias rather than reuse the raw
ternary OSD decision.
\Cref{rem:raw-top-one-entropy-barrier} records the general principle behind
this failure: any symmetric raw top-one Gaussian panel charged at full label
entropy is limited by \(I(A;U)<H(A)\).  Thus the useful code/lattice targets
are not better top-one decoders, but output-sensitive threshold reporters,
quotient or aggregate samplers, and Fano-biased prefix decoders whose charged
entropy is the certified work entropy rather than the whole label universe.
\Cref{lem:information-charge-survivor-test} turns this into the current
screening rule for deep code and lattice proposals: the far-tail charge of the
reported transcript must be no larger than the conditional information that the
near data block retains about that transcript, up to polylogarithmic slack.
\Cref{lem:gaussian-information-charge-contraction} makes the Gaussian version
quantitative, \(I(T;U)\le\chi^2 I(T;Q)\), and
\cref{cor:randomized-aggregate-sampler-information-screen} extends the same
screen to randomized transcripts such as BCJR paths, Construction-A residues,
and discrete-Gaussian lattice samples.
\cref{cor:polylog-raw-list-entropy-barrier} applies it to rule out
equivariant top-\(\polylog m\) raw codeword lists at full label charge.
\Cref{cor:raw-list-rate-lower-bound} gives the corresponding exponential-list
audit: if the only discount is scanning \(K_r\) raw labels, then
\(r^{-1}\log K_r\) must be at least \((1-\chi^2)R-o(1)\) before the
information gap disappears.
\Cref{cor:raw-label-fano-price-no-rescue} adds that deterministic pruning
prices on the same raw labels do not help unless they change the charged
certificate itself.
\Cref{rem:deep-code-lattice-audit} records the resulting candidate map:
algebraic list-recovery is useful as a reduced-cost reporter, low-state
trellises and polar/convolutional recursions are useful as exact aggregate
samplers, Tanner/LDPC factor graphs need an exact small junction tree or a
certified approximation error, Construction-A/D should be analyzed through
theta residue-code partition functions, and lattice enumeration or pruning
only helps when it supplies a Fano-prefix moment or quotient bucket law.
\Cref{lem:min-entropy-information-set} identifies the best chart for a linear
block: assign each coordinate its soft local entropy
\(\lambda_i=\log\sum_a\exp(\beta(\omega_i(a)-m_i))\), then choose a
minimum-weight information set.  For MDS blocks this is just the \(k\) smallest
coordinate entropies; for general linear blocks it is a greedy minimum-basis
computation.  Thus the decoder overhead target reduces to the scalar margin
\(\beta(\sum_im_i-\Theta)+\Lambda_*=O_c(\log\log m)\).
\Cref{lem:superset-product-panel-decoder} handles the fact that OSD and lattice
enumerators often produce a certified superset before exact filtering.
\Cref{cor:osd-superset-block-reporter} gives the resulting product-panel query
certificate: an OSD block contributes the ordinary prefix moment multiplied by
only \(e^{\Lambda_j(q)}\) at the block being decoded.
\Cref{cor:superset-product-panel-rate-bookkeeping} packages this as a
blockwise rate test: the OSD query factor is
\((1+A_j+e^{\Lambda_j})e^{\beta(M_j-\theta_{Q,j})}\), together with the usual
partition factor \(e^{-\beta\theta_{Q,j}}Z_j^Q\).  Thus the remaining product
panel theorem can state query overhead, storage, far load, and near hit as four
ordinary multiplicative block-rate inequalities.
The remaining work is spectrum and rate bookkeeping rather than Lloyd-style
convergence analysis.
\Cref{lem:additive-product-panel-decoder}
makes the decoder side self-contained: once block threshold reporters and
suffix upper scores are available, the live stack is controlled by the product
partition certificate \(P_\beta\), and terminal scan work is controlled by
\(T_\beta\).  The remaining geometric theorem for such panels is therefore
only the random-like spectrum.  \Cref{prop:product-panel-spectrum-compiler}
states the exact certificates: one-panel decoder work \((PP1)\), storage
moment \((PP2)\), far co-load moment \((PP3)\), and near-pair hit probability
\((PP4)\).  The two load conditions are pure exponential-moment inequalities
and factor block-by-block for product panels.
\Cref{lem:product-panel-tensorization} records that reduction explicitly:
after splitting the thresholds by block, the decoder partition, storage
partition, far co-load partition, and a coordinatewise near-hit event all
tensorize.  The remaining code/lattice theorem can therefore be attacked one
block at a time, then multiplied.
\Cref{cor:product-panel-rate-bookkeeping} is the exponent form: prove one-block
rates \(u_j,v_j,w_j,b_j\) with total query and storage rates at most \(\rho\),
total far-separation rate at least \(1-\rho\), and total near-loss
\(O_c(\log\log m)\).  This is the precise product-code analogue of the
spherical exponent calculation.
\Cref{cor:additive-ivf-product-panel} specializes the same certificate to
additive IVF or inverted multi-index style routing: tuple buckets
\((i_0,i_1,\ldots)\) are just product-panel labels, and orthogonal additive
pivots make the Euclidean score exactly block-additive.  The nonorthogonal
additive-quantization case is still useful, but by
\cref{rem:nonorthogonal-additive-ivf} its cross term must be certified as a
small or decodable interaction price rather than hidden inside a Lloyd-style
distortion objective.
\Cref{prop:rectangular-interaction-cover-aq} gives the low-overhead special
case: if preprocessing covers the tuple space by few product rectangles with
certified lower bounds on the interaction price, ordinary product decoders can
list raw-score supersets and exact-filter them back to the true
additive-quantization buckets.  This is the route to exploit practical
low-entropy interaction structure without paying the full prefix-decoder cost.
\Cref{lem:priced-pair-additive-ivf-reporter} and
\cref{prop:priced-pair-additive-ivf-compiler} make this exact for two
nonorthogonal codebooks: after a first pivot \(a\) is chosen, the second
codebook is decoded against the shifted query \(q-a\), and the endpoint follows
from the pair reporter work, pair storage spectrum, pair far co-load spectrum,
and pair near-hit probability.
\Cref{lem:priced-prefix-additive-ivf-reporter} and
\cref{prop:priced-prefix-additive-ivf-compiler} extend this to any finite
additive-codebook stack: each chosen codeword is charged as a query shift, and
admissible suffix scores turn the full tuple search into an output-sensitive
prefix list.  Thus multi-codebook AQ is not a separate theorem object; it is
the same reporter-work, storage-spectrum, far-load-spectrum, and near-hit
certificate over a larger tuple label space.
\Cref{lem:gibbs-prefix-additive-ivf-sampler} gives the sampled counterpart:
exact suffix partition functions sample the true nonorthogonal AQ Gibbs law by
successive residual queries \(q-\sum_i c_i\), so the interaction term is paid
inside the partition recursion rather than by a rectangular lower bound or an
all-listing prefix search.  Conditional on compact partition evaluation,
\cref{prop:gibbs-sampled-additive-ivf-compiler} reduces sampled AQ to three
spectral tests: stored tuple incidences, far sampled co-load, and near Gibbs
mass.  \Cref{lem:gibbs-aq-state-quotient} and
\cref{cor:finite-state-sampled-aq} sharpen the implementation target further:
a compact state graph may sample aggregate Gibbs mass for quotient bucket
labels, so the charged index stores distinct buckets rather than all internal
tuples.  \Cref{lem:stable-quotient-sampled-spectrum} gives the corresponding
loss test: quotienting is harmless up to a polylogarithmic factor whenever each
merged class has polylogarithmic size and only \(O(\log\log m)\) Gibbs log-score
spread at query time.  \Cref{lem:responsibility-thinned-quotient} gives the
softer alternative: large or heterogeneous quotient classes are also safe if
the retained decoder reports points with probability proportional to their
hidden Gibbs responsibility inside the sampled class.  Ordinary IVF union
scanning is exactly the stable special case.  This is the
additive-vector-quantization analogue of the discrete Gaussian code/lattice
route.
\Cref{prop:finite-retained-priced-pair} gives the corresponding retained-index
certificate.  Build time may use \(k\)-means++, random centroids, additive
quantization, list-decoding proposals, or column generation to produce panels,
but the proof trusts only the accepted finite envelopes for reporter work,
stored incidences, far scanned incidences, and near-witness coverage.  This is
the clean way to analyze practical additive IVF: the heuristic proposes a
compact family, and the retained certificate is the theorem object.
\Cref{prop:finite-retained-scored-label},
\cref{lem:finite-scored-label-lp-dual},
\cref{cor:scored-label-column-generation}, and
\cref{cor:fractional-scored-label-terminal} remove the last pair-specific
language from this retained proof: once a panel supplies finite labels,
reported-label work, stored incidences, far scanned incidences, and
near-witness coverage, the same deterministic verifier, fractional LP, dual
obstruction, and exact separator apply.
\Cref{lem:finite-priced-pair-lp-dual},
\cref{lem:fractional-priced-pair-materialization}, and
\cref{cor:fractional-priced-pair-terminal} are the priced-pair specialization
of this finite build-time bridge:
if the pair panels satisfy a fractional signature LP with inverse-polylogarithmic
coverage and polylogarithmic constraint entropy, randomized materialization
gives one deterministic retained pair index.  The dual prices identify the
right replacement for Lloyd distortion: propose panels with positive reduced
gain against witness-value prices and work/storage/load prices.
\Cref{cor:one-sided-reduced-gain-column-generation} is the corresponding
safe approximate interface: a proposal only needs a certified lower bound on
one point score or whole-label gain, and the exact verifier decides whether any
column is retained.
\Cref{prop:sampled-structured-panel} records the corresponding sampler
alternative.  A structured code or lattice panel need not list all active
labels if it can sample labels from a certified Gibbs or discrete-Gaussian law:
stored redundancy, far sampled co-load, and near sampled mass are enough.  This
is a cleaner theoretical version of the empirical multi-assignment lesson and
a possible way around all-reporting overhead in middle-density regimes.
\Cref{cor:gibbs-sampled-product-panel} makes the full-product case algebraic:
far sampled load is a ratio of mixed and query partition functions, while the
near condition is Gibbs mass on labels that store the near point.  These
quantities tensorize block-by-block, so the sampled lattice/code target has the
same rate-bookkeeping shape as the reporting target but no active-list term.
\Cref{cor:gibbs-sampled-rate-bookkeeping} is the exponent form: prove one-block
rates for storage, sampled far separation, and near Gibbs mass with total
storage rate at most \(\rho\), total far-separation rate at least \(1-\rho\),
and total near loss \(O_c(\log\log m)\).  No query-list rate appears.
\Cref{lem:gibbs-near-moment-lower-bound} makes the near condition itself
checkable by a positive tilted-moment margin: under the query Gibbs law, the
storage score of the near point must have a first exponential moment just above
the storage threshold and a controlled second moment.  Thus the sampled
lattice/code route is reduced to three block partition-function estimates.
\Cref{lem:critical-tilted-gaussian-sampled-spectrum} computes the ideal
continuous target at the critical Euclidean normalization: an intensity-\(m\)
Gaussian filter family with query tilt \(N(\beta q,I)\) has storage rate
\(\rho_c\), sampled far-separation rate \(1-\rho_c\), and constant near sampled
mass.  A compact code or lattice sampler would be a finite quadrature for this
calculation.
\Cref{lem:naive-gaussian-quadrature-barrier} explains why this quadrature
cannot be an iid Gaussian label pool analyzed by ordinary importance-sampling
concentration: the label entropy needed to stabilize the tilted partition
function is polynomially larger than the entropy allowed by the storage and far
load exponents.  The finite object must therefore exploit structure, not just
more random labels.
\Cref{lem:construction-a-theta-quotient} records the cleanest Construction-A
interface: the discrete-Gaussian law on the lattice quotients exactly to a soft
theta-reliability law on the residue code, and close-point threshold reporting
reduces to a certified soft list-recovery superset of residues followed by
ordinary integer-lift enumeration.  Thus a Construction-A panel should be
analyzed through residue-code list recovery and tilted partition functions, not
as a black-box nearest-lattice oracle.
\Cref{cor:query-centered-cell-reweighting} gives the posterior analogue of
this decoding normal form.  After the scale-amplified leader law has collapsed
to one max-tilted measure, choosing
\(\alpha=\Theta_c(1/H)\) with \(H\ge\max\{D,\log m\}\) rewrites that measure as
the exact nearest resident cell of a query-centered Gaussian perturbation,
size-biased by a scalar weight whose tail is killed by a polylogarithmic cap.
\Cref{cor:truncated-nearest-cell-compiler} then turns any compact structured
nearest-cell decoder into the max-tilted posterior sampler with only a
polylogarithmic rejection overhead.  \Cref{rem:nearest-cell-structured-decoding}
is the important caveat: this is not a black-box exact-NN assumption, but a
code/lattice/trellis decoder target for smoothed Voronoi or quotient cells.
\Cref{lem:smoothed-witness-list-compiler} weakens this again: the query need
not identify the exact nearest cell of the perturbation, only list the true near
witness with constant tilted mass.  \Cref{cor:facility-bucket-witness} is the
corresponding facility or \(k\)-means++-style form: retained buckets are useful
when their reported union has small scan load and high tilted witness capture.
\Cref{lem:poisson-rate-coverage} turns this into the scalar rate-coverage
certificate \((RC1)\)--\((RC3)\), and
\cref{lem:finite-signature-rate-coverage} gives a conservative all-query
verification route through finite reporter signatures and coefficient
envelopes.
\Cref{lem:finite-poisson-rate-coverage-realization} removes the hidden
randomized-preprocessing layer for finite certificates: after a logarithmic
replication factor, one checkable Poisson bucket realization satisfies all
finite miss, load, and storage constraints simultaneously.
\Cref{cor:finite-signature-retained-buckets} packages the result in the
original query language, so the retained index itself satisfies the tilted
witness-loss and reported-incidence bounds for every finite signature.
\Cref{cor:finite-transcript-rate-coverage} charges compact
decoder transcripts and their reporter work directly.
\Cref{cor:compressed-decoder-dag-rate-coverage} compresses those transcripts to
acyclic decoder state graphs with state-reach envelopes.
\Cref{cor:output-sensitive-decoder-dag-rate-coverage} gives the corresponding
output-sensitive list-enumerator form, with responsibility weights for miss
coverage and ordinary output probabilities for scan load.
\cref{lem:scalar-redundancy-waterfill} gives the optimal scalar redundancy
rule once a reporter and point assignment law are fixed.
\cref{lem:finite-rate-coverage-convex} gives the offline convex verifier and
dual obstruction for a proposed finite panel.  The reduced-cost,
whole-bucket-gain, and column-generation lemmas,
\cref{lem:rate-coverage-column-gain}, \cref{cor:whole-bucket-reduced-gain}, and
\cref{lem:finite-rate-coverage-column-generation}, make expensive build-time
search exact for any finite candidate label family.
\Cref{lem:reduced-gain-variational-separation} turns the nonlinear
whole-bucket objective into a signed weighted coverage problem over label
events, parameterized by candidate intensities.
\Cref{lem:layer-cake-reduced-gain-separation} then reduces positive-gain
exposure to one subset layer and, after truncation, a logarithmic dyadic search
over layer weights.  \Cref{cor:pointwise-reduced-cost-separation} identifies
the exact completeness oracle as a point-label weighted coverage score.
\Cref{cor:soft-list-decoding-reduced-cost-separator} then shows that any
coordinatewise soft list decoder for that score is already an exact implicit
separator after filtering.
\Cref{cor:threshold-event-reduced-cost} gives the exact normal form when the
reporter itself is threshold-decoded: the offline separator is signed
threshold coverage over the reporter tests, not necessarily one additive
codeword score.
\Cref{cor:positive-coverage-screen} then removes the signed part from
candidate generation: list labels with enough positive coverage and use the
negative tests only for exact reduced-cost filtering.
\Cref{cor:dyadic-positive-list-recovery} reduces the weighted positive
coverage lister to dyadic unweighted agreement/list-recovery calls plus exact
filtering.
\Cref{cor:ordinary-list-recovery-positive-coverage} then implements those
unweighted calls by ordinary list recovery on repeated-coordinate projections
whenever the reporter tests are coordinate memberships.
\Cref{cor:unified-soft-decoded-rate-coverage} packages the desired retained
object: the compact query decoder handles online reporter lists, an exact
offline separator drives preprocessing, and the convex certificate charges
empty decoder output, reported incidences, and storage separately.  The
seeded search
compiler \cref{lem:seeded-reduced-gain-search} isolates the useful
code/lattice contribution: a proposal sampler or list decoder only has to
expose a positive reduced-gain label against each surviving dual obstruction;
the finite verifier then decides whether to retain it.  The implicit separator
\cref{lem:implicit-reduced-gain-separation} further shows that a compact
code/lattice quotient does not have to be enumerated in advance: no-positive-gain
separation is itself an infeasibility certificate for every finite-support
panel in that universe.
\Cref{prop:rate-coverage-polylog} records the resulting posterior endpoint.
\Cref{cor:weighted-gaussian-quadrature-panel} records the exact positive
finite certificate: a weighted retained label set only has to pass storage,
sampled far-load, and near-mass checks under the tilted query sampler.  The
weights may be chosen by arbitrary preprocessing; only retained buckets and the
query sampler are charged.
\Cref{cor:bucket-quotient-quadrature} removes a further artificial charge:
labels with the same stored point set may be quotient-merged, so storage
depends on distinct buckets while the query samples their aggregate tilted
weight.  This is the natural form for trellises, code cosets, lattice shells,
and rank-prefix reporters.
\Cref{lem:compressed-aggregate-sampler} gives the corresponding compact
decoder interface: a path-weighted DAG samples the quotient bucket law by a
backward partition-function recursion, so the charged object is graph size and
bucket spectrum rather than raw label count.
\Cref{cor:bcjr-trellis-quotient-sampler} identifies the standard coding
instance of that interface: BCJR/sum-product on a compact acyclic trellis is an
exact aggregate sampler, and the remaining ANN theorem is the induced bucket
spectrum \((BQ1)\)--\((BQ3)\).
\Cref{lem:marked-trellis-spectrum-verifier} turns that spectrum into concrete
transfer-matrix quantities for additive trellis storage scores: sampled far
load and near mass are exactly the marked partition ratios
\(Z_{q,x}^{\ge T}/Z_q\).  The storage side is deliberately separated:
\cref{lem:random-sparse-bucket-no-quotient} shows that random-looking sparse
hidden buckets almost never merge by equality, so useful quotient storage must
come from a designed canonical bucket map, residue/coset identifier, leader
bucket, or responsibility rule.
\Cref{cor:finite-state-trellis-rate-test} is the scalar homogeneous-trellis
audit: with depth \(h=\kappa\log m\), raw storage, sampled far separation, and
near mass reduce to three Perron--Frobenius spectral inequalities against
\(\rho/\kappa\) and \((1-\rho)/\kappa\).
\Cref{cor:raw-trellis-path-information-barrier} gives the corresponding
negative screen: exact path sampling at full raw path entropy still fails the
Gaussian information-charge test, so a trellis success must charge a quotient,
responsibility law, or Fano/list-work prefix object.
\Cref{lem:marked-trellis-responsibility-verifier} makes the responsibility
option checkable: inside a sampled trellis bucket, the exact emission
responsibility of point \(x\) is the marked partition ratio
\(Z_{q,x,\ell}^{\ge T}/Z_{q,\ell}\), and reporting within a polylogarithmic
factor preserves the far and near spectrum.
\Cref{cor:full-bucket-scan-responsibility-barrier} gives the corresponding
barrier for ordinary full-bucket scanning: its overcharge on \(x,\ell\) is
exactly the inverse marked responsibility.
\Cref{cor:heavy-responsibility-trellis-reporter} records the positive target
that remains after this barrier: list and exact-filter the points with
bucket-local marked responsibility at least inverse-polylogarithmic.  Far load
then loses only that polylogarithmic factor, and near recall is exactly the
mass of buckets where the true witness is heavy.
\Cref{cor:marked-heavy-lister-closes-trellis} shows that this heavy near mass
is automatic at the right threshold: marked near mass \(L_m^{-1}\) implies
sampled mass at least \((2L_m)^{-1}\) on buckets where the witness
responsibility is at least \((2L_m)^{-1}\).  Therefore the marked spectrum plus
